resources/what-is-sustainable-manufactur.description: Sustainable manufacturing is the practice of designing, manufacturing, and operating products and processes in a way that minimizes environmental impact.
resources/what-is-sustainable-manufactur.body:
What Is

What is sustainable manufacturing?

Sustainable manufacturing is an AI‑driven, connected system that embeds cost, carbon, compliance, and resilience directly into product design, production, and supply chain execution enabling real-time, data-driven decisions at enterprise scale.

Updated on July 21, 2026

Sustainable manufacturing overview

For more than a century, the manufacturing sector has been evolving and adapting in response to technological innovation and changing market expectations. 40 years ago, sustainable manufacturing practices began to attract attention. Initially, these were often minor, band-aid-type platitudes—seen as inconvenient and costly, but necessary to keep up public appearances. Today, sustainability is a matter of survival for both the manufacturing sector…and the planet—and increasingly a driver of cost efficiency, supply chain resilience, regulatory compliance, and competitive advantage.

In an Autonomous Enterprise, sustainability is no longer managed only through reporting, it becomes a transaction-level decision variable embedded in every production order, sourcing decision, and logistics flow.

Environmental compliance and green manufacturing drivers

The best businesses actually do care a lot about environmental stewardship and ethical corporate values. But of course, it would be naïve to think that green manufacturing initiatives are entirely motivated by altruism and good citizenship. Businesses have a duty to remain profitable and competitive and in today’s market, that means paying attention to risks and opportunities. Corporate sustainability measures are motivated by myriad issues, but the following are some of the most powerful drivers:

  • Reducing costs, carbon, and waste through AI‑optimized production, energy use, and material flows across the manufacturing and supply chain network: To make their operations greener and to succeed amid growing competition, businesses must look for ways to minimize waste and make more efficient use of energy and resources. Apart from the environmental benefits of these efforts, there is also a decided financial benefit to getting this right. Taking a Kaizen approach to operational efficiency and frugality not only helps to reduce waste and cost, it also empowers a culture of productivity and cost-effectiveness that makes business more competitive from end to end.
  • Ensuring real-time compliance by embedding environmental, safety, and regulatory constraints directly into production, sourcing, and logistics decisions: In 2021, the United States EPA levied $1.05 billion USD in civil penalties for corporate environmental compliance violators, and the EU adopted an new directive to tighten compliance by introducing “new criminal offences, increased sanctions and better enforcement”. Every day, in nations around the world, standards are tightening, and new legislation and regulations are being rolled out. Each area of the supply chain—from raw materials sourcing to end-of-life reclamation and waste management—is coming under increased public and governmental scrutiny. Modern manufacturers are looking to smart supply chain solutions that can keep up with compliance requirements in real time and help them automate their operations accordingly.
  • Delivering verifiable, audit-ready sustainability performance through connected data and traceability across products and multi-tier supply chains: In a 2021 survey, PwC found that over 70% of American and British consumers pay close attention to corporate reputations and would modify their purchasing behavior based upon a company’s social and environmental values. This reflects not only the increased level of global concern about environmental issues, but an increased ability to access and share information. Modern businesses know that a single Twitter campaign has the capacity to undo years of reputation-building. This is a powerful motivator to stay on the right side of environmental issues. Smart business systems can be especially valuable in this capacity—being set up to monitor and report social media trends, giving companies the opportunity to get out in front of any concerns, and reassure customers that meaningful measures are being taken.

Principles of sustainability in manufacturing

The EPA defines sustainable manufacturing as: “The creation of manufactured products through economically-sound processes that minimize negative environmental impacts while conserving energy and natural resources.” To achieve scalable sustainability, manufacturers must embed sustainability across the entire value chain from product design to sourcing, production, and delivery powered by connected data and AI-driven decision-making.

  • Recycling and circular supply chains enabled by end-to-end traceability and AI-driven optimization of material flows across circular supply chains: The OECD recommends increasing the percentage of used materials involved in the production process. A closed-loop approach, or circular process manufacturing lifecycle, means that when a product reaches the end of its useful life, it is collected to be reused into a new product. In this way, manufacturers can optimize the use of energy, raw materials, and other resources while reducing waste and emissions.

  • Renewable energy: The Energy Information Administration (EIA) anticipates renewable energy to represent 27% of total global energy consumption by 2030. This will be feasible due to an increase in worldwide initiatives to make renewable energy more accessible and practical—especially for commercial use. Today, many businesses are leaning into more profitable ways to convert to sustainable energy. This includes setting up renewable (usually solar) energy microgrids—and becoming prosumers by storing and redistributing this collected power.

  • Green and ethical raw materials: Managing supplier risk, emissions, and compliance proactively through connected supplier data and real-time supply chain visibility. Vetting and tracking the provenance of raw materials is a vital component of any sustainable manufacturing strategy. Often raw manufacturing materials are sourced from locations that do not uphold reliably strident standards for environmental and labor practices. Traditionally, it is at this stage where businesses are most blind and exposed to enormous potential risk. Quite apart from any unacceptable ethical consequences, the risk of a recall or PR scandal often originates at this stage.

  • Sustainable product design: Embedding sustainability into product design decisions early, balancing cost, carbon, compliance, and market requirements through simulation and AI-driven insights. Einstein said: “We cannot solve our problems with the same thinking we used when we created them”. The best manufacturers realize that “sustainability” is not something you can realistically inject into existing products and processes that were not created with that in mind. Smart manufacturing software helps designers and R&D teams to collaborate on a unified platform—developing simulations, analyzing data, accessing customer feedback, and integrating end-to-end production processes. The practice of sustainable design includes some of the following principles:

    • Uses less packaging
    • Is more minimalist in design with fewer superfluous parts
    • Is designed to minimize complexity in production and assembly
    • Has constituent parts are easily disassembled and recycled
    • Is designed with durability—rather than obsolescence—in mind

  • Conservation: Increasingly, large corporations are supporting global conservation efforts to protect their raw materials suppliers and the natural resources they depend upon. It’s nothing new for large companies to wish to partner their brand with socially responsible initiatives. The difference today, however, is that these partnerships are more than simply financial sponsorships. Modern businesses are taking counsel from conservationists to help them better understand and develop a culture of sustainability across all their teams and along all links of their global supply chains.

Technologies powering AI‑driven sustainable manufacturing and autonomous supply chains

New green industrial technologies are being developed at speed. They vary from industry to industry, including sustainable product design, more efficient raw materials processing (smelters, paper mills, cement), less energy-intensive manufacturing machinery, and eco-friendly packaging. Carbon capture and other alternative and energy-saving technologies are also making huge strides.

Each sector has its own progress milestones and its own set of challenges to analyze and overcome. However, across the board, one of the most important success factors for any green manufacturing initiative is access to smart technology.

When unified on a single platform, AI-enabled and cloud-connected manufacturing solutions turn sustainability data into actionable decisions translating insight into execution across the enterprise. Here are some of the features and tools currently helping to advance green manufacturing.

  • Connected Industrial IoT and enterprise data platforms provide real-time visibility into energy, emissions, and operational performance across manufacturing networks: An IIoT network serves to collect and share disparate and valuable data from assets and machines, all across the business. Unlike IoT devices which tend to operate on a more individual basis, IIoT networks operate within a data ecosystem. The data they collect and share is centrally processed and analyzed and the insights derived can help to inform and automate workflows and processes. This can help to optimize assembly and production lines and inform predictive maintenance efforts, letting machines tell operators when they need maintenance or troubleshooting. IIoT data can even help to improve and streamline human tasks and teams.
  • Predictive analytics: AI-powered predictive analytics enable manufacturers to simulate and optimize trade-offs across cost, carbon, compliance, and resilience. IIoT networks bring machine and device data into the central system. But there are numerous other sources of intel and data to be considered. This can include things like customer feedback, weather or natural occurrences, sudden consumer trends, market and economic information, and even political or social events. In the not-so-distant past, companies were unable to analyze dissimilar types of data all at once, and struggled to get a data-driven, big-picture assessment of their operations. But with AI-powered systems like smart ERPs, businesses can merge and analyze IIoT data, alongside other disparate and diverse data sets—to help them gain valuable insights and inform confident, fast decision making.

Predictive capabilities drawn from the analysis of rich, varied data, help companies made educated and efficient business decisions.

  • Supply chain control tower: AI-driven supply chain control towers enable real-time orchestration of sustainability-aware decisions across sourcing, production, and logistics. As profit margins tighten and competition grows, businesses must leverage every possible opportunity to improve efficiency and agility. This often means working with networks of multiple smaller suppliers and partners, both locally and overseas. This is a shift from the traditional supply chain model and can inject an enormous amount of risk and complexity if not properly managed. A smart supply chain control tower helps to unify operations across the entire supply and value chain. With device agnostic and cloud-connected software, silo walls are broken down. This allows supply chain managers to deal with disruptions or unexpected events in real time, and share and coordinate live action plans across their entire global business.
  • Blockchain and sensors: Tamper-proof RFID sensors can help supply chain managers track and confirm the ethical and environmental provenance of the materials they source. And blockchain acts as an irrefutable source of truth when it comes to materials tracing and is therefore more reliable than any other method of provenance confirmation. Beyond ensuring that materials meet sustainability and ethical standards, blockchain tools can also monitor for potential fraud and other types of risk which help to reassure investors and shareholders. Furthermore, sensors can be configured to gather other types of data such as temperature and handling. These technologies mean that when a shipment of products shows up at a warehouse, supply chain managers never again have to guess who handled it, how long it sat in shipment, or even what kind of materials went into its preparation, growth, or assembly.
  • AI and machine learning: AI not only analyzes sustainability data it increasingly executes decisions through autonomous workflows with built-in governance and auditability. AI helps to manage and process data more quickly and efficiently but its true value comes in the ability to make sense of that data. Structured, relational data is like what you would see in a spreadsheet. It is literal and can be categorized into specific columns and rows. Today, however, it’s the analysis of Big Data that holds the most powerful insights, and Big Data is largely unstructured. That means it doesn’t neatly fit into a spreadsheet. It can include things like IIoT video input, customer feedback, or testing results. AI and Machine Learning come into their own with Big Data. AI technologies can spot patterns, make sense of qualitative content, and compare and contrast unstructured data sets. And machine learning means literally that: the system will learn over time, about what works, what doesn’t, and what leads to the most efficient and accurate outcomes.
  • Automation for sustainability: Autonomous manufacturing enables sustainability policies to be executed automatically within production processes, reducing effort, cost, and risk at scale. Many manufacturers are developing the capacity for ‘lights out’ manufacturing to reduce energy wastage. This involves the integration of collaborative robots (cobots) and other smart assets and tools that can automate production in real time and operate without human intervention. This allows companies to separate certain production lines that can operate without lights or ventilation, boosting efficiency while reducing energy costs.
  • ERP: ERP-centric platforms connect sustainability, financial, and operational data enabling decision-grade insights and execution across the enterprise. A responsive, robust ERP with a powerful database can help to integrate manufacturing technologies and data with other relevant areas of the business such as Finance, HR, or Marketing. Every department across your business has a role to play in streamlining sustainability efforts. An integrated ERP delivers a 360-degree view of your operations, generating data-driven reports that can be used to ensure sustainability and environmental compliance, analyze budgets and costs, connect with customers and employees, and forecast future trends.

Business value of AI‑driven sustainable manufacturing for supply chain leaders

A robust economy is in everyone’s interest—from the customer to the CEO. For sustainability initiatives to be feasible and realistic, they must be undertaken with a win/win spirit—supporting meaningful environmental outcomes, and also helping to drive cost-savings and profitability. With this in mind, we are seeing agencies like the EPA, OECD, and the EU Advisory Board shifting their focus to develop and promote strategies like the ones below, that encourage long-term fiscal growth and corporate success.

  1. Address growing consumer trends. Every year, consumers demonstrate a growing preference for dealing with green and ethical companies. In fact, 73% of Gen Z consumers are willing to pay a premium for a more sustainable product, and many are increasingly suspicious of greenwashing—as opposed to demonstrable and transparent commitments to ethical, sustainable business practices.
  2. Nurture brand equity. Protect and grow revenue with trusted, traceable sustainability performance and compliant products. Today’s consumers demand increased choice, value, and fulfillment speed. The rise in online shopping has also led to a drop in brand loyalty. This means that more than ever, businesses benefit from building unique, verifiable brand attributes such as sustainability and ethical values.
  3. Benefit from subsidies. For many companies, a primary motivator for greening their operations comes from risk aversion and the desire to avoid fines or losses. But for companies that can provide “tangible and visible” evidence of meaningful green initiatives, there may be significant financial subsidies available from their governments. Smart technologies can help support this effort with automated searches for new and emerging subsidies and opportunities.
  4. Be more attractive to investors. Improve financial performance by linking sustainability data to risk, cost of capital, and margin decisions. As Forbes reminds us, a company’s commitment to sustainable and responsible practices, telegraphs an image of success and “…ethical corporate behavior, which reduces investment risk”. Implementing sustainable production solutions can open a company up to new streams of green investors.
  5. Be more attractive to talented job-seekers. We are in a time when even the world’s most successful businesses are struggling to recruit good talent. 49% of Gen Zs surveyed by Deloitte said that a prospective employer’s values play a major part in whether or not they decide to accept a role. In a separate UK survey, 65% of respondents of all ages said that they would be more likely to work for a company with strong environmental policies.
  6. Save money and cut costs. Reduce operational costs by optimizing energy, materials, logistics, and carbon exposure across the supply chain. Every business can benefit from a serious analytical dive into their current practices and how their processes can be streamlined and improved.

Sustainable Manufacturing for Supply Chain Leaders

Supply chain leaders must balance cost, service, resilience, and compliance. AI-driven sustainable manufacturing enables:

  • Carbon-aware sourcing and production planning
  • End-to-end supply chain traceability and compliance
  • Real-time disruption and sustainability risk management
  • Automated execution of sustainability policies at scale

Sustainable manufacturing: Next steps

AI-driven technologies are essential but true impact comes from embedding sustainability into core business processes, enabling organizations to move from insight to autonomous, scalable execution. But ultimately, it starts with your teams—your people. It’s important for businesses to develop communication strategies that go beyond the clichés that everyone has already heard. Your teams need to hear how green initiatives will impact their work, how the success of these measures will be judged, and exactly how a commitment to sustainability will lead to better corporate health and job security.

By focusing on the long-term benefits and communicating successes—and even challenges—with clarity and transparency, companies can set themselves up for a future that is not only greener but also more resilient, agile, and profitable.

resources/what-is-sustainable-procuremen.body:
What Is

What is sustainable procurement?

Sustainable procurement helps you balance cost, risk, and ESG impact across your supply chain.

Published on November 5, 2026

Sustainable procurement definition

Sustainable procurement is the practice of integrating environmental, social, and governance (ESG) criteria into every purchasing decision your team makes. It goes beyond price and quality to consider the full impact of what you buy, who you buy it from, and how those suppliers operate.

When you practice sustainable procurement, you weigh factors like carbon emissions, labor practices, circular metrics, and ethical sourcing alongside traditional cost, quality, and supplier performance metrics.

The goal is to make purchasing decisions that create long-term value for your business, suppliers, and society while conserving resources and protecting communities.

Sustainable procurement is not a separate initiative added to existing procurement processes. It is a core approach to purchasing that builds sustainability into sourcing, supplier management, spend intelligence, and external workforce decisions. By making sustainability part of how you buy, you can manage risk, meet regulatory requirements, and build more resilient supply chains.

Why sustainable procurement matters now

Supply chains face more scrutiny than ever. Investors, customers, regulators, and employees all expect companies to understand and take responsibility for the social and environmental impact of their purchasing decisions. A supply chain is only as responsible as the suppliers within it, and most of a company's environmental and social impact lives in its supply chain, not its direct operations.

Several forces are driving the shift toward sustainable procurement:

  • Regulatory pressure is rising. New laws in the European Union (EU), the United States, and other regions require companies to report on ESG performance, conduct supplier due diligence, and prove their supply chains are free from deforestation and human rights violations. These include the EU Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD), EU Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD), California’s SB 253 and SB 261, Modern Slavery Acts and the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act (UFLPA), the EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), the EU Deforestation Regulation (EUDR), and Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) plastic taxes. Increasingly, businesses face penalties for non-compliance and are being made to bear negative externality costs.
  • Stakeholder expectations are changing. Investors increasingly factor ESG risks into their investment decisions. Fund managers evaluate the ESG performance of the companies they invest in and hold. An example is a company with high incidences of human rights abuses and environmental damage, which could lead to expensive lawsuits and reputational damage, impacting the stock price. Another is a company’s level of compliance with carbon regulations and taxes being paid, where good ESG scores translate to lower carbon costs paid out. Besides regulatory mandates, executive leaders and financial institutions are increasingly seeing useful business cases for supporting environmentally and socially responsible businesses.
  • Supply chain risk is growing.  Global logistics are becoming more vulnerable and disrupted, leading to government policies designed to reduce reliance on fossil fuel supply chains, trade with countries carrying adverse human rights records, imports on critical minerals and commodities, and the impacts of climate disruptions from international trade.
  • Competitive advantage is at stake. Companies that make sustainability part of procurement can reduce costs, build stronger supplier relationships, and differentiate themselves in the market. Naturally, if a company can reduce energy and material waste, it can achieve cost savings.

Sustainable procurement helps organizations reduce supply chain risk, comply with ESG regulations, lower environmental impact, strengthen supplier relationships, and improve long-term business resilience.

Benefits of sustainable procurement:

  • Reduced supply chain risk
  • Improved ESG compliance
  • Lower Scope 3 emissions
  • Stronger supplier relationships
  • Better spend visibility
  • Enhanced brand reputation

The three pillars of sustainable procurement

Sustainable procurement rests on three interconnected pillars: environmental, social, and economic and governance. Together, they form a framework, often called the “triple bottom line,” which essentially looks at business decisions through the lens of environmental, social, and economic outcomes.

Environmental

The environmental pillar focuses on reducing the ecological footprint of your supply chain. This includes measuring and managing Scope 3 procurement emissions, the indirect emissions that come from your suppliers, improving purchases for recycled plastics, and sourcing products responsibly such as licensed wood and timber products. Scope 3 emissions often represent the largest portion of a company's carbon footprint, making them a critical area for action.

Environmentally sustainable procurement practices include:

  • Sourcing from suppliers that use renewable energy or reduce waste.
  • Choosing products and materials with lower carbon footprints.
  • Avoiding goods linked to deforestation, such as those covered by the EU Deforestation Regulation.
  • Prioritizing circular economy principles like recycling, reuse, and reduced packaging.

By addressing environmental impact in your procurement decisions, you can reduce emissions, comply with reporting requirements, and support your company's climate goals.

Social

The social pillar addresses the human impact of your supply chain. It covers labor practices, human rights, health and safety, and supplier diversity. When you practice social sustainable procurement, you look beyond cost to ask whether your suppliers treat their workers fairly and contribute to their communities.

Key social considerations include:

  • Preventing forced labor, child labor, and modern slavery in your supply chain.
  • Promoting supplier diversity by sourcing from minority-owned, women-owned, and small businesses.
  • Supporting safe working conditions throughout your supplier base.
  • Supporting fair wages and ethical labor practices.

Social procurement helps you meet human rights due diligence requirements, protect your reputation, and create positive social impact through your purchasing power.

Economic and governance

The economic and governance pillar focuses on the financial and ethical foundations of your procurement decisions. It covers anti-corruption, fair competition, transparency, and the long-term economic viability of your suppliers.

Sustainable procurement is the process of incorporating economic and governance criteria to purchasing decisions to reduce risk, meet compliance requirements, and create long-term business value.

This pillar includes:

  • Conducting supplier due diligence to assess financial stability and ethical practices.
  • Enforcing anti-bribery and anti-corruption policies across your supply base.
  • Supporting fair competition and ethical sourcing in your bidding processes.
  • Building long-term, mutually beneficial supplier relationships.

Strong governance helps you reduce risk, maintain compliance, and build trust with stakeholders. It also supports the long-term sustainability of your supply chain by helping your suppliers operate responsibly and remain viable partners.

Sustainable procurement regulations and compliance

Regulations are one of the strongest drivers of sustainable procurement. A wave of new laws and frameworks around the world now require companies to understand, report on, and take responsibility for their supply chain impacts.

Key regulations and frameworks include:

  • CSRD: Requires large companies to report on ESG topics, including supply chain impacts and 15 categories of Scope 3 emissions in compliance with European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS).
  • CSDDD: Requires companies to identify, prevent, and mitigate human rights and environmental risks in their operations and supply chains.
  • EUDR: Requires companies to prove that certain commodities do not come from recently deforested land. Learn more with this EU Deforestation Regulation guide.
  • Human rights due diligence legislation such as the German Supply Chain Due Diligence Act (LkSG), Modern Slavery Acts, and the UFLPA: Requires companies exceeding size and/or revenue thresholds to conduct due diligence on suppliers and publish their findings in statement declaration reports.
  • California SB 253 and SB 261: Require large companies doing business in California to disclose greenhouse gas emissions and climate-related financial risks.
  • ISSB IFRS S2: An international framework for sustainability-related financial disclosures, including Scope 3 emissions.

These regulations share a common theme: they push companies to look beyond their direct operations and take responsibility for what happens in their supply chains.

Sustainable procurement helps you meet these requirements by embedding due diligence, reporting, and risk management into your purchasing processes.

Key challenges in sustainable procurement

While the case for sustainable procurement is clear, putting it into practice comes with its challenges:

  • Data quality and availability: Gathering accurate ESG data from suppliers is difficult. Many suppliers lack the systems to measure and report their environmental and social performance, leaving gaps in your sustainability picture.
  • Supplier transparency: Supply chains are often multi-tier and opaque. You may know your direct suppliers, but visibility into their suppliers, and the risks further upstream, is limited.
  • Balancing cost and sustainability: Procurement teams face pressure to control costs while also meeting sustainability goals. Finding the right balance requires clear policies, good data, and tools that help evaluate trade-offs.
  • Regulatory complexity: With regulations varying by region and evolving rapidly, keeping up with compliance requirements is an ongoing challenge.
  • Change management: Shifting from price-driven to sustainable procurement requires new skills, processes, and mindsets across your teams.

Core capabilities of sustainable procurement software

Sustainable procurement applications help make sustainability part of your current workflows. Rather than treating sustainability as a separate initiative, teams can apply sustainability requirements at the moment a purchasing request enters the process, helping guide decisions before sourcing or contracting begins.

Core capabilities of these applications include:

  • Supplier assessment and ESG scoring: Evaluate suppliers against environmental, social, and governance criteria using questionnaires and third-party data from partners like EcoVadis and IntegrityNext.
  • Spend visibility and analysis: Connect spend data with sustainability metrics to understand where your money goes and what impact it has.
  • Risk monitoring: Track supplier risks across multiple dimensions, including financial, environmental, social, and compliance, and get alerts when issues arise.
  • Scope 3 emissions management: Collect and analyze emissions data from suppliers to support reporting and reduction goals.
  • Contract compliance: Incorporate ESG requirements into contracts so suppliers are held accountable for sustainability commitments.
  • AI-supported workflows: Use AI to simplify processes, evaluate supplier responses, support sustainability-driven category strategies, and recommend sustainable options based on policy and available data.

AI plays a supporting role in sustainable procurement applications. It helps teams work more efficiently by surfacing relevant information, evaluating supplier data, and suggesting sustainable alternatives, but people remain at the center of decision-making. AI supports your team; it does not replace their judgment.

SAP Business AI is embedded across these solutions to help procurement teams bring intelligence directly into everyday procurement workflows. Teams can make more informed decisions while keeping people in control of the final outcomes.

Sustainable procurement use cases

Companies across industries are using sustainable procurement to reduce risks and improve compliance.

In fact, when they make sustainability part of procurement, they often discover benefits that extend beyond ESG reporting. When teams have access to the right information at the right time, they can identify potential issues earlier and adapt as supplier or business needs change.

Over time, those decisions add up. Sustainability influences how suppliers are evaluated, how purchases are made, and how businesses work toward their broader goals.

How SAP supports sustainable procurement

Making sustainability part of your everyday procurement requires more than good intentions. You need tools that keep sustainability front and center in your purchasing decisions.

SAP solutions help you build these priorities into everyday procurement workflows, so you can make informed decisions, track progress, and keep moving toward your goals.

Get more perspectives on meeting ESG requirements in sustainable procurement.

FAQ

  • What are the three pillars of sustainable procurement?

    The three pillars of sustainable procurement are environmental, social, and economic and governance. The environmental pillar focuses on reducing ecological impact, including Scope 3 emissions. The social pillar addresses labor practices, human rights, and supplier diversity. The economic and governance pillar covers ethical sourcing, anti-corruption, and supplier due diligence. Together, they form the triple bottom line, a framework for evaluating the full impact of purchasing decisions.

  • What are the seven principles of sustainable procurement?

    The seven principles of sustainable procurement are: (1) vision and strategy, (2) governance, (3) people, (4) engagement and collaboration, (5) measurement and reporting, (6) supply chain risk and compliance, and (7) innovation. These principles guide organizations in building a structured approach to sustainable procurement, from setting a clear vision to measuring progress and driving continuous improvement.

  • What is the difference between sustainable procurement and sustainable sourcing?

    The difference between sustainable procurement and sustainable sourcing is that sustainable sourcing is a subset of sustainable procurement. Sourcing focuses specifically on the upstream process of identifying, evaluating, and selecting suppliers based on sustainability criteria. Sustainable procurement is broader. It covers the entire purchasing lifecycle, including sourcing, supplier management, contract compliance, spend analysis, and external workforce management. In short, sustainable sourcing is about who you buy from; sustainable procurement is about how you buy across the full process.

  • What regulations require sustainable procurement?

    Key regulations that require sustainable procurement include the CSRD, the CSDDD, the EUDR, modern slavery acts (such as the Australian and United Kingdom Modern Slavery Acts, the UFLPA, and the LkSG), and California SB 253 and SB 261. International frameworks like ISSB IFRS S2 also drive sustainable procurement by requiring companies to report on supply chain emissions and ESG impacts. However, regulations are subject to change.

  • What is ESG in procurement?

    ESG in procurement means applying environmental, social, and governance criteria to purchasing decisions. Environmental criteria cover emissions, resource use, and ecological impact. Social criteria cover labor practices, human rights, and supplier diversity. Governance criteria cover ethics, compliance, and transparency. ESG procurement helps organizations manage risk, meet regulatory requirements, and create long-term value through more responsible purchasing.

  • What is a sustainable procurement policy?

    A sustainable procurement policy is a formal document that defines how your business integrates sustainability into purchasing decisions. It sets out the ESG criteria your buyers should consider, the supplier’s due diligence requirements, and the standards suppliers must meet. A strong policy aligns procurement with your company's sustainability goals, provides clear guidance for buyers, and creates a framework for measuring and reporting progress. An example is making it compulsory for suppliers to agree to the buyer’s code of conduct when supplying goods and services and agreeing to disclose human rights records periodically.

resources/what-is-vendor-managed-invento.description: Vendor managed inventory (VMI) simplifies stock management by letting suppliers oversee inventory levels. Learn how VMI can boost efficiency for your business.
resources/what-is-vendor-managed-invento.body:
What Is

What is vendor managed inventory (VMI)?

In the vendor-managed inventory (VMI) model, the supplier manages and maintains inventory at the business's premises, where the business is the final seller and distributor of those products.

Published on August 9, 202410 minutes

The idea of vendor-managed inventory (VMI) is not a new one. Its potential to improve supply chain performance has always been apparent. But what have only become available in the past few years are the AI-powered, cloud-connected technologies that take VMI from a nice idea someday to an essential component of your more collaborative, resilient, and competitive supply chain.

VMI meaning in supply chain

VMI, also known as supplier-managed inventory from a customer’s point of view, is a data-driven initiative where suppliers manage the inventory levels of their own products, components, or materials at the on-site location of the vendor or distributor. This helps to reduce both shortages and surpluses. By shifting inventory management responsibilities in this way, supply chains can run leaner and more efficiently – reducing overheads and improving supply chain responsiveness and agility.

Using automated data flows and advanced analytics, the VMI model improves order accuracy, reduces rework, and increases inventory turnover. Suppliers use real-time sales and demand forecast data to optimize shipments and maintain high in-stock rates, allowing them to respond quickly to market changes and protect against the supply chain bullwhip effect.

Before starting a VMI relationship, you and your suppliers will need to agree upon key performance indicators (KPIs), such as inventory turnover rate, stock-to-sales ratio, and sell-through rate to ensure mutual goals are met. This collaborative model ultimately leads to a more efficient and responsive supply chain, benefiting both suppliers and customers.

How does supplier-managed inventory work?

VMI is a collaborative strategy that can deliver impressive results, particularly when undertaken with commitment, buy-in, and with the proper tools and systems in place. It relies on the synchronization of data and communication to ensure that inventory levels are always aligned with current market demands. Below are some of the critical components of this process:

  • Formal agreements from the start: Before you begin, outline everyone’s roles, responsibilities, and expectations. Both parties must agree on the operational details, such as delivery schedules, inventory levels, return policies, and min/max replenishment levels.
  • Shared technology: Agreements should also include a formal commitment to use shared and integrated technology platforms to their full capacity. The willing exchange of real-time information—such as sales data, inventory levels, and other relevant details — is absolutely essential for the success of this strategy.
  • Inventory management and replenishment process: From initial stock provision to continuous monitoring and demand forecasting, the supplier is responsible for managing your inventory. This is a data-driven process and works best when the supplier can leverage the sophisticated data management and AI-powered analytics within your business and integrated supply chain systems. With controlled access to a broad range of sales and supply chain data sets, your supplier can achieve greater precision and accuracy.
  • Communication link: The most efficient VMI strategies are brought to life on a collaborative business network that makes it easier for all stakeholders to work together, exchange essential documents securely, and act based on shared insights.
  • Vendor control: Vendors do all re-stocking and ordering, allowing you to offload tasks such as determining order times, sizes, and frequency. This data-heavy process becomes smoother and more transparent when your vendor can leverage robust informational sources on expected lead times, production levels, estimated shipping delays, and any other details that may have an impact upon inventory levels and supply and demand.
  • Inventory ownership: “We have great vendors but isn’t it a little risky to put this much faith in them?” This is a common question for those newly learning about this topic. However, with the VMI approach, the vendor actually still owns the inventory. They are placing it on your premises to facilitate fulfillment and minimize time and costs. In other words, it’s a great example of a win/win business strategy.

Benefits of vendor-managed inventory

Every step toward making your supply chain more efficient can have a positive effect across your business. When you adopt VMI, you can not only boost efficiency across your supply chain, but you can also achieve the following results:

  • Streamlined inventory management: By transferring inventory management to your suppliers, you can simplify operations and reduce time spent on managing inventory.
  • Reduced inventory carrying costs: VMI optimizes stock levels to meet demand, minimizing storage costs and freeing up cash flow.
  • Precise production scheduling: Suppliers gain better data-driven visibility into demand trends (or potential disruptions), allowing for more accurate production planning and reduced waste.
  • Timely replenishment: Automated replenishment ensures just-in-time restocking, helping to prevent shortages and surpluses.
  • Better, more collaborative working relationships: The collaborative and communicative nature of VMI can help you foster stronger, more trusting partnerships between you and your suppliers.
  • Optimized inventory levels: When suppliers have access to real-time sales data, it allows them to maintain ideal stock levels and to develop more strategic and precise ordering.
  • Resilience and risk reduction: When this core area of your business is being more strategically managed, you have more time and resources to devote to building a more resilient supply chain that can better predict and respond to disruption or risk.
  • Supplier perks: When suppliers gain early insights, they can use them to drive new sales opportunities, leading to better planning, larger market shares, and, ultimately, happier partners.

Potential risks of a vendor-managed strategy

Below are a few examples of the more common challenges associated with a VMI strategy – and some tips for mitigating them:

  • Lack of control/dependency on supplier: You may lose control over inventory levels and become too dependent on suppliers. Mitigation: Establish clear contracts and SLAs with performance metrics and real-time inventory management systems to maintain visibility and control.
  • Ill-suited systems and messy data: VMI's effectiveness depends on accurate data shared between partners. Mitigation: Invest in built-for-purpose systems that allow parties to transmit and work on documents in a secure way.
  • Communication failures: Miscommunication can lead to inventory discrepancies and inefficiencies. Mitigation: While a collaborative business network is essential, it’s also important to continually encourage and support a silo-smashing and collaborative culture with all your teams and stakeholders.
  • Data security concerns: Sharing sensitive data increases the risk of breaches. Mitigation: Implement advanced cybersecurity measures and encryption protocols to protect data integrity and confidentiality. Undergo regular team training to keep up with the ever-changing landscape of cyber risk.
  • Inflexibility to market changes: Predefined algorithms may hinder swift responses to market shifts. Mitigation: Use flexible AI-driven analytics tools to adjust forecasts and inventory strategies based on real-time data from both inside and outside your supply chain.
  • Demand changes: Unexpected demand spikes or reductions can disrupt forecasts and restocking. Mitigation: Good data analytics will help you forecast many potential scenarios. But it’s essential to have alternate contingency plans and workflows in place with your teams and vendors, so you can pivot quickly if the market demands. And by leveraging a solution that supports integrating your VMI processes with a consignment program, you can keep inventory levels within your ideal upper and lower bound.

VMI vs other types of inventory management

Access to connected technologies and AI-powered tools has unlocked the potential to modernize and optimize numerous inventory management models. Below are some of the more common ones:

  • Traditional inventory management: The business is solely responsible for ordering and managing their own inventory, often leading to larger safety stocks and higher holding costs.
  • Just-in-time (JIT) inventory: JIT reduces inventory costs by receiving goods only as needed, but lacks VMI's flexibility and continuous replenishment, making it more vulnerable to disruptions.
  • Consignment inventory: The supplier owns the inventory at the retailer's premises, reducing the retailer’s capital in stock but without active management by the supplier.
  • Drop shipping: The business does not keep the products it sells in stock but instead transfers customer orders and shipment details to a third party, typically a wholesaler or manufacturer, who then ships the goods directly to the customer.
  • Cross-docking: This model minimizes inventory storage through the direct transfer of materials between inbound and outbound transportation, whereas VMI uses data to optimize stored inventory management.
  • Consignment managed inventory (CMI): With CMI, the vendor owns the inventory until it is sold which reduces retailer financial risk – but it doesn't offer the same level of active inventory management as VMI.

Vendor-managed inventory examples

VMI is effectively employed across an enormous range of industries – each with their own challenges and potential. Below are just a few sectors and scenarios where VMI is helping to ramp up the game:

  • Manufacturing for the automotive industry: Here, VMI is used to effectively manage the supply of critical components like electronics and fasteners directly at assembly sites. Suppliers are responsible for maintaining inventory levels in sync with the manufacturers' production schedules, ensuring timely availability of parts and preventing production delays.
  • Distribution of pharmaceutical medications: To accurately coordinate drug supplies at healthcare facilities and pharmacies, VMI ensures that essential medications are available for distribution, particularly those requiring stringent regulatory compliance and storage conditions.
  • Component supply in the consumer electronics industry: For manufacturers of consumer electronics, such as smartphones and laptops, VMI is ideal for managing component inventories like microchips and displays. Suppliers monitor production forecasts and actual sales data to adjust inventories accordingly, helping to mitigate the risks associated with fluctuating demand and technological upgrades.
  • Aircraft assembly and maintenance in the aerospace sector: VMI systems are used to regulate the inventory of high-value components and maintenance supplies. They allow suppliers to directly control and replenish stocks of critical materials, like aluminum sheets and engine parts, that are crucial to both manufacturing new aircraft and maintaining operational fleets.
  • Retail/consumer packaged goods (CPG): For major retailers and CPG companies like Walmart or Amazon, VMIs are used to optimize inventory management. With SKUs literally in the millions, vendor-managed inventory allows them to keep shelves stocked with minimal overstock, reduce inventory carrying costs, and maintain availability for their customers.

Best practices for a successful VMI strategy

We’ve established that for VMI to be successful, the technological capacity for real-time data sharing and collaboration is mission critical. But for many of your best team leaders and staff, it represents a new (albeit more efficient) way of working. Digital transformation is one part of this process – but never underestimate the importance of good change management strategies and of setting clear expectations and goals. The following practices can help pave the way:

  • Open and transparent communication: In addition to implementing a business network platform, you’ll also need to maintain a commitment to clear and consistent communication channels with every key team member and stakeholder involved in the VMI process.
  • Agreed KPIs (key performance indicators): From the shop floor to the top floor, there are subject specialists across your business. Ensure that you communicate with all relevant team leaders to define and agree upon clear KPIs. In this way, you can be sure to measure and track all the essential moving pieces in your VMI environment.
  • Clear roles, responsibilities, boundaries, and fees: Define these parameters for each party involved in the VMI process to prevent misunderstandings and ensure accountability. And as above, remember to ask the right experts within your team to ensure that these regulations are sufficiently broad and robust.
  • Training and support: Up to 70% of digital transformation projects fail. Not because of the technologies but because of poor planning, siloed cultures, and insufficient training and communication. VMI can be a win/win for everyone in your network. But it’s up to you to ensure that good education and top-down support commitments are in place from the start.
  • Stamping out data squirrels: Information is power and even with the best of intentions, there may be people on your teams who are reluctant to integrate certain data sets into a centralized platform. Establish a consistent and standardized set of data management guidelines to demonstrate your fair and equitable application of necessary regulations.

What to look for in a vendor-managed inventory system

Wherever you are in your digital supply chain journey, it’s important to balance managing your immediate fire-fighting needs with your longer-term commitment to strategic improvement and scalable growth. Here are the VMI system features that deliver the greatest impact on both fronts:

  • Inventory visibility and collaboration: Choose software that provides a real-time view of replenishment orders, scheduling agreements, and inventory levels.
  • Seamless integration: The solution should be able to play well with your ERP system and with your other supply chain and e-commerce platforms. This connectivity allows accurate transaction data to be shared in real time and also supports push-based replenishment based on min/max inventory policies.
  • Shared forecasting: Select a solution that gives all trading partners visibility into forecasts, including demand and production line capacity. The best systems provide alerts about commitments and adjustments for a swifter response to potential disruptions.
  • Real-time data updates: Ensure the system provides real-time updates on inventory and sales data for quick responses.
  • Cloud platforms for real-time access to inventory data: Cloud-based solutions offer flexibility, scalability, and remote access to inventory data.
  • Integrated analytics for decision support: Look for systems with integrated analytics for deep insights into inventory performance.
  • Machine learning for enhanced analytics: Choose systems incorporating machine learning for precise inventory optimization.
  • Scalability: Ensure the system can scale with business growth and increasing inventory demands.
  • User-friendly interface: Select a system with an intuitive interface for easy adoption and efficient use by your team.

Take the next steps

use-cases/joule-assistant/travel-expense.description: Explore SAP’s AI Assistant for travel to plan, estimate, and book trips with policy‑aware guidance, real‑time cost visibility, and smarter spending control.
use-cases/joule-assistant/travel-expense.body:
AUTONOMOUS FINANCE, AUTONOMOUS SPEND MANAGEMENT

Travel Assistant

Streamline individual and team travel planning and booking to improve operational efficiency and enable cost-effective offsite meeting planning.

Published on October 6, 2026
Request a demo

Overview

The Travel Assistant streamlines travel planning and booking, coordinates approvals using AI-generated trip cost estimates that align with company travel policies, and provides personalized itineraries based on traveler preferences. It offers policy guidance, supports cost-effective group travel planning, enables up-front financial controls, and provides a single dashboard showing delegate-managed team travel with insights to improve travel management.

dgl

https://www.sap.com/videos/1354369?type=video&doi=SAP1354369

Tasks this assistant can help with:
  • Estimating trip costs
  • Generating individual travel itineraries
  • Recommending tips based on policy
  • Coordinating logistics for group travel
  • Generating personalized, policy aware trip itineraries
  • Providing in-the-moment policy clarity
  • Providing insights into delegate-managed travel
Example use cases for this assistant:
  • Streamlined pre-trip approval requests
  • Personalized, policy-compliant travel planning and booking
  • Real-time spend estimate visibility with booking-stage pricing breakdowns and travel class justifications
  • Optimized group travel planning for cost and logistics
  • Centralized visibility into team travel and expenses for delegates with proactive recommendations and insights

Benefits

Personalized, policy-aware trip planning and booking
AI agents create more efficient approval workflows and deliver individualized itineraries.

Optimized group travel and meeting planning
AI agents support efficient team trip planning by balancing costs, logistics, and policy compliance across multiple travelers.

Streamlined delegate managed travel and expense
AI agents provide insights and recommendations in a single dashboard to help delegates prioritize their work and save time managing team travel and expenses.

Agents used by this assistant

Use the Travel Assistant to orchestrate specialized AI agents, including Joule Agents that apply SAP’s process expertise or custom agents you create.

Agent

Booking Agent

Plans and books individual travel using conversational AI, aligning preferences with company policy.

Delegates Dashboard Monitoring Agent

Provides delegates with proactive AI-generated briefings, contextual insights, and ready-to-execute actions.

Meeting Planning Agent

Analyzes attendees' locations, flights, travel times, and budgets to recommend destinations and hotels.

Interact directly with SAP solutions through immersive experiences and hear inspirational digital transformation stories through the lens of real-world business scenarios.

about/company/innovation/labs.html.description: SAP Labs are global R&D locations that develop and improve SAP core products in high-tech areas. Each SAP Lab reflects SAP’s culture of diversity and innovation.
about/company/innovation/labs.html.body:
SAP Labs
Overview

SAP Labs Network

Our connected SAP Labs Network around the world focuses on developing and improving key SAP solutions that shape IT and business trends.
Contact us

About SAP Labs Network

The network comprises all of SAP’s major global research and development (R&D) hubs across more than 20 countries and represents more than 80% of SAP’s engineering workforce.

The art of being globally connected

SAP Labs exemplify our culture of diversity and innovation. Each lab partners with local institutions, universities, and startups to develop top-tier enterprise solutions and establish thought leadership in its focus area.

top employer awards for all labs in 2024

SAP Labs in the Americas

SAP Labs United States

Founded in 1996, SAP Labs US has championed design thinking, created award-winning user experiences, and brought deep cloud expertise to help customers become intelligent, sustainable enterprises. SAP Labs US advances SAP Business AI and delivers trusted, industry-grade capabilities embedded across SAP solutions. We collaborate closely with leading technology partners, top universities, and the broader startup ecosystem to stay at the forefront of technology.

Search jobs 

SAP Labs Canada

Operating since 1984 with locations in Montreal, Waterloo, and Vancouver, SAP Labs Canada is a global R&D hub with more than 35 years of expertise in analytics, database technologies, and customer experiences. Recognized as a multi-award-winning employer of choice in Canada and notable for collaborative innovation, AI research, sustainability, and operational excellence at scale, SAP Labs Canada is developing the next frontier of the intelligent enterprise.

Search jobs 

SAP Labs Latin America

Since 2006, SAP Labs Latin America has been a key innovation hub, operating in Brazil and Mexico. Its culture of excellence is rooted in teamwork, accountability, and trust, earning regular recognition from Great Place to Work for a commitment to employee well-being and growth. Deeply committed to social responsibility, SAP Labs Latin America sheltered more than 50 employee families and led donation campaigns after Brazil’s devastating floods in 2024, reflecting the passion for making a difference where it matters most.

Search jobs 

SAP Labs in Europe

SAP Labs Germany Walldorf & Rot

SAP Labs Walldorf & Rot is SAP’s core of engineering, driving innovation through collaboration, turning business knowledge into sustainable, innovative enterprise solutions making use of cutting-edge basis technology

Search jobs 

SAP Labs Germany Berlin/Potsdam

SAP Labs Berlin/Potsdam represents a vibrant and highly diverse ecosystem engaging people, academia, government and economy. Berlin is SAP’s AI, GovTech and Start-up hub, where cutting-edge technologies and process intelligence converge to redefine business models, and shape the future of responsible tech and public services.

Search jobs 

SAP Labs Germany Dresden

At SAP Labs Dresden, we deliver end-to-end cloud expertise – from deep-tech engineering to customer success – enabling and driving seamless business transformation through industry-leading SAP business solutions. We bridge early career potential with seasoned expertise through dynamic vocational programs and collaborative growth. We are more than colleagues – we are a community where trust, curiosity, and collaboration help us grow together and spark innovation.

Search jobs 

SAP Labs Germany Munich

SAP Labs Munich is a significant hub for SAP, driving innovation, development, research, and customer engagement. Located in the heart of Bavaria, SAP Munich contributes to the region's reputation as a leading technology center in Europe. Our offices are not only a workplace but also a community that fosters creativity and collaboration, with a strong commitment to sustainability and employee well-being.

Search jobs 

SAP Labs France

With over 35 nationalities represented, SAP Labs France brings together people with different backgrounds and experiences to turn creativity into powerful software and help the world run better. SAP Labs France is involved in the development of key SAP products, such as SAP Business One, leads security research, and has best-in-class customer care and support teams.

Search jobs 

SAP Labs Paris

With more than 600 developers, SAP Labs Paris has a strong R&D team focused on new technologies, such as conversational AI, automated machine learning, and intelligent robotic process automation. Established in 2009, the lab’s R&D strength in new technologies and its openness to the startup ecosystem provides a unique combination to help customers build intelligent enterprises.

Search jobs 

SAP Labs CEE Hungary

As one of SAP’s key R&D centers, SAP Labs Hungary deals with complex product development in public and private clouds, SAP Business Data Cloud, operations, and customer services and delivery.

Search jobs 

SAP Labs CEE Poland

SAP Labs Poland is dedicated to developing the SAP Commerce Cloud solution, implementing cloud-native SAP BTP Kyma runtime, and delivering intelligent enterprise solutions.

Search jobs 

SAP Labs CEE Czech Republic

SAP Labs Czech Republic develops and maintains core business applications, focusing on finance, sustainability, and business intelligence.

Search jobs 

SAP Labs CEE Slovakia

SAP Labs Slovakia specializes in designing and delivering the SAP Business One solution, along with legal compliance and local best practices.

Search jobs 

SAP Concur Prague

SAP Concur Prague is home to product engineering, delivery, and customer service for SAP Concur, which provides travel and expense management services to customers.

Search jobs 

SAP Labs SEE Bulgaria

SAP Labs Bulgaria has established itself as a preferred employer in the IT sector in Bulgaria over its 25-year history. More than 2,000 colleagues contribute to key development areas such as SAP BTP, SAP Sustainability, and SAP Globalization.

Search jobs 

SAP Labs SEE Romania

SAP Labs Romania was established in 2023, building on SAP’s strong existing offerings. With more than 650 employees in Bucharest, SAP Labs Romania delivers business and technical professional services for SAP Cloud ERP solutions and the extensibility suite, implementing the AI-first, suite-first strategy in direct contact with customers in the EMEA region and globally.

Search jobs 

SAP Labs Ireland

SAP Labs Ireland, with more than 2,300 employees from 60 nationalities, drives innovation through delivering products, services, and support that maximize the value of SAP’s solutions. Our engineering teams specialize in SAP Analytics, SAP Business Data Cloud, and SAP Business AI, and our service, support, and partner teams accelerate adoption and scale transformation. We integrate applications, data, and AI, fostering a culture of collaboration and talent development to create lasting impact for customers, partners, and employees.

Search jobs 

SAP Labs in Asia Pacific Japan

SAP Labs East Asia Singapore

Operating as a dynamic hub for AI innovation and intelligent product capabilities, SAP Labs East Asia Singapore leads the embedding of new technologies and innovation into SAP products and services. Its vision is to bring SAP's strategy to life by developing breakthrough technology, and its goal is to be a thriving engineering and R&D location and a front-runner for AI-driven enterprise solutions.

Search jobs 

SAP Labs India

SAP Labs India is the fastest-growing location within the network and the largest R&D center outside SAP’s headquarters in Walldorf, Germany. Founded in 1998, SAP Labs India represents the entire breadth of SAP’s portfolio, drives SAP’s global product strategy and core solutions, and provides localized products and solutions. Its end-to-end suite of applications and services enables businesses across 25 industries globally to operate profitably, adapt continuously, and make a difference.

Search jobs 

SAP Labs East Asia Japan

Located in Tokyo, the capital city and center of economic dynamism in Japan, SAP Labs East Asia Japan is driven by a mission to unlock the true value of SAP's unmatched line-of-business breadth and end-to-end process coverage — together with customers and the broader ecosystem. As a trusted long-term partner, the Lab champions Japan's next-generation enterprises through true end-to-end process transformation, while shaping markets and ecosystems as an innovation leader with unrivalled Enterprise SaaS expertise.

Search jobs 

SAP Labs East Asia Korea

As a key development location, SAP Labs East Asia Korea is centered around the continual development and enhancement of SAP HANA Cloud. By leveraging Korea's strong technology ecosystem and talent pool, the Lab ensures SAP HANA Cloud remains at the cutting edge of cloud-based enterprise solutions, supporting customers' evolving requirements for speed, security, and scalability.

Search jobs 

SAP Labs China

Established in 2003, SAP Labs China is a strategic R&D hub of SAP, playing a vital role in many of SAP’s core solutions. Headquartered in Shanghai with R&D presence in Beijing, Chengdu, Dalian, Nanjing, and Xi’an, SAP Labs China drives fast-paced innovation through strong technical expertise and delivery capabilities. Guided by the vision “Innovate in China for China and the world,” SAP Labs China is entering a new phase of sustainable excellence.

Search jobs 

SAP Labs East Asia Vietnam

SAP Labs East Asia Vietnam serves as the center for business suite solutions engineering. Its vision is to accelerate SAP Next Generation initiatives through innovation and transformation, foster local collaboration to harness digital economy strengths, and create solutions with a global impact. Committed to a Suite-first mindset and pioneering AI innovations, the Lab delivers top-tier end-to-end products that redefine industry standards and provide outstanding value to customers worldwide.

Search jobs 

SAP Labs in the Middle East and Africa

SAP Labs Israel

Founded in 1998, SAP Labs Israel plays a central role in executing SAP Business AI strategy and leading innovations in multi-cloud strategy, user experience, and privacy. It developed some of the company’s main products, including SAP BTP, SAP Business Data Cloud, SAP Build, and SAP Customer Data Platform. The team combines deep tech expertise with an innovation-driven mindset, working closely with startups, academia, and partners across the tech ecosystem.

Search jobs 

Related resources

Careers

We encourage open, free expression to turn big ideas into reality. And with training, mentors, and a healthy work-life balance, you’ll get more out of your career.

Visit the careers site 

Innovation at SAP

Innovation at SAP drives global collaboration, enhancing the capabilities of SAP’s ecosystem through expertise, technologies, and platforms.

Learn more 

Academic alliances

SAP offers programs for students who are passionate about innovation and technology and want to shape intelligent enterprises as future decision-makers.

Learn more

What is the Autonomous Enterprise?

The Autonomous Enterprise is the future of business—where people set direction and AI executes, with governance at every step.

Move work up the value chain

Start with outcomes, not processes, by partnering with AI to remove busywork and apply human judgment where it creates the most value.

Run it all in real time

Build with total control

Build, run, and manage AI agents and apps on a governed foundation with built‑in security, accountability, and end‑to‑end control.

Our Strategy

We are committed to helping the world run better and improving people’s lives​. Our vision is to bring out the best in every business.

Agile business transformation at scale

SAP Corporate Social Responsibility

SAP brings purpose to life. From scaling social enterprises to preparing youth for the future of work, we turn bold ideas into measurable change for both people and planet.

Contact us

Driving long-term social impact

At SAP, corporate social responsibility (CSR) is integral to our sustainable business strategy. We aim to create lasting social and environmental impact while delivering business value, guided by our purpose to help the world run better and improve lives.

Download the 2024 CSR e-book 
Hemang DesaiInterim Head of Corporate Social Responsibility at SAP
At SAP, we believe real change begins with a deep connection: between companies and communities, between bold ideas and practical infrastructure, and between those who take action and those who benefit from it.

Impact businesses use innovative models to tackle social and environmental issues, reinvesting profits into their mission. We support them in three ways:

Ecosystem building

We advocate for the social and solidarity economy, dedicate financial and non-financial resources, and invest in networks and capacity-building.

Explore our program 

Impact-led procurement

We strengthen impact businesses by integrating them into private and public supply chains, making procurement more socially and environmentally responsible.

Learn more 

Pro bono consulting

We help grow the capacity of impact businesses through professional consulting while developing our own employees.

Find out more 
OUR STRATEGY

Build future skills

We help youth gain essential skills and access to jobs or entrepreneurship pathways, creating a more inclusive and resilient workforce through:

Ecosystem building

We foster strong multistakeholder partnerships, collaborate with leading organizations, and create direct employment opportunities within the SAP ecosystem.

Learn more 

Career exploration

We help youth explore career pathways, develop self-awareness for job planning, and gain hands-on learning experience from industry professionals.

Education

We strengthen employability by investing in education models that open pathways to income—whether through employment or entrepreneurship.

Learn more 

Other initiatives

Tree planting at SAP

SAP is committed to help plant 25 million trees and fund wetland conservation by 2030. This includes supporting partners and communities to reforest a diversity of trees and support forest protection. It also includes funding the conservation and rewetting of coastal and inland wetlands such as bogs and mangrove swamps.

SAP mobilizes employees worldwide for Earth Day through a global volunteer activation. By participating in environmental projects, advancing circular economy initiatives, and reducing our carbon footprint, we unite our workforce to drive real change.
