resources/supply-chain-network.html.body:
What Is

What is a supply chain network?

A supply chain network is a strategic, data-driven digital ecosystem where buyers and sellers collaborate.

Updated on November 2, 20268 minutes

Executive summary

A supply chain network is a digital platform that connects businesses with trading partners across procurement, logistics, and finance processes. These partners can include suppliers, carriers, co-packers, and others. The platform replaces point-to-point integrations with many-to-many connections, enabling real-time collaboration.

No business operates alone. Every transaction, document, and decision flows through a web of external relationships that traditional tools weren't built to handle. Yet most organizations still exchange documents with their supply base using legacy methods like email and fax, and fragmented information limits your ability to respond to disruptions. A supply chain network closes these gaps by digitalizing transaction and document exchange, applying configurable business rules, and giving you shared visibility across your full partner ecosystem.

When your internal and external data is harmonized in one place, it gives AI agents the business context they need to deliver recommendations, evaluate impact, and automate execution—from order and invoice processing to logistics coordination. The results are measurable: improvements in on-time delivery, lower transportation spend and inventory costs, fewer invoice exceptions, and stronger product traceability.

Supply chain network: a definition

A supply chain network is the connected, collaborative system of organizations, facilities, people, processes, and technology involved in delivering products or services to customers. It supports the flow of goods, information, and transactions among suppliers, manufacturers, logistics providers, distributors, and other trading partners, helping them deliver products to customers on time and in the requested quantities.

Modern supply chain challenges

Disruptions caused by geopolitical tensions, natural disasters, and other unexpected events have illustrated our dependence on supply chains and the vulnerabilities that poorly designed networks can create.

  • Lack of visibility: End-to-end visibility has long been a major goal for supply chain managers. Today’s connected and powerful technologies help to mitigate these issues—reducing inefficiencies and delays that businesses face as they struggle to get a complete picture of their network and operations.
  • Volatility in customer demand: We are in a time of unprecedented shifts in consumer behavior and expectations. When supply chains struggle to keep up with these demands, it can result in planning challenges, leading to overstocking or stockouts, and a weakening of the overall agility of the value chain.
  • Complexity of global operations: Regulatory compliance becomes more difficult by the day, exacerbated by shifting geopolitical and environmental issues from region to region. Multi-tier supply chain networks face increased risks and challenges in ensuring consistent quality and performance across the world.
  • Technological limitations: Legacy and outdated technologies are often inadequate in today’s complex environment. Limitations in data analysis capabilities, automation, and real-time tracking can hinder your aims for a more optimized and responsive supply chain.
  • Environmental and sustainability concerns: From consumer expectations to your own robust sustainability goals, balancing growth with environmental and social responsibilities presents a unique challenge.
  • Security: The dual focus on cyber and physical security is critical in safeguarding sensitive data and physical assets against increasing threats. The design of IoT and connected networks must address these complex security challenges.

Key components of a supply chain network

The core components of a supply chain network enable the use of data analytics and centralized supply chain management systems to help you streamline operations and overcome the challenges listed above.

According to an IDC study, “In purchasing and procurement, 71% of professionals state that they receive fragmented/incomplete information due to their current collaboration and/or visibility levels, restricting their ability to react effectively or efficiently to disruptions.”1 The finding highlights the importance of sharing timely, complete information across the organizations and systems in a supply chain network.

Key components of an effective supply chain network include:

  • Cost optimization: A main advantage of being on a supply chain network revolves around balancing operational efficiency and maintaining cost-effectiveness. This includes optimizing logistics, manufacturing, and distribution costs—through better visibility and modeling of your current activities.
  • Risk management: An end-to-end approach to regulatory compliance, data management and analysis, and supply chain transparency is essential. Good risk management practices not only protect your supply chain but also help protect your brand and reputation.
  • Responsiveness and agility: Today’s businesses must rapidly adapt to changes in market conditions, customer preferences, supply dynamics, and global events. Modern technologies are essential to help you map and model contingency plans and pivot safely and quickly when the unexpected occurs.
  • Service-level agreements (SLAs): These help to set clear, measurable standards for performance, quality, and service across the stakeholders in your value chain. This helps to ensure global consistency and reliability in the management and delivery of all your goods.
  • Sustainability and ESG metrics: The stakes are high today to ensure that you integrate environmental, social, and governance considerations into your value chain practices. Smart supply chain solutions help ensure that these practices are transparently upheld across your global operations, including your trading partners.
  • Data analytics and information flow: The role of data and effective information management is essential in ensuring operational efficiency and strategic planning.
  • Technology integration: AI, blockchain, digital twins, advanced analytics, and today’s range of smart, connected solutions—these are the technologies that underpin modern supply chain innovation, and that help to optimize transport, location intelligence, distribution, and fulfillment.

Location intelligence and modeling in supply chain networks

A further essential component of a supply chain network is location intelligence, which provides vital insights for strategic planning and operational efficiency. Through the real-time analysis of geospatial data, your teams can better understand the physical flow of your goods. And by integrating locational data with the rest of your supply chain data, you get an actionable view of your logistics and value chain network. This insight helps you make informed decisions about warehouse locations, transportation routes, and the prediction of market trends. This means spotting and avoiding bottlenecks, tracking the live movement of goods, and forecasting demand based on geolocational patterns.

In addition to geographical optimizations, today’s supply chain network design also incorporates modeling techniques that use advanced analytics for predictive insights, scenario planning, and risk assessment—allowing you to simulate various supply chain scenarios, to improve efficiency, resilience, and responsiveness. This approach lets you integrate data-driven insights into your planning strategies, ensuring better agility and preparedness.

Innovative technologies in a digital supply chain network

Technologies that enable a digital supply chain network include:

  • Big Data analytics: Comprehensive analysis of large and complex data sets helps to improve forecasting accuracy and strategic planning. This includes the application of predictive analytics to anticipate market trends and consumer behaviors.
  • Artificial intelligence (AI): Utilized for sophisticated predictive analytics, demand forecasting, and automation, AI technologies—and the machine learning algorithms that underpin them—significantly streamline operations and decision-making processes.
  • Internet of Things (IoT): IoT devices range across a broad spectrum of assets that can track, automate, communicate, advise, and warn—all in real-time. Cloud connectivity within IoT networks helps improve transparency, tracking, operational control, predictive asset management, and smart supply chain networks.
  • Blockchain technology: Blockchain can support traceability, provenance, and secure transactions through transparent, tamper-resistant records. These records can help supply chain partners verify information and build trust.
  • Cloud computing: Cloud-based solutions facilitate flexible and scalable data storage and processing, enhancing collaboration and information sharing across various supply chain components. Cloud solutions also enable the seamless integration of diverse supply chain activities and systems.
  • Advanced robotics and automation: Improving operational efficiency, particularly in warehousing and logistics, robotics and automation technologies reduce human error and increase productivity. These tools are essential in high-volume and high-speed operational environments.

Together, these technologies help connect the people, processes, and partners involved in supply chain operations.

Through SAP Supply Chain Management solutions and SAP Business Network, we help organizations align teams, connect processes, integrate partners, and embed AI into core supply chain activities—enabling better decisions, faster execution, and sustained enterprise impact in a constantly changing world. 2

Hagen Heubach, CMO for Supply Chain Management at SAP

Digital twins in supply chain network

In addition to the important technologies listed above, digital twins represent a breakthrough in how supply chains are managed and optimized. Through the creation of virtual replicas of physical supply chains, digital twins allow for detailed analysis, simulation, and optimization. Because testing a digital twin does not risk damaging a physical asset, supply chain managers can simulate routine operations and extreme disruptions. The integration of real-time data with these models further allows for continuous refinement and adaptation, making digital twins an invaluable tool for a dynamic and resilient supply chain network.

Key benefits of an optimized supply chain network

Potential benefits of an optimized supply chain network include:

  • Efficiency and cost reduction: Every bit of wasted space in a vehicle or warehouse, all the little delays that add up to big ones, each of the unnecessary miles your teams have to go—these can all hurt your bottom line. An effective supply chain network can help you spot these weaknesses and coordinate more predictive responses, saving on production, streamlining operations, and minimizing waste.
  • Sustainability and reverse supply chain integration: Meeting and exceeding your sustainability targets doesn’t have to be challenging. The visibility into your supply chain provided by a network can help you see areas where energy, packaging, and carbon usage savings can be made—including the costly and resource-heavy area of reverse logistics.
  • Enhanced customer satisfaction and brand reputation: Of course, fast, reliable deliveries remain high priority. But with a well-designed and integrated supply chain, you’re also able to deliver on the tracking, service, support, and real-time assistance that helps build your reputation. Quality collaboration and material traceability further strengthen customer trust and your brand.
  • Increased agility: A supply chain not only generates and gathers data but also uses advanced analytics to understand and apply that data more responsively. Higher visibility and digital collaboration with trading partners increases business resilience amid unexpected disruption.
  • Better decision-making: A major component of increased agility is the ability to act on information quickly. When your data is reliable, you can make decisions with confidence.

Emerging supply chain trends

Current trends in supply chain networks include:

  • AI-driven planning and execution: AI is moving from pilot projects into core supply chain operations, powering demand forecasting, predictive analytics, and increasingly autonomous decision-making across planning, logistics, and procurement.
  • Greater focus on sustainability: Businesses are looking for ways to reduce waste, conserve resources, and improve reverse logistics.
  • Stronger resilience and risk management: Businesses are diversifying suppliers and building greater flexibility into their supply chain networks.
  • More customer-centric operations: Supply chains are adapting to changing customer expectations, including the demands of e-commerce.
  • More complex trade management: Businesses must navigate evolving trade regulations and compliance requirements across markets.
  • Growth in near sourcing and local production: Shorter supply chains can reduce dependence on extended global networks and improve responsiveness to market changes.

Why SAP for supply chain networks?

SAP’s perspective

No business does business alone. An effective supply chain network connects internal operations with suppliers, logistics providers, manufacturers, service providers, and other trading partners. SAP’s approach brings these partners, processes, and data together to improve visibility, collaboration, and coordinated decision-making.

SAP Business Network is a cloud-based collaboration offering that modernizes how procurement and supply chain processes connect across organizations. It helps you build stronger supply chains, gain visibility into your supply chain, increase operational efficiency, and ensure compliance. It closes the break points between trading partners through transaction exchange, information sharing, and trading partner discovery.

SAP Business Network Supply Chain Collaboration supports planning, inventory, quality, procurement, and manufacturing collaboration with trading partners.

In an IDC study of buyer organizations using SAP Business Network, respondents reported 30% faster go-to-market speed and 27% faster product or order delivery.3 These results illustrate the potential value of improving collaboration and information sharing across trading partners.

How leading supply chains differ

Discover what high-performing supply chains do differently to strengthen resilience.

Read the report

FAQ

  • What is a supply chain network?

    A supply chain network is the connected system of organizations, facilities, people, processes, and technology involved in delivering products or services to customers. Goods, information, and money move through the network among suppliers, manufacturers, logistics providers, distributors, business partners, and customers. Supply chain network design uses data and models to help businesses decide how to structure and improve these connections. An effective network provides the visibility and coordination businesses need to respond to changing supply, demand, and operating conditions.

  • What are the main benefits of a supply chain network?

    The main benefits of a supply chain network are greater visibility, efficiency, resilience, and responsiveness. Better visibility helps businesses detect delays earlier and respond when conditions change. Network design and modeling also enable decisions about where to source materials, hold inventory, and locate facilities. These capabilities can help businesses control costs and reduce waste. They can also support more reliable customer service and better preparation for disruptions.

  • What are the key components of a supply chain network?

    The key components of a supply chain network are the organizations, locations, processes, data, and technology that support the flow of products and information. Organizations include suppliers, manufacturers, logistics providers, distributors, and customers. Locations include factories, warehouses, and distribution centers. Shared processes and data help these participants plan and coordinate their work. Technology provides the visibility and modeling capabilities needed to monitor the network, assess risks, and support informed decisions.

  • What is a digital twin in a supply chain network?

    A digital twin in a supply chain network is a digital representation of a physical asset, process, or network. The digital twin uses current data to reflect conditions in the physical world. Businesses can use the model to test scenarios without disrupting operations. The resulting insights support planning, risk assessment, and maintenance decisions. By showing how a change could affect the wider network, a digital twin helps teams prepare for disruptions and improve supply chain performance.

  • How does a supply chain network help optimize my supply chain?

    A supply chain network helps optimize your supply chain by improving coordination and visibility across the businesses involved. Access to timely information helps teams identify delays and respond when supply or demand changes. Businesses can also use network data to improve planning and make informed decisions about inventory, sourcing, and delivery. These capabilities help the supply chain operate more efficiently while remaining responsive to customers and disruptions.

  • Is participating in a supply chain network useful for my industry?

    Yes, participating in a supply chain network is useful across many industries, although the benefits vary by operating model. In production-centric industries, a connected network supports the flow of materials between suppliers, manufacturers, and logistics providers. This helps businesses coordinate production and respond to supply issues. In service-centric industries, a network supports collaboration with external providers and improves access to shared information. Each business can shape its network around how it operates and serves customers while accounting for industry requirements and risks.

resources/supply-chain-risk-management.h.body:
What Is

Supply chain risk management

Build supply chain resilience, gain real-time risk visibility, and operate confidently through disruptions.

Updated on October 26, 2026

Executive summary

Supply chain risk management (SCRM) is a coordinated approach to protecting supply chain operations from risks and disruptions. As supply chains have grown more global and interconnected, risks can escalate and disruptions can cascade farther and faster, making early detection and effective response strategic priorities. A recent IDC study states, “99% of organizations are actively working to improve their ability to respond to disruptions in supply chains.”¹ SAP Supply Chain Management solutions help businesses meet this challenge by bringing together AI-enabled risk detection, collaboration, and visibility so teams can identify emerging threats, respond sooner, and ensure operational continuity.

What is supply chain risk management?

Supply chain risk management (SCRM) is the process of identifying, assessing, and mitigating risks that could disrupt the flow of goods, services, or information across a company’s supply chain. It involves both proactive planning and real-time response to minimize potential disruptions, protect business continuity, and strengthen operational resilience. These risks can range from natural disasters and geopolitical instability to supplier insolvency or cyberattacks.

As supply chains have become increasingly global, interconnected, and digital, the complexity and urgency of risk management have grown. An effective SCRM strategy not only reduces the impact of potential disruptions but also strengthens a company’s agility and competitive edge.

Organizations that prioritize SCRM are often better positioned to safeguard customer satisfaction, maintain consistent revenue streams, and navigate compliance demands. Whether you're managing a vast global network or a localized operation, risk management is a core competency for supply chain success.

Why supply chain risk management matters today

Supply chain disruptions have always existed, but today they can occur more frequently, overlap, and spread faster across increasingly complex global networks.

Port congestion, material shortages, and climate-related events are now routine challenges. At the same time, customers and regulators expect faster delivery, quality products, greater transparency, and stronger compliance.

Reflecting these pressures, an IDC study reports, “35% of organizations cite supply chain resilience and risk management as a top priority.”1 This focus reinforces the role of SCRM in maintaining continuity and adapting to disruption.

Without a structured approach to risk management, organizations can face delayed shipments, increased costs, and dissatisfied customers. At the same time, many supply chain leaders still struggle with limited visibility, siloed processes, and reactive decision-making. Investing in SCRM helps businesses anticipate issues before they escalate—and recover faster when they do.

But effective supply chain risk management isn’t just about avoiding disruptions. It’s about protecting margins, building resilience, and creating the operational adaptability that supports growth.

Understanding the risks: What can disrupt your supply chain?

Supply chain risk comes in many forms, both internal and external. Common types include:

  • Operational risks: Equipment failures, labor shortages, production delays.
  • Financial risks: Supplier bankruptcy, currency fluctuations, inflation.
  • Environmental risks: Natural disasters, climate events, resource scarcity.
  • Geopolitical risks: Trade disputes, sanctions, regulatory changes.
  • Cyber risks: Data breaches, ransomware, IT system outages.

Other overlooked risks include quality failures, intellectual property theft, or shifts in customer demand that ripple through sourcing and production. Because many supply chains rely on multi-tiered networks of suppliers, risks can emerge from deep within the ecosystem—often undetected until it’s too late.

A key challenge is risk interdependency: one disruption can cascade through the entire supply chain, amplifying the impact. For instance, a cyberattack on a logistics provider may delay material deliveries, stall manufacturing, and lead to lost sales.

Benefits and challenges of effective supply chain risk management

Organizations that prioritize supply chain risk management gain critical advantages, including better risk visibility, faster response times, stronger supplier collaboration, and regulatory compliance. But realizing these benefits isn’t always easy. Global complexity, siloed domains and systems, isolated decision-making, and limited resources can create major roadblocks. Understanding both the value and the obstacles is key to building a resilient, future-ready supply chain.

Organizations are already seeing measurable value from connecting risk management with supply chain orchestration. Risk management helps identify and prioritize threats, while orchestration enables a coordinated response across the supply chain.

In a survey of 300 supply chain executives, 68% of respondents who had adopted supply chain orchestration tools selected improved supply chain agility or flexibility as a benefit.2 The finding illustrates how connecting risk intelligence with coordinated decisions and actions can help organizations adapt faster when disruptions emerge.

Benefits

An effective supply chain risk management strategy delivers benefits across operations, supplier relationships, compliance, and customer service:

  • Increased visibility and control: A well-implemented SCRM strategy provides insight into supplier performance, inventory status, logistics flows, and emerging risks—enabling proactive rather than reactive decisions.
  • Stronger supplier compliance and collaboration: Companies can better align with suppliers on risk protocols, improve contract adherence, and create a more resilient, transparent supplier ecosystem.
  • Faster, more confident responses to disruption: With standardized procedures, live data, and predictive alerts, teams can act quickly and decisively when issues arise—reducing delays, costs, and customer impact.
  • Improved regulatory adherence and risk reporting: Standardized processes and better data governance make it easier to comply with industry regulations and document responses to supply chain threats.
  • Competitive differentiation in volatile markets: Organizations that manage risk effectively can maintain service levels, preserve revenue, and earn customer trust even during industry-wide disruption.

Potential challenges

Several barriers can make effective supply chain risk management difficult to implement:

  • Complexity of global, multi-tier networks: Many risks originate from tier-2 or tier-3 suppliers, making it difficult to track vulnerabilities across the full supply base without modern tools and processes.
  • Fragmented data across systems and partners: Disconnected platforms and siloed workflows hinder a unified view of risk and delay response time when it matters most.
  • Limited resources for planning and monitoring: Many supply chain teams are under pressure to deliver on cost containment and efficiency, leaving little time or budget for proactive risk management initiatives.
  • Balancing efficiency with resilience: It’s often challenging to justify redundancy, safety stock, or alternate sourcing strategies in cost-driven environments—especially without clear ROI data.

Despite these challenges, organizations with a supply chain risk management strategy and the right technology can anticipate risks, respond to disruptions, and strengthen resilience across the supply chain.

What makes an effective supply chain risk management plan

A comprehensive SCRM plan includes:

  • Risk identification: Mapping and monitoring suppliers, sites, and logistics routes to uncover potential vulnerabilities
  • Risk assessment: Scoring risks by likelihood and potential impact
  • Risk mitigation: Creating action plans to reduce exposure or recover quickly
  • Monitoring and reporting: Establishing dashboards and alerts to detect early warning signs

It also requires cross-functional alignment between procurement, logistics, operations, finance, and IT. Governance frameworks and scenario-based planning help ensure teams are prepared for a range of alternatives and outcomes.

Another critical aspect is continuous improvement: as threats evolve and the business grows, the plan should be revisited and refined. Embedding a risk-aware culture across departments can also increase overall organizational resilience.

10 proven strategies for managing supply chain risk

There is no one-size-fits-all approach, but many successful organizations rely on a combination of these strategies:

  1. Diversify suppliers and logistics partners to avoid single points of failure.
  2. Invest in nearshoring or reshoring to reduce geographic exposure.
  3. Strengthen collaboration with tier-1 and sub-tier suppliers, subcontractors, and contract manufacturers for better visibility and faster response times.
  4. Optimize planning processes with data from suppliers and contract manufacturing partners.
  5. Use applications, data, and AI together to detect risks, assess impacts, and coordinate responses across the supply chain.
  6. Use digital twins and scenario modeling to test risk response plans.
  7. Establish redundant inventory or safety stock for critical materials.
  8. Adopt agile manufacturing and fulfillment models to respond to change faster.
  9. Create contingency plans and crisis response teams trained for rapid deployment.
  10. Segment supply chains based on risk tolerance, product criticality, or customer needs.

Companies that use a portfolio approach to risk—mixing cost-efficient and resilient models—can achieve both stability and scalability.

SAP Product

Strengthen supply chain resilience

Work smarter with suppliers and partners through SAP Business Network—and boost visibility and control when it matters most, at scale.

Learn more

How to conduct a supply chain risk assessment

A structured assessment can help organizations prioritize where to focus. Key steps include:

  1. Map the full supply chain: Identify key suppliers, routes, facilities, and interdependencies.
  2. Categorize potential risks: Look across operational, geopolitical, environmental, and digital factors.
  3. Assess likelihood and impact: Use a risk matrix to rate severity and probability.
  4. Prioritize and address: Focus on high-impact, high-likelihood risks first.
  5. Repeat regularly: Risks evolve over time, and assessments should too.

Tools like heat maps, scorecards, and scenario planning platforms can support this process.

For global businesses, localization also matters. Risk assessments should account for regional nuances such as infrastructure reliability, regulatory environments, and climate risk.

How technology supports smarter supply chain risk management

Where supply chain risk management once relied on spreadsheets and isolated expertise, today it’s powered by real-time data and advanced technologies, including:

  • Predictive analytics and AI to sense and respond to changes earlier.
  • Control towers to provide end-to-end visibility and alerts.
  • Integrated business planning platforms to align demand, supply, and finance.
  • Multi-enterprise business networks to collaborate and share information with partners in real time.
  • Automation tools to reduce manual data input, tracking, and reporting.
  • Supply chain orchestration connects people, processes, data, and technology to coordinate decisions, assess impacts, and execute responses across the end-to-end supply chain.

AI is already changing how organizations identify and manage supply chain threats. An IDC study reports, “AI-powered cybersecurity threat detection for supply chain systems is implemented across 45% of supply chains.”3 This level of adoption demonstrates the growing role of AI in detecting emerging threats and supporting faster risk responses.

We offer a range of solutions that support smarter SCRM. From synchronized planning to AI-enabled risk detection and collaborative platforms like SAP Business Network, our tools help organizations turn insight into action.

Real-world examples: SCRM in action

Across industries, organizations are modernizing their approach to supply chain risk management—shifting from reactive, manual processes to proactive, data-driven strategies. These examples highlight how businesses are applying technology to strengthen resilience, maintain continuity, and stay competitive in the face of disruption:

  • In electronics and high-tech manufacturing, supply chain teams use integrated business planning tools to model supplier disruptions, obtain supplier commitments to demand plans, simulate alternate sourcing strategies, and adjust production plans in real time. This allows them to minimize downtime and protect inventory flow during unforeseen events.
  • In the food and beverage industry, companies rely on collaborative networks to maintain cold chain logistics during extreme weather or transportation delays. By sharing real-time data with suppliers and logistics providers, they can reallocate inventory and maintain product integrity even in challenging conditions.
  • In pharmaceuticals and life sciences, organizations use predictive analytics and automated compliance tools to monitor supplier risk, excipient quality, and regulatory adherence. This early detection helps prevent disruptions, protect patient safety, and avoid costly violations.
  • In consumer products and retail, businesses are adopting control towers and AI-enabled alerts to quickly respond to shifts in demand, supply shortages, or geopolitical events. These tools enable faster decisions and more agile adjustments to sourcing, production, and fulfillment strategies.

Together, these examples demonstrate the power of combining visibility, planning, AI-assisted analysis, and extensive collaboration. With the right technology, companies can turn risk management into a source of strength—ensuring stability today while preparing for whatever comes next.

FAQ

  • What is supply chain risk management (SCRM)?

    Supply chain risk management (SCRM) is a coordinated approach to identifying and assessing risks, preparing appropriate responses, and managing disruptions when they occur. It assigns clear ownership and response plans to priority threats, while ongoing monitoring helps teams recognize changing conditions. When a disruption occurs, SCRM provides the processes and information needed to evaluate impacts, coordinate decisions, maintain operations, and support recovery. This combination of preparation and response helps businesses protect supply chain performance, continuity, compliance, and customer commitments.

  • Why is supply chain risk management important?

    Supply chain risk management is important because disruptions rarely remain isolated. A supplier failure, cyberattack, or port closure can spread across the business, affecting production and customer commitments. SCRM provides a structured way to recognize those effects earlier and determine which threats require attention. Instead of waiting for a problem to interrupt operations, the business can adjust its plans in advance. This preparation supports continuity and can shorten recovery because teams already understand the risk and know how to respond. By helping the business deliver on its commitments, effective SCRM can also protect customer satisfaction and trust.

  • What are the main types of supply chain risks?

    The main types of supply chain risks include operational, financial, environmental, geopolitical, cyber, and supplier-related threats. These risks often overlap, and a disruption in one area can create consequences across several others. For example, a trade restriction may limit access to a supplier, delaying production and increasing costs. Extreme weather can interrupt transportation and affect customer delivery commitments. Understanding these connections helps businesses assess the broader impact and prioritize an appropriate response.

  • How do you conduct a supply chain risk assessment?

    A supply chain risk assessment begins by mapping the relationships and resources that support critical operations. This map shows where disruption could spread and which dependencies require the most attention. The business then evaluates each threat according to how likely it is to occur and how seriously it could affect operations. This comparison guides mitigation planning and clarifies who should lead the response. Because the supply chain changes over time, regular reviews are necessary to keep priorities and response plans aligned with current operating conditions.

  • What are the best strategies for managing supply chain risk?

    Effective supply chain risk management strategies reduce exposure while preparing the business to respond when disruptions occur. Alternative suppliers and routes reduce dependence on a single source, while visibility across multiple supplier tiers and earlier alerts help teams respond more quickly. Collaboration also gives businesses greater awareness of vulnerabilities across supplier relationships and helps trading partners coordinate solutions when issues arise. Scenario modeling then tests whether these preparations will hold up under different conditions, allowing the business to correct weaknesses before an actual disruption exposes them.

  • How does technology improve supply chain risk management?

    Technology improves supply chain risk management by giving decision-makers greater visibility, earlier insight into changing conditions, and a clearer basis for action. Predictive analytics and AI identify patterns that may require attention, while control towers bring relevant alerts and operational information into a shared view. Integrated planning reveals how a change in demand or supply could affect financial and operational decisions. Business networks support information sharing with external partners, and automation reduces routine monitoring. Together, these capabilities support a more informed and coordinated response when risks emerge.

resources/supply-chain-visibility.html.body:
What Is

What is supply chain visibility and why is it important?

Supply chain visibility improves transparency across multitier supply chains, from raw materials to final delivery, enabling faster risk identification and better decision-making.

Updated on October 27, 2026

Executive summary

Supply chain visibility enables you to digitally monitor and manage the movement of products and materials across your entire supply chain, from sourcing and delivery to recycling. With this level of transparency, you can react to market changes faster, forecast demand with greater accuracy, improve customer service, reduce risk, and meet sustainability goals.

Supply chain visibility depends on integrated platforms such as those from SAP, which, together with AI like predictive analytics and intelligent automation, support deeper insights and faster decisions. By connecting data, processes, and partners across the supply chain, these technologies help your business minimize disruption, improve collaboration, and build a more resilient and competitive supply chain.

Supply chains are at the heart of so many businesses. They support growth and success, yet they can also be the most complex and vulnerable area of your company—especially when every new year seems to bring with it some previously unheard-of complexity or disruption. And while you can’t control politics or the weather, you do have the power to apply data and AI-powered technologies to enhance your supply chain visibility, driving a more agile and competitive enterprise.

What is supply chain visibility?

Supply chain visibility is the strategic capability to monitor every component of the supply chain. By providing insights into inventory levels, shipment status, production schedules, and warehouse management, enhanced visibility can help you create a more responsive and resilient supply chain to better manage the unpredictability inherent in global markets. This not only boosts operational efficiency, but also supports regulatory compliance and shows you areas where you can improve the overall sustainability of your supply chain operations.

Supply chain visibility also enables better trading partner collaboration. This can reduce risks and delays while helping improve customer satisfaction and loyalty. Ultimately, supply chain visibility translates to quicker decision-making and more efficient operations, helping you meet and even exceed customer expectations.

Comparing supply chain visibility, tracking, transparency, and autonomy

While supply chain tracking focuses on the movement of products and transparency focuses on sharing supply chain information with stakeholders, supply chain visibility provides the operational insight needed to manage supply chain performance. AI-enhanced supply chain visibility uses real-time data, predictive analytics, and automation to help organizations anticipate risks and make faster, more proactive decisions.

Concept

Focus

Scope

Benefits

Supply chain visibility (traditional)

Provides insight into supply chain operations through reports, system integrations, and historical or periodic data updates

End-to-end supply chain activities, including inventory, orders, suppliers, and logistics

Improves operational awareness and supports informed decision-making

Supply chain tracking

Monitors the location and status of products, assets, or shipments

Individual items, orders, containers, or shipments moving through the supply chain

Helps organizations locate goods, monitor delivery progress, and identify delays

Supply chain transparency

Shares information about sourcing, compliance, sustainability, and business practices with stakeholders

Supplier networks, environmental impact, ethical practices, and regulatory compliance

Builds trust, supports accountability, and demonstrates responsible business practices

Visibility in an autonomous supply chain

Combines real-time data, AI, machine learning, and analytics to generate predictive and prescriptive insights

End-to-end supply chain operations, risks, disruptions, inventory, and partner networks

Enables organizations to anticipate disruptions, automate decisions, and respond proactively to changing conditions

How does supply chain visibility work?

Supply chain visibility is enabled through these components:

  • Data integration: It’s one thing to amass an enormous amount of informative data, but its value can only be realized when it’s integrated into enterprise-wide systems—and strategically analyzed to deliver powerful insights and inform automation and decision-making. A unified data pool is essential for breaking down silos within the organization and ensuring that all stakeholders have access to better supply chain visibility.
  • Continuous monitoring: A supply chain control tower represents cloud-connected tools that can monitor operations from end to end. Connecting IoT devices, systems, sensors, suppliers, and partners to a centralized vantage point helps you identify and address disruptions proactively. By integrating contextualized data from all supply chain components into a harmonized data model, a control tower helps to boost your confidence and arm you with the intel you need to pivot and respond to both opportunities and threats through timely alerts and notifications.
  • Analytics and reporting: From sales and operational planning (S&OP) to inventory management, and planning/forecasting, supply chain visibility relies upon your team’s ability to obtain information and commitments from partners across your supply chain, from tier one to lower tiers. Here is where all that data capture and integration pay off: AI-powered analytics and integrated, connected systems allow you to understand and apply the big data sets you need to work with to compete in today’s market.

Benefits of visibility in the supply chain

Below are some examples of how you can benefit from deeper insight into your supply chain:

  • Greater agility and resilience: It’s essential to gather and analyze all your supply chain data so that you can quickly act upon it. True agility means you have the capacity to respond from end to end across your supply chain, to pivot, and to optimize your operations for a new business paradigm. Knowing when a challenge or opportunity is on its way is the first crucial step.
  • Improved inventory planning and optimization: By providing a real-time view of inventory levels and operational status, companies can streamline operations and reduce excess inventory. Well-managed inventory optimization leads to cost savings and improved efficiency.
  • Accurate forecasting and demand management: Access to real-time and historical data enhances the accuracy of demand forecasting. Companies can align their production and inventory management more closely with actual market demand, reducing the risk of overproduction and stockouts.
  • Enhanced customer satisfaction: Greater supply chain visibility improves the accuracy and reliability of order fulfillment processes. Timely and transparent shipping information increases customer trust and satisfaction by keeping them informed about the status of their orders.
  • Documented environmental and social responsibility: Depending upon the nature of your business, your supply chain can contribute up to 90% of your total carbon and pollution output. Visibility is critical for achieving sustainability goals and for meeting consumer expectations of ethical and responsible business practices.
  • Risk management: Supply chain visibility helps organizations identify potential risks earlier, from supplier disruptions to compliance issues. With a clearer view of vulnerabilities across the network, leaders can take proactive steps to mitigate risk and improve resilience.
  • Regulatory and policy compliance: With improved visibility into the supply chain, organizations can better monitor compliance across suppliers, operations, and logistics. This transparency helps identify potential regulatory and policy issues early, enabling proactive action to address them.

Overcoming challenges through visibility into supply chains

Of course, there are often hiccups when you try to initiate change and new strategic directions. But the good news is that—unlike global events and supply chain disruptions—these practical challenges are within your control to manage and overcome.

  • Inconsistent data: Many supply chain managers are grappling with disconnected global systems and wildly disparate data sources.
    • Mitigation: By implementing AI-powered data integration platforms to harmonize and cleanse disparate data, you can establish a single, consistent source of information that enhances decision-making.
  • Disconnected processes and process gaps: Siloed operations can disrupt the flow of information.
    • Mitigation: A unified operational platform is an essential tool to boost collaboration. But ultimately, it’s equally important to work toward a business culture that is communicative and team oriented.
  • Technologies that are not integrated: Often with the best of intentions, suppliers, partners, and staff across your supply chain invest in isolated solutions.
    • Mitigation: Acquiring the powerful tools and software you need is the first step. But it’s also essential to establish protocols and training to help people use it optimally, and to wean them off unapproved applications and disconnected technologies.
  • Poor communication between buyers and suppliers: Advanced collaboration tools are often underutilized.
    • Mitigation: A supply chain network connects data, processes, and trading partners for better collaboration, document exchange, and visibility.
  • Over-reliance on manual data handling: Manual processes for data management slow operations and increase the risk of errors.
    • Mitigation: Adopt automation tools employing AI and machine learning to overhaul data collection and processing, significantly boosting efficiency and accuracy across the supply chain.

Trends in supply chain visibility technology

New technologies continue to improve supply chain visibility and responsiveness. Here are the key trends that are shaping the future of supply chain management:

  • Extended transparency: Today’s business leaders seek deeper, real-time insights into their global operations supply—including tier two and tier three suppliers, going as far back as their raw materials suppliers’ sourcing and production practices. This helps them root out non-compliant suppliers and unacceptable practices.
  • Environmental, social, and governance (ESG) and emissions tracking: Companies are increasingly leveraging smart technologies to track emissions and other environmental impacts (in real time) along their supply chains. This helps them improve their sustainability practices and adhere to their environmental, social, and governance (ESG) commitments.
  • Automation and AI: AI is moving beyond analytics to help supply chains anticipate disruptions, make decisions, and take action. AI assistants and agents can analyze real-time data, identify risks and opportunities, recommend responses, and automate routine tasks while enabling teams to guide critical decisions.
  • IoT integration: Just a few years ago, IoT networks were largely relegated to the manufacturing floor. But as connectivity continues to improve, there is a marked rise in touchpoints, devices, tools, and even people who are sending powerful data into a centralized IoT network.
  • Blockchain for transparency: From combating cybercrime to building a more reliable and transparent supplier network, blockchain can provide a tamper-resistant transaction record that helps build trust and transparency.

What to look for in supply chain visibility solutions

When selecting supply chain visibility software, it's crucial to choose a solution that aligns with your organization's specific needs and goals. Here are key factors to consider as you proceed on your digital transformation journey:

  • Trading partner collaboration: Ensure the software connects buyers, suppliers, manufacturers, and logistics partners on a single platform, facilitating seamless collaboration across the supply chain.
  • Digital document exchange: Look for capabilities that support digital document exchange for planning, purchasing, and invoicing processes, streamlining these activities and reducing manual errors.
  • Process automation: Choose software with robust automation features, such as automated invoice reconciliation and other processes based on historical and real-time data.
  • Integration with business systems: The solution should integrate smoothly with existing ERP and CRM systems, enabling a unified view of the supply chain and enhancing data consistency.
  • Real-time tracking: Select software that offers real-time tracking of materials, inventory, and shipments, providing immediate insights and alerts for better decision-making.
  • Inventory management: Effective supply chain visibility software should support supplier-managed inventory, helping to maintain optimal stock levels and prevent overstock or stockouts.
  • Frequent updates and scalability: Ensure the software receives regular updates and improvements—and that it can scale as your business grows and adapt to your evolving needs.

Take the next steps

Explore supply chain network solutions that can seamlessly integrate with your existing business systems to provide powerful tracking and advanced analytics. With features like automated processes, digital document exchange, and robust collaboration tools, you can now ensure that all your global stakeholders can efficiently share and manage critical supply chain data. This enhances transparency, reduces risks, and powers more confident and accurate decision-making across your supply chain—and your business.

FAQ

  • What is supply chain visibility?

    Supply chain visibility is the ability to see what's happening across your supply chain from end to end. By connecting data from the full supply chain ecosystem, businesses gain a clearer understanding of inventory, orders, shipments, forecasts, and invoices. This shared view helps teams spot issues sooner, respond more quickly to disruptions, and make decisions with greater confidence.

  • Why is supply chain visibility important?

    Supply chain visibility is important because businesses can't respond to problems they can't see. When decision-makers have access to timely, accurate information, they can identify risks before they escalate and adjust plans as conditions change. This leads to more reliable forecasting, better inventory decisions, and stronger collaboration across partners. As a result, organizations can improve service, reduce costs, and build more resilient operations.

  • What is software for supply chain visibility?

    Software for supply chain visibility brings together data from across the supply chain to create a unified view of operations. Rather than relying on disconnected systems, organizations can track inventory, orders, shipments, and potential disruptions in one place. By analyzing this information in real time, the software helps teams understand what's happening, anticipate challenges, and take action before small issues become larger problems.

  • How does AI improve supply chain visibility?

    AI improves supply chain visibility by turning large volumes of operational data into useful insights. Instead of simply showing what has happened, AI helps explain why it happened and what may happen next. As patterns emerge, businesses can forecast demand more accurately, identify risks earlier, and respond to disruptions before they affect customers. This allows teams to make faster, more proactive decisions across the supply chain.

  • What is the difference between supply chain visibility and tracking?

    Supply chain visibility and tracking are related, but answer different questions. Visibility focuses on understanding what is happening across day-to-day supply chain operations—inventory levels, order status, supplier performance, and disruptions—so teams can manage and optimize the network. Tracking focuses on following the location and status of specific shipments or assets as they move from point to point. In short: visibility supports operational control across the supply chain, while tracking confirms where a particular item is right now.

  • What technology is needed to achieve end-to-end supply chain visibility?

    End-to-end supply chain visibility requires technology that connects information from every stage of the supply chain into a single, shared view. Integration platforms link data from suppliers, logistics providers, customers, and internal systems; tracking tools capture location and status updates as goods move; and analytics dashboards turn that shared data into early disruption alerts and coordinated responses.

resources/what-are-multi-agent-systems.h.description: Learn how a multi-agent system coordinates artificial intelligence (AI) software programs that collaborate with each other so they can perform complex tasks.
resources/what-are-multi-agent-systems.h.body:
What Is

What are multi-agent systems?

AI agents, collaborating in one system, are solving today’s increasingly complex business challenges.

Published on March 15, 2025

A multi-agent system consists of multiple artificial intelligence (AI) agents that act autonomously but work collaboratively to understand user inputs, make decisions, and perform tasks to achieve a collective goal.

Multi-agent systems solve complex, multi-step, large-scale problems, freeing teams to focus on higher-value work.

A few examples of multi-agent systems in business include:

  • Customer service: AI agents can work together to track a customer’s issue in a tech support call, recommend fixes, escalate the solution, and adjust billing or issue a refund.
  • Supply chain: Agents representing different suppliers can collaborate in real-time to predict inventory needs, allocate resources, and adjust operations as needed.
  • Security and fraud detection: AI agents can monitor for fraudulent activity, assess the risk, and adapt an organization’s actions to reduce threats.

Understanding multi-agent systems

The capabilities of multi-agent systems go far beyond simply automating workflows, in part, thanks to AI agents, which are essentially the next frontier of generative AI. AI agents will far exceed the capabilities of simple chatbots and advance what is possible with AI copilots. Think of a single human operating independently: One person can only have so much expertise and, working in isolation, can accomplish only so much. The same is true of AI agents: Collaborating achieves much more than working solo. Multi-agent systems autonomously collaborating with one another to handle more complex workflows can improve an organization’s productivity and efficiency.

One real-world example of a multi-agent system is in HR, where agents autonomously support the recruiting process through screening, ranking, and recommending candidates.

Another example is across the supply chain, where AI agents autonomously assess the impact of machines’ downtime, reschedule impacted orders, reallocate inventory, and plan and schedule maintenance.

  • AI: The brain power at the core of an AI agent
  • AI agent: A subset of intelligent agents that takes its own agency a step further through specialization, and autonomously making decisions and performing tasks
  • Large language models (LLMs): An AI system trained on massive amounts of data so that AI agents can understand human language and respond conversationally—answering questions, generating text, and making other decisions based on the context it’s learned.
  • Orchestration: The information exchanges between AI agents
  • Environment: Physical, digital, and simulated space where AI functions

How does a multi-agent system work?

A multi-agent system distributes tasks and communication among individual agents, each of which brings their specialized talent to collectively achieve a goal and learn from it in a shared environment. This dividing of tasks is the key to a multi-agent system’s ability to solve complex problems.

Key multi-agent systems architectures

A multi-agent system typically operates as either a centralized or decentralized network.

  • In a centralized network, a single server controls the AI agents’ interactions and information. This orchestrator (in a human scenario, the project manager) has the ability to reason over the overall process and system, simplifying communications and standardizing information. The primary drawback for using a centralized multi-agent system is that it can create a single point of failure.
  • In a decentralized network, AI agents control their own direct interactions with each other instead of a single server (“project manager”) controlling them. The specialized AI agents have a common understanding and shared responsibility of what they’re trying to accomplish. While more robust and scalable than a centralized network, the primary drawback for using a decentralized multi-agent system is that it requires more complex coordination.

What's the difference between a multi-agent system and a single agent?

There are several differences between multi-agent systems and single agent systems.

  • Single AI agents work autonomously within their own environment to perform a requested task. They use LLMs to understand user inputs, they design workflows, and they can call on tools to execute the workflows they plan.
  • In a multi-agent system, multiple AI agents interact with each other fluidly and iteratively, bringing together their individual properties and expertise to not only to achieve the task, but also to learn. A multi-agent system can have thousands of individual agents.

Collaboration is a strategy every business uses to make teams greater than the sum of their parts, and these tactics can include project management, scrum meetings, and discussion forums. Collaboration allows AI agents to achieve more than when they act independently; for example, missing opportunities outside their specialization. By talking to each other, AI agents act more like a human team does and can fill gaps that otherwise go unaddressed.

The difference between the two systems is having a single expert performing their individual specialty as a cog in a wheel versus a team of experts coordinating and succeeding in real time.

A key distinction between a single agent system and a multi-agent system is the latter’s superior ability to understand the problem’s complexity and its effectiveness in addressing that problem.

Think of a project manager who brings together a team of individual specialists—for example, a software engineer, a designer, a product manager, and so on—to do greater things by collaborating. A multi-agent system is like a project manager or a project plan; it can do more using a team of specialists. Assigning AI agents to tasks according to their specialization helps the LLM prioritize what to focus on so it can deliver a better performance.

Using specialized AI agents in a multi-agent system also gives developers a framework to follow, allowing them to break down their tasks into subtasks that are easier to code. Finally, many teams using multi-agent systems may see them outperform single agent systems, driving new innovations and developer productivity.

When to choose a multi-agent system

Generally speaking, any organization already using AI agents can realize the benefits of a multi-agent system. Choosing between a single agent system and a multi-agent system depends on an organization’s or project’s specific needs; achieving the goal comes down to training, maintenance, and processing outputs—the same tasks that are required to grow a team of humans.

  • A single agent system is ideal when tasks are straightforward and well-defined.
  • A multi-agent system is ideal when tasks are complex and require expertise across multiple disciplines.

Examples of real-world multi-agent systems

Thanks to their flexibility and adaptability, multi-agent systems are ideal for roles in nearly every industry.

  • Automated manufacturing lines: Reducing downtime with predictive maintenance AI agents that audit equipment and communicates with another agent to schedule necessary repairs
  • Smart power grids: Optimizing energy distribution using one agent to monitor weather systems and a second agent to use that data to predict energy demand
  • Autonomous vehicles: Increasing safety with the AI agent controlling the camera systems collaborating with the on-screen display agent to guide the driver
  • Patient healthcare and coordination: Accelerating diagnosis and intervention using agents representing different healthcare specialists that work together to design a comprehensive treatment plan
  • Supply chain management: Responding faster to changes using one AI agent to monitor sales trends and communicate with another agent to adjust reordering levels
  • Transportation systems: Improving navigation using one agent to monitor traffic conditions that it shares with a second agent that optimize routes for public transportation

Benefits of multi-agent systems applications in technology and AI

Given a complex task like writing code, a multi-agent system would distribute the job as assignments for individual agents representing the software engineer, product manager, designer, quality assurance engineer, and other roles needed for the task. Each AI agent does its part, and the overall multi-agent system coordinates the collective work and enables the agents to collaborate, reasoning on next steps and beyond to ultimately accomplish the overall goal.

While single AI agents are powerful on their own, they can deliver even more accuracy, scalability, and flexibility when part of a multi-agent system. A multi-agent system can free up staff to focus on higher value, more strategic work instead of spending time overseeing manual, repetitive, and labor-intensive workflows.

Overall benefits of a multi-agent system include:

  • Collaboration: Leveraging the collective intelligence of a team of AI agents can understand and solve increasingly complex problems.
  • Performance: Enabling a bigger pool of specialized AI agents to interact and learn in their environment can accomplish more, faster, than single agents acting independently.
  • Efficiency: The multi-agent system design pattern gives developers a framework for how to break down complex tasks into subtasks that are easier to code.

Building a multi-agent system

When building a multi-agent system, it’s important to consider the quality and depth of the data available to an organization.

Designing a multi-agent system

Empowering smarter decisions and achieving efficiencies at scale starts with a system tailored to an organization’s unique data landscape and the nuances of its industry. This ensures the AI agents comprising the organization’s multi-agent system have the most relevant, reliable, and trustworthy data available.

  1. Determine project needs and choose the most ideal LLM to meet those needs. The best LLMs for multi-agent systems offer advanced reasoning capabilities, reading comprehension, language understanding, and code generation.
  2. Define the role and objectives for each AI agent. Make sure each AI agent knows what to do as part of the greater goal. Assign the correct LLM and any necessary tools the AI agents might need.
  3. Initiate a workflow for each AI agent. Orchestrate AI agents so their tasks are done correctly, and collaboration is harmonious and effective. Workflow initiation includes establishing the AI environment, defining tasks, launching agents, monitoring communication, and generating outputs.

SAP Product

Modernize, innovate, automate

Jump-start and simplify application development and extension, and automate processes using pre-built solutions and generative AI tools in SAP Build.

Learn more

Key considerations when implementing a multi-agent system

Every system an organization deploys must operate efficiently, ethically, and within established regulations, which requires constant evaluation and a governance framework.

  • Establish ethical practices for using AI.

  • Identify metrics for how each AI agent performs.

  • Retest system performance when the number of AI agents and/or tasks increases.

  • Evaluate the system’s ability to recover from errors, adapt to changes, and deliver business continuity.

  • Continually monitor and audit the multi-agent system to identify areas for improvement.

Governance-specific considerations

  • Enforce standards that protect data privacy and prevent bias and comply with regulatory laws and industry standards.
  • Program AI agents to monitor the activity of other agents and identify any ethical breaches.
  • Maintain visibility on AI agent decision-making to establish trust.
  • Establish transparency on multi-agent system operations to meet regulation compliance.
  • Identify and mitigate risk to reduce errors and increase reliability.

Human oversight

  • Use a human-in-the-loop model for workflows to maintain alignment with human value.
  • Include human touch points to monitor and prevent unsanctioned autonomous actions.

Challenges of multi-agent systems

While multi-agent systems are highly capable, they come with some challenges to consider.

  • AI still needs to become proficient in addressing complex tasks, workflows, and business processes that are not easily preconfigured or require multiple steps to complete.
  • Having more AI agents increases the system’s complexity, configuration, and needed maintenance.
  • A decentralized multi-agent system can experience unpredictable behavior among its AI agents that pass along incorrect information on the basis it’s true. Detecting the source of the inaccuracy and managing behavior based on bad data can be difficult.
  • Humans using AI must also follow the rules and guidelines for the ethical use of AI.

What's next for using AI multi-agent systems

AI agents represent a major shift in the way work gets done, from improving operational efficiencies to delivering more service value for less effort.

Emerging trends and predictions

As AI becomes more capable and data management more rigorous, multi-agent systems will evolve to generate increasingly accurate, applicable, and adaptive outcomes. Some scenarios include virtual customer service to answer common questions, monitoring supply chains and managing inventory, forecasting market trends and recommending potential growth opportunities, updating job postings and generating candidate lists, and tracking and preventing fraud by monitoring transactions in real time.

One future trend will be to combine multi-agent systems with increasingly dynamic machine learning algorithms to advance data analyzation and application development. Another trend leverages the increasing intelligence and capabilities of the individual AI agents that contribute to the efficacy of a multi-agent system.

Implications for AI and technology

As AI agents continue to adapt and learn, multi-agent systems will drive AI deeper into more complex problems facing organizations of every size, focus, and industry. These capabilities position AI to have a much bigger impact on businesses and society.

FAQ

  • What is an AI agent?

    An AI agent is a specialized program that autonomously interacts with its environment and plans workflows, reasons, makes decisions, and performs tasks to achieve a goal.

  • What does an AI agent do?

    AI agents can automate specialized tasks, make decisions, and improve performance over time without human intervention.

  • How do I create my own AI agent?
