about/what-is-sap.html.description: Learn what SAP is, what SAP software does, and how organizations use SAP ERP, cloud applications, business AI, and GROW with SAP to run and grow.
about/what-is-sap.html.body:
What is SAP?
Overview

What is SAP?

SAP is a global company that develops software that helps organizations run, manage, and improve their businesses.
Contact us
Explore our products

Overview of SAP—ERP, business software, AI, and solutions

SAP is best known today for enterprise resource planning (ERP) software, cloud business applications, and AI-powered business solutions that help organizations make better decisions, automate work, and adapt to changing business conditions. 

 

SAP solutions connect core business processes such as finance, procurement, supply chain management, manufacturing, human resources, customer experience, and analytics in a single, integrated environment.

 

From small and midsize companies to many of the world's largest enterprises, organizations use SAP software and solutions to connect operations, data, and AI across the business.

SAP at a glance

 Company name : SAP 

Founded : 1972 

Headquarters : Walldorf, Germany 

Industry : Enterprise software 

Best known for : ERP and business applications 

Serves : Organizations of all sizes across industries 

Core focus : Helping businesses run, adapt, and transform through integrated applications, data, and AI

Flagship ERP : SAP S/4HANA

Growth offerings : SAP GROW, SAP Cloud ERP, SAP Business AI Platform, and modular business applications

What does SAP stand for? 

SAP stands for Systems, Applications, and Products in Data Processing.  The original SAP meaning comes from the company's German name when it was founded, SystemAnalyse Programmentwicklung, which translates to "Systems Analysis Program Development."

Explore SAP company information

What does SAP do, and why do companies use it?

SAP helps organizations manage and optimize the processes that keep businesses running.

 

Most companies generate information across many departments, systems, and teams. Finance has its own data. Procurement has another set of information. HR, manufacturing, customer service, and operations often rely on different tools and workflows.

 

SAP helps bring those processes and data together. Instead of relying on disconnected systems, spreadsheets, or manual processes, organizations can use SAP solutions to operate with greater visibility, consistency, and efficiency.

What SAP helps businesses manage:

  • Finance and accounting

  • Procurement and sourcing

  • Supply chain operations

  • Manufacturing and production planning

  • Inventory and warehouse management

  • Sales and customer service

  • Human resources and workforce management

  • Business analytics and planning

  • Sustainability reporting and compliance

  • Enterprise-wide data management

Organizations often choose SAP for five key reasons

A centralized source of business information

SAP helps organizations create a trusted view of data across business functions, reducing silos, and improving decision-making.

Global standardization

Many businesses operate across countries, business units, and subsidiaries. SAP helps establish consistent processes while supporting local requirements.

Deep industry and business process expertise

Over decades of working with organizations worldwide, SAP has developed specialized capabilities for industries including manufacturing, retail, healthcare, energy, consumer products, public sector, and financial services.

Integrated applications

The SAP portfolio spans finance, supply chain, HR, procurement, analytics, customer experience, and business technology, helping organizations connect critical processes.

Continuous innovation

SAP continues to evolve its cloud applications, business data capabilities, and AI-powered experiences to help customers operate more intelligently and efficiently.

What are the main SAP products categories and solutions?

SAP offers a broad portfolio of business offerings. Some customers adopt a comprehensive ERP platform, while others start with specific business applications that solve individual business challenges.

  • Business AI Platform

  • Cloud ERP

  • Finance

  • Supply chain

  • Business Technology Platform

  • Procurement

  • Human resources

  • Customer experience

  • Analytics

  • SAP Business AI Platform

  • SAP S/4HANA

  • Joule

  • SAP GROW

  • SAP Business One

  • SAP SuccessFactors

  • SAP Ariba

  • SAP Concur

  • SAP Fieldglass

  • SAP Analytics Cloud

Try SAP products

Which industries use SAP?

SAP software supports industry-specific needs across a wide range of sectors. Industry capabilities help organizations address unique operational, regulatory, and market requirements while maintaining integrated business processes.

Common industries that use SAP include:

  • Automotive

  • Retail

  • Consumer products

  • Life sciences and healthcare

  • Government

  • Financial services

  • Oil, gas, and energy

  • Telecommunications

  • Education and research

  • Travel and transportation

  • Industrial manufacturing

  • Professional services

Explore all industries

How is SAP software used in business?

Organizations use SAP software in different ways, depending on their goals, industry, and operational needs.

Enterprise finance

Manage accounting, reporting, financial planning, compliance, and close processes.

Procurement automation

Standardize purchasing activities, supplier collaboration, and spend management.

Manufacturing planning

Improve production scheduling, resource utilization, and operational visibility.

Inventory tracking

Track inventory levels, warehouse activities, and product movement in real time.

Workforce data

Support recruiting, employee development, payroll integration, and workforce analytics.

Customer experience

Improve sales processes, service delivery, and customer experience.

Business analytics

Turn operational data into actionable insights for planning and decision-making.

Sustainability management

Measure, monitor, and report sustainability metrics and business impact.

See how customers are using SAP

What’s the difference between SAP and ERP?

For those asking, "What is ERP?,” ERP software helps organizations manage and integrate core business processes across finance, procurement, supply chain, HR, and operations. ERP is a category of software, while SAP is the brand or company manufacturing that software; just like automobiles are a product category and BMW is a brand under that category.

Here’s a closer look at how ERP, SAP, and SAP S/4HANA fit together.

What is ERP?

ERP is a category of software that helps organizations manage and integrate core business processes.

What is SAP?

SAP is a company that develops ERP software and solutions, as well as many other business applications.

What is SAP S/4HANA?

SAP S/4HANA is a leading ERP solution from SAP.

How is SAP incorporating AI?  

As enterprises make AI a fundamental part of how they operate, SAP is embedding AI directly into business applications and workflows.

 

Rather than treating AI as a separate tool, SAP increasingly integrates AI into the software people already use for finance, procurement, supply chain, HR, customer service, and other business functions.

SAP Business AI Platform helps organizations

  • Automate repetitive tasks

  • Generate insights from business dat

  • Improve decision-making

  • Increase productivity

  • Streamline business processes

  • Support faster responses to changing business conditions

Learn more about SAP Business AI Platform 

AI with business context

One of SAP's strengths is the business context available across enterprise workflows, processes, and data derived from over 50 years of deep business process experience, industry experience, and approach to governance. This allows AI capabilities to be applied where organizations need practical outcomes, such as improving forecasting, accelerating approvals, identifying risks, or helping employees work more efficiently.

SAP's long-term vision is to help organizations operate with greater intelligence, automation, and adaptability while maintaining enterprise-grade governance, control, and human oversight.

Joule

Joule refers to SAP's context-aware AI agents and AI assistants. It helps users interact with SAP applications more naturally, access relevant information, complete tasks, and navigate processes more efficiently.

Learn more about Joule 

Is SAP only for large enterprises?

A common misconception is that SAP is only for the world's largest enterprises. Although SAP does have a long history serving large global organizations, the company also offers solutions designed for growing and midsize businesses.

SAP for small and midsize businesses

SAP Business One provides ERP capabilities designed specifically for small and midsize organizations.

SAP for growing companies

SAP GROW helps companies adopt cloud ERP with preconfigured best practices, implementation guidance, and scalability for future growth. Companies that adopt cloud ERP benefit from embedded AI, digitization of data and processes, and the ability to scale without complexity.

SAP for large enterprises

SAP continues to support complex global organizations that require sophisticated business process management, governance, and operational scale.

How to learn SAP

Like any enterprise software platform, learning SAP requires time and practice.

The difficulty depends on:

  • Your role

  • The SAP products being used

  • Your familiarity with business processes

  • Your technical background

Finance professionals, procurement specialists, analysts, HR practitioners, and developers often focus on different areas of SAP.

For those interested in learning SAP, resources are available through SAP Learning, including training and certification options, free courses, premium learning resources like hands-on practice, and instructor-led courses to build your skills and advance your career.

How long does SAP implementation take?

How long does SAP implementation take?

There is no single implementation timeline. The duration depends on factors such as:

  • Business scope

  • Implementation readiness

  • Number of users

  • Data quality and migration needs

  • Integration requirements

  • Project resources

  • Deployment approach

Some standalone SAP solutions can be adopted relatively quickly, while large enterprise transformations may require significantly more planning.

Offerings like SAP GROW, which leverage processes like SAP Activate, help organizations accelerate adoption through proven methodologies and best practices.

FAQs

SAP is both. SAP is the company, and SAP software refers to the business applications the company develops and sells.

The SAP acronym stands for Systems, Applications, and Products in Data Processing.

SAP is best known for ERP solutions and enterprise business applications.

SAP supports industries including manufacturing, retail, healthcare, financial services, energy, public sector, telecommunications, and many others.

Companies use SAP to integrate business processes, improve visibility, standardize operations, automate work, and support better decision-making.

SAP software is used by organizations of all sizes across industries, including manufacturing, retail, healthcare, finance, government, and technology, to manage and streamline business operations. SAP customers include:

  • Large multinational enterprises

  • Fortune Global 500 organizations

  • Midmarket and growing businesses

  • Public sector organizations

  • Educational institutions

  • Healthcare providers

  • Retailers

  • Manufacturers

  • Energy and utility companies

  • Financial services organizations

SAP is a software company that provides ERP solutions, while ERP (enterprise resource planning) is the category of software used to manage core business processes across an organization.

SAP’s main products include SAP S/4HANA, SAP Business Technology Platform, SAP SuccessFactors, SAP Ariba, SAP Concur, and SAP Customer Experience.

Some SAP products have free trials, before committing to a purchase you can explore and find the right fit for your needs.

Historically, SAP users often referred to major business functions as "modules." Many of these abbreviations remain common in job descriptions, training materials, and customer discussions.

 

  • FI - Financial accounting - Finance 

  • CO - Controlling - Management accounting and performance tracking 

  • MM - Materials management - Procurement and inventory 

  • SD - Sales and distribution - Sales and order management 

  • HCM - Human capital management - Workforce and HR management 

 

Although modern SAP solutions are increasingly cloud-based and integrated, these terms continue to be widely used throughout the SAP ecosystem. 

SAP S/4HANA is SAP's flagship ERP solution for managing core business operations.

SAP embeds AI into business processes through SAP Business AI Platform and Joule to help users automate work, gain insights, and improve productivity.

No, SAP isn’t just for large enterprises. SAP offers solutions for small, midsize, growing, and large organizations, including SAP Business One and SAP GROW. 

No, SAP isn’t too complex for small or midsize businesses. SAP offers cloud-based and scalable solutions designed specifically for small and midsize businesses, making implementation and management more practical and cost-effective.

No, you don’t need SAP ERP to use SAP products. Many SAP products can integrate with SAP ERP, but they can also work with other systems depending on your business needs.

Yes. Many solutions, including SAP Concur, SAP Ariba, SAP Fieldglass, SAP SuccessFactors, and SAP Analytics Cloud, can be adopted independently.

It doesn’t necessarily take 18 months or more to implement SAP. Implementation timelines vary widely, and many modern cloud deployments can be completed in a matter of weeks or months rather than 18+ months. Organizations can use the SAP Activate methodology, which supports the process to streamline deployment.

Yes. SAP continues to modernize the user experience across cloud applications and AI-powered interactions.

While SAP can be complex, its modern user interfaces, training resources, and role-based tools make it accessible for users at all experience levels.

The SAP Learning site, SAP Learning Hub, certifications, and training programs provide multiple paths for building SAP skills.

“SAP experience” in a job description typically means familiarity with using, configuring, supporting, or managing SAP software to perform business processes such as finance, supply chain, procurement, HR, or reporting.

Microsoft Excel is excellent for individual analysis, calculations, models, and reporting. SAP, however, is designed to manage governed business processes across teams, departments, and organizations. Excel typically helps individuals analyze data. SAP helps organizations run their business. Many organizations use both SAP and Excel because they solve different business needs.

blogs/ext-how-ai-powered-cybersecurity-c.body:
Blog

How AI-powered cybersecurity combats growing AI threats

Gabriele FiataUpdated on July 25, 2024

The threats related to AI are expanding as systems gain autonomy and sophistication at an alarming rate. From January to February 2023 alone, Darktrace researchers observed a 135% increase in “novel social engineering attacks,” corresponding to “the widespread adoption of ChatGPT.”

Malicious actors can now use artificial intelligence to launch targeted cyberattacks and exploit vulnerabilities at speeds, scales, and levels of precision previously unattainable by human hackers. AI can also be used to craft highly convincing phishing e-mails, create malware that adapts to security measures, and even automate the extraction of valuable data from compromised systems. Traditional cybersecurity measures—such as signature-based antivirus software, firewalls, and rule-based intrusion detection systems—struggle to keep pace with these types of AI-driven attacks, highlighting the need for more adaptive and advanced, AI-enabled cybersecurity strategies.

It’s the perfect time to discuss how leaders can fortify their strategies to mitigate these risks.

The best defense against AI is … AI

Ironically, AI itself can be a potent tool in defending against AI threats. Machine learning algorithms can analyze vast data sets to identify anomalies and detect potential security breaches in real time. AI-driven threat detection systems can recognize patterns of behavior that human analysts might miss. This proactive approach to cybersecurity can significantly reduce response times and limit the damage caused by AI-driven attacks.

To tackle evolving AI threats, SAP is working together with Splunk—creator of prominent technology for data analysis and security—to address the unique challenges posed by AI in the realm of cybersecurity. The following are key initiatives behind their collaboration.

Keys to the cybersecurity strategy refresh

  • AI-specific threat detection
    AI-powered threat detection systems are being designed to detect AI-driven attacks. These systems identify anomalies such as an unexpected surge in data requests outside of business hours or a sudden influx of simultaneous user login attempts. These specific indicators serve as early alerts, signaling potential cyber threats or unauthorized access and helping organizations fortify their security posture.
  • Real-time monitoring
    In the age of AI, real-time monitoring is crucial. SAP and Splunk's collaborative efforts focus on providing businesses with tools to continuously monitor their AI systems. This allows for immediate responses to security threats as they arise, reducing the potential for damage.
  • Strong security community
    Engaging with industry experts and cybersecurity professionals facilitates better information exchange, best practices, and threat intelligence sharing. Technical workshops and thought leadership conferences can also foster collective defense strategies. Events like these help security professionals and businesses stay resilient in the face of evolving AI-related security risks, encouraging a proactive and collaborative response within the community.

What leaders can do to tackle AI threats

Stay informed: Keep up to date with the latest developments in AI security threats and solutions. Attend industry webinars, such as the SAP User Groups on Security, and conferences such as SAPinsider and.conf24, to gain insights from experts.

Regular security audits: Conduct regular security audits of your AI infrastructure to identify vulnerabilities and weaknesses. Collaborate with AI security experts to ensure comprehensive protection.

Invest in AI-enabled cybersecurity solutions: Recognize that AI demands specialized security measures. Explore products, such as those provided by SAP and Splunk, that are capable of early detection. These products can identify abnormal user and system behaviors and safeguard your business data against AI-driven cyber attacks.

Train your team: Invest in AI security training for your cybersecurity professionals, and equip them with the knowledge and skills needed to defend against AI-specific threats. Key focus areas include:

  • Ensuring security is an integral part of the AI development process, from inception to deployment
  • Simulating potential AI attacks to identify vulnerabilities and reinforce defensive measures
  • Conducting drills to enhance the team's ability to respond effectively to AI-specific incidents, establishing strong processes for detection, response, and recovery strategies

Stronger AI security hinges on collaboration

The collaboration between industry leaders like SAP and Splunk is indicative of the growing recognition of the need for collective action in the face of AI threats. By pooling resources, knowledge, and expertise, organizations can develop more effective AI-enabled security products. This collaborative approach is essential for staying ahead of cyber adversaries who continually update their tactics.

As AI continues to shape our world, companies must have strong cybersecurity strategies to ensure that AI is used safely.

blogs/sap-and-mistral-ai-building-europe.body:
Blog

European Innovation, Enterprise Scale for AI: SAP and Mistral

Joining forces to deliver sovereign, enterprise, generative AI for the autonomous enterprise.

Pierpaolo VezzosiPublished on August 11, 2026

SAP and Mistral AI have teamed up to bring a sovereign, enterprise grade AI platform to Europe, with a particular focus on regulated industries and the public sector. Delivered as “Mistral on SAP Business AI Platform,” this joint solution is a key building block in SAP’s broader strategy for digital sovereignty for AI, giving customers choice from locally hosted AI all the way to SAP Sovereign Cloud.

A European partnership built for sovereignty

SAP and Mistral AI are two of Europe’s most important software innovators: SAP as the global leader in enterprise applications and business AI, and Mistral AI as a fast‑growing European AI model and platform provider headquartered in Paris. Together, they combine deep industry process expertise with state‑of‑the‑art generative AI to address the needs of European customers that must balance innovation with strict regulatory and sovereignty requirements.

The result is a partnership that is not only about embedding models, but about operating AI in a way that respects European rules, values, and control expectations around data, infrastructure, and operations.

What is “Mistral on SAP Business AI Platform”?

“Mistral on SAP Business AI Platform” is an out‑of‑the‑box solution where SAP hosts, operates, and supports Mistral’s AI models and products, available also on the SAP cloud infrastructure. Customers get access to Mistral Vibe and Studio through SAP Business AI Platform, enabling them to design, customize, and deploy AI agents and workflows that are deeply integrated with their SAP landscape.

The solution is based on a consumption model with a unified AI Unit metric and a single SAP contract, reducing the legal and operational complexity of dealing with multiple independent AI providers. SAP manages lifecycle, metering, and maintenance, so customers avoid infrastructure overhead while still retaining the deployment controls they need for sovereignty.

Designed for regulated industries and public sector, available for all

Regulated industries and public institutions face unique requirements around data residency, operational controls, security clearances, and compliance with regulations such as GDPR, NIS2, the EU AI Act, export controls, and cloud‑in‑country mandates. Mistral on SAP Business AI Platform is explicitly positioned to meet these needs by supporting different sovereignty levels, from secure public cloud to fully sovereign deployments on SAP infrastructure or certified partner environments.

For public sector and other highly regulated customers, the solution is planned to be delivered as well via SAP Sovereign Cloud by end of year, providing legal, operational, technical, and data sovereignty, backed by attestation and certification programs for handling sensitive or even classified government information. This gives ministries, regulators, healthcare providers, and critical‑infrastructure operators a pathway to adopt generative AI while keeping AI operations aligned with national and European rules.

Foundation for digital sovereignty for AI in Europe

SAP defines digital sovereignty for AI as the ability to use AI while maintaining control over where sensitive data is processed, who can access it, and how AI is operated, always in alignment with regional and industry regulations. In practice, that means reducing cross‑border exposure, strengthening governance and auditability, and allowing organizations to adopt AI without losing control of their most critical information assets.

Mistral on SAP Business AI Platform directly supports these outcomes by keeping AI data, prompts, models, and execution in‑region under SAP managed controls and by ensuring that SAP does not share customer data with third parties for model training. For Europe, and especially for Germany and France, this partnership is a strategic step toward “AI made in Europe,” aligning innovation with European digital‑sovereignty ambitions.

A spectrum of SAP solutions for digital sovereignty

The SAP–Mistral solution is one part of a broader portfolio of digital‑sovereignty options that can be tailored to each customer’s risk profile, regulatory context, and transformation roadmap. SAP offers multiple programs that span from regionally hosted AI to fully sovereign cloud deployments, so customers can choose the right level of control for each workload.

Key elements include:

  • Locally hosted AI with sovereign capabilities: AI workloads run within a specific region on SAP‑controlled or certified partner infrastructure, keeping data, prompts, models, and execution in‑region and reducing cross‑border exposure.  EU AI Cloud and Industrial AI Cloud are locally hosted regional initiatives that provide secure, compliant environments for AI, with governed access to LLMs
  • SAP Sovereign Cloud: a full‑fledged sovereign cloud offering that extends beyond data residency to legal, operational, technical, and data sovereignty through controls such as locally deployed control planes, restricted data flows, tenant isolation, local personnel, and locally aligned legal entities.

This range of options means customers can evolve over time, from early pilots on locally hosted AI to fully sovereign architectures where required, without having to redesign their entire landscape or compromise on innovation.

What this means for you

For business and IT leaders in regulated industries and public sector, the SAP–Mistral AI partnership offers a pragmatic path to adopt gen‑AI that is powerful, compliant, and sovereign by design. They can build AI agents that understand their specific SAP data and processes, automate complex workflows, and unlock new efficiencies, all while keeping AI under control and in‑region.

By choosing Mistral on SAP Business AI Platform as part of SAP’s broader digital‑sovereignty portfolio, European organizations can move faster with Artificial Intelligence on their own terms, aligned with their legal obligations and strategic autonomy goals.

Blog

Supply Chain trends for 2026 – From Agentic AI to orchestration

Supply chains will not get a year off in 2026. They will be expected to do more, with less, while becoming smarter, greener, and more resilient – all at the same time.

Richard HowellsPublished on February 3, 2026

From firefighting to orchestration

Over the past few years, many supply chains have lived in permanent crisis mode, reacting to disruptions as they happen rather than anticipating them. In 2026, leading organizations will start to move from firefighting to true orchestration – connecting planning, logistics, procurement, manufacturing, and the extended business network on a common, real‑time data foundation.​

In a recent Future of Supply Chain podcast episode, Domonik Metzgar, President & Chief Product Officer, Supply Chain Management at SAP described orchestration as “ that central intelligence that makes the multiple silos and departments work in much better harmony together for better decisions, faster time to response and ultimately better business outcomes”.

Instead of isolated functional decisions, companies will increasingly run synchronized cross departmental processes that span from demand sensing to last‑mile delivery. This shift will be powered by AI‑driven impact analysis that can simulate upstream and downstream consequences of a decision before it is executed, making trade‑offs between cost, service, risk, and sustainability explicit and measurable.​

As Metzger continued, “supply chain orchestration is the conductor. It is that central intelligence that makes the multiple silos, departments and companies work in harmony together for better decisions, faster time to response and ultimately better business outcomes”.

AI agents become team members

In 2026, AI in the supply chain will move from proof‑of‑concept experiments to embedded, agentic capabilities that sit inside core business processes. Instead of only delivering dashboards and recommendations, AI agents will identify risks and opportunities, propose workarounds, onboard suppliers, and even trigger corrective actions automatically within trusted guardrails.​

This does not replace planners and logistics experts; it augments them. The emerging pattern is “human plus machine,” where copilots embedded in planning workspaces and logistics processes handle repetitive analysis while people focus on scenario choice, exception management, and stakeholder communication. The supply chain of 2026 will be defined as much by the quality of its digital colleagues as by the skills of its human workforce.​   As Dominik Metzger explained, “for each persona, we are launching an AI assistant, so this is essentially an assistant made for that role with Agentic capabilities. What gets me super excited is when these agents actually collaborate with each other in a workflow.  So you may have a material planner assistant, a commercial assistant, and maybe a demand forecast assistant collaborating with each other to give you a recommendation on what you should do”.

Continuous Planning at the speed of business

Traditional planning cycles – monthly S&OP, weekly supply planning, daily scheduling – struggle to keep pace with volatility and geopolitical uncertainty. In response, planning capabilities are converging into unified, end-to-end models that support strategic, tactical, and operational decisions on one harmonized data set.​

More companies will work in a single planning environment that blends time‑series and order‑based planning, enabling rapid zoom‑in and zoom‑out from a board‑level scenario to a shop‑floor order impact in just a few clicks. Embedded simulations will let planners test disruptions – a port closure, a regulatory change, a demand spike – and instantly see implications for inventory, capacity, and service levels across multiple horizons.​

The supply Chain Balancing Act - Resilience meets cost discipline

One of the defining tensions of the last several years has been the pendulum swing between resilience and cost. After a period of “resilience at any price,” boards are once again asking hard questions about profitability, even as risks from climate events, cyberattacks, and geopolitical fragmentation increase.​

I see supply chains measured on “total value delivered”, not just on unit cost or inventory turns. That means balancing working capital, service levels, risk exposure, and sustainability outcomes in a single performance conversation – and expressing supply chain contributions in the language of growth, margin protection, and market share. Metrics and dashboards will evolve accordingly, tying operational KPIs directly to financial and ESG outcomes.​

The Three “R”’s - Regional, resilient, and regulated

The debate about reshoring, nearshoring, and multi‑sourcing will not be settled in 2026, but it will become more nuanced. Many companies have already started to regionalize critical value chains, yet the economics and timelines of structural moves remain challenging.​

Expect more hybrid models. For example, core production or critical inventory placed closer to demand, supported by digital risk assessment and dual sourcing strategies that can be activated when disruption thresholds are breached. At the same time, trade regulations, tariffs, and compliance requirements will grow more complex, making tax and regulatory optimization an integral part of network design rather than a late‑stage check.​

Sustainability is operationalized

Sustainability has moved from marketing slide to board mandate, but many organizations still struggle to operationalize it in day‑to‑day supply chain decisions. I expect to see emissions and circularity becoming native parameters in planning, logistics, and procurement, not after‑the‑fact reports.​

This means route selection, sourcing choices, and production planning will increasingly be optimized not only for cost and service, but also for carbon intensity and resource utilization. Digital networks connecting buyers, suppliers, logistics providers, and partners will improve data quality for Scope 3 emissions and enable collaborative programs for reduction, reuse, and recycling across the value chain.​

Cloud ERP as the control tower

All of these trends rely on a consistent, trusted view of data across the business. We are constantly seeing cloud ERP, tightly integrated with planning, manufacturing, and business networks, functioning as the digital backbone and de‑facto control tower for the intelligent, sustainable supply chain.​

Instead of stitching together dozens of disconnected tools, organizations will favor platforms that natively connect financials, logistics, procurement, and asset management, with embedded analytics and AI. This will reduce integration debt, accelerate innovation cycles, and enable new business models such as outcome‑based services, product‑as‑a‑service, and dynamic collaboration with partners in real time.​

The 2026 mandate to orchestrate don’t just operate supply chains

Looking ahead to 2026, the winners will be those who embrace AI as a team member, use unified planning to see around corners, balance resilience with cost and sustainability, and run all of this on a cloud‑based digital core that connects the extended value chain.​

Supply chain is no longer a backstage function; it is where customer promises, brand trust, and sustainable growth are delivered – or lost. The organizations that act now will be best positioned to turn uncertainty into competitive advantage.

To keep up with the latest trends, challenges and opportunities for supply chain executives, join me on the weekly, Future of Supply chain Podcast.

Blog

The digital thread: Closing the loop on growth opportunities

Discover why leading aerospace and defense firms see the digital thread as a strategic imperative

Dave BlatnerPublished on August 7, 2026

For aerospace and defense firms, the digital thread can’t wait

Aerospace and defense (A&D) manufacturers are entering one of the strongest growth cycles in recent memory. Rising defense budgets, growing geopolitical instability, and sustained investments in military modernization are creating significant opportunities. According to a report by Kearney, global annual revenue will approach $750 billion this year and exceed $900 billion by 2030.

Despite the opportunity, many A&D manufacturers continue to face persistent challenges as they compete for new contracts, including labor shortages, supply chain volatility, aging infrastructure, increasing program complexity, and more stringent regulatory requirements.

Production capacity or pricing alone won’t guarantee success. Rather, the winners in the A&D industry will be those organizations that can make faster, better-informed decisions across the enterprise. This requires a level of visibility and coordination that many A&D organizations still lack today.

The solution isn’t simply to increase IT investments. For years, A&D manufacturers have invested heavily in digital tools and enterprise systems. Despite this, critical information often remains fragmented across engineering, production, finance, supply chain, and sustainment functions, resulting in delayed decision-making, reduced transparency, and limited ability to anticipate program risks before they impact operations.

To close these gaps, organizations must connect information across the entire product ecosystem so that decisions made in one area immediately inform actions elsewhere. This continuous flow of contextualized information is known as the digital thread.

The digital thread represents a shift from isolated decision-making toward enterprise-wide lifecycle intelligence. For organizations seeking to compete in the next generation of defense programs, it is rapidly becoming a strategic necessity.

The silent cost of fragmented operations

A&D organizations have historically adopted an incremental, patchwork approach to digital transformation where each investment addressed a specific business need:

  • Engineering teams invested in product lifecycle management (PLM) platforms to manage product data.
  • Finance and operations teams implemented enterprise resource planning (ERP) systems.
  • Manufacturing organizations deployed manufacturing execution systems (MES) and shop-floor technologies.
  • Sustainment teams introduced specialized maintenance and field-service applications.

Few of these investments, however, were designed to operate as part of an integrated data architecture.

The cost of fragmented operations, invisible at first, inevitably surfaces as market pressures place more demands on real-time intelligence, appearing as:

  • Decision-makers who spend too much time reconciling conflicting reports.
  • Program managers who struggle to understand how engineering changes affect cost and schedule performance.
  • Manufacturing teams that must wait for engineering data to be manually translated across systems.
  • Sustainment organizations that lack insight into the design and production history of deployed assets

The underlying issue is rarely a lack of data; A&D organizations possess more information than ever before. The challenge is that critical context remains trapped inside functional silos.

The digital thread as an enterprise operating model

A digital thread creates a continuous, traceable flow of information across the product lifecycle—from concept and design through production, deployment, and sustainment. Data retains its context as it moves through the enterprise, allowing stakeholders to understand not only what happened, but why it happened and what is likely to happen next.

In contrast to traditional technology capabilities, a digital thread is better understood as an operating model for managing complex products and processes. It’s a departure from digital transformation initiatives of the past, from ERP modernization efforts to PLM deployments.

The digital thread reframes these investments as components of a broader enterprise capability. Rather than optimizing individual functions, organizations create a shared source of product intelligence that enables more synchronized decision-making across teams. The result is not simply greater clarity, but greater organizational agility to align with expanding and emerging opportunities.

The results to date have been hard to ignore. Organizations that establish a robust digital thread can improve schedule predictability by as much as 25%, reduce unplanned maintenance events by up to 30%, and dramatically reduce the manual effort required for program reporting and earned value management (EVM).1

Connecting engineering decisions to business outcomes

Let’s take a closer look at how the digital thread impacts design and development. Engineering organizations historically operate within specialized environments such as PLM, CAD, and model-based systems engineering platforms. Procurement, finance, supply chain, and program management functions, meanwhile, usually work from entirely different systems. This separation creates an intelligence gap between technical decisions and business consequences.

A seemingly routine engineering change can affect supplier qualifications, procurement timelines, production schedules, workforce requirements, and overall program cost. Yet those downstream implications frequently take weeks to become visible throughout the organization.

A digital thread fundamentally changes this dynamic. When engineering data is connected to operational and financial systems, stakeholders gain understanding into the broader impact of design decisions almost immediately. Manufacturing requirements remain synchronized with engineering intent, procurement teams receive earlier signals regarding sourcing implications, and program managers gain clearer insight into cost and schedule impacts before they escalate.

Organizations that strengthen these lifecycle connections have reported reductions of 20% to 30% in engineering change cycle times,1 accelerating the transition from concept to production while reducing costly rework. The strategic benefit is not merely speed, but the ability to make engineering decisions with a more complete understanding of operational, financial, and mission impacts.

Bringing production, finance, and program execution into alignment

Production environments operate in a constant state of change. Supplier delays, engineering revisions, workforce constraints, material shortages, and funding shifts can all influence program performance. Yet many executives still rely on reporting structures built around historical snapshots rather than current conditions.

This challenge is most keenly felt with government contracts, where earned value management, estimate-at-completion (EAC), and estimate-to-complete (ETC) metrics play a critical role in financial oversight. Without integrated operational data, these measures often require extensive manual reconciliation across multiple systems before leadership can act on them.

A digital thread allows for a more dynamic approach. By connecting manufacturing operations, program accounting, funding structures, and execution data, organizations can monitor performance as conditions evolve. Variances become visible earlier, forecasts become more reliable, and decision-makers gain greater confidence in both operational and financial reporting.

The shift is profound. Organizations that have implemented digital thread technologies have reported reductions of 30% to 50% in manual EVM reconciliation efforts while improving EAC forecast accuracy by 10% to 20%.1 Equally important, program management moves beyond explaining yesterday's performance and begins anticipating tomorrow's challenges.

Transforming sustainment into a strategic asset

For many defense programs, the cost of maintaining in-service equipment—known as sustainment—can account for as much as 70% of total program cost.1 Despite its importance, sustainment often remains one of the least integrated parts of the enterprise. Maintenance records, for example, may be separated from production history, or operational performance data may never reach engineering teams.

A digital thread closes this loop.

Linking field performance data with manufacturing history, engineering configurations, and supply information enables A&D organizations to gain a more complete understanding of asset behavior in operational environments. This enables predictive maintenance strategies, more effective spare-parts planning, and faster root-cause analysis of failures. Equally important, it provides engineering teams with a continuous feedback mechanism that can improve future designs.

With the aid of a digital thread, sustainment ceases to be a downstream support function and instead becomes an active driver of operational and financial performance. Organizations equipped with this kind of mature lifecycle awareness have seen reductions of 20% to 30% in unplanned maintenance events while improving readiness rates by 10% to 20%.1

Business area

Traditional fragmented environment

Digital thread environment

Engineering and design

Engineering data resides in PLM, CAD, and model-based systems with limited view into downstream impacts.

Engineering data is linked to operational and financial systems, enabling near real-time insight into business impacts.

Change management

Engineering changes can take weeks to reveal impacts on cost, schedule, suppliers, and production.

Stakeholders quickly understand the operational, financial, and program implications of design changes.

Manufacturing

Teams often wait for engineering data to be manually translated across systems.

Manufacturing requirements remain synchronized with engineering intent.

Procurement and supply chain

Sourcing implications are identified late, creating delays and uncertainty.

Procurement teams receive earlier signals regarding supplier and sourcing impacts.

Program management

Limited transparency into cost and schedule impacts until issues escalate.

Program managers gain proactive insight into cost, schedule, and execution risks.

Finance and earned value management reporting

Extensive manual reconciliation is required across multiple systems.

Integrated operational and financial data supports more dynamic monitoring and reporting.

Production operations

Decisions are based on historical snapshots and siloed reporting.

Performance can be monitored continuously as conditions evolve.

Sustainment and maintenance

Maintenance records, production history, and operational data remain disconnected.

Field performance, manufacturing history, and engineering configurations are linked.

Asset readiness

Reactive maintenance and limited failure visibility.

Predictive maintenance, faster root-cause analysis, and improved readiness.

Executive decision-making

Leaders spend time reconciling conflicting reports and data sources.

Leaders operate from a shared source of lifecycle intelligence.

Why the digital thread is an imperative for all executives

Digital thread initiatives often turn up first on a CIO’s radar because implementation involves systems, data, and integration. For CIOs, a digital thread provides a framework that turns isolated modernization projects into a coordinated enterprise capability.

But the value of digital thread investments extends well beyond the CIO's office. COOs, for example, stand to gain greater awareness across production, supply networks, and program execution from it. For CFOs, a digital thread can lead to greater forecasting confidence and stronger financial controls. For strategy leaders, benefits include increased competitiveness through better bid accuracy, lower program risk, and improved operational predictability.

More importantly, a digital thread establishes the foundation for the next phase of digital transformation. AI, automation, digital engineering, and predictive analytics all depend on trusted, contextualized, and consolidated data.

Without a digital thread, A&D organizations risk scaling their business intelligence on top of a fragmented foundation. With it, they gain the ability to automate decisions, identify emerging risks earlier, and execute with greater speed and precision.

The next decade will belong to enterprises that know how to leverage their lifecycle data

The aerospace and defense organizations best positioned to meet the rising tide of the future won’t simply be those with the biggest facilities or the largest workforces. They will be the organizations that know how to turn their data into a strategic differentiator.

As defense demand accelerates and program complexity grows, competitive advantage will increasingly be defined by decision velocity—the ability to translate information into action faster than your competitors. The digital thread provides the foundation for that decision velocity. More than a connectivity initiative, it establishes the data architecture needed to support predictive operations, autonomous workflows, AI-driven decision support, and mission-ready execution at scale.

The issue facing A&D leaders isn’t whether they’re capturing enough data. It’s whether that data can move across the enterprise with sufficient context, traceability, and intelligence to create measurable business value.

Those that solve this challenge will do more than merely participate in the industry's next growth cycle; they will define it.

If you’d like a detailed blueprint on how leading A&D organizations are building lifecycle data connectivity at enterprise scale, read the complete Kearney and SAP whitepaper, The digital thread imperative in aerospace and defense.

1Ameer Ali et al, The digital thread imperative in aerospace and defense, Kearney, May 7, 2026.

    Lead architect of SAP Cloud Application Services

    SAP Cloud Application Services: The Hidden Engine Behind Trusted Cloud Operations

Frequently asked questions

  • What are SAP Cloud Application Services?

    SAP Cloud Application Services are SAP’s application management offerings, delivered as service subscriptions designed for SAP private, public, and hybrid cloud contracts. These services run your entire solution landscape with practical, proactive support to help facilitate smooth daily operations.

  • What kind of support and expertise can customers expect from SAP Cloud Application Services?

    Customers can expect application management support that includes:

    • An application service manager as the primary point of contact, working closely with customers.
    • A service desk that processes all requests and ensures they are handled within the agreed service times.
    • A service delivery team that handles incident resolution, problems, change requests, service requests, and activity monitoring.
    • 24/7 support from the service desk and the delivery team, depending on contract terms.

  • What are the benefits of SAP Cloud Application Services?

    SAP Cloud Application Services help ensure smooth operation of your SAP private, public, and hybrid cloud solutions. Customers benefit from SAP’s expertise and experience in running digital business in real time and can adopt cloud solutions more quickly and efficiently, increasing customer satisfaction.

  • How can SAP Cloud Application Services increase profitability?

    Using SAP Cloud Application Services can increase profitability by improving user experience, delivering clearly defined services at fixed annual prices, customizing SAP solution management to your specific requirements, and handling technical and functional services end to end. The services are available globally and can be adapted to meet regional, language, sovereignty, and industry requirements.

  • Who should use SAP Cloud Application Services?

    SAP Cloud Application Services are designed for businesses running SAP solutions in private, public, or hybrid clouds that want to strengthen their application management capabilities, improve operational efficiency, and redirect existing personnel to more strategic priorities—including analyzing and adopting SAP innovations.

  • How does SAP ensure data security and compliance in SAP Cloud Application Services?

    SAP Cloud Application Services are delivered by certified experts who follow global security frameworks. The offerings are designed to meet regional and industry-specific compliance requirements, including GDPR, GxP, and EU access, and support audit readiness and data protection best practices.

  • Which SAP cloud solutions are eligible for SAP Cloud Application Services?

    SAP Cloud Application Services support most application areas within SAP Business Suite, along with SAP Business Technology Platform, SAP Business Data Cloud, SAP SuccessFactors, and SAP Customer Experience. These services also support SAP Business AI, including Joule. Solutions deployed on hyperscaler-hosted and SAP-managed infrastructures are supported globally.

  • How do SAP Cloud Application Services work with success plans?

    Success plans and SAP Cloud Application Services are designed to complement each other across your cloud journey. Success plans provide advisory and activation services, including strategic guidance, defined objectives, and enablement. SAP Cloud Application Services focus on operations, delivering day-to-day application management and continuous optimization.

    Together, they create a comprehensive framework: Success plans help you plan and activate your SAP strategy, while SAP Cloud Application Services help ensure your solutions run smoothly in production, aligning strategic goals with operational excellence.

Frequently asked questions

  • What is SAP Services and Support?

    SAP Services and Support offers customers the unified, enterprise-wide engagement needed to maximize the value of individual applications, accelerate complex transformations, and consistently adopt new innovations and AI, all while keeping business-critical systems running smoothly.

  • What is a success plan?

    Success plans are tiered engagements that provide a rich set of features ranging from self-guided resources to a personalized partnership. Customers can choose the plan they need to ensure their continuous success.

  • Why has the SAP Services and Support portfolio evolved?

    We’ve evolved the SAP Services and Support portfolio to deliver a simpler, more powerful experience that meets your individual needs while driving measurable results.

    Whether you are a new or existing SAP customer, you expect choice, clarity, and simplicity, backed by a consistent experience across your SAP journey. And you can expect predictable costs and reliable ROI—not only at go-live, but throughout your entire innovation journey with SAP.

    With our success plans, you can expect a stronger, tiered engagement model. Designed for transparency, speed, and flexibility, the plans make adopting SAP solutions—and continuously innovating with them—easier than ever.

  • Does a customer need to subscribe to the same success plan across SAP Business Suite solutions?

    We offer customers the flexibility to choose the success plan they want to subscribe to for each cloud solution depending on the level of engagement they require. Customers are not limited to one success plan across all their solutions. Instead, they can pick the success plan that suits them for each solution area. For example, a customer can choose the Advanced Success Plan for SAP Customer Experience and the Max Success Plan for finance and spend management.

Frequently asked questions

To get SAP-certified, choose a certification that aligns with your role or career goals and prepare using SAP Learning Hub, SAP's recommended learning experience. SAP Learning Hub provides learning content, live sessions, hands-on practice systems, and four exam attempts to help you build the skills and confidence needed to succeed. You can also purchase a standalone certification exam attempt.

 

For more information, see our step-by-step guide to SAP Certification.

An SAP Certification exam is a comprehensive evaluation of the skills required for a specific SAP solution or role. 

 

Assessments are short, non-proctored quizzes with unlimited attempts that focus only on the knowledge introduced between software releases.

 

These assessments help learners stay up to date with the latest solution updates and maintain their certification. Assessments to stay certified are available exclusively through an SAP Learning Hub subscription.

SAP Certification pricing varies based on your certification pathway. You can purchase standalone SAP Certification exam attempts or an SAP Learning Hub subscription that includes certification attempts, guided preparation, hands-on practice, and certification maintenance support. Partners can log in to SAP PartnerEdge for partner-specific pricing information.

SAP Certification uses a practical, open-book exam format designed to assess how candidates apply SAP skills in realistic scenarios. Depending on the certification, exams may include system-based or scenario-based tasks supported by learning journeys, hands-on practice, and other preparation resources. 
 
Learn more about SAP Certification exam formats.

SAP Activate offers a structured approach to implementing SAP solutions supported by ready-to-run best practice processes, tools, and AI-assisted guidance.

 

The framework’s task content—including setup guidance, enablement resources, templates and accelerators for fit-to-standard workshops, and detailed guidance for test sprints—is embedded in SAP Cloud ALM, offering detailed, role-based guidance for all project team members across every step of the implementation journey. 

The SAP Activate framework provides a structured approach to activation and implementation of SAP solutions with six distinct phases supported by best practices and tools. It builds on SAP’s strong foundation of fit-to-standard and clean core principles to assist customers with implementing robust and agile environments that enable continuous innovation.

The RISE with SAP Methodology encompasses a standardized framework, an integrated toolchain, and expert guidance to support your transition to the cloud. SAP Activate is the framework. It provides best practice and road map recommendations, guidelines, and checkpoints organized into six distinct phases.

The SAP Activate framework includes guidance that’s organized into six phases:

  1. Discover: Understand solution options and define the scope at a high level.
  2. Prepare: Finalize the project plan, set up the environment, and get the team aligned.
  3. Explore: Conduct fit-to-standard workshops and confirm the solution design.
  4. Realize: Configure, build, test, and validate the solution.
  5. Deploy: Cut over to the new system and transition to production.
  6. Run: Operate, support, and continuously optimize the solution.

 

The road map viewer in SAP for Me is the main hub for project teams—as well as customers, partners, and registered users—to access implementation road maps, deliverables, tasks, and accelerators such as templates and guides.

SAP Activate provides a structured framework, comprehensive support, and valuable resources that guide organizations through each phase of their adoption journey. This approach ensures that potential risks are identified and mitigated early, leading to a smoother and more predictable project outcome. Additionally, SAP Activate offers self-enablement resources, preconfigured business processes, AI-assisted guidance, fit-to-standard workshops, agile implementation cycles, and SAP Cloud ALM capabilities to further accelerate the process.

SAP Activate supports continuous adoption of new capabilities with minimal disruption through ready-to-run best practices that are updated regularly. The Run phase is also focused on supporting operations, optimizing processes, and enabling iterative improvements so teams can continuously innovate without needing a major reimplementation.

AI Readiness

SAP Business One brings AI into analytics, contextual assistance, ​and partner innovation, allowing each customer to choose the solution that meets that customer’s needs while also keeping users in control of shared data.​

Integration to SAP AI Core

Supports out of the box AI functionality as well as partner extensions in SAP Business One Web client; SAP AI Core setup and metered- consumption are separate from the SAP Business One license.​

AI User-Defined Query (AI UDQ): from plain language to reviewable SQL to a reusable dataset in the Web client. AI UDQs only read and analyze ​data without changing SAP Business One data.

Ask AI: contextual questions on values you select, answered as text in the Web client. Available in header and rows of most documents and master data records; ​ You choose which values are shared with SAP AI services.

Partners extensions: - Inviting partners to leverage SAP AI Core for developing the next generation of extensions.

MCP server (code samples)

Support for AI agent adoption with partner extensions​.

Rich portfolio of AI partner extensions for SAP Business One is available

Financial management

Accounting

Automate the handling of key accounting processes, such as journal entries, accounts receivable, and accounts payable.

Align your operations to the needs of modern consumers, so you can anticipate, plan, and manage demand and deliver the consumer goods and products shoppers crave.

Manufacturing

Meet customer demand and develop new revenue streams by shrinking supply chain costs, speeding time to profit, shortening cycle times, and minimizing scrap and rework.

Deliver consistent, high-value services by establishing a repeatable process for service delivery while improving resource planning, project management, and billing.

Give consumers the products, information, and personalized experiences they want by harnessing real-time customer and point-of-sale insights and optimizing operations.

Respond to customer and supplier demand with flexible, tightly integrated processes, while improving your business from planning to inventory and supply chain management.

Mobile apps

Manage leads, customer accounts, view stock, and place an order with your iOS or Android mobile device. Designed for busy sales teams on the move, SAP Business One mobile apps give immediate access to the most relevant information to run your business from anywhere, anytime.

Create, process, and update marketing documents and master data, including approval processes. SAP Business One, Web client enables activity creation and tracking and provides sophisticated charting capabilities and predefined analytics, regardless of deployment method.

products/erp/digitization-vs-digitalizat.description: Get a clear, practical overview of the differences between digitization and digitalization and their impact on accelerating digital transformation in business.
products/erp/digitization-vs-digitalizat.body:
What Is

Digitization vs. digitalization in digital transformation

Digitization and digitalization aren't the same—knowing the difference is crucial for transformation.

Updated on January 26, 2026

Digitization vs. digitalization: Key differences

Before exploring the broader impact of digital transformation, it’s essential to distinguish between two often-confused concepts: digitization and digitalization. The difference is more than semantic—it helps organizations understand whether they’re simply modernizing infrastructure or actively transforming how they work and compete.

What is digitization? Definition and examples

Digitization is the process of converting analog information into digital formats, enabling data to be stored, accessed, and processed by computers and digital systems.

In a business context, digitization often involves transforming physical records like printed invoices, contracts, or handwritten notes into structured digital data that can be integrated into enterprise systems. Scanning paper-based customer files into a digital database or converting analog sensor readings into digital signals for real-time monitoring are common digitization practices.

The origins of digitization trace back to the early days of computing, when businesses began using mainframes to store and process data previously kept in filing cabinets or on paper ledgers. Over time, the practice evolved alongside advances in hardware and software, becoming more sophisticated and widespread.

Today, digitization is a foundational step in digital transformation, enabling organizations to unlock efficiencies, improve data accessibility, and lay the groundwork for automation and analytics. While it doesn’t inherently change how a business operates, it is a critical enabler for more advanced digital initiatives.

What is digitalization? Definition and examples

Digitalization is the use of digital technologies to transform business operations, models, and customer experiences.

Once digitization has converted analog data into digital formats, digitalization leverages that digital data to drive innovation, efficiency, and strategic change. In practice, this might look like automating supply chain workflows using AI, implementing predictive analytics to optimize customer engagement, or redesigning service delivery through digital platforms.

The concept of digitalization gained momentum as businesses began to realize that simply having digital data wasn’t enough—they needed to use it to rethink how they operate. Early examples include enterprise resource planning (ERP) systems that integrated and centralized data across business departments, enabling more agile decision-making.

Today, digitalization is central to digital transformation strategies, encompassing cloud computing, machine learning, Internet of Things (IoT), and more. It’s not just about tools—it’s about reimagining processes to be faster, smarter, and more responsive to change.

Why the distinction between digitization and digitalization matters

Understanding the difference between digitization and digitalization is crucial for organizations aiming to thrive in a digital-first world. While digitization is a critical transformation step, it is largely technical and does not intrinsically alter an organization’s operations.

Digitalization, on the other hand, involves using digital tech to transform business processes, models, and customer experiences. It’s about leveraging digital tools to create new value, improve efficiency, and enable innovation.

The distinction matters because conflating the two can lead to missed opportunities and misaligned strategies. A company that focuses solely on digitization may end up with digital records but still rely on outdated workflows. In contrast, digitalization encourages rethinking how work gets done—automating tasks, enabling remote collaboration, and using data to drive decisions.

Recognizing this difference helps leaders set clearer goals, allocate resources more effectively, and measure progress in terms of transformation rather than just conversion.

Why digitalization is important for businesses

The technologies underlying digitalization continue to evolve rapidly, even as they are being adopted throughout business and society. Digitalization, however, is not simply a matter of “more technology.” Digitalization is important because it unlocks new thinking and approaches in how a business perceives its role within its ecosystem and its opportunity for increased profitability. The technology is not an end in itself.

With digitalization in place, companies can begin to create new value chains and experiences that are collaborative, interactive, sustainable, and profitable.

Here are some examples of enterprises that have used digitalization to deliver tangible business value:

  • Nestlé, one of the world’s largest food and beverage companies, undertook a global IT transformation to standardize ERP systems and migrate to the cloud. The initiative delivered a 99.97% system availability, enabled one unified digital entry point for 275,000 employees, and moved over 1,200 TB of data to cloud infrastructure.
  • The Mercedes-AMG PETRONAS Formula One Team enhanced racing performance and resource efficiency using real‑time analytics and cost-cap management. By building a robust cloud environment, they optimized physical and financial operations while maintaining elite performance standards.
  • The band Coldplay launched an app to help minimize the environmental impact of its global concert tour and track fan travel-related carbon emissions. The app achieved over 1 million downloads, offered real-time sustainability insights, and encouraged greener travel choices across more than 150 countries.

Enabling technologies: Cloud, AI, IoT, and automation

Digitalization is powered by a set of transformative technologies that enable businesses to operate more intelligently, efficiently, and responsively, even while on the go:

  • Cloud computing: Provides scalable infrastructure and real-time access to data and applications, allowing organizations to break down silos and collaborate across geographies
  • AI: Enhances decision-making by analyzing vast datasets, identifying patterns, and automating complex tasks—from customer service chatbots to predictive maintenance
  • IoT: Connects physical assets to digital systems, enabling real-time monitoring, data collection, and remote control of equipment and environments
  • Automation: Streamlines repetitive processes, reduces human error, and accelerates workflows—freeing up teams to focus on strategic initiatives

Together, these technologies form the backbone of digitalization, enabling organizations to innovate, adapt, and scale in a fast-changing digital landscape.

Drive transformation and AI readiness

Learn what’s top-of-mind for CIOs when it comes to AI, ERP, and modernizing their IT landscape.

Read now

Business benefits of digitalization

Digitalization offers a wide range of strategic and operational benefits that can significantly enhance an organization’s competitiveness and agility. By integrating digital technologies into core business processes, companies can streamline workflows, reduce manual effort, and improve overall efficiency. For example, automating routine tasks such as invoice processing or inventory management not only saves time but also minimizes errors and frees up resources for higher-value work.

Beyond operational gains, digitalization enables better decision-making through real-time data access and advanced analytics. Businesses can respond more quickly to market changes, personalize customer experiences, and uncover new revenue opportunities.

Digitalization also supports scalability, allowing organizations to adapt and grow without being constrained by legacy systems. Ultimately, digitalization is not just about adopting new tools—it’s about creating a more responsive, data-driven, and innovative business environment that creates value through:

  • Improved productivity
  • Reduced risk
  • Increased scalability
  • Higher cross-regional consistency

Digitalization challenges and risks

While digitalization offers significant benefits, it also introduces challenges and risks that organizations must navigate carefully. Common hurdles include:

  • Integration complexity: Ensuring that new digital tools work seamlessly with existing infrastructure can require substantial time, investment, and expertise—especially when legacy systems are involved.
  • Market expectations of digitalized services: Companies face increasing pressure to provide more services in a digital form, such as online or mobile apps. This requires proactive planning to predict needs and pick strategies that future-proof the business for the next digital wave.
  • Technology overreach: Overreach can occur when businesses invest in tools without a clear strategy, often resulting in underutilized systems or fragmented processes.
  • Data security and privacy: As digital systems handle increasing volumes of sensitive information, organizations become more vulnerable to cyber threats and compliance issues—risks that they can’t afford to ignore.
  • Change management: Digitalization often requires shifts in culture, roles, and workflows, which can meet resistance from employees or leadership. Without clear communication and training, adoption may stall.

To mitigate these risks, businesses must approach digitalization with a well-defined roadmap, strong governance, and a focus on aligning technology with business goals.

How to move from digitization to digitalization: A roadmap

Moving from digitization to digitalization is not just a technical upgrade—it’s a strategic transformation. Digitization lays the groundwork, but digitalization builds on that foundation to reimagine how work is done, decisions are made, and value is delivered. For modern enterprises, this shift requires a clear roadmap that integrates technology with business goals.

  1. Cloud ERP
    The first step is investing in a cloud ERP. Whether you're a first-time buyer of an ERP system or want to migrate from an on-premises one, a cloud ERP enables scalable infrastructure, centralized data access, and real-time collaboration across teams and geographies. Cloud ERP platforms eliminate the limitations of on-premises systems and provide the flexibility needed to innovate quickly.
  2. Automation
    Next, organizations should implement automation through software, applications, and integrated systems. This includes automating repetitive tasks, streamlining workflows, and connecting systems to reduce friction and improve efficiency. Automation helps unlock the full potential of digitized data by making processes faster and more intelligent.
  3. Mobile enablement
    Going mobile is essential for enabling a modern, flexible workforce. Employees should be able to access platforms, perform tasks, and make decisions from smartphones or tablets—whether they’re in the office, on the road, or working remotely. Mobile access ensures continuity and responsiveness in a fast-paced business environment.
  4. Centralization on a global scale
    To operate globally, businesses must embrace centralization through synchronized databases, platforms, reporting portals, and live dashboards. This allows for unified management and oversight, eliminating time zones and physical location as barriers to decision-making and execution.
  5. AI integration
    Finally, organizations should leverage AI and modern technologies across every aspect of the business. From predictive analytics in financial planning to intelligent automation in supply chains and personalized customer experiences, AI enhances agility, insight, and innovation. Integrating these technologies into workflows, security protocols, and strategic planning ensures that digitalization delivers long-term value.

Measuring success: digitalization metrics and maturity models

Successfully transitioning from digitization to digitalization demands continuous measurement and evaluation. Organizations can track progress using digitalization metrics such as:

  • Process automation rates
  • System integration levels
  • Data accessibility
  • User adoption
  • Time-to-decision improvements

These indicators help assess how effectively digital tools are transforming operations and delivering value.

To gain a broader view, many enterprises use digital maturity models. These frameworks evaluate an organization’s digital capabilities across dimensions like:

  • Strategy
  • Culture
  • Technology
  • Customer experience

Maturity levels typically range from basic digitization, such as digital records and isolated tools, to advanced digitalization, including AI-driven decision-making and fully integrated platforms. By benchmarking against these models, businesses can identify gaps, prioritize investments, and align digital initiatives with long-term goals.

Digitalization and the broader digital transformation journey

Digitalization is a critical phase within the larger arc of digital transformation, using data converted via digitization to enhance and automate business processes. Digital transformation encompasses a more holistic reinvention of how an organization operates, competes, and delivers value in a digital world.

True digital transformation involves rethinking business models, customer engagement strategies, and organizational culture. It’s not just about adopting new technologies—it’s about aligning those technologies with strategic goals, fostering innovation, and building resilience.

Digitalization serves as the bridge between foundational digitization and full-scale transformation, enabling businesses to move from simply having digital tools to using them in ways that fundamentally reshape operations and outcomes.

By understanding where digitalization fits within this journey, organizations can better assess their current maturity, identify gaps, and chart a path forward that leads to sustained growth, agility, and relevance in an increasingly digital economy.

FAQs

  • What is digital enablement?

    Digital enablement refers to equipping an organization with the tools, technologies, and capabilities needed to operate effectively in a digital environment. It involves preparing systems, processes, and people to adopt and benefit from digital solutions.

  • What is digital technology?

    Digital technology encompasses electronic tools, systems, devices, and resources that generate, store, or process data. Examples include cloud computing, artificial intelligence, mobile applications, and IoT devices—all of which support digital transformation.

  • Are there disadvantages to digitalization?

    Yes, digitalization can introduce challenges such as cybersecurity risks, high implementation costs, and resistance to change. Without proper planning and training, organizations may struggle with integration or fail to realize the full value of their digital investments.

  • What is the ROI of digitalization?

    The return on investment (ROI) from digitalization varies by industry and implementation, but it often includes increased efficiency, reduced operational costs, improved customer experiences, and faster decision-making. Long-term ROI also comes from enhanced agility and innovation.

  • When is digitization enough vs. when do you need to digitalize?

    Digitization is sufficient when the goal is to preserve or access information more efficiently—such as scanning documents or converting records. Digitalization becomes necessary when an organization wants to transform its operations, utilizing digital tools to automate, optimize, and innovate across processes.
