Overview

SAP Ariba Sourcing software features

Request a demo
Download solution brief

Simplified sourcing intake

Streamline sourcing projects with efficient capture and conversion of project information for faster execution.

Execute sourcing projects from initial request to RFx delivery with a solution that helps you:

  • Easily capture sourcing project information and requirements with an intuitive intake form.

  • Receive sourcing requests from integrated systems and convert them into sourcing projects, propagating associated information to the new RFx document.

  • Collect structured data from casual users, ensuring all necessary details are captured.

AI‑assisted sourcing from request to award

Unify sourcing intake, event creation, and award with AI-‑generated recommendations that increase productivity, accelerate decisions, and streamline execution.

Enhance productivity with advanced AI and machine learning capabilities that help you:

  • Drive better sourcing outcomes by creating events faster with AI-generated content recommendations, comparing best-matched suppliers and bids, and tracking progress and pricing in real time.

  • Use Joule to navigate quickly to key workflows such as sourcing requests, project creation, and task management.

  • Reduce manual effort and accelerate processes by automating routine tasks such as bid reminders, event status checks, and approvals.

Supplier discovery

SAP Business Network Discovery is integrated with SAP Ariba Sourcing, making it easier to find and select the best suppliers.

Easily connect with reliable, diverse suppliers worldwide with a network that allows you to:

  • Find alternative sources during disruptions, uncover new supplier opportunities with speed, and drive competitive pricing.

  • Search for suppliers based on specific industry, item, or service needs.

  • Find robust and trusted information in supplier profiles including certifications; environmental, social, and governance (ESG) data; and assessments.

  • Select top suppliers and add them directly to your sourcing event—without leaving the event screen.

Supplier network collaboration

Collaborate securely on SAP Business Network to boost efficiency and streamline workflows.

Explore capabilities that help you find, evaluate, and engage the right suppliers—all in one connected experience—to:

  • Invite your strategic suppliers to participate in sourcing events by joining the network and to share data and proprietary information in a secure environment.

  • View detailed supplier profiles and use collaboration tools to request pricing or availability.

  • Use filters to refine supplier searches by category, keywords, certifications, and sustainability criteria.

WalkMe for SAP Ariba Sourcing

Stay focused, confident, and prepared for what’s next though integration of WalkMe with guided sourcing for intelligent, in-workflow guidance.

Get step-by-step guidance for faster, smarter sourcing that helps you:

  • Enhance task completion, reduce errors, and accelerate processes with detailed walkthroughs, contextual guidance, and automated data entry.

  • Identify workflow bottlenecks, pain points, and inefficiencies through advanced analytics to streamline tasks and eliminate unnecessary steps.

  • Guide users with personalized messages and a conversational interface, delivering task-specific support for a more intuitive and engaging experience.

Bid analysis and optimization

Use AI to compare scenarios, optimize awards, and select strategies that maximize value.

Accelerate sourcing decisions with AI and natural language capabilities that let you:

  • Compare bids with advanced filters and confidently trigger single or split awards.

  • Extract key insights from supplier responses with AI-assisted bid summaries that surface risks, opportunities, and anomalies in real time.

  • Optimize awards using a natural language–based scenario setup.

  • Align stakeholders by sharing constraints, using preconfigured optimization templates, and evaluating multiple scenarios with clear, side-by-side comparisons.

SAP Ariba Category Management is a solution that digitalizes and streamlines the development, execution, and monitoring of category strategies. Built on SAP Business Technology Platform, the solution provides category analytics, process guidance, analysis frameworks, and system-enabled recommendations that help procurement organizations move rapidly toward intelligence-driven category management and improved spend management performance.

Because SAP Ariba Category Management is natively integrated with the SAP Ariba Sourcing, SAP Ariba Contracts, and SAP Spend Control Tower solutions, as well as other procurement solutions, it delivers a smooth user experience across source-to-pay processes without requiring expensive and time-consuming point-to-point integrations.

 

SAP Ariba Sourcing offers valuable tools to develop your sourcing strategy. SAP Ariba Category Management is built with a common data layer that forms the foundation for comprehensive analytics, insights, and opportunity analysis.

 

Category profiling capabilities, guided strategy frameworks, system-recommended opportunities, and integrated execution and tracking of metrics enable you to create and attain spend management goals with a high degree of speed and efficiency.

SAP Ariba Category Management is natively integrated with the guided sourcing capability for SAP Ariba Sourcing, allowing category managers to create a guided sourcing project from an initiative in SAP Ariba Category Management. They can also navigate to the guided sourcing user interface from SAP Ariba Category Management to execute sourcing projects. Task progression of the guided sourcing project is visible from the SAP Ariba Category Management initiative screen. Active projects are also visible in the planning calendar on the workbench and on the active projects screen.

 

Beyond this, SAP Ariba Category Management is fully integrated with and allows for free flow of information from SAP Ariba Contracts, SAP Ariba Supplier Lifecycle and Performance, SAP Ariba Supplier Risk, and SAP Ariba Spend Analysis.

You can either manage the process on your own or by purchasing additional SAP services or partner services.

What is SAP Ariba Direct Materials Sourcing for Automotive and Industrial Manufacturing in SAP S/4HANA?

It is direct procurement software that helps solve industry-specific source-to-contract problems by streamlining the process and integrating it with engineering, supply chain, and payables workflows.

Place procurement at the center of the product lifecycle and integrate it with design and supply chain flows through:

  • NPDI planning and design collaboration to accelerate time to market

Operationalize the complex terms and pricing conditions of procurement contracts and long-term agreements without the cost of system and data integration.

products/spend-management/services-procu.title: What Is Services Procurement? Benefits and Strategies | SAP
products/spend-management/services-procu.description: Services procurement focuses on how companies source, manage, and optimize external service providers to fill skill gaps and accelerate business goals.
products/spend-management/services-procu.body:
What Is

What is services procurement?

Services procurement oversees how companies source and manage external service providers.

Updated on May 28, 2026

Services procurement: An overview

Services procurement refers to the hiring and managing of external service providers to support internal teams. These partners focus on people-based services like consulting, technical support, or maintenance. Today, more businesses than ever depend on outside expertise to fill operational gaps. This approach gives companies flexible access to specialized capabilities for both short-term projects and ongoing functions.

Why services procurement matters?

In today’s competitive climate, companies need greater workforce agility to stay ahead. But building specialized in-house teams can be challenging for many organizations. According to research from Ardent Partners, 73% of businesses report difficulty finding and hiring qualified candidates, and 71% say a tight labor market limited their talent acquisition strategies.1

Services procurement helps organizations overcome these constraints. Partners offer streamlined access to talent and tools purpose-built for specific business needs. When done well, services procurement empowers organizations to:

  • Save time and costs: Outsourcing to specialized providers often saves time and costs compared to building new in‑house teams from scratch.
  • Boost efficiency: Providers take on time‑consuming work so internal teams can stay focused on high‑value initiatives.
  • Improve project outcomes: Extra support empowers teams to keep projects on schedule, on budget, and focused on business goals.
  • Drive innovation and growth: External experts introduce fresh insights and niche capabilities that accelerate new ideas and business expansion.

Services procurement vs. contingent labor vs. traditional procurement

Services procurement is just one part of the broader procurement role—responsible for securing all the resources businesses need to operate and grow. Together, these procurement processes form a complete picture of enterprise spend and supplier engagement.

Traditional procurement

Traditional procurement refers to the purchase of physical goods that organizations need to function. This includes both:

  • Direct procurement of raw materials used for production
  • Indirect procurement of supplies for day-to-day operations

This type of procurement prioritizes sourcing goods at the right price and quality standards, while meeting deadlines.

Services procurement

Services procurement focuses on securing an external workforce with specialized skills to target specific business needs. Instead of buying goods, companies contract providers to complete defined tasks or projects. This approach is used when businesses need expert support that directly contributes to their goals.

Contingent labor

Contingent labor refers to temporary workers from staffing agencies or talent suppliers. These workers help fill short‑term capacity needs but are not company employees. The focus is on managing their assignments, compliance, and hours worked rather than project outcomes.

Service procurement in action

See how Energy Queensland optimizes its contingent workforce with SAP Fieldglass solutions.

Watch the video

Types of services procurement

Services procurement takes several forms depending on the project scope, flexibility, and target outcomes. Each format offers companies a different approach to defining work, tracking progress, and structuring payments.

Statement of work

Statement of work (SOW) engagements clearly outline up front what work needs to be done, when it’s due, and how success will be measured. Payments are tied to completed deliverables—not hours worked.

Best for: Projects with well‑defined goals and clear expectations, such as system implementations, marketing campaigns, or audits.

Time and materials

Under time-and-materials agreements, companies pay for the actual hours worked and any materials used. This model offers organizations more flexibility when project scopes shift or when specialized skills are needed quickly. Stronger controls also help keep spending on track.

Best for: Work that may evolve over time, such as research, discovery phases, or short‑term capacity support.

Milestone‑based contracts

Milestone‑based contracts break down a project into stages, with payment issued after each approved milestone. This approach relies on regular checkpoints to ensure work stays on schedule, on budget, and meets quality expectations.

Best for: Multiphase projects like system rollouts, integrations, or transformation initiatives.

Managed services

Managed services transfer ongoing responsibility for a specific business function to an external provider under a long‑term agreement. The provider commits to executing the operational responsibilities, freeing internal teams to focus on higher-value strategic work.

Best for: Ongoing operations such as IT support, customer service, facilities management, and marketing.

The services procurement lifecycle

The services procurement lifecycle should follow a structured framework for sourcing, managing, and completing work delivered by external service providers. By breaking the process into clear, repeatable stages, organizations can streamline collaborations, reduce risk, and ensure each engagement delivers real operational value.

Identify procurement needs

Set a solid foundation for supplier relationships by pinpointing what work needs attention and what outcomes matter most. Whether the collaboration lasts a few weeks or several years, clear requirements help teams set budgets, choose the right suppliers, and avoid confusion later.

Evaluate and select service providers

Compare different potential service providers to choose the one best suited for the role. The right choice can improve performance quality and reduce risk for both short-term projects and ongoing operations. Teams should evaluate experience, pricing, capacity, and past performance to make sure suppliers deliver consistently.

Negotiate and confirm service contract

Formalize the agreement with the service partner, outlining the project scope, timelines, pricing models, and responsibilities. A clear contract protects both parties and sets the tone for the contract duration, whether brief or long-term. Companies should establish measurable goals, define how progress will be tracked, and outline how changes or issues will be handled.

Onboard and integrate service suppliers

To streamline the launching process, give service providers access to the necessary tools, systems, and contacts. Timely onboarding gives short-term providers a faster jump start, while allowing long-term partners to integrate smoothly into ongoing processes. A simple kickoff meeting helps confirm goals, expectations, and communication routines.

Monitor supplier performance and risk exposure

Measure progress using the metrics defined in the contract. Evaluate whether work meets quality standards, supports business goals, and stays within budget and on schedule. This step is vital for mitigating any operational delays or budget issues.

Approve service vendor payments

Review completed deliverables, hours, or milestones before issuing payment. Confirm that invoices reflect the contract terms and the value delivered. Maintain clear records to support financial accuracy and audit readiness.

Close and review projects

After work is complete—or at regular intervals for ongoing providers—review the results and document performance. This ensures a clean handoff and closure for short-term work and supports continuous improvement for more long-term partnerships. Companies should record what worked well to improve future collaborations.

Common services procurement challenges

Despite the strategic value of external service providers, many organizations still struggle to manage them effectively. Eventually, inadequate sourcing and management can turn these partnerships from assets to potential liabilities. Here are common hurdles to consider when building external collaborations.

  • Lack of visibility: Teams may struggle to ensure projects meet expectations without clear insights into service providers’ progress and performance metrics.
  • Difficulty tracking deliverables: Limited monitoring of milestones and outputs means teams may miss early signs of delays or quality issues.
  • Compliance and security exposure: Insufficient oversight of supplier access, credentials, and training increases exposure to regulatory and security gaps.
  • Budget overruns and timeline slippage: Poorly defined scopes and weak controls allow projects to drift off track, leading to missed deadlines and overspending.

Best practices checklist for services procurement

External service providers are a powerful driver for business productivity, growth, and innovation. However, companies need a clear services procurement strategy to maximize these benefits. Here are a few key steps that help organizations get better results from their suppliers.

  • Standardize sourcing processes: Use consistent criteria to assess experience, capabilities, pricing models, and past performance to select providers who best fit business needs.
  • Maintain consistent communication: Schedule regular check‑ins and progress updates to keep work aligned with expectations and address issues before they escalate.
  • Track performance with objective metrics: Monitor progress against milestones, quality standards, timelines, and budgets to identify risks and adjust plans as needed.
  • Enforce compliance and access controls: Verify that providers have the right credentials, training, and system access to support secure, compliant collaboration.
  • Use procurement technology: Deploy centralized platforms and efficiency tools to unify sourcing, performance tracking, compliance checks, and communication across all providers.

Technology supporting services procurement

Today, digital tools optimize every stage of the services procurement process—offering greater visibility, automation, and data-driven insights. Here are a few ways that modern services procurement solutions improve efficiency and support strategic decision-making.

Automated sourcing and contracts

Automation helps teams move through supplier sourcing and contract reviews faster. These tools can assist with preparing SOWs, creating sourcing events, and comparing proposals. By reducing repetitive steps, these solutions shorten cycle times and confirm contracts stay consistent and aligned with project expectations.

Spend analytics and reporting

Analytics tools consolidate service spend and activity data to show where money goes, how providers perform, and where cost‑saving opportunities may exist. Real‑time dashboards and impact analysis allow stakeholders to monitor milestones, quality, and budget variances, enabling quick course correction.

Supplier and risk management tools

These tools enable organizations to flag potential service-provider risk factors. Dashboards, risk analysis features, and performance evaluations make it easier to spot delays, compliance issues, or other concerns early. With stronger visibility, teams can address challenges sooner and maintain more reliable partnerships.

Vendor management systems

Vendor management systems (VMS) act as central hubs for managing service providers, combining sourcing, onboarding, progress tracking, and spend information on one platform. By unifying relevant data and processes, VMS platforms streamline vendor monitoring and communication. With a single source of truth, procurement teams can smoothly coordinate with finance and HR. Integrated tools also enhance related tasks such as compliance checks, contract management, and budget analysis.

AI

AI supports services procurement by automating routine work and turning large amounts of data into practical insights. Modern AI agents further enhance this by autonomously handling more complex tasks behind the scenes, such as analyzing bids, summarizing supplier information, and generating SOW contracts. These capabilities allow teams to spend less time on supplier management tasks and more time on higher‑value activities.

Turning services procurement into a strategic advantage

A clear strategy can turn services procurement from routine transactions into real business assets. With clear processes, performance metrics, and modern tools like analytics, automation, and AI, companies can channel outside expertise toward their highest‑value goals. Ultimately, companies can remain resilient against shifting markets and drive new opportunities forward.

FAQ

  • What is services procurement?

    Services procurement is the process of sourcing, managing, and optimizing work delivered by external service providers. This process helps organizations access specialized skills, improve performance visibility, and manage spend more effectively.

  • Why is services procurement important?

    Businesses increasingly rely on external expertise to fill skill gaps and support critical initiatives. Effective services procurement helps reduce costs, increase operational efficiency, and ensure project outcomes stay aligned with business goals.

  • What types of work fall under services procurement?

    Services procurement covers project‑based or outcome‑based work—such as IT services, consulting, marketing, maintenance, or repair services.

  • How does services procurement differ from contingent labor management?

    Services procurement focuses on outcome-centric engagements, while contingent labor management uses temporary workers paid by the hour. Services procurement tracks deliverables while contingent labor tracks hours and compliance.

  • What technology helps improve services procurement?

    Common tools include vendor management systems (VMS), AI and AI agents, automated sourcing workflows, spend analytics, and risk and compliance monitoring. These tools streamline sourcing, improve visibility, and support smarter decision‑making.

  • How does services procurement reduce costs?

    By clearly defining scope, improving spend management, and helping teams source the right expertise at the right price, services procurement minimizes overspending, reduces contract leakage, and ensures organizations only pay for work that meets set targets.

1Christopher J. Dwyer, Innovating Workforce Agility, Ardent Partners, February 2026.

What is SAP Strategic Procurement?

SAP Strategic Procurement is an integrated solution that bundles sourcing, contracting, and supplier management to streamline the source-to-contract process.

Running these procurement capabilities together means:

  • Negotiated savings flow directly into contracts.

  • Contract terms are monitored against what suppliers deliver.

  • Supplier data is visible at every stage.

Key benefits

Increase savings and spend under management (SUM)

Run optimized sourcing events, analyze bids against business objectives, and model award scenarios to negotiate better outcomes.

Improve consistency and compliance

Author and execute contracts with standardized templates, managed clause libraries, and automated approval workflows. Monitor compliance against contracted terms throughout the agreement lifecycle.

Engage suppliers through a structured, data-driven process that supports qualification, performance evaluation, and ongoing development within a single shared system.

Turn connected data into smarter decisions

Link sourcing, contracting, and execution so every outcome informs the next decision and expanding data continuously sharpens AI-driven recommendations.

Translate awarded terms into contracts and enforce them consistently across channels to realize savings, reduce risk, and ensure compliance.

  • Track obligations, milestones, and renewals automatically.

  • Assess and qualify suppliers based on category, region, and business unit.

  • Manage supplier performance with a centralized information portal.

  • Streamline supplier onboarding processes, including workflows and approvals, while assessing compliance and mitigating supply risk.

SAP Strategic Procurement is designed for organizations seeking a unified strategic sourcing and source-to-contract solution, instead of siloed e-sourcing and contract lifecycle management (CLM) and software lifecycle management (SLM) tools that don’t share data. It’s a strong fit if your team is losing savings between negotiation and contract, lacks supplier intelligence and risk visibility, or spends more time building RFx events than making strategic award decisions grounded in contract, market, and supplier data.

SAP Strategic Procurement includes three products: SAP Ariba Sourcing, SAP Ariba Contracts, and SAP Ariba Supplier Lifecycle and Performance. Together, they cover the full source-to-contract process: running sourcing events and analyzing bids, authoring and managing contracts, onboarding, and monitoring supplier performance.

A connected source-to-contract process delivers increased savings, accelerated source-to-contract cycles, improved supplier collaboration, and proactive risk and compliance monitoring.

Yes. SAP Strategic Procurement runs on the SAP Business AI Platform and can integrate with non–SAP ERP environments. It provides sourcing, contracting, and supplier management capabilities to organizations regardless of their ERP landscape.

SAP Strategic Procurement is the source-to-contract layer within SAP's Autonomous Spend Management domain—one of five functional domains in SAP's Autonomous Enterprise vision.

 

Most enterprise AI gets stuck in pilot mode because it lacks business context, connected data, and governance. SAP's position is that its combination of deep process knowledge, semantically rich business data, and enterprise-grade AI governance solves all three.

products/acquired-brands.html.body:
Acquired Brands and Companies

Acquired brands

Acquired brands and companies

Every day, we invest in the development of our products and technologies to improve the speed and number of innovations we bring to market. But we also acquire targeted, strategic technology and software to augment our broad portfolio and improve our coverage in critical markets. With this approach, we strive to best support our customers’ demand for simplified operations.

AppGyver Oy

In 2021, SAP acquired AppGyver Oy, a pioneer in no-code development platforms that enable users with no coding skills to build applications for Web and mobile use. SAP Build Apps evolved from SAP AppGyver and other SAP technologies. SAP Build Apps adds additional application-building capabilities for use in enterprises that address authentication, data integration, and lifecycle management needs. A community edition of SAP AppGyver remains available but does not include the features developed for use in enterprises.

Learn more about AppGyver Oy 

Ariba

In 2012, SAP acquired Ariba, a long-time leader in spend management software.  Our cloud-based solutions for strategic sourcing, contract management, procurement, and supplier management help companies control costs and minimize risks as they collaborate with suppliers on the purchase of goods and services. Their transactions take place over Ariba Network, where millions of trading partners do trillions of dollars in business every year. 

Learn more about SAP Ariba solutions 

Callidus Software

Known for its CallidusCloud lead-to-cash and configure, price, quote (CPQ) solutions, this sales performance management company was acquired by SAP in April 2018. Most of the CallidusCloud offerings are now in the SAP Sales Cloud portfolio and the SAP SuccessFactors HCM suite.

Learn how the CallidusCloud brand evolved into SAP Sales Cloud 

CallidusCloud Clicktools

CallidusCloud Clicktools, an enterprise survey software for businesses, is now part of the SAP Customer Experience portfolio.

Learn more about CallidusCloud Clicktools 

Coresystems

The crowdsourcing and field service management company was acquired by SAP in June 2018. Enabled by AI, Coresystems software provides advanced capabilities for field service scheduling, which are now in the SAP Service Cloud portfolio and part of the SAP Customer Experience solutions suite.

Learn how the Coresystems brand evolved into SAP Service Cloud 
Learn more about SAP Service Cloud 

Datahug

A leader in intelligent forecasting and pipeline management, is now part of the SAP Sales Cloud solution portfolio.

Learn more about Datahug 

Fieldglass

SAP Fieldglass, a longstanding leader in external workforce management and services procurement, is used by organizations around the world to find, engage, and manage all types of flexible resources. Our cloud-based, open platform has been deployed in more than 180 countries and helps companies transform how work gets done, increase operational agility, and accelerate business outcomes in a rapidly evolving, AI-driven world.

Learn more about SAP Fieldglass solutions 

Gigya

The leader of customer identity and access management solutions was acquired by SAP in September 2017. Its technology supports best practices for data privacy, compliance, and security in the SAP Customer Data Cloud portfolio and the SAP Customer Experience solutions suite.

Learn how the Gigya brand evolved into SAP Customer Data Cloud 
Learn more about SAP Customer Data Cloud 

hybris AG

The leading e-commerce and product content management software provider was acquired by SAP in June 2013 and initially available as SAP Hybris solutions. SAP Hybris solutions were integrated under the SAP masterbrand into the wider SAP Customer Experience solutions portfolio – a complete suite of industry-leading cloud solutions that delivers an end-to-end consumer journey.

Learn how the SAP Hybris brand evolved into SAP Customer Experience 
Learn more about SAP Customer Experience solutions 

LeanIX

In 2023, SAP acquired LeanIX,  a market leader for enterprise architecture and IT modernization. SAP LeanIX’s software-as-a-service solutions empower organizational transparency, enabling businesses to visualize, assess, and achieve their target IT architectures.

Learn more about SAP LeanIX 

Signavio

Signavio, acquired by SAP in 2021, helps organizations quickly understand, transform, and manage their business processes at scale. SAP Signavio solutions combine advanced process analytics and data mining to delivers fast, data-driven insights to your current business processes. These quantitative and qualitative insights form a solid foundation for continued improvement, secure cloud transformations, and accelerated innovation.

Learn more about SAP Signavio 

SuccessFactors

The cloud-native SAP SuccessFactors HCM suite spans core HR and payroll, talent management, HR analytics and workforce planning, and employee experience management. These leading solutions go beyond transactional human capital management (HCM) processes and deliver individualized experiences that enable employees to do their best and the business to be its best. Founded in 2001 and acquired by SAP in 2012, SAP SuccessFactors solutions are used by over 10,000 organizations in 200+ countries and territories.

Learn more about SAP SuccessFactors 

Sybase

Sybase is an industry leader in delivering enterprise and mobile software to manage, analyze and mobilize information. The company is recognized globally as a performance leader, proven in the most data-intensive industries and across all major systems, networks and devices. Sybase’s information management, analytics and enterprise mobility solutions have powered the world’s most mission-critical systems in financial services, telecommunications, manufacturing and government.
Date: May 2010. Purchase Price: US$ 5.8 billion.

Learn more about our database products 

WalkMe

WalkMe, acquired by SAP in 2024, pioneered the world’s leading digital adoption platform for organizations to navigate technological changes across any application or system. This platform integrates generative AI to deliver proactive, accessible, and actionable insights. WalkMe solutions are designed to simplify workflows, eliminate digital friction, and prioritize the user experience to foster fast and effective technology adoption.

Learn more about WalkMe

Frequently asked questions

Sustainability in finance is the practice of incorporating environmental, social, and governance (ESG) factors into financial strategy, planning, and reporting alongside traditional financial metrics. Rather than treating sustainability as a separate initiative, organizations integrate carbon, climate risk, and ESG data into core financial decisions, such as capital allocation, budgeting, and risk management, to better understand both long-term value and exposure to regulatory and market pressures.

ESG reporting software helps organizations collect, manage, and report on environmental, social, and governance data in compliance with regulatory frameworks such as CSRD and IFRS. It centralizes data from across the business, enables audit-ready reporting on metrics like emissions, energy use, and workforce diversity, and supports target setting and performance tracking. It replaces manual, spreadsheet-based processes with automated, verifiable data flows.

Carbon management and carbon accounting software enables organizations to measure, track, and reduce their greenhouse gas emissions across Scope 1, 2, and 3. It calculates corporate and product-level carbon footprints using actual operational data, rather than estimates, and supports compliance with emission reporting standards such as the GHG Protocol. Leading solutions embed carbon data directly into financial and procurement systems so that emissions become a factor in everyday business decisions.

 

Integrating sustainability into finance and business planning gives organizations a more complete picture of risk and performance. It connects emissions and ESG data to financial outcomes, enabling more informed decisions on capital allocation, supplier selection, and cost management. It also streamlines regulatory compliance by generating audit-ready sustainability disclosures from the same data used for financial reporting, reducing duplication and the risk of inconsistency across reports.

SAP offers an integrated sustainability portfolio—including SAP Sustainability Control Tower, SAP Sustainability Footprint Management, SAP Sustainability Data Exchange, and SAP Green Ledger—that embeds carbon and ESG data directly into ERP and financial processes. Because sustainability is integrated into SAP's core business systems rather than added as a separate tool, organizations can use actual transactional data to comply with regulations, produce auditable Scope 1, 2, and 3 emissions reports, and factor carbon costs into financial planning.

Connecting financial and ESG performance​

Since 2012, SAP has issued our annual Integrated Report to present a holistic view of our business performance across environmental, social, and governance (ESG) metrics.​

View the SAP Integrated Report 

Human rights at SAP

We're committed to respecting and promoting human rights across our operations, extended supply chain, and product lifecycle.

To integrate human rights considerations into our standard business practices, we take guidance from the United Nations’ Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights. We have a range of policies and procedures in place to ensure we treat everyone with respect and to mitigate human rights risks occurring in our own business and along the value chain. We also expect all our business partners to respect human rights and avoid complicity in any abuse.

Learn more about Human Rights at SAP 

Compliance, policies, and commitments

Ethics and compliance

Find out how we strive to undertake business with integrity by doing the right thing and following both the spirit and the letter of the law in all the markets we operate in.

Learn more 

Policies, codes, and commitments

Explore our policies and commitments to employing and safeguarding responsible business practices, based on respecting the Ten Principles of the UN Global Compact.

Learn more 

Energy and environmental management

Discover our environmental and energy management approach for achieving our targets.

Learn more 

Ethics and compliance at SAP

By doing business the right way, SAP can positively impact social and economic development, furthering education, justice, democracy, prosperity, development, and health worldwide.

SAP is committed to the highest standards of ethical business. We strive to undertake business with integrity by doing the right thing and following both the spirit and the letter of the law in all the markets we operate in.

Teaching prevention

SAP has a strong culture of ethical business. We actively and continuously nurture our culture of integrity, providing our employees, partners and suppliers with clear and comprehensive guidance on our ethics and compliance standards via our Codes of Conduct, policies, and due diligence processes, and continuous advice, communication, and training.

Identifying concerns

At SAP, every employee has equal responsibility for upholding our standards of ethical business and is encouraged to voice their concerns about any situation, without fearing personal retribution. We equally encourage those who do business with us to speak out. Reports about any suspected issues can be made confidentially through our network of Field and People Compliance Officers, or anonymously – if desired – using our reporting tool, Speak Out at SAP.*

Addressing issues

We share reported concerns only with the relevant SAP department for assessment and next steps. For instance, matters of compliance relating to potential bribery, corruption, or fraud are investigated by a dedicated team within our Office of Ethics & Compliance. This team enacts appropriate measures to address any parties – employees, partners, or suppliers – found to have breached our Codes of Conduct. We also actively integrate learning from audits, investigations, data analytics, and industry best practices to continuously strengthen the elements of our compliance management system.

We rely on our employees and our ecosystem to assess every decision and action made on behalf of the organization to be legal and compliant with our Codes of Conduct and policies - as well as respectful towards people and the environment.

SAP encourages you to speak out and report any breaches of the Codes, including concerns over potential violations relating to compliance, the law and/or regulations.

There are multiple ways of raising a concern, including a direct approach to the responsible department, for example the Office of Ethics & Compliance, or the Global People Compliance Office, or by using the Speak Out at SAP tool. All submissions and identities are maintained confidentially to the greatest extent practical (in light of the need to take further steps).

There are also third-party channels for reporting potential misconduct that involves breaches of EU laws and national implementations thereof according to the EU Directive 2019/1937 on the protection of whistleblowers.

SAP has a strict non-retaliation policy and does not tolerate any threatened or actual retaliation toward individuals speaking up and reporting concerns about potential non-compliance in good faith.

If you believe you have been or are being subjected to retaliation for raising a concern, please use via Speak Out at SAP.

Note that anyone reporting a concern using the Speak Out tool is subject to the protections granted to them by the European Union Directive 2019/1937 on the protection of persons who report breaches of Union law (EU Whistleblower Directive), in as far as the requirements of the Directive and/or of national implementations thereof apply.

Our sustainability policies, codes, and commitments

As a signatory of the United Nations (UN) Global Compact initiative, SAP is committed to respecting and promoting human rights across our operations, extended supply chain, and product lifecycle.

We are committed to the highest standards of Ethical Business and expect the same from our ecosystem. Our Code is a cornerstone for this commitment: it guides all SAP employees in fulfilling our purpose and promise with integrity.  

Read the Code (PDF) 

We are committed to reducing our impact on the environment in our operations, throughout our value chain, and with our solutions.

The SAP Global Environmental Policy guides our efforts to minimize our ecological footprint, provide environmental performance transparency, and demonstrate leadership in sustainability through transformational strategies and by offering solutions that enable customers to increase resource productivity.

Read the SAP Global Environmental Policy (PDF) 

This statement is an extension of SAP’s public commitment to the Human Rights Commitment Statement, Luxembourg Declaration on Workplace Health Promotion, the International Labor Organization (ILO) Declaration on Fundamental Principles and Rights at Work and the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (specifically SDG 3 “Good Health” and SDG 8 “Decent Workplaces”).

Read the SAP Health, Safety and Well-Being Commitment Statement 

SAP is committed to respecting and advancing human rights across its own operations, extended supply chain, and product life cycle.

Our policy statement outlines our commitment, human rights-related action areas, human rights governance and risk management system, prioritized risks, preventive and remedial measures as well as expectations placed on employees and suppliers.

Read the SAP Global Human Rights Commitment statement 

We are committed to the highest standards of ethical business and expect the same from our ecosystem. The SAP Partner Code of Conduct (“Code”) is a cornerstone of this commitment to integrity; all work performed for SAP must be in full compliance with this Code and all applicable laws, rules, regulations, and policies.

Read the SAP Partner Code of Conduct (PDF) 

To learn more about the Code or to report potential violations, e-mail SAP at ethicalbusiness@sap.com or submit your concern via Speak Out at SAP.

Please note that the SAP Office of Ethics & Compliance can answer questions about the SAP Partner Code of Conduct but cannot give legal advice.

We encourage our suppliers to adopt sustainable business practices as set forth in the SAP Supplier Code of Conduct.

We regard our supplier base as a critical and necessary extension of our operations and success. To help our suppliers, we created the SAP Supplier Code of Conduct, a statement of integrity that SAP expects from our contractors, consultants, suppliers, vendors, and all other third-party companies that comprise SAP's supply chain ("Suppliers"). All work performed for SAP must be in full compliance with this SAP Supplier Code of Conduct and all applicable laws, rules, regulations, and policies.

We encourage our contractors, consultants, suppliers, and agents to: 

  • Comply with regional and federal laws, rules, and regulations

  • Uphold the human rights of workers and treat them with dignity and respect

  • Operate with sustainable business practices and mindful, responsible use of environmental resources

  • Provide a safe and professional work environment that protects SAP's intellectual property

  • Refrain from any action that may be considered a conflict of interest

The code of conduct is in place for SAP, the parent company of the SAP Group, and all its entities.

Read the SAP Supplier Code of Conduct 

The Sarbanes-Oxley Act requires companies listed in the United States to declare whether they have a code of ethics that, at minimum, applies to certain levels of management. The SAP Supplier Code of Conduct meets the standards set by the Sarbanes-Oxley Act and the regulations pursuant to the act.

To learn more about the Code or to report potential violations, e-mail SAP at ethicalbusiness@sap.com or submit your concern via Speak Out at SAP.

SAP believes that Artificial Intelligence has the potential to unlock boundless potential for businesses, governments, and society. However, AI may also create economic, political, and societal challenges, depending upon how it is used and implemented.

Our brand-new SAP Global AI Ethics Policy therefore governs the development, deployment, use, and sale of AI systems at SAP, by defining clear rules of ethics that are aligned with SAP’s established guiding principles for AI and its core organizational values.  

The policy covers essential elements which are vital to build trust in AI solutions, such as transparency and traceability, human agency and oversight, addressing bias and discrimination as well as civic society.

Read the SAP Global AI Ethics Policy (PDF) 

Acknowledging that tax is an essential element of our overall corporate social responsibility, we have set out guiding principles which determine SAP’s responsible and sustainable approach to tax.

Read about SAP Global Tax Principles (PDF) 

SAP is committed to the highest standards of integrity and sustainable business practices in all the markets in which it operates. SAP recognizes the importance of controls relating to anti-money laundering (AML) and to combat the financing of terrorism (CFT) in support of the 2030 Sustainable Development Goals set by the United Nations General Assembly.

Read the SAP Global Commitment to Anti-Money Laundering & Combating the Financing of Terrorism (PDF) 

SAP is dedicated to ensuring that our software and services are not used in connection with controversial weapons. The SAP Controversial Weapons Commitment Statement, which has been binding since 2023, lays down principles and restrictions on conducting business with companies involved in controversial weapons.

Read the SAP Controversial Weapons Commitment Statement

Frequently asked questions

SAP’s purpose is to help the world run better and improve people's lives with sustainability at the core. Our objective is to create a positive economic, environmental, and social impact worldwide within planetary boundaries. We bring this to life by providing products and services that meet the sustainability challenges and opportunities of our customers (enabler) and leading by example in our own sustainable business operations and practices (exemplar). Learn about our approach to sustainability.

Yes, we are working with companies of all sizes, across geographies and industries, at various stages of maturity from pilots to full deployment.  Hear the stories of our visionary customers using SAP Sustainability solutions.

SAP has been serious about climate action for more than 15 years, setting its first carbon reduction targets in 2009. SAP is committed to achieving net-zero emissions along its entire value chain in line with a 1.5°C future in 2030 - 20 years earlier than originally targeted.

 

In the transition to net zero 2030, SAP follows a three-pillar carbon mitigation hierarchy: avoid, reduce, contribute. This means avoiding the creation of greenhouse gases in the first place, for example by using virtual collaboration technology instead of business travel. Secondly, SAP aims to significantly reduce its unavoidable emissions through innovations, for example by increasing the energy efficiency of our offices and data centers or transitioning to an emission-free car fleet. SAP has put in place a portfolio of measures to continuously reduce emissions along the value chain. Thirdly, SAP is committed to contribute to climate change mitigation by financing climate solutions outside our value chain that equal in size the annual carbon footprint of our own operations until 2030. At net-zero, SAP will neutralize its remaining value chain emissions via carbon removals. 

SAP is committed to protecting the environment and continuously improving our own environmental performance. Therefore, we are gradually introducing an EMS reflecting the ISO 14001 standard at SAP sites worldwide. We aim to increase the EMS scope to 100% of SAP’s major company-owned sites by 2025 (2022: 85%). In addition, an ISO 50001-certified energy management system is integrated with existing management systems at selected sites, such as SAP’s headquarters. View our ISO certificates on sap.com (go to “Energy and environmental management”).

In alignment with SAP’s Global Environmental Policy, we remain committed to Zero Waste by striving for zero e-waste in our operations and diverting at least 90% of our discarded SAP equipment from incineration and landfill by 2030. By the end of 2025, 96% of our total discarded equipment had been reused or recycled. In addition, we are committed to embedding circularity principles across our operations and improving SAP’s overall waste performance. To advance our global goals, we continuously collaborate with suppliers, service providers, partners, our internal global network of sustainability champions, and other stakeholders.

 

As an enabler, SAP offers a variety of solutions to support our customers’ transition to a circular economy. For example, SAP RDP addresses compliance topics associated with the PPWR. For more information on implemented measures and initiatives, see our Integrated Report, section “Resource Use and Circular Economy.”

Since 2012, we annually release an Integrated Report which combines our full-year financial, social, and environmental performance, allowing us to present a clear and holistic overview of what drives our company and our long-term success. The current SAP Integrated Report can be found at www.sapintegratedreport.com.

Yes. In our Integrated Report 2025, we continue to fulfill our reporting obligations under the EU Non‑Financial Reporting Directive (NFRD). In addition, we have voluntarily prepared our Sustainability Statement in accordance with the European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS), in anticipation of the EU Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD), which will become mandatory once transposed into German law.

 

In addition, our reporting covers:

  • EU Taxonomy Disclosures

  • Task Force on Climate-Related Financial Disclosures (TCFD)

  • Greenhouse Gas (GHG) Protocol for carbon accounting

  • Science Based Targets initiative (SBTi) alignment for our climate targets

 

 

SAP is committed to the highest standards of ethical business. We have a robust compliance framework to support employees in acting ethically and compliantly and within the law in all the markets in which we operate. The framework includes clear Policies, Codes, and a Global network of experts, all underpinned by a Global Code of Ethics & Business Conduct (the Code) which includes, amongst other topics, loyalty, bribery and corruption, and confidentiality.

 

For more information, please see the chapter “Business Conduct” in the SAP Integrated Report and/or Ethics and Compliance at SAP on sap.com.

We have implemented safeguards to help protect the fundamental rights of everyone whose data is processed by SAP, whether they are our customers, prospects, employees, or partners. In addition, we work toward compliance with all relevant legal requirements for data protection. You can find more information in the chapter "Security, Cloud Compliance, and Data Protection and Privacy" of the SAP Integrated Report, on SAP Trust Center, in the SAP Privacy Statement.

As a signatory of the UN Global Compact since 2000, SAP believes companies have a responsibility to respect human rights throughout all business operations. SAP is committed to respecting and promoting human rights across our operations, extended supply chain, and product lifecycle. We set high standards of fairness, diversity, and inclusion for ourselves, and expect all of our business partners to respect human rights and avoid complicity in any abuse.

We take guidance from the UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights as well as legal requirements like the German Supply Chain Due Diligence Act (Lieferkettensorgfaltspflichtengesetz, LkSG), to operationalize our commitment.

 

Further key References:

  • SAP Integrated Report 2022, chapter Human Rights

  • SAP Human Rights Commitment Statement

  • SAP’s Artificial Intelligence (AI) web site where you find SAP’s Guiding Principles for Artificial Intelligence, the SAP Global AI Ethics Policy, and the AI Ethics Handbook

  • SAP Supplier Code of Conduct

SAP embraces the 17 UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and embedded the framework as a foundation to our strategic approach to sustainability. We use this framework to evaluate global progress – both for our roles as a role model and exemplar and as an enabler. Our contribution to the SDGs is a cross-company effort driven by experts from almost every board area and aligned through the internal SDG Network. Engagement with customers and other activities contributing to the SDGs are published in our continuously updated Web book “SAP and the UN Global Goals” and addressed in our Integrated Report, where we describe the potential positive and negative direct or indirect impacts of our company and of our products and services related to the SDGs.

Yes. SAP’s ongoing sustainability efforts have been acknowledged externally and SAP continues receiving excellent scores. In 2025, SAP maintained industry leadership as one of the top companies in the software industry in the S&P Global Corporate Sustainability Assessment, received an A-score in CDP’s Climate Change rating, and was awarded the EcoVadis Gold medal ranking in the top 2% of companies scored. In 2024, SAP was recognized as one of the world’s most sustainable companies by TIME magazine and data firm Statista. More about SAP's sustainability awards and recognitions can be found on sap.com.

SAP discloses information on purchased carbon credits retired to uphold SAP’s climate finance commitment in 2025 here. This disclosure complements the SAP Integrated Report to ensure full compliance with The Voluntary Carbon Market Disclosures Act (California Assembly Bill No. 1305).

SAP discloses information on GHG Emissions Scopes 1, 2, and 3 Upstream and Downstream as part of SAP Integrated Report 2025 to ensure full compliance with California Climate Corporate Data Accountability Act (Senate Bill No. 253).

Frequently asked questions

Sustainability in finance is the practice of incorporating environmental, social, and governance (ESG) factors into financial strategy, planning, and reporting alongside traditional financial metrics. Rather than treating sustainability as a separate initiative, organizations integrate carbon, climate risk, and ESG data into core financial decisions, such as capital allocation, budgeting, and risk management, to better understand both long-term value and exposure to regulatory and market pressures.

ESG reporting software helps organizations collect, manage, and report on environmental, social, and governance data in compliance with regulatory frameworks such as CSRD and IFRS. It centralizes data from across the business, enables audit-ready reporting on metrics like emissions, energy use, and workforce diversity, and supports target setting and performance tracking. It replaces manual, spreadsheet-based processes with automated, verifiable data flows.

Carbon management and carbon accounting software enables organizations to measure, track, and reduce their greenhouse gas emissions across Scope 1, 2, and 3. It calculates corporate and product-level carbon footprints using actual operational data, rather than estimates, and supports compliance with emission reporting standards such as the GHG Protocol. Leading solutions embed carbon data directly into financial and procurement systems so that emissions become a factor in everyday business decisions.

 

Integrating sustainability into finance and business planning gives organizations a more complete picture of risk and performance. It connects emissions and ESG data to financial outcomes, enabling more informed decisions on capital allocation, supplier selection, and cost management. It also streamlines regulatory compliance by generating audit-ready sustainability disclosures from the same data used for financial reporting, reducing duplication and the risk of inconsistency across reports.

SAP offers an integrated sustainability portfolio—including SAP Sustainability Control Tower, SAP Sustainability Footprint Management, SAP Sustainability Data Exchange, and SAP Green Ledger—that embeds carbon and ESG data directly into ERP and financial processes. Because sustainability is integrated into SAP's core business systems rather than added as a separate tool, organizations can use actual transactional data to comply with regulations, produce auditable Scope 1, 2, and 3 emissions reports, and factor carbon costs into financial planning.

products/sustainability/sustainable-proc.description: Sustainable procurement integrates environmental, social, and governance criteria into purchasing. Learn how it helps you manage risk and create value.
products/sustainability/sustainable-proc.body:
What Is

What is sustainable procurement?

Sustainable procurement helps you balance cost, risk, and ESG impact across your supply chain.

Published on November 5, 2026

Sustainable procurement definition

Sustainable procurement is the practice of integrating environmental, social, and governance (ESG) criteria into every purchasing decision your team makes. It goes beyond price and quality to consider the full impact of what you buy, who you buy it from, and how those suppliers operate.

When you practice sustainable procurement, you weigh factors like carbon emissions, labor practices, circular metrics, and ethical sourcing alongside traditional cost, quality, and supplier performance metrics.

The goal is to make purchasing decisions that create long-term value for your business, suppliers, and society while conserving resources and protecting communities.

Sustainable procurement is not a separate initiative added to existing procurement processes. It is a core approach to purchasing that builds sustainability into sourcing, supplier management, spend intelligence, and external workforce decisions. By making sustainability part of how you buy, you can manage risk, meet regulatory requirements, and build more resilient supply chains.

Why sustainable procurement matters now

Supply chains face more scrutiny than ever. Investors, customers, regulators, and employees all expect companies to understand and take responsibility for the social and environmental impact of their purchasing decisions. A supply chain is only as responsible as the suppliers within it, and most of a company's environmental and social impact lives in its supply chain, not its direct operations.

Several forces are driving the shift toward sustainable procurement:

  • Regulatory pressure is rising. New laws in the European Union (EU), the United States, and other regions require companies to report on ESG performance, conduct supplier due diligence, and prove their supply chains are free from deforestation and human rights violations. These include the EU Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD), EU Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD), California’s SB 253 and SB 261, Modern Slavery Acts and the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act (UFLPA), the EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), the EU Deforestation Regulation (EUDR), and Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) plastic taxes. Increasingly, businesses face penalties for non-compliance and are being made to bear negative externality costs.
  • Stakeholder expectations are changing. Investors increasingly factor ESG risks into their investment decisions. Fund managers evaluate the ESG performance of the companies they invest in and hold. An example is a company with high incidences of human rights abuses and environmental damage, which could lead to expensive lawsuits and reputational damage, impacting the stock price. Another is a company’s level of compliance with carbon regulations and taxes being paid, where good ESG scores translate to lower carbon costs paid out. Besides regulatory mandates, executive leaders and financial institutions are increasingly seeing useful business cases for supporting environmentally and socially responsible businesses.
  • Supply chain risk is growing.  Global logistics are becoming more vulnerable and disrupted, leading to government policies designed to reduce reliance on fossil fuel supply chains, trade with countries carrying adverse human rights records, imports on critical minerals and commodities, and the impacts of climate disruptions from international trade.
  • Competitive advantage is at stake. Companies that make sustainability part of procurement can reduce costs, build stronger supplier relationships, and differentiate themselves in the market. Naturally, if a company can reduce energy and material waste, it can achieve cost savings.

Sustainable procurement helps organizations reduce supply chain risk, comply with ESG regulations, lower environmental impact, strengthen supplier relationships, and improve long-term business resilience.

Benefits of sustainable procurement:

  • Reduced supply chain risk
  • Improved ESG compliance
  • Lower Scope 3 emissions
  • Stronger supplier relationships
  • Better spend visibility
  • Enhanced brand reputation

The three pillars of sustainable procurement

Sustainable procurement rests on three interconnected pillars: environmental, social, and economic and governance. Together, they form a framework, often called the “triple bottom line,” which essentially looks at business decisions through the lens of environmental, social, and economic outcomes.

Environmental

The environmental pillar focuses on reducing the ecological footprint of your supply chain. This includes measuring and managing Scope 3 procurement emissions, the indirect emissions that come from your suppliers, improving purchases for recycled plastics, and sourcing products responsibly such as licensed wood and timber products. Scope 3 emissions often represent the largest portion of a company's carbon footprint, making them a critical area for action.

Environmentally sustainable procurement practices include:

  • Sourcing from suppliers that use renewable energy or reduce waste.
  • Choosing products and materials with lower carbon footprints.
  • Avoiding goods linked to deforestation, such as those covered by the EU Deforestation Regulation.
  • Prioritizing circular economy principles like recycling, reuse, and reduced packaging.

By addressing environmental impact in your procurement decisions, you can reduce emissions, comply with reporting requirements, and support your company's climate goals.

Social

The social pillar addresses the human impact of your supply chain. It covers labor practices, human rights, health and safety, and supplier diversity. When you practice social sustainable procurement, you look beyond cost to ask whether your suppliers treat their workers fairly and contribute to their communities.

Key social considerations include:

  • Preventing forced labor, child labor, and modern slavery in your supply chain.
  • Promoting supplier diversity by sourcing from minority-owned, women-owned, and small businesses.
  • Supporting safe working conditions throughout your supplier base.
  • Supporting fair wages and ethical labor practices.

Social procurement helps you meet human rights due diligence requirements, protect your reputation, and create positive social impact through your purchasing power.

Economic and governance

The economic and governance pillar focuses on the financial and ethical foundations of your procurement decisions. It covers anti-corruption, fair competition, transparency, and the long-term economic viability of your suppliers.

Sustainable procurement is the process of incorporating economic and governance criteria to purchasing decisions to reduce risk, meet compliance requirements, and create long-term business value.

This pillar includes:

  • Conducting supplier due diligence to assess financial stability and ethical practices.
  • Enforcing anti-bribery and anti-corruption policies across your supply base.
  • Supporting fair competition and ethical sourcing in your bidding processes.
  • Building long-term, mutually beneficial supplier relationships.

Strong governance helps you reduce risk, maintain compliance, and build trust with stakeholders. It also supports the long-term sustainability of your supply chain by helping your suppliers operate responsibly and remain viable partners.

Sustainable procurement regulations and compliance

Regulations are one of the strongest drivers of sustainable procurement. A wave of new laws and frameworks around the world now require companies to understand, report on, and take responsibility for their supply chain impacts.

Key regulations and frameworks include:

  • CSRD: Requires large companies to report on ESG topics, including supply chain impacts and 15 categories of Scope 3 emissions in compliance with European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS).
  • CSDDD: Requires companies to identify, prevent, and mitigate human rights and environmental risks in their operations and supply chains.
  • EUDR: Requires companies to prove that certain commodities do not come from recently deforested land. Learn more with this EU Deforestation Regulation guide.
  • Human rights due diligence legislation such as the German Supply Chain Due Diligence Act (LkSG), Modern Slavery Acts, and the UFLPA: Requires companies exceeding size and/or revenue thresholds to conduct due diligence on suppliers and publish their findings in statement declaration reports.
  • California SB 253 and SB 261: Require large companies doing business in California to disclose greenhouse gas emissions and climate-related financial risks.
  • ISSB IFRS S2: An international framework for sustainability-related financial disclosures, including Scope 3 emissions.

These regulations share a common theme: they push companies to look beyond their direct operations and take responsibility for what happens in their supply chains.

Sustainable procurement helps you meet these requirements by embedding due diligence, reporting, and risk management into your purchasing processes.

Key challenges in sustainable procurement

While the case for sustainable procurement is clear, putting it into practice comes with its challenges:

  • Data quality and availability: Gathering accurate ESG data from suppliers is difficult. Many suppliers lack the systems to measure and report their environmental and social performance, leaving gaps in your sustainability picture.
  • Supplier transparency: Supply chains are often multi-tier and opaque. You may know your direct suppliers, but visibility into their suppliers, and the risks further upstream, is limited.
  • Balancing cost and sustainability: Procurement teams face pressure to control costs while also meeting sustainability goals. Finding the right balance requires clear policies, good data, and tools that help evaluate trade-offs.
  • Regulatory complexity: With regulations varying by region and evolving rapidly, keeping up with compliance requirements is an ongoing challenge.
  • Change management: Shifting from price-driven to sustainable procurement requires new skills, processes, and mindsets across your teams.

Core capabilities of sustainable procurement software

Sustainable procurement applications help make sustainability part of your current workflows. Rather than treating sustainability as a separate initiative, teams can apply sustainability requirements at the moment a purchasing request enters the process, helping guide decisions before sourcing or contracting begins.

Core capabilities of these applications include:

  • Supplier assessment and ESG scoring: Evaluate suppliers against environmental, social, and governance criteria using questionnaires and third-party data from partners like EcoVadis and IntegrityNext.
  • Spend visibility and analysis: Connect spend data with sustainability metrics to understand where your money goes and what impact it has.
  • Risk monitoring: Track supplier risks across multiple dimensions, including financial, environmental, social, and compliance, and get alerts when issues arise.
  • Scope 3 emissions management: Collect and analyze emissions data from suppliers to support reporting and reduction goals.
  • Contract compliance: Incorporate ESG requirements into contracts so suppliers are held accountable for sustainability commitments.
  • AI-supported workflows: Use AI to simplify processes, evaluate supplier responses, support sustainability-driven category strategies, and recommend sustainable options based on policy and available data.

AI plays a supporting role in sustainable procurement applications. It helps teams work more efficiently by surfacing relevant information, evaluating supplier data, and suggesting sustainable alternatives, but people remain at the center of decision-making. AI supports your team; it does not replace their judgment.

SAP Business AI is embedded across these solutions to help procurement teams bring intelligence directly into everyday procurement workflows. Teams can make more informed decisions while keeping people in control of the final outcomes.

Sustainable procurement use cases

Companies across industries are using sustainable procurement to reduce risks and improve compliance.

In fact, when they make sustainability part of procurement, they often discover benefits that extend beyond ESG reporting. When teams have access to the right information at the right time, they can identify potential issues earlier and adapt as supplier or business needs change.

Over time, those decisions add up. Sustainability influences how suppliers are evaluated, how purchases are made, and how businesses work toward their broader goals.

How SAP supports sustainable procurement

Making sustainability part of your everyday procurement requires more than good intentions. You need tools that keep sustainability front and center in your purchasing decisions.

SAP solutions help you build these priorities into everyday procurement workflows, so you can make informed decisions, track progress, and keep moving toward your goals.

Get more perspectives on meeting ESG requirements in sustainable procurement.

FAQ

  • What are the three pillars of sustainable procurement?

    The three pillars of sustainable procurement are environmental, social, and economic and governance. The environmental pillar focuses on reducing ecological impact, including Scope 3 emissions. The social pillar addresses labor practices, human rights, and supplier diversity. The economic and governance pillar covers ethical sourcing, anti-corruption, and supplier due diligence. Together, they form the triple bottom line, a framework for evaluating the full impact of purchasing decisions.

  • What are the seven principles of sustainable procurement?

    The seven principles of sustainable procurement are: (1) vision and strategy, (2) governance, (3) people, (4) engagement and collaboration, (5) measurement and reporting, (6) supply chain risk and compliance, and (7) innovation. These principles guide organizations in building a structured approach to sustainable procurement, from setting a clear vision to measuring progress and driving continuous improvement.

  • What is the difference between sustainable procurement and sustainable sourcing?

    The difference between sustainable procurement and sustainable sourcing is that sustainable sourcing is a subset of sustainable procurement. Sourcing focuses specifically on the upstream process of identifying, evaluating, and selecting suppliers based on sustainability criteria. Sustainable procurement is broader. It covers the entire purchasing lifecycle, including sourcing, supplier management, contract compliance, spend analysis, and external workforce management. In short, sustainable sourcing is about who you buy from; sustainable procurement is about how you buy across the full process.

  • What regulations require sustainable procurement?

    Key regulations that require sustainable procurement include the CSRD, the CSDDD, the EUDR, modern slavery acts (such as the Australian and United Kingdom Modern Slavery Acts, the UFLPA, and the LkSG), and California SB 253 and SB 261. International frameworks like ISSB IFRS S2 also drive sustainable procurement by requiring companies to report on supply chain emissions and ESG impacts. However, regulations are subject to change.

  • What is ESG in procurement?

    ESG in procurement means applying environmental, social, and governance criteria to purchasing decisions. Environmental criteria cover emissions, resource use, and ecological impact. Social criteria cover labor practices, human rights, and supplier diversity. Governance criteria cover ethics, compliance, and transparency. ESG procurement helps organizations manage risk, meet regulatory requirements, and create long-term value through more responsible purchasing.

  • What is a sustainable procurement policy?

    A sustainable procurement policy is a formal document that defines how your business integrates sustainability into purchasing decisions. It sets out the ESG criteria your buyers should consider, the supplier’s due diligence requirements, and the standards suppliers must meet. A strong policy aligns procurement with your company's sustainability goals, provides clear guidance for buyers, and creates a framework for measuring and reporting progress. An example is making it compulsory for suppliers to agree to the buyer’s code of conduct when supplying goods and services and agreeing to disclose human rights records periodically.
