products/data-cloud/master-data-governan.body:
What Is

What is data governance?

Data governance defines the policies and processes ensuring data accuracy, security, and accessibility.

Updated on January 26, 2026

Data governance definition

Data governance refers to the set of policies, procedures, and technology tools used to manage an organization’s data assets throughout their lifecycle. As a vital part of data management, this process helps secure data quality, integrity, and privacy for all end users. With clear systems and standards in place, data governance enables organizations to reduce risks, comply with regulations, and extract maximum value from their enterprise data.

Why data governance matters

Modern organizations are flooded with vast amounts of data. Without a straightforward way to manage this heavy volume, data quickly becomes fragmented, inaccurate, and insecure. This disorder can turn data from an asset into a liability amid today’s strict privacy regulations and cyber threats.

Data governance addresses these risks by establishing clear protocols to maintain data consistency, security, and trustworthiness. This approach reduces costly errors and compliance risks while enabling better analytics and decision-making. Ultimately, data governance helps organizations transform raw information into a strategic advantage.

Key components of data governance

Good data governance requires a few core features to ensure that data remains accurate and secure. These key data governance components work together to manage data throughout its lifecycle—from creation to disposal. Learn how these fundamental data governance pillars support data consistency, mitigate risks, and uncover vital business insights.

Data rules and regulations

Data governance rules and regulations define how data is collected, stored, accessed, and shared in an organization. Having precise controls supports privacy and security standards, ensuring that all data complies with relevant regulations. Good data governance rules also should not remain static. Regular updates are key for adapting to new operational and compliance requirements.

Data quality

Data quality measures the accuracy, completeness, consistency, timeliness, relevance, and usability of data. Data governance regulates the rules and systems necessary to maintain these high standards. This includes protocols and tools for data standardization, validation, monitoring, and cleansing. Structured data quality management helps prevent data errors, redundancies, and inconsistencies.

Data stewardship

Data stewardship refers to the role responsible for maintaining data quality, integrity, and usability across the organization. Stewards act as primary custodians for specific data domains, ensuring compliance and proper usage among teams while monitoring data quality standards. Effective data stewardship is crucial for bridging the gap between technical systems and business needs, enabling accurate decision-making and regulatory compliance.

Data compliance

Data compliance ensures that organizations follow legal, regulatory, and industry-specific data standards. This includes following privacy laws, security mandates, and auditing requirements. Compliance usually involves regular data auditing, which reviews data practices and access logs to detect any issues. Effective compliance practices protect organizations from penalties while fostering trust with customers and other stakeholders.

Data cataloging

To generate valuable business insights, teams must first find the relevant data. Cataloging supports this process by organizing all data assets into a searchable inventory—making it easier for users to locate and curate the information they need quickly. A robust data catalog should include comprehensive metadata, ownership details, data lineage information, and access rules.

Data monitoring

Data monitoring refers to the tracking and evaluation of data-related activities against established quality and security standards. This process involves validating new data, identifying anomalies, and managing user access. Ongoing monitoring reduces compliance risks and ensures data remains trustworthy for informed decision-making.

How data governance works

Data governance involves a multistep process to maintain consistent and secure data. Each step—from assigning roles to integrating technology—helps create a foundation that supports accountability and adaptability. Follow these key steps to build and sustain successful data governance initiatives that drive value across the organization.

1. Establish a data governance framework

Develop a strategic blueprint outlining how data governance runs within the organization. Having a strong data governance structure helps align team efforts toward the same goal. A practical data governance framework should include:

  • Objective and scope: Define which data domains will be governed and why.
  • Organizational structure: Outline a clear data governance operating model that determines how data decisions will flow through the organization.
  • Data standards: Document clear standards and metrics for managing data.
  • Processes and workflows: Identify key operational steps for handling data throughout its lifecycle.
  • Data technology: Specify tools needed to automate and support key governance tasks.

2. Outline clear data governance policies

With a clear data governance framework in place, introduce policies that translate these high-level standards into actionable rules for day-to-day tasks. This includes detailed orders for managing data quality, compliance, privacy, and security. Clear policies reduce operational ambiguity, allowing teams to comply confidently with regulatory requirements.

3. Assign data governance roles and responsibilities

Outline specific data governance roles to define who’s responsible for particular tasks, which helps prevent confusion and ensure accountability. Data stewards lead the day-to-day management of specific data assets. Other key data governance roles include:

  • Data governance committee: Provides strategic oversight, approves data governance policies, and resolves conflicts across data domains.
  • Data owners: Oversee the accuracy, quality, and consistency of specific datasets, and authorize data access and use.
  • Data custodians: Implement technical data security controls, including data encryption, data access controls, and data privacy.
  • Data users: Consume data responsibly according to governance policies and report any discrepancies or issues.

4. Implement data governance processes

Establish clear workflows for creating, managing, and protecting data across its lifecycle. Standardized processes are crucial for maintaining trust, mitigating risks, and ensuring compliance with regulations. Key data governance processes include:

  • Data classification: Categorize data based on sensitivity, usage, and regulatory requirements to determine appropriate handling and protection measures.
  • Access control: Define and enforce who can view, edit, or share specific datasets to maintain security and prevent unauthorized use.
  • Data governance documentation: Record processes to create transparency and enable operational consistency across teams.
  • Data validation: Use tools to verify that data meets defined quality and format standards before it is stored or used, reducing errors and improving reliability.
  • Incident resolution: Set up procedures for identifying, reporting, and correcting data errors or breaches quickly and effectively.

5. Integrate data governance technology

Data platforms and tools are vital for scaling governance policies and processes. Modern data management tools can help automate tasks, monitor compliance, and provide visibility into data assets. With these capabilities, teams can reduce manual workloads and improve their performance accuracy.

6. Audit and continuously improve

Effective data governance requires ongoing assessments and continuous improvement. Conduct regular audits to refine policies and processes. Quality checks should verify accuracy, completeness, and consistency across datasets. Stakeholder feedback loops can also provide valuable guidance to adapt to shifting business goals.

Data governance benefits

As organizations navigate today’s rapidly shifting markets, robust data governance equips decision-makers with powerful tools to stay ahead. They can extract the full value of their enterprise data to uncover new strategic insights and opportunities. Here are just a few ways data governance helps companies strengthen resilience and drive sustainable growth.

Faster, smarter decision-making

Reliable, high-quality data allows leaders to make faster, more informed decisions. Teams can spend less time validating information and more time acting on insights, boosting overall productivity. This efficiency frees up resources for strategic initiatives rather than troubleshooting data issues.

Greater business agility

Accurate data supports better forecasting and scenario planning, enabling organizations to respond quickly to market changes. Leaders can pivot strategies confidently with decisions grounded in trustworthy insights. This gives organizations a competitive edge, allowing them to anticipate issues and shifting trends.

Enhanced collaboration

Good governance ensures teams across departments can access and use accurate, consistent data, which is crucial for effective collaboration. When everyone works from a single source of truth, teams can quickly identify issues and brainstorm solutions. This alignment fosters a culture of transparency and teamwork across the organization.

Accelerated AI innovations

Data governance lays the foundation for advanced AI automation and analytics. Clean, well-managed data fuels AI models, enabling organizations to develop new products, optimize processes, and deliver personalized customer experiences. Innovation thrives when teams can experiment confidently with reliable data.

Reduced risks

Organizations can significantly reduce their regulatory compliance and security risks with thorough data governance programs. Clear documentation of data policies, workflows, and decisions creates transparency and simplifies compliance audits. Protective data measures also defend systems against costly breaches before they occur. These practices reduce legal and financial exposure.

Improved customer and partner trust

Strong data governance safeguards sensitive information. This signals trustworthiness to customers, which reassures them about sharing vital data to enhance products and services. Partners are also more willing to share data and align processes, which helps improve efficiency and profitability across the value chain.

Lower costs

Reliable data reduces errors and inefficiencies that drive up operational expenses. Governance also streamlines audits and improves resource allocation, freeing budgets for more strategic initiatives. Over time, these efficiencies translate into significant cost savings and improved profitability.

Common data governance challenges

Organizations can often face hurdles when trying to implement a data governance program. Challenges may stem from technology, people, or processes. Understanding the source of these common governance risks can help teams build more robust programs.

Data sprawl

Data spawl occurs when information becomes scattered across cloud platforms, SaaS tools, on-premises systems, and employee devices. This fragmentation makes it hard for teams to maintain data quality, security, and compliance. Organizations need tools to harmonize their data environments and improve visibility.

Unstructured data

Companies generate vast amounts of unstructured data, including emails, reports, contracts, and financial records. These datasets often lack clear formats and metadata, making it more difficult to classify, govern, and protect them. Teams will require tools to discover, classify, and secure unstructured data at scale.

Data silos

Different departments often store their data in isolated systems, creating data silos that fragment information and limit visibility. Silos also lead to duplication and inconsistencies that eventually degrade data integrity. Breaking down these barriers requires governance models that enable unified oversight without disrupting departmental workflows.

Environment complexity

Hybrid and multi-cloud environments introduce multiple security models and compliance requirements, which makes maintaining consistent policies and procedures difficult. To resolve these data governance issues, teams need integrated tools that function smoothly across on-premises and cloud systems.

Organizational challenges

Unclear roles and accountability will eventually undermine data governance efforts. From the top down, everyone needs to understand their responsibilities for maintaining data integrity and security. Training and ongoing guidance are necessary to ensure that all teams view data management as a strategic priority.

Data governance tools and technology

New technologies are making data governance simpler than ever. From harmonizing environments to automating routine tasks, this new generation of tools helps teams collect, manage, and secure data more effectively across diverse systems. Companies can boost efficiency, strengthen security, and enable data-driven decisions. To achieve these goals, consider the following features when evaluating data governance solutions.

Master data governance

Master data governance solutions enable users to consolidate, monitor, and manage all their master data through a central portal. By creating a single, trusted source of truth, these solutions can improve data accuracy, reduce duplication, and ensure consistency across systems.

Metadata management

Metadata management solutions enable data stewards to define and maintain consistent information about specific data assets, including their origin, structure, and usage. This makes data easier to find, understand, and manage while supporting compliance and traceability.

Data catalog management

Catalog management tools can generate a centralized inventory of all data assets, recording their metadata, lineage, and usage information. By improving visibility, this approach makes data easier for end users to discover and understand. Greater transparency also helps data governance stewards enforce compliance standards and monitor usage.

Data quality management

Quality management solutions ensure information remains accurate, complete, and reliable. Core features include cleansing, validation, and standardization tools that filter through data to fix errors and improve consistency. Integrated quality checks, data health monitoring, and anomaly detection can also proactively catch issues before they affect operations.

AI-enabled features

Integrated AI automation features can help accelerate many daily governance tasks, including classification, metadata tagging, and anomaly detection. AI-driven knowledge graphs also help track data lineage, context, and connections. These features are key to supporting quality and compliance audits.

Zero-copy architecture

Zero-copy data architecture enables users to share secure, real-time data across systems without physical transfers. This feature helps simplify governance across data landscapes by reducing data silos, maintaining data integrity, and preserving rich metadata.

Security features

To protect sensitive data, governance teams can integrate a wide range of security features, including access controls, encryption, and identity management. These capabilities help enforce governance policies by preventing unauthorized access and ensuring compliance with regulatory requirements.

Data governance best practices

Data governance is not a one-time project, but an ongoing process. That’s why successful implementation requires not just new policies, but also a cultural shift in how teams collaborate and share information. With the right approach, however, companies can build sustainable frameworks that grow with their businesses. Here’s how to implement data governance initiatives to build a solid foundation for long-term success.

  • Start small: Begin with a pilot project to test and validate data governance processes, while keeping the organization’s high-level data governance goals in mind.
  • Secure leadership support: Ensure an executive business sponsor is appointed to advocate for the program, enforce accountability, and resolve cross-functional data conflicts.
  • Build a solid business case: Outline clear objectives, expected benefits, timelines, and progress milestones to keep the project on track.
  • Define meaningful metrics: Focus on a handful of relevant measurements to monitor progress without overwhelming the team.
  • Communicate openly: Encourage collaboration by actively engaging relevant teams in the data governance planning and implementation process.

Data governance FAQ

  • How does data governance compare to data management?

    Data governance sets the policies, standards, and roles that define how data should be managed. Data management refers to the operational execution of those policies—covering tasks such as storage, integration, and processing.

  • What is the difference between data governance and data stewardship?

    Data governance is the overall framework of policies and processes for managing data across the organization. Data stewardship is a specific role within that framework, responsible for enforcing governance standards and maintaining data quality and compliance in assigned domains.

  • How does data governance help with compliance and risk management?

    Governance ensures organizations follow legal, regulatory, and industry standards by defining clear policies for data privacy, security, and usage. This process reduces risks by preventing unauthorized access, enhancing audit readiness, and minimizing errors that could result in financial penalties or reputational damage.

  • What are examples of data governance?

    Examples of data governance include establishing clear policies for data access and usage, maintaining data quality standards, and ensuring compliance with relevant data protection and privacy regulations. Organizations often use tools like data catalogs to organize assets with metadata and lineage details, while assigning roles such as data stewards and custodians to ensure accountability.

  • Why is data governance important?

    Data governance keeps data accurate, secure, and accessible, which helps organizations reduce their compliance risks and make more informed decisions. Strong governance turns raw data into a trusted asset that supports analytics, innovation, and business growth.

  • How does data governance work?

    Data governance begins with defining a clear framework of objectives, roles, and standards. Policies translate these principles into actionable rules to enforce quality, compliance, and security standards. Teams then implement workflows for classification, validation, and access control, supported by technology that automates tasks and monitors compliance. Regular audits and updates ensure governance also adapts to changing business needs and regulations.

SAP Key Management Service
Overview

SAP Key Management Service

Take control of your business data using your own encryption keys.
Request a demo

What is SAP Key Management Service?

SAP Key Management Service is a security service that safeguards data with customer-controlled encryption keys and compliant key management across your SAP cloud solutions.

Meet data protection and audit requirements with:

  • Cloud deployment.

  • Simplified and transparent custom key management.

  • Intuitive user experience.

  • Better compliance within business regulations.

  • Adaptive and scalable capabilities.

Key benefits

Enhance security and resilience

Limit provider and insider access with exclusive key control and quickly revoke or rotate keys for swift incident containment and secure offboarding.

Ensure compliance goals

Streamline audits and certifications by using proven key custody, hardware security module-backed (HSM) controls, and clear separation of duties.

Lower overhead

Reduce operational efforts, errors, and total cost of ownership using a centralized, automated key lifecycle.

Adopt cloud services confidently

Use SAP cloud services while maintaining data sovereignty and a consistent, high-assurance security posture.

Key features

Enhance security

  • Import, register, enable, disable, rotate, and delete keys within your secure SAP KMS tenant.

  • Lock SAP cloud systems to immediately prevent data access.

  • Enforce dual control and workflow approvals for key operations.

  • View policies, status, and audit logs through a central management UI.

  • Protect key handling with a cryptographic keychain.

Meet your compliance goals

  • Trace all key activities using audit logs.

  • Authenticate using cloud identity services.

  • Ensure regulatory compliance with FIPS-validated and HSM-backed key storage.

  • Enforce least privilege-access through role-based access control.

  • Control SAP system-to-key mapping.

Improve flexibility

  • Import, register, and store keys using bring your own key (BYOK) or hold your own key (HYOK).

  • Support centralized or distributed SAP KMS models.

  • Dynamically assign and update customer-managed key mappings.

  • Connect SAP cloud solutions to designated SAP KMS tenants.

  • Operate across all major hyperscalers.

Frequently asked questions

SAP Key Management Service (SAP KMS) is a security service that allows customers to manage their own encryption keys for SAP cloud products and the SAP Business AI Platform to protect data at rest. It provides consistent key governance and auditability to help meet compliance and regulatory requirements. With SAP KMS, customers keep control of their encryption keys, ensuring data remains inaccessible to any external party.

Customer-managed encryption means that you, the customer, control the encryption keys that protect your data at rest in SAP cloud services. With SAP KMS, you decide who can access your data and when. Revoke a key, and the data becomes inaccessible to anyone, including SAP. This gives your organization full sovereignty over sensitive data and helps meet compliance requirements such as GDPR and CCPA. Options include bring your own key (BYOK) and hold your own key (HYOK).

A cryptographic key is the secret value used to encrypt and decrypt your data. Think of it as a digital lock—only someone with the right key can access the information it protects. In SAP cloud services, every piece of data at rest is secured by one of these keys. By default, SAP generates and manages the keys for you. With SAP Key Management Service (SAP KMS), you take over that control by creating, rotating, and revoking your own keys so your data stays inaccessible to anyone you haven't authorized.

SAP Key Management Service (SAP KMS) protects your business data by putting encryption key control in your hands. Generate, rotate, and revoke your own keys across SAP cloud products and the SAP Business AI Platform. If a key is revoked, the data it protects becomes cryptographically locked to everyone. SAP KMS also provides consistent key governance and auditability to help you meet compliance and regulatory requirements, giving your organization a proactive, centralized approach to data security.

With bring your own key (BYOK), you generate your encryption key and import it into SAP Key Management Service (SAP KMS). Your key lives inside SAP's secure environment, but you—not SAP—create and control it. With hold your own key (HYOK), your key never leaves your infrastructure. SAP KMS connects to your external keystore and requests permission to use it. If you cut access, the data is immediately inaccessible. BYOK offers control with easier cloud integration. HYOK offers maximum sovereignty for stricter security requirements.

Many regulations, including GDPR and PCI DSS, require organizations to protect sensitive data, control who can access it, and prove that controls are in place. SAP Key Management Service (SAP KMS) helps you meet those requirements in three ways: it gives you full control over your encryption keys, supports consistent key governance across SAP cloud products, and provides auditability so you can demonstrate compliance. Regular key rotation, access revocation, and flexible key scenarios like bring your own key (BYOK) and hold your own key (HYOK) add further layers of accountability.

SAP Key Management Service (SAP KMS) manages encryption keys across their full lifecycle. You start by generating a key, which SAP KMS stores securely and distributes to the services that need it. When you rotate a key, a new primary version encrypts the keychain while the older version stays active to decrypt existing data. When a key is no longer needed, you can disable or delete it, immediately blocking access to the data it protects. Every step is logged for full auditability.

When using bring your own key (BYOK), SAP Key Management Service (SAP KMS) relies on a FIPS 140-2 Level 3 compliant hardware security module (HSM) for key storage. This means the physical device that stores your encryption keys has passed rigorous testing to validate its security mechanisms. For organizations in regulated industries, this provides a verified, standards-backed foundation for BYOK key storage.

SAP Real Estate and Facilities Management is a cloud-based solution that integrates Planon’s real estate and facility management software with SAP S/4HANA Cloud for the entire building management lifecycle. It is a comprehensive tool for portfolio, space, maintenance, and sustainability management that helps organizations optimize building efficiency and costs.

 

The combined strengths of SAP and Planon holistically connect buildings, people, and processes. SAP Cloud ERP serves as the backbone for managing end-to-end business processes, while Planon provides vertical real estate and facility management software. Planon is part of Schneider Electric, a global specialist in energy management and automation for buildings.

SAP Contract and Lease Management continues to be the SAP solution for processing leasing (in compliance with standards set by IFRS 16, GAAP 842, and the local commercial code) for all types of leased assets.

SAP S/4HANA for contract, lease, and real estate management functions remain available. However, all future innovations—including AI capabilities, Fiori UI enhancements, and SAP Business Data Cloud products—will be developed exclusively for SAP Contract and Lease Management and its integration with SAP Real Estate and Facilities Management by Planon.

SAP Real Estate and Facilities Management by Planon reflects operational activity accurately reflected in transactions and financial reporting on SAP S/4HANA. It is an out-of-the-box integration via the Business Technology Platform (BTP).

/content/sapdx/countries/en_us/registration/request-demo.html

Integration with External Trading Platforms

SAP trading platform integration for SAP Treasury and Risk Management and SAP Cash Management enables you to streamline, automate and integrate SAP S/4HANA trading activities into trading platforms. This service covers outbound process for trade requests and inbound process for trades.

Benefits

  • Automated Trading Platform Connection for Treasury System

    Connect to the leading trading platform providers like 360T, FXall and others by leveraging a single service powered by SAP Business Technology Platform (BTP) for inbound and outbound service.

  • SMART Trading

    Straight through processing capability without multiple data entries and disrupted workflows, as well as fully automated end-to-end workflow for Smart Trading using SAP BTP. Includes system landscape simplification by getting rid of any middleware.

  • Fast Implementation and Reduced Cost

    Features include very fast setup by configuration, automatic execution of trade requests and replication into SAP Treasury System. Control, monitor and audit all relevant trading activities with a fully automated rule-based execution process.

Features

View media gallery

Inbound Service to Manage Trade

Transfer treasury deals to SAP S/4HANA automatically, manage inter-company trades, store competitive bids in the application, update treasury transactions with additional information before sending to SAP S/4HANA and receive notifications on successful transactions.

Outbound Service to Manage Trade

Including trade requests originated from Cash Management and Hedge Management, inter-company trade requests, trade request processing (splitting and block trade) and manual trade requests including back-to-back mirroring of internal trade requests and internal deals.

Manage Trade Requests for different Users

Fully automated end-to-end workflow for Smart Trading for different users and scenarios, including for subsidiaries and headquarters risk managers using Hedge Management Cockpit and Balance Sheet Exposure as well as for cash managers to initiate cash requests from SAP Cash Management.

Treasury and working capital management software from SAP is a software solution that is designed to help organizations manage their treasury and working capital more effectively and efficiently. Here are some of the software’s key features and functionalities:

  • Cash management

  • Financial risk, debt, and investment management

  • Payments and bank communication

  • Receivables and payables management

  • SAP Taulia Dynamic Discounting, Taulia Supply Chain Finance, Taulia Receivables, and Taulia Virtual Cards

By using treasury and working capital management software from SAP, organizations can improve their financial performance, reduce risks, enhance operational efficiency, and gain real-time insights into their financial health.

Treasury and working capital management software from SAP helps improve cash visibility and liquidity through several key features and functionalities, such as:

  1. Real-time cash positioning and instance cash balances
  2. Short-term, medium-term, and long-term cash forecasting
  3. Liquidity planning
  4. Bank connectivity and statement reconciliation
  5. Cash AI agent as a digital assistant 

By leveraging these features, the solution enables organizations to enhance cash visibility, optimize liquidity, reduce borrowing costs, and make informed decisions on cash management and investment strategies.

SAP Working Capital Management (WCM) improves visibility into receivables and payables through a range of features and functionalities designed to provide organizations with real-time insights into their financial position, such as:

  • Accounts receivables and payables aging analysis

  • Real-time receivables and payables monitoring

What is SAP SuccessFactors HCM?

As a vital part of SAP since 2012, SAP SuccessFactors HCM enables organizations to manage all HR and talent management processes from a single AI-driven cloud solution.

Why SAP SuccessFactors solutions?

SAP SuccessFactors HCM helps organizations improve workforce performance, optimize operations, and accelerate business impact. It brings together truly global HR capabilities, trusted people data, and powerful agentic experiences in a single connected suite.

Joule Work mobile app requires internet access to function and exchange data. Offline capabilities are supported through separate native or offline-enabled apps.

Joule Work mobile app supports secure single sign-on (SSO) using SAML or OIDC and integrates with common identity providers (IdPs) such as SAP IAS, Microsoft Azure AD, Okta, Ping, and ADFS. It works with mobile device management (MDM) and unified endpoint management (UEM) for conditional access, app protection, and remote wipe. Security is further defined by backend authorizations, content security policy, and SAP BTP or SAP Build Work Zone settings to determine the final security posture. Once configured, users can securely access SAP applications without repeated logins.

products/scm/apm/what-is-predictive-main.title: What Is Predictive Maintenance? | SAP
products/scm/apm/what-is-predictive-main.description: Learn what predictive maintenance is, how it works, key technologies involved, and how businesses can implement effective, data‑driven maintenance programs.
products/scm/apm/what-is-predictive-main.body:
What Is

What is predictive maintenance?

Predictive maintenance is the continuous, real-time assessment of equipment health to maximize performance and lifespan.

Updated on May 28, 2026

Predictive maintenance definition

Predictive maintenance is a proactive approach to equipment upkeep that uses data, sensors, and analytics to determine the real-time condition of machinery.

At a high level, predictive maintenance helps businesses reduce downtime, extend equipment life, and optimize maintenance resources. By acting only when data indicates a need, companies avoid unnecessary service calls and minimize unexpected breakdowns, ultimately improving efficiency and lowering total operating costs.

Predictive maintenance vs. preventive maintenance

Both predictive and preventive maintenance involve performing the same types of maintenance tasks—be it replacing parts, servicing equipment, or fixing malfunctions—the key difference isn’t in the “how,” but the “when.”

Preventive maintenance follows a fixed schedule informed by past performance and the knowledge and experience of engineers and operators. It helps avoid obvious failures or breakdowns, but is also imprecise, relying on the expected condition of equipment. This can lead to expensive maintenance before it’s needed or to unnoticed weaknesses in the maintenance process.

Predictive maintenance, in contrast, provides continuous, real-time insight into the equipment's actual condition. By monitoring performance indicators—such as vibration, temperature, or usage patterns—to identify early signs of wear or failure and then applying advanced analytics to that data, businesses can anticipate equipment failures and schedule maintenance when and where it’s immediately needed.

The importance of predictive maintenance

Predictive maintenance has become essential as businesses increasingly rely on complex, digitally connected equipment to keep operations running smoothly. Even brief, unplanned outages can create costly production delays, missed service commitments, and downstream operational disruption.

By applying technologies like AI and machine learning (ML), predictive maintenance helps teams detect subtle patterns and anomalies in equipment behavior. Being able to spot issues long before they disrupt operations enables smoother, more reliable performance across the business.

It also plays a strategic role in resource optimization. Modern operations depend on the efficient use of labor, parts, and capital assets, and predictive maintenance enables teams to deploy these resources with greater precision. Rather than reacting to failures or performing maintenance simply because it’s “time,” organizations can target their efforts based on actual conditions. This results in fewer emergency repairs, less wasted maintenance effort, and more predictable budgeting.

Over time, this translates to lower replacement costs and a more resilient operational foundation—an increasingly important advantage as companies work to maintain reliability while managing tight margins and complex supply chains.

How does predictive maintenance work?

Predictive maintenance works by capturing and analyzing equipment data in real time to predict potential issues before they lead to equipment failure. There are four basic stages of operation in the predictive maintenance process:

  1. Gathering machine data through physical sensors
  2. Transmitting live data from the sensors to a central business system
  3. Using smart technologies like AI and ML analytics to draw insights from the data
  4. Taking action based on these predictive insights

Key predictive maintenance technologies

The following technologies form the backbone of modern predictive maintenance, enabling organizations to capture equipment data, analyze it intelligently, and translate insights into timely, proactive action.

  • IoT networks connect equipment, sensors, and devices across facilities to capture real-time data. IoT networks act as the foundation of predictive maintenance by enabling continuous condition monitoring at scale.
  • Cloud-connectivity enables seamless transmission, storage, and access to equipment data across distributed sites. Cloud-connected systems support real-time monitoring, faster analytics, and centralized visibility—making it easier for teams to act on predictive maintenance insights from anywhere.
  • IoT gateways serve as intermediaries between equipment and the cloud, securely aggregating, filtering, and transmitting sensor data. They ensure high-quality, reliable data reaches the analytical systems.
  • A modern ERP consolidates operational, maintenance, and financial data in one system. Cloud ERP platforms support predictive maintenance by integrating real-time sensor data with work orders, inventory availability, and asset histories to streamline response and planning.
  • AI and machine learning analyze large volumes of equipment data to detect anomalies, identify emerging patterns, and predict failures earlier and more accurately than manual methods. These models improve over time as more data is collected.
  • Advanced analytics apply statistical models, trend analysis, and visualization techniques to help teams interpret equipment behavior. They provide actionable insights that guide maintenance timing, resource allocation, and long-term asset strategy.
  • Digital twins create virtual models of physical assets, allowing organizations to simulate performance, predict behavior, and test “what‑if” scenarios. Digital twins make predictive maintenance more precise by combining real-time data with virtual modeling.

Real-world predictive maintenance use cases

Predictive maintenance plays a vital role across many industries, with well‑established, real‑world applications that help keep critical assets running reliably and efficiently.

Automotive manufacturing

Robotics‑driven assembly lines use predictive maintenance to track joint torque, actuator heat, and welding arm alignment. Small deviations can signal calibration drift or mechanical fatigue, allowing maintenance teams to fix issues before they cause production errors or quality defects.

Alternative energy

Wind farms monitor gearbox vibration signatures, blade pitch adjustments, and generator temperature to detect micro‑fractures or lubrication issues. Predictive models help schedule repairs during low‑wind periods, maximizing power output while preventing catastrophic turbine failures.

Rail transportation

Rail operators use predictive maintenance to analyze wheel‑rail interaction forces, axle temperature, and braking system wear. Early detection of flat spots or bearing degradation helps avoid derailments and keeps trains running safely on schedule.

Oil and gas

In upstream and downstream operations, predictive maintenance monitors equipment like drills, compressors, pipelines, and pumps operating in harsh conditions. By analyzing pressure data, flow rates, and material fatigue indicators, companies can detect corrosion or mechanical stress early to prevent large‑scale environmental incidents and avoid costly emergency shutdowns.

Commercial facilities and smart buildings

Commercial buildings use predictive maintenance to manage HVAC systems, elevators, generators, and other critical infrastructure. Sensors and AI models detect anomalies such as inefficient airflow or abnormal energy consumption. This ensures comfortable environments, reduces energy usage, and cuts the cost of reactive repairs.

What are the benefits of predictive maintenance?

Predictive maintenance delivers value far beyond reducing equipment failures and avoiding unnecessary or expensive repairs—other significant benefits of implementing a predictive maintenance model include:

  • Improved employee safety
    By identifying equipment risks early, predictive maintenance reduces the likelihood of accidents, ensuring safer conditions for technicians, operators, and frontline teams.
  • Higher workforce productivity
    Maintenance teams spend less time on unnecessary inspections or emergency repairs and more time on strategic, planned work. This leads to smoother workflows, fewer disruptions, and better use of employee expertise.
  • More reliable and consistent operations
    Predictive insights enable teams to schedule maintenance at optimal times, minimizing workflow interruptions and helping operations maintain steady performance throughout the day.
  • Enhanced coordination across departments
    Because predictive maintenance integrates data across IoT systems, ERP platforms, and analytics tools, it improves communication between operations, maintenance, finance, and procurement teams. Everyone works from the same real-time information, reducing delays and rework.
  • Stronger regulatory and compliance performance
    In industries with strict safety, environmental, or quality standards, predictive maintenance helps organizations demonstrate proper asset monitoring and timely intervention—simplifying audits and reducing compliance risk.
  • A better customer experience
    Reliable equipment leads to more dependable production schedules, consistent product quality, and fewer service delays—all of which improve customer satisfaction and strengthen trust.
  • More sustainable operations
    Early detection of inefficiencies helps reduce waste, lower energy consumption, and support corporate sustainability goals.

Drive asset reliability with AI

See how asset-intensive companies can use AI-assisted visual inspection to improve reliability and lower costs.

Watch video

Overcoming common predictive maintenance challenges

Implementing predictive maintenance can unlock substantial value, but the adoption process is not without challenges. Fortunately, many of these obstacles can be overcome with thoughtful planning, the right tools, and strong cross‑functional alignment.

  • Data quality and consistency
    Many predictive maintenance programs struggle because equipment data is incomplete, inconsistent, or siloed. Standardizing data collection, ensuring sensors are properly calibrated, and integrating systems can help create a reliable foundation for accurate insights.
  • Lack of technical skills or specialized expertise
    Teams may not initially have the analytics or AI skills needed to build and interpret predictive models. Upskilling maintenance staff, partnering with technology vendors, or using solutions with built-in automation and user-friendly dashboards can make advanced capabilities more accessible.
  • Legacy equipment
    Older machines were not built with sensors or connectivity in mind, making data collection challenging. Retrofitting them with add-on sensors, edge devices, or IoT gateways allows organizations to capture meaningful data without replacing costly assets.
  • Change management and cultural resistance
    Maintenance teams accustomed to reactive or scheduled maintenance may hesitate to rely on data-driven approaches. Clear communication, hands-on training, and demonstrating early wins can help build trust and encourage adoption.
  • Cybersecurity and data governance risks
    Connected equipment increases exposure to cybersecurity risks. Implementing strong access controls, secure data transmission practices, and regular security audits ensures that predictive maintenance systems remain protected while still delivering value.

How to implement a predictive maintenance program

Implementing a predictive maintenance program requires a structured, step‑by‑step approach that aligns the right technologies, processes, and people to deliver reliable, scalable results.

1. Define your goals and decide where to start

Begin by identifying what you want predictive maintenance to achieve—whether that’s improving safety, reducing last‑minute emergencies, or making daily operations run more smoothly. From there, decide which equipment or processes you want to include first. Starting with a specific group of high‑value or high‑risk assets keeps the effort manageable and helps you demonstrate quick wins.

2. Match each piece of equipment with the right monitoring approach

Different machines show early warning signs in different ways, so the next step is deciding how to monitor them. For example, rotating equipment may require vibration sensing, while slow‑moving machines are better suited for oil or sound analysis. The goal is simply to understand what “healthy” looks like for each asset and choose the right tools to spot changes.

3. Install sensors and begin collecting data

Once you know what you want to measure, add the appropriate sensors to your equipment so you can begin gathering information. These might measure heat, vibration, sound, fluid quality, or other indicators of asset health. Starting with a small, focused set of sensors helps you avoid unnecessary complexity and ensures the data you collect is actually useful.

4. Connect your systems so data flows smoothly

To make the information meaningful, ensure that sensor data can be viewed and used in the systems your teams already rely on—such as your maintenance software or ERP. This often involves sending data to a central, ideally cloud-based platform where it can be organized and shared. When everything is connected, maintenance teams, operations, and planners can all see the same information and act quickly.

5. Turn your data into insights

After your data is flowing, use analytical tools, including AI and ML, to spot unusual patterns or signs that something may be starting to fail. These tools help you highlight issues early, often before a person would notice them. The goal isn’t to replace expertise, but to give your teams another set of “eyes and ears” on the equipment.

6. Create clear processes for responding to alerts

Once your system identifies a potential issue, your teams need a consistent way to respond. This could include sending an automatic notification, creating a maintenance work order, or routing a task to the right technician. Clear, agreed‑upon steps help ensure issues get addressed quickly and efficiently—without confusion or delays.

7. Start with a pilot and learn as you go

Run your predictive maintenance program on a small scale first to test your approach and understand what’s working. Use this time to gather feedback from technicians, adjust thresholds that trigger alerts, and refine data collection. Small pilots help build confidence and create early success stories before expanding to more assets or sites.

8. Keep refining your program

Predictive maintenance isn’t a one‑time project—it’s an ongoing improvement effort. Continue collecting feedback, updating your processes, retraining models, and fine‑tuning how alerts are handled. As your program matures, it will become more accurate, more trusted, and more valuable to the entire business.

Together, these practices and technologies empower organizations to operate more safely, efficiently, and intelligently—delivering long‑term reliability and resilience across the entire business.

products/scm/commodity-management/featur.body:
Features
Overview

SAP Commodity Management features

Request a demo
Contact us

Commodity Physicals

Advanced commodity pricing engine

  • Integrate commodity pricing and calculation capabilities across purchase and sales orders, contracts, invoices, and settlement processes.

  • Define pricing formulas using a flexible, rules-based framework aligned to your business and market requirements. 

  • Use centralized commodity market data as a single source of truth for consistency, accuracy, and transparency across transactions. 

Expense management for commodity businesses

  • Centralize and govern your expense rule framework in a single, flexible model to ensure consistency, transparency, and control.

  • Automatically assign expenses to relevant documents across the process chain to ensure accurate and consistent financial tracking.

  • Adapt to changing business requirements with a fully flexible and configurable expense management approach.

  • Integrate expense data into reporting and analytics to gain clear visibility into cost drivers, compliance, and financial performance.

 

FX risk management for commodity businesses

  • Automatically determine commodity price exposure directly from physical documents, ensuring timely and accurate risk visibility. 

  • Execute a fully automated hedging flow to reduce manual intervention and improve operational efficiency. 

  • Support multiple hedging strategies, including accumulation, netting, and direct hedging, for diverse risk management approaches. 

  • Utilize native integration with treasury and risk management systems for seamless processing and control across operations. 

SAP Commodity Management, AI-assisted commodity work center

  • Generate contracts using natural language, accelerating contract creation while maintaining consistency and control. 

  • Reduce manual effort and operational complexity with a highly automated framework that adapts across contract types. 

  • Guide users with prefiltered, context-aware options to ensure accurate contract outcomes when inputs are incomplete or ambiguous. 

SAP Agricultural Contract Management

  • Consolidate complex agricultural terms and conditions into a single source of truth, to govern commodity contracts and mitigate risk. 

  • Support partial and differential pricing with fixed and unfixed prices, from contract to invoice.  

  • Track delivered load details and apply them during contract application and settlement, with adjustments created automatically. 

Link to ACM product page 

Commodity derivatives

Manage derivatives

  • Support a broad range of exchange-traded instruments, including futures and listed options, as well as OTC instruments.

  • Operate on centralized commodity market data to ensure consistent valuation, pricing, and risk assessment across instruments.

  • Integrate into valuation processes and accounting postings to ensure accurate financial representation and compliance.

  • Use the Derivative Contract Specification framework with position management to maintain control over derivative exposures.

Commodity derivative order and trade execution

  • Create and place hedge orders directly from physical documents, simplifying the transition from operational exposure to risk management.

  • Receive and process broker confirmations via FIX protocol messages to ensure fast, reliable, and standardized communication. 

  • Automatically create corresponding hedge positions within your system, reducing manual effort and operational risk. 

  • Feed hedge transactions directly into risk reporting to provide real-time visibility into exposure and hedging effectiveness. 

Commodity hedge accounting

  • Enable IFRS 9–compliant cash flow hedge accounting to ensure regulatory adherence and financial transparency.

  • Support commodity swaps and commodity forwards to cover a wide range of hedging instruments. 

  • Automate hedge accounting postings to reduce manual effort and operational risk. 

  • Support fully automated on‑behalf‑of hedging scenarios to manage centralized risk strategies across entities. 

Broker reconciliation for commodity derivatives

  • Automate reconciliation processes to investigate and resolve deviations with less human intervention.

  • Efficiently identify missing and erroneous trades and positions to decrease commodity risk exposure. 

  • Support fast, efficient, and accurate commodity trade and position reconciliation with a standardized cloud solution. 

Link to Broker Reconciliation product page 

Commodity risk analytics

Commodity risk analytics is key in assessing risk resulting from commodity transactions and enables timely hedging to protect margins

  • Gain a full view of commodity price risk exposure across both physical documents and derivative instruments.

  • Obtain a quantity-based overview of hedged and unhedged positions to clearly understand your current risk profile. 

  • Value physical documents and derivative contracts against current market data using mark-to-market risk reports for accurate assessments. 

  • Analyze trading performance with detailed profit and loss reporting to identify gains, losses, and key value drivers.
