Workflow management technologies

Modern workflow technology offers a broad range of capabilities to automate tasks and support strategic decision-making. These technologies enable organizations to streamline operations and improve outcomes. Discover how these key technologies can enhance workflow efficiency.

Big Data technology

Big Data refers to the vast datasets that traditional data processing tools can’t handle efficiently. Big Data technologies allow organizations to store, process, and analyze this complex information. In workflow management, Big Data technology channels accurate, real-time data into workflows, which helps teams automate tasks and optimize processes.

Workflow automation use case: Collect and organize data from both structured and unstructured sources to automatically generate financial reports.

AI agents

AI agents are autonomous systems that use artificial intelligence to make decisions and perform tasks without constant human input. With proper IT oversight and reliable data to maintain clear business context, these applications can automate more complex, multistep workflows. Agents can be tailored to perform roles for specific business areas and collaborate to complete cross-functional tasks.

Workflow automation use case: Deploy AI agents to monitor incoming service requests, prioritize them based on urgency, and automatically assign tasks to the appropriate team.

Machine learning

Machine learning (ML) is a branch of artificial intelligence (AI) that allows systems to analyze data, recognize patterns, and make predictions. ML-enabled systems can also learn from past data to fine-tune their performance over time. This makes ML ideal for automating workflows with dynamic variables, such as forecasting, anomaly detection, and recommendation engines.

Workflow automation use case: Predict inventory needs by analyzing historical sales, weather patterns, and seasonal trends—reducing stockouts and waste.

Natural language processing

Natural language processing (NLP) helps systems interpret and generate written or spoken human language. This technology powers modern features like chatbots, virtual assistants, and automated document handling. For workflow management tasks, these capabilities reduce manual interventions in communication-heavy processes by automating routine inquiries and approvals.

Workflow automation use case: Use an NLP-driven chatbot to handle high-volume queries about invoice status or purchase orders, freeing staff for more complex tasks.

Computer vision

Computer vision enables systems to interpret and analyze visual data from images and videos. In workflows, this AI tool helps organizations automate inspections, monitor infrastructure, and support predictive maintenance by extracting actionable insights from visual inputs. Teams can reduce their reliance on manual checks and improve accuracy in processes that require visual validation.

Workflow automation use case: Prevent costly outages by analyzing satellite images to detect infrastructure risks and automatically launch maintenance workflows.

Robotic process automation

Robotic process automation (RPA) uses software bots to mimic human interactions with digital systems, executing repetitive tasks quickly and accurately. In workflow management, RPA can bridge integration gaps, reduce manual data entry, and accelerate processes without major system overhauls. RPA is ideal for high-volume, rule-based tasks that consume valuable time and resources.

Workflow automation use case: Automate the transfer of supplier data from emails into ERP systems, eliminating manual processing.

Business workflow management and automation trends

Organizations are seeking faster, smarter, and more scalable ways to automate processes. To meet these demands, today’s workflow management innovations focus on reducing manual effort and improving system agility. From AI-enabled solutions to smarter analytics, these key trends are reshaping how businesses design and execute workflows.

  • Intelligent automation: Advanced workflows combine AI tools like agents, NLP, and RPA to handle complex tasks and unstructured data for smarter automation.
  • Predictive workflow optimization: Process analytics uses workflow data to identify bottlenecks and recommend improvements to enhance efficiency.
  • Ecosystem integration: Workflow management platforms can connect across disparate systems and applications to support fluid workflows across teams.
  • Prebuilt content: Solutions provide ready-made templates and workflow components to accelerate deployment and reduce development workloads.
  • Built-in security and governance: Compliance checks, encryption, and access controls are directly embedded into workflows to ensure trust and regulatory adherence.

Roles and skills for workflow management

Effective workflow management isn’t just about adopting the right technology—it’s also about fostering collaboration. Processes work best when teams can combine their skill sets and coordinate across departments. When people understand their responsibilities and work together, workflows become more efficient and adaptable. Here are a few team development strategies to consider when building a strong workflow management foundation.

Core workflow management skills

Companies don’t need major technical or organizational overhauls to start improving workflows. Modern business applications often include preconfigured workflows built on best practices. Many advanced tools are also business user-friendly, making workflow optimization accessible for organizations of all sizes. To make the most of these applications, focus on nurturing these essential skills:

  • Project management: Coordinate responsibilities to complete workflow tasks on time and within scope.
  • Technical proficiency: Understand how to use the relevant workflow management platforms and automation tools.
  • Communication and collaboration: Work effectively with cross-functional teams to streamline workflows.
  • Adaptability: Learn and adopt emerging technologies like low-code workflows and AI.
  • Compliance and risk awareness: Comply with workflow regulatory requirements and risk management policies.

Common workflow management roles

Organizations will also need specialized business and technical roles to harmonize strategic goals and execution. Together, these roles ensure that workflows are well-designed, properly implemented, and continuously fine-tuned.

Business-oriented roles:

  • Workflow manager: Oversees workflow design and implementation to confirm they align with business goals and compliance.
  • Business process analyst: Maps and analyzes workflows to identify inefficiencies and recommend improvements for operational efficiency.
  • Project manager: Plans and executes workflow-related projects—managing timelines, resources, and stakeholder communications to deliver successful results.

Technical roles:

  • Solution architect: Designs the overall workflow automation architecture to enable scalability, integration, and security.
  • Automation developer: Builds and maintains automated workflows to streamline repetitive tasks.
  • System administrator: Manages workflow platforms by configuring systems, handling permissions, and troubleshooting technical issues.

How to get started with workflow management

Implementing a new workflow management program requires a structured, strategic approach. People, processes, and systems must adapt to new ways of operating. This alignment is critical for creating workflows that deliver measurable business value. Learn how to implement workflow management transformations to build and sustain a successful transformation.

Workflow management best practices:

  • Assess processes and define goals: Review existing workflows to identify inefficiencies and set clear goals to target areas needing improvement.
  • Prepare data systems: Ensure data is clean, consistent, and reliable so automation runs smoothly and delivers accurate results.
  • Engage stakeholders: Involve business and technical teams early to support alignment and collaboration.
  • Choose the right tools: Select workflow management platforms and automation technologies that fit specific organizational needs.
  • Design and document workflows: Map out processes visually and document responsibilities to ensure clarity.
  • Implement and optimize: Start with a pilot program to measure results and expand workflows gradually across departments, tracking metrics to refine performance results.

Quick answers: How can midsize organizations jump-start workflow automation?

Midsize companies can still reap the benefits of workflow automation—all without major technical infrastructure and team investments. Prebuilt workflows in modern business applications enable organizations to automate processes quickly and cost-effectively, allowing teams to focus on growth and innovation.

FAQ

  • What is a workflow process?

    A workflow process is a sequence of tasks that moves work from initiation to completion. For example, an approval workflow might include submitting a request, reviewing details, approving or revising content, and notifying stakeholders.

  • What is meant by workflow management?

    Workflow management is the practice of designing, executing, and monitoring workflows so tasks remain efficient, consistent, and aligned with business goals.

  • Can workflow software solve all my process automation needs?

    Workflow software can automate routine tasks and improve visibility, but some complex automation scenarios may require additional tools like business process management (BPM) platforms or custom integrations.

  • What are some examples of workflow management?

    Examples include employee onboarding, invoice approvals, content publishing, customer support ticket handling, and procurement processes—all structured to streamline tasks and reduce delays.

  • What skills are needed for workflow management?

    Key skills include project management, technical proficiency with workflow tools, communication and collaboration, adaptability to new technologies, and compliance awareness.

  • What are the basic steps of a workflow?

    Typical steps include:

    • Initiation: Define the task or request.
    • Assignment: Allocate responsibilities.
    • Execution: Perform the tasks.
    • Review: Check for accuracy and compliance.
    • Completion: Close the workflow and record outcomes.

products/scm/asset-management-eam/what-i.body:
What Is

What is enterprise asset management?

Enterprise asset management (EAM) manages physical assets across their lifecycles. This article explains how it works and why it matters.

Updated on May 28, 2026

Enterprise asset management overview

Enterprise asset management is the practice of managing physical assets so they are available, reliable, and safe to use over time.

For organizations that depend on equipment, vehicles, facilities, or infrastructure, assets affect everyday operations. When an asset fails, work stops. Costs rise. Safety risks increase. Customer commitments can be missed. EAM helps organizations avoid those outcomes by keeping asset information accurate, current, and shared across teams.

EAM software brings together data about assets, maintenance work, inspections, spare parts, and people. Instead of being scattered across spreadsheets, paper records, or disconnected tools, this information lives in one place and follows the asset through its lifecycle.

This makes it easier for maintenance, operations, finance, and planning teams to coordinate their work. Maintenance can be scheduled before failures occur. Asset availability can be aligned with production and service plans. Decisions about repair, replacement, or retirement can be based on real conditions rather than assumptions.

In short, EAM helps organizations take better care of the assets they rely on while supporting reliable operations, lower costs, and safer working environments.

How does an EAM system work?

Modern EAM systems are typically run on a cloud platform and are designed to operate alongside supply chain management systems, finance, and workforce applications. Rather than functioning in isolation, EAM contributes asset intelligence to a harmonized, semantically consistent data foundation that spans operational, transactional, and network-level systems.

This shared foundation helps ensure that asset information—such as condition, availability, risk, and maintenance status—is consistent, contextualized, and usable across planning, manufacturing, logistics, service, and finance processes.

At a practical level, EAM systems focus on a few core activities that help teams understand asset condition, plan maintenance, and coordinate work.

Centralizing and governing asset data

EAM systems collect and manage asset data from multiple sources, including inspections, work orders, maintenance histories, sensor readings, and connected enterprise applications. This information is consolidated into a single, governed view of each asset and its lifecycle.

By maintaining consistent definitions and data structures, organizations reduce errors, eliminate duplication, and improve trust in asset information across the business.

Interpreting asset data in context

Once asset data is harmonized, analytics can be applied to understand how assets behave under real operating conditions. Performance trends, degradation patterns, and risk indicators become visible when asset data is evaluated alongside production plans, demand signals, and supply constraints.

This contextual insight supports more proactive maintenance strategies and helps organizations detect potential disruptions earlier—before they affect service levels or customer commitments.

Planning and executing maintenance work

EAM systems integrate maintenance planning, scheduling, and execution. Work orders can be prioritized based on asset criticality, operational impact, safety risk, and regulatory requirements.

By coordinating maintenance activities with workforce availability, spare parts, and production schedules, organizations reduce unplanned downtime and improve schedule adherence.

Supporting mobile and field-based teams

Many asset-intensive operations rely on workers in the field. EAM systems provide mobile access to asset records, inspection checklists, work instructions, and maintenance histories, even in offline environments.

Capturing updates at the point of work improves data accuracy and helps ensure that asset information remains current and actionable across the organization.

Key capabilities of enterprise asset management

While implementations vary by industry, most enterprise asset management systems support a common set of capabilities:

  • Asset lifecycle tracking: Maintains a complete history of each asset, including digital twin representations that reflect condition and performance over time.
  • Maintenance management: Plans, schedules, and executes preventive, corrective, and condition-based maintenance.
  • Inspection and compliance management: Standardizes inspections, captures results, and maintains auditable records.
  • Workforce and resource coordination: Aligns skills, tools, materials, and schedules with maintenance needs.
  • Performance monitoring and analytics: Tracks reliability, cost drivers, and asset health over time.
  • Integration with enterprise systems: Connects asset data with finance, supply chain, human resources, and geographic information systems.

Together, these capabilities allow organizations to manage assets as interconnected components of their supply chain rather than as standalone pieces of equipment.

Benefits of EAM systems

When enterprise asset management is applied consistently, organizations typically see improvements across cost control, asset reliability, and resource efficiency. These benefits are driven by better visibility into asset condition, more disciplined maintenance processes, and stronger coordination between maintenance and operations.

Lower maintenance and operating costs

Industry research shows that organizations using structured maintenance systems can significantly reduce maintenance spend while improving asset availability. Studies of CMMS and EAM practices indicate maintenance cost reductions in the range of 10% to 15%, alongside uptime improvements of up to 20%, when maintenance activities are planned and executed more consistently.

When maintenance systems are integrated with connected asset data, organizations can detect abnormal operating conditions earlier and intervene before failures occur. This earlier intervention helps avoid emergency repairs and secondary damage, contributing to maintenance cost reductions of up to 30% in more mature, data-enabled environments.

Improved asset availability and reliability

By standardizing maintenance processes and improving visibility into asset condition, EAM helps organizations reduce unplanned downtime. Maintenance work can be prioritized based on asset criticality and operational impact, rather than reacting to failures after they occur.

As a result, assets remain available for production, service, and transportation more consistently, supporting operational stability and customer commitments.

More effective spare parts management

Spare parts management is a persistent challenge in asset-intensive operations. Without reliable asset data, organizations often overstock parts to reduce risk or struggle with shortages when failures occur.

Research on maintenance and inventory practices shows that EAM supports better spare parts decisions by linking parts usage to actual asset condition, failure history, and maintenance plans. This improves forecasting accuracy, reduces excess inventory, and lowers the risk of stockouts—without relying on blanket safety stock strategies.

Energy efficiency and resource optimization

Asset condition has a direct impact on energy consumption. Industry guidance from the US Department of Energy shows that well-maintained equipment can operate with 15% to 20% less energy than degraded or poorly maintained assets.

By keeping assets operating within design parameters and addressing inefficiencies early, EAM helps organizations reduce energy waste, lower operating costs, and support sustainability goals—particularly in energy-intensive industries.

Stronger safety, compliance, and risk management

EAM systems support standardized inspections, documented maintenance histories, and auditable records. This consistency helps organizations demonstrate compliance with regulatory requirements and manage operational risk more effectively.

Proactive maintenance also reduces the likelihood of asset failures that can lead to safety incidents, environmental damage, or service disruptions—protecting workers, communities, and the business.

The role of asset collaboration in EAM

Asset collaboration extends enterprise asset management beyond organizational boundaries by enabling coordinated processes and information sharing among stakeholders involved in asset design, construction, operation, and maintenance.

Effective asset collaboration software supports EAM in several ways, including:

  • Shared asset data: A single source of truth accessible to internal teams and external partners.
  • Knowledge sharing and documentation: Field-accessible manuals, warranties, inspection records, and asset documentation.
  • Cross-functional coordination: Structured handovers between engineering, operations, and maintenance teams.
  • Collaborative maintenance planning: Better alignment among owners, operators, service providers, and suppliers.
  • Workflow automation: Digital processes that reduce manual effort and minimize errors across the asset lifecycle.

By breaking down silos, asset collaboration helps organizations improve reliability while reducing commissioning, maintenance, and lifecycle costs.

The evolution of enterprise asset management

Historically, asset management systems were deployed on premises and designed to support specific asset types or locations. Data was fragmented across multiple systems, making it difficult to gain a cohesive view of asset performance.

Maintenance decisions often relied on manual inspections, paper-based processes, and individual experience. As a result, information was frequently outdated or incomplete, and maintenance strategies were largely reactive.

Today, enterprise asset management has evolved into a connected, cloud-based discipline. Modern systems collect data from diverse assets and systems in real time, enabling faster analysis and more informed decision-making. Advances in artificial intelligence help organizations interpret this asset data in context and support earlier risk identification.

Several complementary technologies have contributed to this evolution, including:

  • Advanced analytics to identify trends and risks.
  • Integration with supply chain systems to align maintenance with parts availability.
  • Location technologies such as GIS and GPS for managing linear and remote assets.
  • Imaging technologies, including drones and satellite data, for inspections.
  • IoT sensors that provide continuous visibility into asset condition.

Together, these capabilities allow organizations to manage assets proactively and at scale while adapting to changing market and supply conditions.

EAM vs. CMMS: What’s the difference?

A computerized maintenance management system (CMMS) focuses on managing maintenance activities that keep equipment running, such as work orders, preventive maintenance schedules, and repairs.

Enterprise asset management addresses a broader scope by managing assets across their full lifecycle and connecting maintenance activities to financial, operational, and strategic outcomes.

Feature

CMMS

EAM

Primary goal

Maximize equipment uptime

Optimize total cost of ownership

Core users

Maintenance and operations

Maintenance, finance, HR, procurement

Asset lifecycle coverage

Operation and maintenance

Design through retirement

Scope

Typically single-site

Multi-site and enterprise-wide

Integrations

Limited

Deep enterprise integration

Maintenance approach

Preventive and reactive

Predictive, prescriptive, reliability-centered

Organizations often adopt CMMS to improve maintenance efficiency, then move to EAM as asset complexity increases and lifecycle visibility becomes more important.

EAM examples across industries

Enterprise asset management supports a wide range of asset-intensive industries by adapting to different asset types, operating environments, and regulatory requirements.

Production asset management

In manufacturing, warehouse, and assembly environments, asset availability directly affects production output, work safety, and environmental performance. EAM helps organizations coordinate maintenance activities with production schedules, helping ensure that critical equipment is serviced before failures disrupt operations.

For example, Hungrana uses enterprise asset management to support world-class maintenance across its production facilities. By standardizing maintenance processes and improving visibility into asset condition, Hungrana strengthened equipment reliability while also supporting worker safety and environmental protection across its operations.

Linear asset management

Organizations responsible for roads, railways, pipelines, and electricity transmission lines manage assets that are geographically dispersed and continuously in use. EAM supports these environments by combining asset hierarchies, inspection histories, and location data to help teams plan maintenance without interrupting service.

In the rail sector, DSB relies on digital asset management to maintain more than 3,000 kilometers of track and support over 500,000 daily travelers. By managing linear assets with consistent data and planning processes, DSB improves service reliability while coordinating maintenance across a complex national network.

Mobile workforce management

Many asset-intensive organizations depend on technicians working in the field to inspect, maintain, and repair equipment. EAM enables mobile workforce management by giving workers access to asset information, inspection checklists, and maintenance histories wherever the work happens.

At Jet Aviation, mobile access to asset data supports technicians performing inspections and maintenance across global operations. Field teams can capture updates as work is completed so asset records remain accurate and immediately available for planning and compliance purposes.

Natural resources and mining

In mining and natural resource production, asset performance and availability are critical for both safety and productivity. Equipment often operates in harsh or regulated environments, making consistent inspection and maintenance essential.

Spirit Energy uses enterprise asset management to support inspections of equipment operating in potentially explosive (Ex/ATEX) environments. By improving visibility into asset condition and inspection status, Spirit Energy strengthened operational safety while reducing the risk of unplanned disruptions.

EAM FAQs

  • How is an EAM system deployed?

    While EAM systems were traditionally deployed on premises, most modern implementations are cloud-based. Cloud deployment supports scalability, faster updates, and easier integration, making EAM accessible to organizations of all sizes.

  • How does EAM integrate with existing systems?

    EAM systems integrate with enterprise applications such as finance, supply chain, human resources, and geographic information systems. This integration helps ensure asset decisions are aligned with broader business processes and constraints.

  • How does EAM support sustainability goals?

    By improving asset performance and reducing unnecessary maintenance activities, EAM helps organizations lower energy consumption, reduce emissions, and minimize environmental impact. Optimized maintenance routes also reduce fuel use and waste.

  • How does EAM help manage risk and liability?

    EAM provides standardized inspection records, maintenance histories, and audit trails that support compliance and accountability. Proactive maintenance reduces the likelihood of failures that can result in safety incidents, environmental damage, or regulatory penalties.

  • Why would an organization choose CMMS instead of EAM?

    Organizations focused primarily on maintenance execution and asset uptime may choose CMMS. Those that require full lifecycle visibility, cross-functional coordination, and enterprise-wide asset insight typically adopt EAM.

resources/api-integration.html.body:
What Is

What API integration is and how it transforms enterprise IT

APIs are building blocks. Learn how API integration connects them and enables data flow, automation, and agility across enterprise systems.

Published on June 18, 2025

What is API integration?

API integration, in its simplest form, enables applications, systems, and services to work together as a cohesive whole.

Using an integration platform is perhaps the best way to combine and manage multiple APIs to help achieve business transformation goals. It prevents API sprawl, bridges the gap between old and new systems, strengthens security, and helps maintain compliance—making businesses more agile and future-ready.

Understanding the difference between API integration and APIs

APIs and API integration are closely related, but are not the same:

  • API: A set of rules that allows different software applications to communicate with one another. APIs define how data is requested, sent, and received—making connections between systems possible.
  • API integration: The process of using APIs to connect systems, enabling seamless data exchanges and coordinated functionality across applications, platforms, departments, and environments.

The difference between an API and API integration lies in capability versus implementation. An API provides the rules and protocols that enable communication between systems—it’s the interface.

An API integration uses those APIs to build real, functioning connections between applications. It turns potential into performance by allowing data, services, and workflows to move fluidly across a company’s digital ecosystem.

Commonly used APIs for business integration

Before diving into integrations, it’s important to understand the common architectural APIs to enable integration across departments, platforms, and ecosystems.

  • RESTful APIs are the most used type for web-based services and are ideal for cloud services, mobile applications, and IOT devices.
  • SOAP APIs handle transaction management and offer a high level of security, which makes them a good fit for CRM systems and financial services enterprise applications.
  • OData APIs promote efficient data retrieval and are ideal for organizations looking to improve interoperability and streamline data access.
  • GraphQL APIs provide a flexible alternative to REST and allow clients to request the data they need.

These APIs power integrations between HR platforms, finance systems, logistics platforms, customer engagement tools, and more—turning disparate systems into a cohesive digital ecosystem.

The critical role of API integration in enterprise architecture

API integrations enable connectivity across platforms, automate workflows, and strengthen the user experience for modern enterprise systems. API integration provides the connective tissue that ensures systems like ERP, CRM, HCM, and data platforms speak the same language.

Some of the most common API integrations involve connecting CRM software with other enterprise systems, such as ERP. Through the transfer of data, the integration creates a single, accurate source.

4 benefits of API integration services for enterprises

1. Connecting fragmented landscapes

Enterprises operate across diverse ecosystems that include:

  • SaaS applications that evolve rapidly and need to integrate with core business processes
  • On-premises systems that are deeply embedded and still critical to operations
  • Data lakes and analytics platforms that require real-time, high-quality data inputs
  • Mobile applications and edge devices that need to connect to backend systems securely

2. Scaling and agility

Agility is no longer just a competitive advantage—it’s a necessity. API integration gives enterprises the flexibility and resilience needed to move business forward by allowing them to:

  • Scale operations efficiently and handle increased workloads and new users without architectural rewrites
  • Adapt to change and integrate new services without disruption to core systems
  • Reduce technical debt by decoupling applications and fostering loosely coupled services

3. Composability

API integration tools enable the composable enterprise—an architectural model that delivers digital capabilities as modular, reusable components. By exposing services and data through APIs, organizations can:

  • Orchestrate workflows across departments and platforms
  • Rapidly build and reconfigure digital experiences
  • Accelerate time-to-value with reusable integrations

Modularity helps reduce development time and increase innovation because it allows enterprises to mix and match capabilities without rebuilding from scratch.

4. Improve governance

Strong governance is key to addressing increasing integration complexity. API integration helps enterprises maintain:

  • Consistent security policies and role-based access controls
  • Compliance by ensuring integrations meet industry and regional regulatory standards
  • Visibility into performance, failures, and optimizations

API integration use cases

Businesses are using API integration to unlock new opportunities for growth on the front and back ends. Here are a few practical ways enterprise organizations are using API integration to break down barriers between systems, accelerate transformation, and build a composable foundation for growth:

Omnichannel engagement

Retailers integrate their CRM systems, e-commerce platforms, and mobile apps to create a personalized and consistent customer journey to unify disconnected systems and support real-time visibility.

Connected supply chain

Manufacturing and logistics firms integrate supplier, warehouse, and transportation data to enable real-time tracking, demand-driven replenishment, and faster response to disruptions.

Finance and compliance automation

Enterprises connect financial systems, banks, and compliance tools to automate reconciliations, monitor transactions, and ensure data consistency across reporting environments.

Employee lifecycle management

HR and payroll systems exchange employee data securely to streamline onboarding, benefits management, and workforce planning—supporting a more responsive and integrated people strategy.

Platform-driven innovation

Businesses share their capabilities and systems with partners or developers to extend reach, fuel growth, and unlock new revenue streams through platform business models.  Data providers can also provide API integration services that enable other companies to integrate valuable data into their applications.

The value of API integration platforms

Integration platforms are essential for reducing API sprawl. They enable enterprises to implement APIs at scale across applications, data, processes, services, and events—including bridging cloud and on-premises environments.

Centralized API management and governance

Managing a growing number of APIs requires a secure, centralized approach. Integration platforms with built-in API management help organizations register, publish, secure, and monitor APIs throughout their lifecycle. These API integration tools streamline access control, enforce usage policies, and ensure consistent performance.

Hybrid integrations for evolving IT landscapes

To modernize without disrupting existing operations, organizations often adopt hybrid integration strategies. These strategies connect legacy on-premises systems with cloud-based applications through pre-built connectors and integration flows—enabling gradual digital transformation while preserving critical infrastructure.

Complex data transformations and routings

API integrations simplify the conversion of complex data formats such as XML, JSON, CSV, EDIFACT, Parquet, and Avro while applying business logic. Integration platforms offer private landscapes that support secure routing and transformation of sensitive data to help ensure compliance with privacy and governance standards.

Event-driven architecture

Modern integration platforms support event-driven architectures that facilitate real-time, asynchronous communication across distributed environments. By triggering workflows based on events like customer actions or sensor alerts, businesses can monitor key events and respond instantly to changing conditions.

Low-code/no-code integration

Integration platforms offer intuitive low-code/no-code tools to reduce IT dependency. These platforms enable users to create and modify integrations through graphical interfaces and pre-built components to customize processes and scale digital initiatives.

B2B integration and collaboration

Sharing information with business partners often involves navigating diverse systems and protocols. Integration platforms secure and scale B2B communications by automating partner interactions, streamlining document exchange, and supporting industry standards. Resulting in expanded reach and increased operational efficiency.

Strategic integration planning

A successful integration strategy aligns people, processes, data, and technology. Integration platforms offer guided tools, digital assistants, and pre-built content to lessen the complexity of enterprise integrations. This helps organizations confidently plan, execute, and evolve their integration to support long-term agility and resilience for their enterprise.

The role of AI in API integration

AI is most effective when it can access a wide array of data. Integration platforms incorporating APIs provide AI with the information it needs to drive the most value for businesses.

Increased security and governance

By spotting unusual patterns and potential threats in traffic, AI strengthens the overall security of APIs. Automated compliance monitoring uses AI to maintain operational integrity and ensure API integrations align with data governance policies and regulatory requirements.

Root cause and predictive maintenance

Through analysis of logs and error messages, AI can identify the underlying causes of integration failures and reduce investigation efforts. It can analyze historical performance data to forecast API or integration flow failures, allowing preventative maintenance before a deployment.

Informed integration development and decision-making

AI can also evaluate the integrations and the most-used APIs. Combining this analysis with organizational data flow can inform future integration strategies.

Within integration platforms, AI can auto-generate parts of integration flows based on common patterns and best practices to accelerate development.

Best practices for API integration

A comprehensive plan that accounts for research, updates, security, and processes helps organizations get the most out of API integrations.

Know the API prior to implementation

Thorough research and understanding are essential for successful API integration. At a minimum, organizations need to know the data model, structure, and formatting.

Organizations should also know how to handle error reports and understand the API’s response formats to maintain smooth operations. Following established API design principles—such as using appropriate HTTP methods and adhering to RESTful practices—ensures consistency and efficiency.

Accommodate API versioning

Planning for change is crucial as APIs evolve. Regularly upgrading to the latest version helps organizations prevent operational disruptions, while maintaining clear communication channels ensures swift resolution if updates introduce missing properties.

Incorporate authentication and authorization security methods

Select the securest method, like OAuth 2.0, to secure API access. Businesses need to have the proper mechanisms and workflows to acquire, store, and refresh OAuth tokens. Businesses should also protect API endpoints from unauthorized access by using firewalls, API gateways, and rate limiting.

It’s necessary to regularly review and update security protocols and dependencies to help maintain a strong defense against evolving threats.

Use consistent deployment practices

Maintaining a consistent and automated integration process across development, testing, and production ensures stability and efficiency.

Keeping everything centralized streamlines troubleshooting and analysis, with logs from integrated systems compiled in one location. Up-to-date API documentation, flow diagrams, and troubleshooting guides help businesses further support smooth operations and ongoing improvements.

Final thoughts on API integration

By unifying systems, applications, and data, API integration helps enterprises move fast, work efficiently, and enable future growth. Integration platforms make this possible at scale—offering the tools, governance, and flexibility enterprises need to build and manage API connections with confidence.

resources/data-fabric-vs-data-mesh.html.body:
Best Practice How-To Guide

Data fabric vs. data mesh

Data fabric and data mesh are distinct, yet complementary methods for optimizing business data.

Published on April 14, 2026

Businesses today generate more data than ever before, often scattered across many systems, teams, and tools. Without a clear strategy to manage this information, leadership loses out on vital insights for decision‑making.

In response, data fabric and data mesh offer innovative ways to maximize the business value of data assets. Data mesh focuses on how data responsibility is distributed, while data fabric focuses on how data is connected, governed, and made usable across the enterprise.

Both approaches can be combined to solve information gaps and inconsistencies. Understanding these methods, how they operate, and where they work together helps businesses find data management solutions that fit their unique needs.

What is data fabric?

Data fabric describes a type of data architecture that connects all data across hybrid and multi-cloud environments. Users can access and manage both historical and real-time data—no matter where it resides—through a single unified layer. The result is a strong enterprise backbone that’s vital for cross‑domain use, consistent governance, and AI innovation.

How data fabric works

Together, these capabilities allow organizations to operate data consistently—even as ownership, tools, and use cases expand.

  • Connect systems: Data connectors link data stored across on-premises systems, cloud platforms, applications, and sensor networks to a central location.
  • Automate integration: Enriched metadata is used to discover, classify, and harmonize data automatically.
  • Preserve context: Data modeling keeps business logic and meaning intact, ensuring data remains governed, trustworthy, and semantically rich when shared.
  • Synchronize data: Automated pipelines support real‑time updates so users always have the latest information.
  • Enforce governance: Shared rules apply consistent standards for data security, access, and quality.
  • Create and manage data products: The data fabric facilitates the full data product lifecycle, from design and publishing to versioning, monitoring, and retirement.

The true value of unified data

Learn how data fabric reduces total cost of ownership and fuels AI in this GigaOm report.

Read the report

What is data mesh?

Data mesh is an organizational model where each business area—such as finance, HR, or marketing—owns and manages its own data. Instead of sending everything through a central data team, users access data directly from the teams that create and understand it the most.

How data mesh works

Backed by solid data architecture, these data mesh practices help domain teams maintain data quality and clarity, even as organizations grow more complex.

  • Distribute ownership: Each business domain is responsible for managing and governing the data it creates.
  • Create domain-focused data products: Domain teams package information as ready‑to‑use data products for others across the organization to easily consume.
  • Enable self-service: Self‑service platforms with no-code and low-code tools allow domain teams to manage data more independently, while data professionals handle technical upkeep.
  • Federate governance: Domain teams govern their own data, while data professionals set shared standards to ensure consistency.

Key differences between data fabric and data mesh

Ultimately, data fabric is the technical foundation that defines the underlying technologies and processes of data management. Data mesh, by contrast, refers to a way of working rather than a specific technology system, focusing on how teams own, manage, and share data.

Used together, the data fabric’s shared infrastructure strengthens data mesh strategies by ensuring domain‑driven data is consistent, governed, and ready for enterprise use. By understanding where the two approaches differ, organizations can more effectively decide how to combine them.

Core focus

  • Data fabric: Unifies and automates data integration across systems, preserving business context to support analytics and AI.
  • Data mesh: Distributes data responsibilities so domain teams can deliver high‑quality, context‑rich data products.

Data management approach

  • Data fabric: Focuses on technology-driven connectivity and automation.
  • Data mesh: Creates an organizational model to support autonomy for domain teams.

Data governance approach

  • Data fabric: Embeds central governance by design, enforcing consistent policies and security so data remains traceable and compliant as systems and AI tools scale.
  • Data mesh: Adopts federated governance, where domains govern their own data while data professionals set shared standards to maintain alignment across teams.

How to choose between data fabric and data mesh

Selecting the right approach depends on whether the organization’s primary challenges are technical, organizational, or a mix of both. Consider the following factors to determine whether either approach or a combination aligns best with core business data needs.

When to use data fabric

This approach works best for companies with data scattered across many systems, clouds, and applications. When data sources don’t connect cleanly, teams struggle to locate, access, and combine the information they need.

Data fabrics channel this disparate data into a central hub where teams can search, query, and use information without navigating separate systems. The data fabric architecture also preserves the data’s business context by keeping the metadata, relationships, and governance rules intact. This approach works well when consistent access, real‑time integration, and centralized governance are top priorities.

When to use data mesh

Data mesh is ideal when an organization’s biggest challenge is process, not technology. For many large companies, data is technically accessible but slow to deliver because one central team controls every pipeline, definition, and approval. This creates backlogs, preventing business areas from publishing or updating data quickly.

Data mesh shifts ownership to the teams that create and understand the data, allowing them to manage quality, definitions, and delivery directly. This approach is ideal when domain autonomy and faster delivery cycles are the main goals. Data mesh, however, works best with a reliable data architecture to streamline integration and maintain governance standards.

Can data fabric and data mesh work together?

Data fabric and data mesh often complement each other when used in the right context. Here’s how a combined approach can improve each method’s unique strengths.

Stronger data product reach

Both data fabric and data mesh enable the creation of high‑quality, context-rich data products. Data fabric then makes those products easier to find and use through consistent access, search, and discovery tools.

More reliable metadata

Domain teams supply precise, context‑rich metadata for their data products. The data fabric then preserves and standardizes this metadata as it moves across systems, improving trust and consistency organization‑wide.

Lower operational burden for domain teams

The data fabric provides self‑service infrastructure, automated governance, and built‑in services for tasks like access control, classification, and quality checks. This reduces the technical overhead for domain teams.

Enterprise‑wide data transparency

Data mesh contributes structured, meaningful metadata from each domain. In turn, the data fabric connects these fragments into a unified view through catalogs, knowledge graphs, and cross‑domain insights. This gives organizations a more complete and navigable data map.

When to use both data fabric and data mesh

For many businesses, technical and organizational challenges often go hand in hand. Data may be scattered across systems, while domain teams need more autonomy to deliver insights quickly. In these cases, relying on one approach may leave important gaps unaddressed.

A combined approach can resolve both issues for organizations. Data mesh gives domain teams greater agency over their data, while data fabric provides the technical backbone that makes their data usable across the enterprise. The result is the best of both worlds—harmonized, domain-guided data products that can drive strategic decision-making.

Data fabric vs. data mesh vs. data lakehouse

A data lakehouse can also work in tandem with these data management strategies and technologies. While data fabric and data mesh describe how organizations structure, govern, and deliver data, a data lakehouse refers to the technical platform for storing and processing that data. Understanding the relationship between these three concepts helps clarify where each one adds value—and why they’re often used together rather than in competition.

What is a data lakehouse?

A data lakehouse is a single system that stores large volumes of data in one place, while also organizing and managing that data for analytics, business intelligence (BI), and machine learning. This approach combines the flexibility, scale, and low cost of a data lake with the structured data management and performance of a data warehouse. By joining the best of both worlds, a data lakehouse can reduce data duplication, simplify pipelines, and optimize data for storage and analytics.

How do data lakehouse, data fabric, and data mesh work together?

  • Data lakehouse acts as the unified platform for large‑scale data storage and analytics.
  • Data fabric connects the data lakehouse with all other data sources, automating data integration and governance.
  • Data mesh uses the lakehouse as a central environment for domain teams to build and publish their data products without duplicating storage or tools.

Together, these approaches help organizations address different dimensions of the same challenge—making data accessible, trustworthy, and ready for use across the business.

Examples of data fabric and data mesh in practice

Organizations often apply data fabric and data mesh to solve very different challenges, yet both approaches can deliver meaningful results when matched to the right business need. Here’s how both can be applied to support operations across diverse business areas and industries.

Data fabric use cases

  • Customer service: Data fabric brings together customer information from many systems, so service teams can respond faster and deliver more personalized support.
  • Fraud detection and risk management: By connecting signals across internal and external systems, the data fabric helps businesses spot unusual activity early and reduce financial and operational risks.
  • Sales forecasting: By integrating real‑time data, a data fabric improves forecast accuracy and supports better planning and market responsiveness.

Data mesh use cases

  • Financial planning: Data mesh allows finance teams to own revenue, expense, and investment data domains, ensuring accurate forecasting and scenario modeling.
  • Human resources: HR domains govern sensitive recruiting, payroll, and performance data independently, enabling compliant, real‑time workforce reporting and planning.
  • Manufacturing: Plant-level teams can own sensor and machine performance data, improving predictive maintenance and reducing unexpected downtime.

Combined data fabric and data mesh use cases

  • Healthcare analytics: Healthcare providers gain a unified, governed view that supports better patient care when clinical data products combine with a data fabric that connects medical records, lab results, and scheduling systems.
  • Supply chain and logistics: Data fabric can integrate data products from procurement, inventory, and logistics into supplier and warehouse systems, which strengthens system visibility and forecast accuracy.
  • AI and machine learning: Combining domain‑curated datasets with unified enterprise data accelerates model development and scales AI initiatives.

Challenges to consider before choosing data fabric or data mesh

Although data fabric and data mesh offer significant benefits, each has considerations that may affect readiness and success.

Common challenges with data fabric implementation

  • Metadata dependency: If existing metadata is incomplete or inconsistent, automation and unified access become less reliable.
  • Complex integrations: Data fabrics may require system modernization to connect legacy systems, multi-cloud platforms, and real-time pipelines.
  • Governance alignment: Centralizing data governance becomes difficult if existing rules differ across teams or regions.

Common challenges with data mesh implementation

  • Domain ownership: Data products can quickly become disjointed without strong ownership from each business area.
  • Shared standards: Independent domain teams must align on shared data definitions and practices to ensure reliable governance.
  • Skills gaps: Domain teams may lack enough data and technical skills to manage and maintain their own data products.

Data fabric and data mesh best practices

Successful data fabric or data mesh implementation can’t be achieved overnight. These approaches require well‑defined standards, the right supporting tools, and close coordination across technical and business teams. The following best practices can help organizations apply each method effectively and avoid common pitfalls.

Data fabric best practices

  • Phase adoption: Phase data fabric implementation in stages so teams can manage changes with minimal disruptions.
  • Enforce quality: Implement regular data quality checks and controls to ensure information remains reliable and trustworthy.
  • Define governance: Establish clear governance for secure data use and consistent policy enforcement.
  • Automate integration: Use AI and machine learning tools to reduce manual integration workloads, such as data discovery, anomaly detection, and metadata classification.
  • Strengthen alignment: Foster collaboration between IT and business teams to ensure the data fabric supports real operational needs.

Data mesh best practices

  • Start small: Start small with pilot programs, using core domain teams to refine processes before scaling.
  • Productize data: Treat data as a product by defining clear ownership and usability standards for every dataset.
  • Standardize tools: Invest in shared tools to make publishing, accessing, and discovering data products easier for domain teams.
  • Embed governance: Establish strong governance standards early to balance domain autonomy with compliance needs.
  • Encourage partnership: Foster collaboration between data and business teams to ensure domain data owners get enough technical support.

FAQ

  • What is the difference between data fabric and data mesh?

    Data fabric is a technology‑driven data architecture that unifies, connects, and governs data across systems. Data mesh is an architectural framework that distributes data ownership to domain teams and treats data as a product.

  • Can data fabric and data mesh work together?

    Yes, the two approaches complement each other. Data fabric provides integrated, governed access to enterprise data. In contrast, data mesh enables domain‑level accountability and faster delivery of high‑quality data products.

  • When should an organization use data fabric?

    Data fabric is most effective when a business needs consistent, real‑time access to data spread across multiple systems, clouds, and applications without creating new data silos.

  • When should an organization use data mesh?

    Data mesh is helpful when organizational bottlenecks slow down analytics and when domain experts need more autonomy to manage, publish, and maintain their own data products.

  • How do data fabric and data mesh support AI and analytics?

    Data fabric provides unified, governed data pipelines for analytics and AI, while data mesh ensures high‑quality, domain‑curated datasets that improve model accuracy and accelerate development.

resources/effective-ai-implementation-in.body:
Best Practice How-To Guide

Effective AI implementation in business: Steps for success

A successful AI implementation is about adopting technology as quickly as possible, aligning AI with business goals, setting up the foundation for sustainable value, and empowering people to lead the transformation.

Published on July 2, 2025

Artificial intelligence (AI) offers incredible potential to automate processes, enhance decision-making, and reimagine business models. However, many organizations face an uncertain starting point. These companies know how crucial AI adoption has become—but aren’t sure how to align it with their specific needs, develop internal readiness, or measure ROI effectively.

A successful AI implementation is about more than just adopting technology as quickly as possible, it’s about aligning AI with business goals, setting up the foundation for sustainable value, and empowering people to lead the transformation.

What to consider before starting your AI implementation

Success with AI begins long before the first line of code is written. Steps must be taken to create an environment for AI to thrive, such as aligning leadership, assessing readiness, and building in resources and support.

Developing an AI strategy and governance framework

First, an organization will need to create a strategic foundation that aligns AI initiatives with business priorities and embeds responsible governance from the outset. Key elements of an effective AI strategy include:

  • Defining clear, measurable goals aligned with strategic objectives
  • Identifying success metrics and key performance indicators (KPIs)
  • Establishing an AI governance framework that ensures ethical use, transparency, and regulatory compliance

Responsible AI isn’t a “nice to have”—it’s a business imperative. Bias, explainability, and data privacy must be embedded into AI design and deployment processes. Building trust is foundational to realizing sustainable AI value.

Identifying value areas and selecting tools based on business needs

AI readiness starts with knowing where AI can create real value by identifying high-impact use cases, such as:

  • Automating repetitive manual processes
  • Enhancing customer experiences
  • Improving decision-making and agility
  • Unlocking new insights from existing data

Tool selection is another pivotal first step—and one that should be driven by business needs, not technology trends. Organizations will need to assess their needs based on factors like:

  • The maturity of their existing IT infrastructure
  • Integration capabilities with current platforms
  • Vendor support
  • Security features

By connecting AI implementation to clear business outcomes and selecting tools that align with their AI strategy and data landscape, organizations can avoid the common pitfall of pursuing AI for AI’s sake.

Considering the potential of outside support

Finally, many businesses may also need external expertise to accelerate their AI journey. Engaging a management consultant or participating in structured workshops can provide:

  • Cross-functional alignment
  • Change management guidance
  • Critical expertise in data integration and readiness

How to implement AI in business operations

Once the actual implementation begins, it should start with clear-eyed and strategic integration into business processes. Effective AI integration means embedding it into existing business workflows—not bolting it on as an afterthought.

Matching AI systems with business processes

Companies should take the time to map out how AI tools will:

  • Interact with current applications
  • Support specific business processes
  • Enhance—not disrupt—employee workflows

This alignment is key to driving adoption and ensuring AI delivers measurable improvements.

Assessing data quality

Data readiness is another key aspect of AI implementation, and for good reason. AI depends on high-quality, well-governed data, so it’s critical that organizations objectively assess factors like:

  • Data accessibility, accuracy, and completeness
  • Governance and privacy controls
  • Data integration across disparate systems
  • Real-time data availability

Investing in a unified data foundation can dramatically accelerate AI success.

Testing and evaluating

Before scaling, companies should conduct structured pilots to validate business value and technical feasibility. Key best practices include:

  • Defining clear success metrics
  • Running pilots in a controlled environment
  • Iterating based on feedback
  • Documenting lessons learned

Pilots help refine both the technology and the change management approach—building a strong case for broader AI adoption.

Training and upskilling teams

People are at the heart of any successful AI implementation, which is why businesses can’t afford to neglect investing in employee upskilling in areas such as:

  • AI literacy and ethical principles
  • Hands-on tools and workflows
  • Evolving roles and responsibilities
  • Cross-functional collaboration

Empowering employees ensures that AI becomes a tool for augmentation—not alienation.

Scaling

With successful pilots and trained teams, the next phase is scaling AI across the enterprise. Effective scaling should be based on the following:

  • Proven ROI from pilots
  • Readiness of supporting infrastructure
  • Cross-departmental alignment
  • Robust governance and monitoring frameworks

Scaling is not just about deploying more AI—it’s about scaling what works responsibly and sustainably.

Realizing value

Scaling AI successfully leads to the realization of measurable value. Businesses should monitor AI usage and performance by tracking:

  • Financial ROI
  • Efficiency gains
  • Enhanced customer and employee experiences
  • Improved decision-making agility

This helps objectively measure business value and ensures that deployments remain aligned with strategic objectives.

Reflecting and measuring

AI is not a one-time project—it’s an ongoing evolution. Organizations are encouraged to maintain continuous reflection and measurement through:

  • Regular KPI reviews
  • Audits of AI fairness, accuracy, and compliance
  • Stakeholder feedback loops
  • Iterative improvements based on new learnings

By embedding a culture of continuous improvement, organizations can future-proof their AI investments and sustain value over time.

Overcoming AI implementation challenges

AI implementation unlocks new possibilities for businesses—but it’s certainly not without challenges. Hurdles such as resistance to change, misaligned incentives, and unrealistic expectations can quickly derail AI efforts.

Strong leadership is essential to keeping AI implementation focused and resilient. Key success strategies for managers include:

  • Securing executive sponsorship
  • Setting transparent expectations and timelines
  • Communicating AI’s role as an enabler, not a threat
  • Aligning incentives across business units

AI is inherently cross-functional—requiring collaboration between IT, data teams, legal, compliance, operations, and business units. Organizations must take the necessary steps to ensure cross-functionality, such as:

  • Building cross-functional AI coalitions early
  • Establishing governance structures with shared ownership
  • Creating spaces for ongoing dialogue and feedback
  • Fostering a culture of curiosity and experimentation

Without this alignment, even the best AI technologies will fail to deliver sustainable business value.

Get expert guidance on AI implementation in business

AI holds extraordinary promise—but realizing its potential requires more than just adopting new tools. It requires a strategic, responsible, and people-centered approach to transformation.

Our new e-book, “The Path to AI Implementation,” provides a clear, actionable roadmap for every stage of the AI integration journey, from strategy and readiness to scaling and sustaining value. Get guidance and best practices on:

  • Aligning AI initiatives with business goals
  • Building a unified data foundation
  • Embedding responsible governance
  • Investing in workforce enablement
  • Driving continuous measurement and improvement

Develop your AI Implementation roadmap

resources/employee-time-tracking.html.body:
What Is

What is employee time tracking?

Employee time tracking refers to the process of recording and managing the hours employees work. Beyond basic attendance, modern systems use AI to automate time capture, flag inconsistencies, and deliver insights that help HR teams optimize schedules, ensure compliance, and improve payroll accuracy.

Updated on January 26, 2026

Why time tracking is important for productivity and compliance

Time tracking is key to understanding employee productivity and attendance, helping ensure employees are paid correctly and working as efficiently as possible. By knowing how much time is spent on tasks and projects, organizations can identify inefficiencies and implement solutions, such as reallocating tasks or providing additional training or support, and make more informed decisions about future assignments and project timelines. For service-based organizations, time tracking is essential for creating accurate invoices and building customer trust.

As hybrid and remote work continue to shape the modern workplace, reliable and accessible time tracking remains essential for confirming when employees are working and how productively they’re spending their time. Time tracking also plays a foundational role in workforce management, helping organizations align talent with business goals, optimize staffing, and maintain visibility across distributed teams.

Additionally, AI-enabled time tracking tools are helping organizations automate time capture, detect anomalies, and generate predictive insights that support smarter scheduling and improved compliance.

What does time tracking software do?

Time tracking software digitalizes and automates time tracking processes, such as clock-ins and clock-outs, time sheets, GPS tracking, reporting, and analysis. This software helps organizations accurately track and manage employee work hours, attendance, and productivity. It also helps guarantee that employees are paid correctly for the hours they work, including overtime.

Organizations use employee time tracking software for:

Employee time and attendance tracking

A clock-in and clock-out system provides a centralized view of employee arrival times, absences, breaks, overtime, vacation, and personal time, helping organizations schedule resources and projects, identify inefficiencies, and calculate payroll and overtime.

Resource and task allocation

By monitoring productivity and workload across teams, time tracking software helps organizations make informed decisions about resource and task allocation, keeping projects on schedule and making the best use of employees’ time.

Client billing

Automated time tracking eliminates manual steps and errors to help ensure client billing is accurate and timely, helping build trust between organizations and clients and improving on-time payments.

Project management

By tracking time spent on each phase of a project—from planning through review—time tracking software enables organizations to better manage timelines, resources, and costs, keeping projects running on time and on budget.

Performance evaluation

Time tracking software that collects data on task completion times and employee productivity provides valuable insights into skills gaps and employee time management, enabling managers to provide constructive feedback in performance reviews and set attainable goals.

Compliance reporting

Consistent and reliable time tracking methods enable organizations to record and report accurate working hours, helping ensure all employees are treated fairly and in accordance with labor laws and regulations for working hours, breaks, and overtime.

Display employees’ planned and recorded working time for a seven-day period in a clear, user-friendly interface.

How does employee time tracking software work?

Time tracking software works by allowing employees to easily record their work hours and tasks completed throughout the day, week, or month. The software then compiles and organizes this data, providing reports and insights to managers and HR. Cloud-based time tracking software integrates with other business systems to provide a unified view of employee time and attendance.

Key time tracking terms:

  • Time tracking is the act of recording time spent on a specific task or project.
  • Time sheet is a paper or digital document used for recording employees’ arrival and departure times and the amount of time spent on a task or project.
  • Time tracking software is a digital tool that records and analyzes time spent on tasks or projects, in place of manual time tracking methods, such as punch cards and sign-in sheets.
  • AI-enabled features enhance this process by automatically detecting anomalies, validating entries in real time, and providing predictive insights that help HR teams optimize staffing and reduce compliance risks.

Empower operational leaders and stakeholders to understand the financial impacts and potential risks of decisions related to overtime, productivity, and compliance.

Time tracking methods

The methods of capturing time have evolved over the years—from paper and pen to employee time clock with a punch-card system (credited to Willard Legrand Bundy) to AI-enabled time recording, analysis, and reporting. Some of the most common methods used today include:

  • Excel templates, which use formulas to calculate time, and require manual data entry and analysis.
  • Mechanical punch clocks that stamp times on a piece of paper employees insert into a machine to record time in and time out.
  • Biometric control systems that scan employees’ fingerprints or pupils to verify their identity and record the time they enter and exit the workplace.
  • Swipe cards (like credit cards), which are swiped through a card reader at the front desk or workstation when employees start or end their workday.
  • Paper spreadsheets, which are completed and submitted by hand, stamped, and retained for future reference.
  • Digital spreadsheets that record, calculate, and store time tracking data on a hard drive or USB stick.
  • Mobile apps that use GPS and geofencing features to track employees’ time and location, remind employees to clock in and clock out, and provide detailed reporting.

What are the benefits of time tracking software?

By centralizing and streamlining time tracking processes, time tracking software makes it easier for organizations to collect accurate, real-time information that leads to improvements in:

  • Productivity: Accurate time tracking helps organizations increase employee accountability, provide constructive feedback during reviews, prioritize projects and tasks, and optimize workflows.
  • Cost savings: Insights into labor cost inefficiencies, such as excessive overtime, lengthy processes, and inappropriate staffing levels, can help organizations implement cost-effective solutions.
  • Compliance with local, industry, and company policies: Maintaining a clear, accurate record of employee working hours helps organizations comply with labor laws and union rules for overtime, breaks, and minimum wage, which can be crucial during labor audits.
  • Employee satisfaction: By giving employees visibility into their work hours, overtime, and pay, organizations can boost employee motivation, morale, and trust.
  • Forecasting: The data from time tracking can help predict future labor needs and costs, helping organizations create reliable, cost-effective budgets and financial forecasts.

Simplify time management to support rotating schedules, cross-midnight time recording, auto and mass approvals, alerts, automated recalculations, and embedded reporting.

Challenges of implementing time tracking software

While time tracking software offers many benefits to employers and employees, cost and integration can present challenges for organizations preparing to move to cloud-based time tracking. Some of the key challenges organizations should consider include:

  • Cost: To alleviate the costs associated with time tracking software, organizations can start with just the features they need and choose pricing plans and solutions that best fit their budget.
  • Compliance: Taking compliance into consideration, organizations must ensure the software can scale to meet all relevant labor laws, local and regional regulations, and union rules.
  • Integration: To provide a seamless user experience, time tracking software should smoothly integrate with existing HR, project management, and payroll systems.
  • Technical difficulties: Unpredictable system performance, software bugs, and compatibility issues can prevent users from consistently using time tracking tools, which makes the data less reliable.
  • Training and support: Additional time and resources are needed to provide sufficient training and ongoing support to ensure all employees can use time tracking tools effectively.

By understanding business goals and challenges upfront and taking the time to explore different cloud and on-premise software options, payment plans, and vendors, organizations can find the best time tracking software to fit their business needs and budget.

Easing adoption of time tracking software

To simplify the adoption of employee time tracking software and ensure employees are using it consistently and correctly, organizations should:

  • Provide training sessions tailored to different types of users and organizations
  • Create self-paced demos on recording time and reviewing working hours, payroll, and overtime
  • Hold open forums to discuss concerns about time tracking processes and highlight the benefits, such as eliminating time spent on manual processes and ensuring more accurate, timely paychecks

Key features of effective employee time tracking software

With time tracking software, it’s easier than ever to keep track of employee time, attendance, and productivity without relying on manual, error-prone processes. Time tracking software offers a range of features that can help organizations manage projects, timelines, payroll, and client billing more effectively.

  • Automated clock-in and clock-out records start and end times, breaks, and intervals during employee work hours for both onsite and remote workers, eliminating errors and gaps from manual processes.
  • Mobile accessibility allows users to track time and manage tasks on the go using any mobile device.
  • Customization enables users to customize time tracking settings and features based on individual or team needs, as well as local regulations and union rules.
  • Geolocation tracks where employees are working around the globe, which is especially valuable for remote employee time tracking and analysis.
  • Artificial intelligence (AI) automates time tracking processes, analyzes patterns, and generates real-time insights about productivity trends and potential issues and solutions.
  • Real-time reporting summarizes recorded hours, project progress, and other relevant data to help keep projects and people on schedule.
  • Monitoring and analytics provide insights into time usage and efficiency, supporting better decision-making and performance improvements.
  • Integration connects time tracking software with other tools and software used in the workplace, such as payroll time tracking, project management systems, and accounting software.
  • User permission settings allow managers to set different levels of access and permissions for users or teams within the organization.
  • Security measures protect sensitive employee data both within and outside the organization.

FAQs

  • How do employees track hours?

    Employees track hours by clocking in and clocking out of work and tasks using a variety of paper-based, digitalized, manual, and automated processes. Many companies have moved away from manual, paper-based time tracking, such as punch clocks, swipe cards, and spreadsheets, to cloud-based, AI-enabled time tracking software that automates and streamlines time tracking, analysis, reporting, and invoicing.

  • Why is employee time tracking important?

    Time and attendance tracking provides essential insights that can help organizations manage efficiencies, resource allocation, invoicing, and costs for all types of workers across onsite, remote, and hybrid working models.

  • How does employee time tracking help with payroll and billing?

    A time and attendance system works by recording the amount of time employees work, including time in and time out, breaks, overtime, and time off. Some systems automatically track employee time while other systems require employees to enter their time manually.
