resources/what-is-lms.html.description: Learn how an enterprise learning management system (LMS) works and how organizations use an LMS to increase employee engagement and improve the learning experience.
resources/what-is-lms.html.body:
What Is

What is a learning management system (LMS)?

An LMS is a software application used for planning, delivering, and tracking training and educational programs. Organizations use LMS software to make learning more engaging and accessible to employees, helping improve employee skills, compliance, retention, and productivity.

Updated on May 28, 2026

LMS meaning and definition

A learning management system, often referred to as an LMS, is a software application that provides organizations with a framework for creating, managing, delivering, and tracking educational courses, training programs, or learning and development programs throughout the employee lifecycle. An LMS uses artificial intelligence (AI) and smart technologies to assess individual and organizational training needs, create personalized learning paths, and track learning and compliance training.

Why is learning management important today?

Major demographic changes, emerging technologies, new regulations, and a highly competitive job market are creating talent gaps and skills shortages. Technology, particularly AI, is leading to new types of jobs, such as prompt engineers, AI trainers, and AI ethicists, and a lack of people trained to perform these jobs. Learning management is essential for driving continuous learning and development—from training through upskilling and reskilling—to help fill these gaps and empower people to drive the business forward.

What’s the difference between upskilling and reskilling?

  • Upskilling helps people develop new or more advanced technology and human skills, including decision-making and problem-solving skills, to perform better in their current roles.
  • Reskilling helps people learn new skills for a completely different role or career change.

As a result, businesses are putting employee skills at the center of HR practices, according to a 2024 HR trends report. Based on a study of 100 reputable business press resources, the report determined that “Reskilling and upskilling initiatives, especially for urgent skills needs like AI, will lead to increased motivation in employees, so it must also see greater prioritization by organizations.”

What are learning management systems used for?

Organizations—from educational institutions to corporations and government agencies—use learning management systems to meet their educational, training, and compliance goals. For example, a university uses an LMS to deliver online courses to its students worldwide, while a government agency uses an LMS to provide the latest compliance training to employees and send reminders until it’s completed. Most organizations use an LMS for:

Onboarding

It’s essential for HR teams to provide consistent and regionally accurate onboarding training from day one. LMS solutions can help HR personalize, automate, and deliver onboarding tasks and development goals quickly and cost-effectively to help new hires hit the ground running.

Employee training

An LMS can help team leaders and learning and development (L&D) professionals get a centralized view of each employee’s assessed skill levels and current and past training activities to help them deliver the right training to the right people—and keep track of their progress and compliance status.

Upskilling and reskilling

Every employee has unique learning styles and needs based on current and future roles and responsibilities. An LMS supports skills-driven learning by using AI and smart technologies to generate personalized learning recommendations and learning paths that align with specific skills, learning styles, and strategic business goals.

Continuing education and professional development

An LMS connects corporate priorities and skills needs with an existing workforce and its training and professional development activities. It can also help employees identify potential career paths and personalized development goals.

Extended enterprise and channel training

From franchisees to gig workers, anyone who represents a brand must be well-versed in operational rules and guidelines. Smart LMS technologies can help companies create training and brand initiation programs that align with the roles and tasks of each vendor, consultant, or external partner.

Compliance training

To help ensure safety and well-being and minimize risk and loss, businesses must take an organized and consistent approach to regulatory and safety compliance. In addition to assigning training based on nearly any criteria and keeping track of training compliance targets, organizations can use an LMS to develop mandatory training packages that employees won’t dread—and may even enjoy!

Personalized learner homepage with required learning courses and personalized recommendations.

What are the benefits of using an LMS?

By centralizing and streamlining learning content and delivery, an LMS can help organizations achieve many long- and short-term benefits, such as:

  • Higher course completion rates: Accessible, always-on learning opportunities make it easier for employees to attend training and development programs, complete courses, and maintain compliance on any device.
  • Increased engagement: Interactive and innovative learning options, such as virtual reality trainings and gamification integrated into an LMS, help make learning more appealing and engaging for learners.
  • Time and cost savings: Virtual and on-demand training allows organizations to eliminate travel and off-site expenses (for both employees and instructors) and reduce administrative and training consultancy costs.
  • Continuous learning culture: An LMS can track, recommend, and deliver each new stage or learning unit in a continuous learning journey, encouraging employees to never stop learning.
  • Improved compliance: With capabilities such as workflow monitoring, notification, and e-signature processes, an LMS offers a transparent global view of an organization’s compliance status for training and certification to all stakeholders involved.
  • Future-ready workforce: An LMS uses data and individualized insights to create courses and suggests skills that are relevant and digestible, increasing attendance, completion, and retention. This translates to faster and more strategic upskilling and reskilling of the talent pool.

Future of work predictions

Proactively guide your company towards a future that is mutually beneficial to both your people and your business.

Dive into the research

Challenges of implementing and maintaining an LMS

While there are many benefits of an LMS, organizations should be prepared for the challenges of implementing, managing, and maintaining a learning management system, including:

  • User adoption: Users who are uncomfortable with change or new technology may be slow to adopt and effectively use an LMS.
  • Implementation and maintenance costs: Because the costs of developing, implementing, and maintaining an LMS can be substantial, an LMS may not be affordable for some organizations.
  • Technical issues: Poor connections, compatibility issues, and software bugs can disrupt the learning experience and deter users from finishing courses or starting new ones.
  • Content creation and customization: Additional resources and skills are needed to effectively develop fresh, high-quality content that meets users’ needs and keeps them engaged.
  • Updates and maintenance: To keep an LMS running smoothly and securely, organizations must perform regular maintenance and updates, which could put a burden on resources and create talent gaps that need to be filled.

Encouraging user adoption of an LMS

As with any digital transformation, implementation starts with people first—and a clear and open communication strategy. The initial reaction to news of an LMS implementation may include some pessimism due to longstanding perceptions of traditional training as boring and inconvenient. To get ahead of this, organizations can start their LMS journey by:

  • Customizing the LMS rollout plan to resonate with different teams
  • Building multimedia and access-anywhere components into LMS user training
  • Offering microlearning units, fun and gamified elements, and social and personal exchanges—instead of exhausting, day-long training sessions
  • Demonstrating how an LMS can help users achieve their personal and professional goals, advance their careers, and maintain their compliance

How do learning management systems work?

An LMS works by providing a digital platform for creating, managing, and delivering courses, training programs, or learning and development programs enhanced by AI and smart technologies. Users can access the platform to track training, compliance, or development goals; develop new training courses; complete live and on-demand training from any mobile device; and more.

Common features of an LMS include:

  • AI-enabled
    Organizations can use AI features to generate personalized recommendations for learning, mentors, assignments, career paths, dynamic teams, and more to help close talent gaps, reduce skills shortages, and improve employee satisfaction—quickly and effectively.
  • Intuitive interface
    A user-friendly, customizable interface that’s easy to access and navigate helps speed user adoption and participation.
  • Mobile-friendly
    Today, organizations are not only allowing employees to use personal devices—they’re depending on them to do so. To maximize employee engagement and participation, an LMS enables learners to access and complete learning materials and assessments from any mobile device.
  • Data tracking
    A centralized portal synchronizes learning progress when learners are online, helping HR and L&D professionals track learners’ journeys and progress across departments and regions. By tracking and comparing different learning models, L&D teams can hone and customize training programs.
  • Personalized user experience
    Intelligent LMS solutions supported by AI and machine learning can analyze multiple data sets—including a learner’s history, preferences, and performance—to align with the latest corporate priorities as well as personal skills, needs, and interests to help create personalized learning paths.
  • Centralized learning materials
    Users should be able to easily find and access the full range of learning content for their learning path. An LMS can provide centralized access to learning materials—from on-demand courses to quizzes to documentation—using AI and enhanced search capabilities with filtering options.
  • Flexible reporting and analytics
    An LMS can help tailor reporting and analytics to align with specific criteria and learning objectives. The ability to customize reports in real time and get clear visual representations helps L&D teams spot patterns and get a better idea of specific challenges and ways to improve learning courses and materials.
  • Compliance
    Emerging technologies are driving new laws and legal rules, such as the EU AI Act, reflecting globally changing levels of scrutiny, regulations, and workforce expectations. An LMS can help organizations centralize, organize, and keep track of each employee’s status for mandatory compliance training and certification.
  • Flexible range of assessment tools
    Different metrics require different assessment tools, such as exam engines, branching scenarios, and other types of simulations. With a more robust range of assessment tools, learners can be given feedback that’s actionable and specific to their unique challenges and needs.
  • Course creation
    Flexible course creation options allow users to create a course from scratch by developing a lesson right inside the LMS or by importing existing training material in a wide variety of media—from documents to webinars, videos, and interactive training modules.
  • Learning integrated into the employee lifecycle
    An LMS can help organizations align employee growth goals with organizational skills needs—from onboarding to succession—by setting up development goals and fostering internal mobility through always-on learning opportunities, such as projects, fellowships, coaching, and mentoring.
  • Interoperability
    As learning management systems become more sophisticated, so do the technical standards and data models that support interoperability between learning activities across technical systems. An LMS must be able to integrate with third-party systems and enable the exchange and sharing of information between different systems through e-learning content standards, such as SCORM, xAPI, and Tin-Can.
  • Social learning
    According to a Forbes article on social media statistics and trends in 2024, the average person spends about 2 hours and 25 minutes on social media every day. By engaging learners through social channels, an LMS can help build enthusiasm and increase participation and collaboration.
  • Flexible implementation
    An LMS that offers flexible implementation and configuration can scale to meet an organization’s future business needs and integrate solution add-ons to meet new requirements, such as gamification from third-party partners. This flexibility helps reduce upfront costs and enable ongoing innovation.
  • Ease of integration and use
    By enabling seamless cloud integration with other business systems, an LMS can provide a more accurate and actionable picture of learning and development needs and opportunities—and ease of access for all users.
  • Gamified learning
    In an LMS, gamification keeps learners engaged through points, ratings, badges, and more. When a learner can work toward a specific level or standing, experience shows that they’re more likely to engage with the content and better retain what they’ve learned.
  • Microlearning
    Microlearning is an educational strategy that takes broad or complex topics and breaks them down into bite-sized study units. In an LMS, these units can be viewed whenever and wherever the learner needs a refresher and can be incorporated into more formal or longer-term educational goals.
  • Learning in the flow of work
    By learning in the flow of work, learners can quickly gain access to answers or bite-sized microlearning chunks while they’re working and engaging in a task that’s relevant to the learning unit in question.
  • Open platform
    An LMS solution with an open ecosystem can help organizations take advantage of diverse content from Massive Open Online Course (MOOC) providers, for example, as well as benefit from new innovations from a variety of sources.

Types of learning management systems

Learning management systems are always evolving to meet different business and technology requirements and learner types. By understanding the unique features of each LMS, an organization can select the one that best fits its needs. Types of LMS include:

Cloud LMS (SaaS-based solutions): SaaS-based solutions offer a range of capabilities and integrations with smooth scalability and updates in the cloud. Typically hosted by a software provider, this type of LMS can easily scale up or down based on demand and is more cost-effective to maintain and upgrade than on-premise systems.

Self-hosted LMS: For businesses that wish to install and host their own LMS and content, this system allows for full control but compromises on scalability, speed, costs, and ease of integration.

Open LMS: Open source is great for smaller businesses that are prepared to take the prebuilt free public code and implement it in their own systems.

Mobile LMS: This isn’t a distinct “type” of LMS but rather an LMS that comes with device-friendly components and dashboards (which open and self-hosted systems may not).

Corporate LMS: While an educational LMS can be adapted for corporate use, these systems are designed with corporate users in mind. A corporate LMS can either be a cloud-based or self-hosted system.

Educational LMS: These systems formed the foundation for many of today’s corporate LMS systems but are not natively structured for corporate needs and priorities. An educational LMS, such as Canvas, Blackboard, and Google Classroom, can either be a cloud-based or self-hosted system.

Build a future-ready workforce

Upskilling and reskilling can shape the skills and agility needed for the future.

Learn how to get started

FAQ

  • What does LMS mean?

    LMS stands for learning management system (LMS). An LMS is a software application that helps organizations administer, document, track, report, automate, and deliver educational courses, training programs, or learning and development programs.

  • What is e-learning?

    E-learning is learning that is done outside of a classroom, usually over the Web and often conducted through a cloud-based LMS.

  • What is microlearning?

    Microlearning is a highly focused educational session delivered in small pieces, such as a tutorial about a specific problem. It plays a key role in the gamification of learning.

resources/what-is-people-analytics.html.body:
What Is

What is people analytics?

People analytics can give you the insight and context you need to make better workforce decisions. Here’s how it works.

Published on October 2, 2025

People analytics—also known as HR analytics or workforce analytics—is a data-driven approach to understanding and improving workforce decisions. It goes beyond simple reporting to connect information across HR and business systems—recruiting, onboarding, learning, performance, and more—to create a complete view of the workforce.

Done well, people analytics empowers human resource management teams to act with clarity. Employees benefit from fairer, more personalized experiences, while organizations gain the insight to reduce costs, strengthen engagement, and plan with confidence for the future.

Why people analytics is important

The world of work is changing fast. New skills, hybrid work models, and evolving expectations around fairness and opportunity mean organizations need a clearer view of their workforce. Relying on instinct or isolated reports is no longer enough.

People analytics can help by:

  • Replacing guesswork with evidence so leaders can make decisions that improve hiring, development, and retention.
  • Revealing hidden patterns that explain why employees stay, leave, or thrive—helping organizations act sooner.
  • Supporting business agility by connecting strategic insights to workforce planning so organizations can adapt quickly to change.
  • Improving the employee experience through transparent career pathways and effective development opportunities.

Common challenges in people analytics

Even with clear benefits, organizations often face hurdles when getting started with people analytics. These challenges can slow adoption, limit impact, and create resistance if they aren’t addressed early.

Data silos

Workforce information is typically scattered across multiple systems—recruiting, onboarding, learning, performance, payroll, and business operations. Without integration, leaders only see fragments of the picture, making it hard to connect employee growth to business outcomes.

Data quality and consistency

People analytics is only as strong as the data behind it. Incomplete, outdated, or inconsistent records can lead to misleading results, eroding trust in the process and discouraging managers from relying on insights to guide decisions.

Limited adoption

Even the most advanced analytics tools are ineffective if HR teams and managers don’t use them. Complex interfaces, unclear outputs, or a lack of training often limit adoption, leaving valuable insights unused.

Privacy and compliance concerns

People analytics requires access to sensitive employee data. Organizations must strike a balance between generating insights and protecting privacy while also navigating regulatory requirements around data usage and storage.

Skills and expertise gaps

Many HR professionals have strong expertise in people management but less experience with data analysis. Without support, teams may find it challenging to interpret analytics, translate results into action, or communicate insights effectively to business leaders.

Short-term focus

Some organizations treat people analytics as a reporting exercise rather than a strategic discipline. Focusing only on short-term metrics—like turnover rates or time-to-fill—misses the bigger opportunity to connect workforce insights to long-term business planning and resilience.

Key components of people analytics

Effective people analytics comes down to a few key components that turn data into meaningful insight:

  • Unified data foundation: By consolidating information across HR and business systems, people analytics gives leaders a single source of truth. That clarity helps HR professionals move from reactive to proactive decision-making.
  • Predictive analysis: AI and machine learning can enhance your human resource management system by spotting patterns people might miss, including attrition risk, skills shortages, or productivity bottlenecks.
  • Accessible dashboards and reporting: Modern platforms make insights easy to explore. Interactive dashboards, visualizations, and scenario modeling help HR teams and executives answer key workforce questions quickly.
  • Employee experience improvement: Analytics can reveal where onboarding falters, where learning programs need updating, or where career progression is unclear. Addressing these issues leads to stronger engagement and retention.
  • Strategic alignment: By linking workforce data with business outcomes, people analytics helps ensure talent acquisition is grounded in business priorities, from expanding into new markets to preparing for digital transformation.

Use cases and examples

The real value of people analytics comes through practical application. These examples highlight how organizations are using it to solve workforce challenges:

  • Improve retention: Analytics can identify the leading drivers of turnover and flag employees who may be at risk of leaving. Leaders can then target interventions—such as development opportunities or manager coaching—before valuable talent walks out the door.
  • Advance diversity and inclusion: By analyzing hiring, promotion, and pay equity data, organizations can see where disparities exist and design initiatives that improve fairness and representation.
  • Optimize hiring and onboarding: Workforce planning and analytics tracks recruiting funnel performance and onboarding effectiveness, helping organizations shorten time-to-hire and get new employees up to speed.
  • Plan future skills: By mapping skills across the workforce, HR can identify emerging gaps, guide upskilling and reskilling efforts, and prepare the organization for future demands.
  • Boost engagement: Combining survey results with workforce data highlights the factors that shape employee satisfaction. Leaders can then design programs that address these factors and improve overall performance.

The difference between people analytics and talent intelligence

While closely related, people analytics and talent intelligence serve different purposes:

  • People analytics looks inward. Sometimes referred to as People Intelligence, it focuses on workforce data generated inside the organization—HR systems, performance metrics, and surveys—to improve employee engagement, retention, and planning.
  • Talent intelligence combines internal data with external labor market information. It provides a broader view, showing how an organization’s workforce compares to industry benchmarks and where external talent pools are strongest.

Together, they provide a full picture: people analytics helps leaders optimize the workforce they already have, while talent intelligence helps them anticipate and compete for the talent they will need.

What to look for in a people analytics solution

To get the most out of your investment, look for solutions that provide both immediate insight and long-term strategic support. Key considerations include:

  • Unify data across systems: HR and business information should come together in one source of truth.
  • Deliver deeper insights: AI and machine learning should reveal patterns, forecast risks, and recommend actions.
  • Support scenario planning: Leaders should be able to model what-if situations to anticipate shifts in demand or workforce mix.
  • Provide clear dashboards: Visualizations should make insights easy for HR teams, managers, and executives to use every day.
  • Highlight workforce skills: The system should map capabilities, reveal gaps, and link employees to learning and development.
  • Integrate with talent processes: Analytics should connect seamlessly with succession planning, career growth, learning, and performance.
  • Scale with the business: The platform should adapt as the workforce grows while staying simple enough for broad adoption.

FAQs

  • What’s the difference between people analytics, HR analytics, workforce analytics, and talent analytics?

    These terms are often used interchangeably. “People analytics” and “HR analytics” usually describe the same practice of using workforce data for better decision-making. “Workforce analytics” sometimes refers to a broader scope, including contingent labor. “Talent analytics” typically zeroes in on areas like recruiting, succession, or development.

  • Is people analytics only for large enterprises?

    No. While global companies often lead adoption, mid-size organizations are increasingly adopting people analytics thanks to cloud-based platforms that make it scalable and cost-effective.

  • How does AI enhance people analytics?

    AI for HR improves the predictive power of people analytics. It identifies trends, forecasts risks such as attrition, and recommends personalized actions for both employees and managers.

  • How does people analytics connect with other SAP solutions?

    When combined with SAP SuccessFactors HCM and SAP Business Data Cloud, people analytics becomes part of a larger SAP HR ecosystem—connecting workforce insights to learning, succession, and overall business strategy.

resources/what-is-procurement.html.body:
What Is

What is procurement? A comprehensive guide

Procurement is the process of sourcing, purchasing, receiving, and inspecting all of the goods and services your business needs to operate—everything from raw manufacturing materials to software to office supplies.

Updated on January 26, 2026

The procurement function is often taken for granted—until something impedes it. Responsible for keeping a company’s wheels moving, procurement ensures that the right materials and supplies are on hand when needed. Operational in focus, procurement hasn’t typically been considered a strategic discipline—until now.

Cost containment continues to be a priority, particularly given inflation and the rising cost of supplies. However, cost control is only one of the pressures bearing down on procurement today. Squeezed between the threat of supply shortages and the expense of stocking extra inventory, procurement must somehow support supply chain resiliency, even when climate events or other disruptions impede delivery. The need to procure sustainable goods and comply with expanding regulatory requirements means companies must add an extra layer of data collection and scrutiny to their sourcing processes. Add geopolitical pressures and risk to the equation—with resulting material scarcity—and procurement is suddenly at the eye of the storm.

Today, the chief procurement officer (CPO) role is no longer a back-office function chiefly concerned with cost reduction and compliance.

Procurement definition

Procurement is a vital business function, responsible for securing all the goods and services needed by an organization. For manufacturing companies, supply availability is particularly critical as it’s impossible to create finished goods without the necessary materials. Procurement departments must liaise with internal stakeholders to gather their forecasts and requirements, and then source the best suppliers at the best cost.

Thanks to papyrus scrolls that record supply and transportation details, the procurement function can be traced back to the construction of the pyramids. Over time, procurement has undergone numerous transformations—evolving from a simple record-keeping task to a discipline that requires strategic thinking and negotiation.

During the Industrial Revolution, procurement gained importance as burgeoning manufacturing operations needed to source, purchase, and transport materials. In the mid-20th century, when the economy was booming, opportunity and competitive bidding helped redefine the practice again. Individuals were trained in various aspects of supply chain management, gaining professional status. Procurement became regarded as a management function rather than a clerical one.

Today, procurement is again going through a dramatic transformation—arguably as significant as any of the shifts in the past.

Why is procurement so important in business today?

What has been a back-office management function is now center stage—a strategic partner in complex C-suite strategy decisions.

Procurement also controls a big slice of a company’s costs—40% to 80% according to some estimates—so it is essential for budgetary considerations. But effective procurement practices also enhance risk assessment, supplier oversight, and the potential for value creation within the supply chain.

Here are some key ways procurement is important in business:

  • Cost savings: Procurement is the first line of defense for reducing cost and stabilizing cash flow in a business, affecting profit margins and the bottom line. Competitive product sourcing and contract negotiations can deliver significant cost savings. In addition, the streamlining of purchasing processes can have a real impact on financial results.
  • Quality: Procuring the right raw materials at the right time is crucial for manufacturing high-quality products. Quality encompasses every aspect of the procurement process, as the choice of materials and suppliers directly impacts product and service quality. Prioritizing quality is key to mitigating risks related to reputation, production, and legal concerns.
  • Goal alignment: Strategic sourcing aligns procurement purchases with a company’s goals. For example, if enhancing agility and resilience is a core value of your business, tools to meet these targets should be embedded in your procurement process. A detailed analysis of the market as well as your internal requirements can help identify suppliers best positioned to meet your needs.
  • Risk mitigation: Risk can occur at every step of the procurement process—from inaccurate needs analysis to supplier delivery issues. Additional risk comes from ineffective responses to compliance obligations, unclear ethical standards, weather-related incidents, global disruptions, and similar challenges. Today’s technology-powered procurement processes can provide the visibility needed to proactively identify, evaluate, and mitigate risks.
  • Sustainability and ethics: The procurement team must align with their company’s values around environmental impact, ethical sourcing, environmental, social, and governance (ESG) commitments, and more to ensure compliance and protect against risk, reputational damage, and unnecessary expense. Managing sustainable sourcing and compliance is a key responsibility of the procurement function.

Procurement risk management is paramount

Explore results from a new study about risk management and resilience in procurement functions.

Learn more

Types of procurement management

There are four main types of procurement:

  1. Direct procurement: This includes procuring anything that directly supports the production of the goods a company sells, including raw materials, components, parts, services, and wholesale items. These all have an impact upon revenue, growth, and reputation, so supplier relationships are crucial in direct procurement.
  2. Indirect procurement: Anything not directly related to production, including materials, goods, and services for internal use and daily business operations, falls under indirect procurement. This includes items such as office supplies, utilities, and travel expenses.
  3. Goods procurement: Both direct and indirect procurement can fall under goods procurement, which includes procuring any tangible object, whether finished or unfinished—everything from equipment to raw materials to office chairs.
  4. Services procurement: Professional, people-based services such as consultancies, agencies, law firms, outsourced IT, security services, software as a service (SaaS) delivery, and facilities repair all fall under services procurement. These are necessary for efficient workflow and filling in any workforce gaps.

12 steps in the procurement process

While the procurement process can vary from company to company, it generally includes the following 12 steps:

1. Identify needs: The first step of any procurement process is identifying the specific materials, products, software, or services needed due to shortages, new projects, or regular operational requirements. This stage includes demand planning and forecasting.

2. Source suppliers: Researching and assessing the best potential suppliers for your business needs happens early in the procurement process. Developing alternative suppliers can help with risk management by giving you options in case of shortages or disruptions.

3. Submit a purchase requisition: Submitting a purchase request with specifications such as price, time frame, and quantity for internal review and approval triggers the purchasing process.

4. Evaluate and select suppliers: Choosing the best supplier through a competitive bidding process such as putting out a request for proposal (RFP), request for quote (RFQ), e-auctions, or “three bids and a buy” involves assessing vendors on cost as well as quality, reputation, reliability, speed, and sustainability.

5. Negotiate price and terms: After a supplier has been selected, the procurement team negotiates various purchase terms, including price, quantity, delivery timelines, and payment conditions.

6. Create a purchase order (PO): Once a supplier has been chosen and the terms finalized, the company issues a formal PO to that supplier detailing the exact goods, services, and terms included in the order.

7. Receive goods and check quality: When the goods have been received, the next step is to ensure that their quality and quantity match what was ordered by carefully inspecting them for damage or errors.

8. Process invoice and fulfill payment terms: Upon confirming a delivery of goods has passed the quantity and quality check, the supplier’s invoice can be processed through accounts payable (AP) to ensure timely payment. Depending on the terms of the contract, early-payment discounts may apply, and a variety of payment methods may be used.

9. Establish and manage good supplier relationships: It’s strategic for the procurement team to build positive ongoing relationships with suppliers. The benefits include better supplier performance, terms, discounts, collaboration, and reliability.

10. Manage contracts: Procurement contract management covers monitoring contracts, ensuring compliance, and renegotiating terms as needed. It’s important for identifying and addressing potential issues, to ensure that negotiated savings are being realized—and reaching your bottom line.

11. Manage risk: Part of what makes the procurement team so integral to an organization is their role in risk management. It is essential to anticipate and manage potential problems such as shortages, supply chain disruptions, and implementing measures to mitigate them. Staying on top of regulatory and requirements—and spotting any threat of noncompliance—is also an essential component of managing risk.

12. Review and analyze: This final step in the procurement process is ongoing. Reviewing and analyzing procurement KPIs to identify gaps and uncover new opportunities for savings and risk reduction plays a key role in business success.

These 12 steps are commonly thought of as the procurement lifecycle—as the tasks overlap and the process is continuous. A successful procurement lifecycle requires integration with other key business areas, such as budgeting, forecasting, and supply chain management.

Procurement vs. purchasing and other related workflows

Many organizations use the terms “procurement,” “purchasing,” “sourcing,” and “supply chain management” interchangeably, but they are not the same thing. Here’s how they differ:

Procurement vs. purchasing: Purchasing is the part of the procurement process that focuses on transactions. It includes negotiating, ordering products, receiving goods and services, and submitting payments. While purchasing is a crucial part of procurement, the overall procurement process is much broader.

Procurement vs. sourcing: Sourcing is an essential early-stage part of the overall procurement process, covering identifying needs, finding suppliers, issuing purchase requests, evaluating and selecting suppliers, and negotiating prices and terms. The sourcing stage is where strong supplier relationships can be built.

Procurement vs. supply chain management: Procurement is the part of the overall supply chain management process that focuses on acquiring the goods and services needed to manufacture products and maintain internal operations. Procurement dynamically interacts with other supply chain segments, such as logistics, inventory management, and demand planning.

Sustainable procurement management

Sustainable procurement, which integrates ESG criteria into procurement practices and decision-making, isn’t just a procurement trend; it’s a critical consideration.

Sustainable procurement challenges include supply chain complexity and transparency, measuring performance, ensuring compliance with standards, and building capacity. It’s already hard to source materials with low emissions intensity, such as green steel and recycled aluminum and plastic, and it will only get harder. Plus, customers increasingly want to purchase from brands that can prove their sustainable bona fides, which makes sustainable procurement integral for business.

Take just one aspect of sustainable procurement—reducing supply chain emissions. The process can take years, so starting the transition now will set businesses up to be more competitive and resilient in the future.

Here are a few examples of sustainable procurement:

  • Green sourcing or green procurement: Green sourcing involves strategically purchasing products and services with a smaller environmental impact. Green procurement includes eliminating single-use plastics and other disposable items, incorporating recycled or upcycled raw materials, and adopting clean technology or fuel. Green procurement can reduce production costs, contribute to your company's corporate social responsibility initiatives, and even boost sales by appealing to environmentally-conscious consumers.
  • Ethically-sourced materials: Sustainable procurement relies upon ethical sourcing. This means purchasing products from companies that guarantee a living wage, offer good working conditions, don’t engage in child labor, make positive contributions to the communities they’re part of, and meet other ethical standards.
  • Reduced carbon footprint and energy consumption: Lowering your company’s carbon emissions and energy consumption isn’t just about reducing the emissions created directly from your day-to-day operations from factories and transport; it’s also about reducing emissions all along your supply chain.

AI in procurement: Smarter automation and insights

AI in procurement can automate and streamline complex tasks such as spend analysis, contract management, strategic sourcing, and compliance management. It can also support smarter analytics and decision making; help you spot opportunities, potential cost savings, and anomalies; and make it easier to identify new suppliers—while helping to eliminate procurement fraud and reduce errors.

AI can also be used to create business value by deconstructing what the business really needs, challenging established processes, leveraging knowledge from new points of reference, and designing the supply chain in new and different ways.

Generative AI also has huge potential for procurement. Its ability to automate tasks, provide insights, and improve transparency supports efficiency, productivity, and better supplier selection and management. Generative AI can also help mitigate risk and reduce spend.

Using AI to support procurement in making better decisions, identifying new opportunities, automating tasks, and improving operational efficiency means your procurement team can focus on where their human expertise is most valuable.

AI in procurement: A comprehensive guide

AI is bringing exciting new opportunities and transforming long-established processes and practices in procurement.

Read the guide

What to look for in procurement software

When selecting procurement software, prioritize tools that not only digitize and streamline your procurement processes but also enhance your strategic decision-making. Ideal software should boast robust cloud-based infrastructure and artificial intelligence capabilities, simplifying complex procurement tasks. Essential features include seamless integration with existing financial and supply chain systems, user-friendly interfaces, and comprehensive analytics for in-depth spend analysis.

Opt for solutions that provide real-time insights and reporting, facilitating proactive management of procurement activities. Ensure the software is scalable, capable of evolving with your business, and contributes actively to your company’s growth trajectory.

FAQ

  • What is procure-to-pay?

    Procure-to-pay specifically focuses on the latter stages of the procurement process. It involves selecting specific goods and services, enforcing compliance and order procedures, receiving and quality-checking goods, followed by the final steps of invoicing and payment. This process is more concentrated on the transactional phase of procurement, from the point of order to financial settlement. Learn more about procure to pay

  • What is source-to-pay?

    In contrast, source-to-pay is a broader, more comprehensive process. It covers the entire procurement cycle, beginning with identifying the initial needs for products and services, then extending to sourcing, contracting, and managing supplier relationships. This process culminates in processing invoices and fulfilling payment terms for the procured product or service. Source-to-pay is typically supported by advanced procurement software that integrates big data and digital technologies, thereby optimizing the entire procurement lifecycle. Learn more about source to pay

  • What is strategic sourcing?

    Strategic sourcing connects data collection, market research, spend analysis, and negotiation. Strategic sourcing aims to create efficiencies, improve supplier selection, and maximize visibility into pricing and forecasting. Learn more about strategic sourcing

  • What is spend management?

    Spend management is a process that controls how a company spends money to help regulate expenses while reducing costs, risk, and errors. Spend management includes spending for procurement from source to settle but generally does not include payroll or costs of goods sold. Learn more about spend management

  • What is e-procurement?

    E-procurement, or electronic or digital procurement, is the process of requisitioning, ordering, and purchasing goods and services online. E-procurement centralizes and automates interactions, tasks, and transactions in the procurement process. With its technological foundation, it improves efficiency, enhances customer/supplier relationships, streamlines business processes, and offers opportunities for significant cost savings.

What Is

What is source-to-pay (S2P)?

Source-to-pay (S2P) is a business process that encompasses all activities related to the procurement of goods and services, from identifying the need for a product or service to making the final payment to the supplier.

resources/what-is-workforce-management.h.body:
What Is

What is workforce management (WFM)?

Workforce management comprises the tools and processes to manage and maintain a productive workforce.

Updated on April 22, 2026

Workforce management trends and evolutions

Workforce management (WFM) has undergone a significant transformation in recent years, driven by changes in how and where work gets done. Fortunately, workforce management software has evolved right along with it to help you better navigate this shifting landscape. Today’s WFM solutions include AI-enabled tools that help ensure the right employees and skillsets are available to meet demand. Modern WFM solutions must go beyond operational efficiency. They should support evolving employee lifestyles and expectations while promoting workforce well-being and engagement.

Workforce management definition

WFM is a comprehensive and integrated set of processes and tools used to accurately budget for, schedule, track, and forecast working times and workloads. WFM tasks include time and attendance, employee scheduling, and labor law compliance. By providing data-driven insights, WFM helps you better align your HR activities with your business goals—and quickly spot opportunities to streamline and boost productivity.

Modern WFM platforms leverage AI to automate scheduling, optimize staffing, and deliver predictive insights that help organizations stay agile and competitive.

Key components of workforce management

Workforce management software capabilities can range from the core functionalities of time management, scheduling, and compliance to more advanced integration and predictive analytics.

  • Time and attendance management: Top workforce management solutions should support time tracking from a multitude of sources, such as mobile applications and online timesheets. Self-service capabilities to request time off and grant approvals make life easier for both employees and managers, while alerts for overtime can help organizations avoid excessive payroll costs.
  • Forecasting, scheduling, and budgeting: Solutions that use predictive modeling, AI analytics, in-memory data processing, and other advanced technologies can create the most accurate forecasts and scheduling. With these solutions, scheduling can be automated based on workloads as well as factors like people’s skills, preferences, and availability.
  • Analytics dashboards and metrics: Based on real-time workforce data, analytics dashboards and metrics provide insights into employee performance, scheduling effectiveness, and more. When WFM systems can integrate with other HR and operational data, businesses can measure the impact of workforce strategies across the organization and tweak where needed.
  • Worker wellness, health, and safety: Having a good management and communication structure is essential to maintaining employee wellness. Today’s WMF solutions can also help you use real-time workplace data and personalized reporting to ensure you’re on top of any risks or challenging situations your teams may be facing.
  • Regulatory compliance: Configurable tools help companies track and comply with local and global laws, certification requirements, labor standards, union agreements, and more. With increasingly remote and geographically distributed teams, it’s essential to have a centralized view of regulations as they can vary greatly from region to region.
  • Mobile workforce management: Secure, anywhere access to workforce management data and processes helps field teams, remote workers, and on-site employees and managers stay connected and work more efficiently.
  • Integration: Integration with HR, procurement, and ERP systems can help you gain unprecedented insights. This means on-demand reporting and analysis, predictive planning for spikes and dips in hiring, and the ability to attach ROI to your cross-business workforce activities.

Top nine benefits of workforce management solutions

Using real-time data, AI, and cloud-based workforce management solutions, you can gain a competitive edge. With strong communication and planning strategies, you can optimize these WFM solutions by ensuring your management protocols and values are evenly applied across your business.

An engaged, happy, and motivated workforce is the core benefit from which all other WFM benefits can arise, including:

  1. AI-enabled analytics: Forecasts demand, identify workforce trends, and support data-driven decision making
  2. Automated attendance tracking: Streamlines the process of monitoring employee hours, reducing errors and administrative workload
  3. Lower costs: Optimizes staffing levels and schedules, minimizing overstaffing and reducing labor costs
  4. Improved workforce productivity: Aligns employee skills and schedules with business needs, enhancing workforce efficiency
  5. Compliance assurance: Helps ensure adherence to labor laws and regulations, reducing the risk of non-compliance penalties
  6. Increased employee satisfaction: Offers tools for self-service and flexible scheduling, improving employee engagement and retention
  7. Enhanced absence management: Centralizes leave requests and gives managers visibility into team availability
  8. Increased agility and resilience: Quickly scales talent and resources to respond to changing business needs
  9. Unified workforce data: Integrates employee and contingent worker information for better decision-making and strategic planning

Challenges of traditional workforce management solutions

Traditional workforce management solutions are increasingly strained under the weight of modern demands. Designed for more static, predictable environments, legacy systems often fall short in today’s digital-first landscape due to:

  • Limited agility and responsiveness
  • Fragmented workforce visibility
  • Inflexible scheduling and resource allocation
  • Lack of strategic insight
  • Risk exposure and compliance gaps
  • Inability to support skills-based transformation

Forbes highlights that mobility and flexibility are dismantling the traditional four walls of the enterprise, creating a “borderless workplace” where employees can work anytime, anywhere. Mobile solutions and unified device management enable secure access across all devices, while application-based interfaces and dynamic provisioning deliver a seamless, consumer-like experience. These changes fundamentally transform the relationship between employee and employer, and require modern IT infrastructures and agile cultures.

Organizations that proactively integrate AI into their WFM strategies are better positioned to build more adaptable, future-ready teams. This shift to automation, real-time responsiveness, and unified workforce visibility allows businesses to align their workforce to meet evolving demands and stay competitive.

What are the functions and features of WFM solutions?

Modern WFM solutions are designed to help organizations optimize labor resources, improve compliance, and enhance employee experiences.

Key WFM functions and features include:

  • Labor forecasting: Predicting where, when, what kind, and how many employees will be required to meet anticipated demand, enabling businesses to avoid overstaffing or understaffing and optimize productivity and labor costs
  • Scheduling: Aligning workforce availability, skills, and labor demand, ensuring the right people are assigned to the right tasks at the right time and helping organizations adapt in real time and engage employees
  • Time tracking: Recording employees’ time spent on tasks, projects, and work activities, enabling organizations to monitor productivity, manage attendance, ensure accurate payroll, and make informed decisions about resource allocation and project timelines
  • Absence management: Handling employee leave requests and tracking time away from work while ensuring compliance with labor regulations, maintaining workforce productivity, and supporting employee well-being
  • Analytics: Connecting data across HR and business systems to provide a complete view of the workforce, enabling organizations to make informed decisions, enhance employee experiences, reduce costs, and plan confidently for the future
  • Compliance: Consistently following legal, regulatory, and contractual standards related to employment to ensure fair treatment, reduce risk, and protect both employees and the business across jurisdictions
  • Mobile accessibility: Enabling the workforce to securely access and perform work using mobile devices, helping to ensure productivity, engagement, and a seamless, responsive experience across platforms, anytime, anywhere

What is external workforce management?

External workforce management is the strategic process of sourcing, engaging, and overseeing non-employee talent—also known as contingent workers—including freelancers, contractors, consultants, and service providers. Core functions of external workforce management include:

  • Sourcing and onboarding non-payroll talent
  • Managing services procurement
  • Ensuring compliance with labor laws
  • Controlling costs and optimizing spend
  • Gaining visibility into performance and outcomes

An external workforce is critical for modern organizations because it provides flexibility, scalability, and access to specialized skills that may not exist internally. The rise in remote work and a steadily growing dependence upon contingent workforces and services procurement has made external workforce management a priority in modern workforce strategies. Using contractors, freelancers, and service providers delivers strategic value by empowering companies to quickly adapt to changing market demands, control costs, accelerate innovation, and maintain business continuity. This flexibility is even more essential during periods of growth, transformation, or disruption.

Keeping a strong focus on external workforce management is crucial for ensuring agility and resilience in a fast-paced market. Using modern vendor management systems (VMS) and integrated workforce management solutions helps you:

  • Efficiently manage the entire lifecycle of external talent
  • Ensure seamless, compliant engagements that align with your company’s goals
  • Boost flexibility and innovation, allowing rapid incorporation of new skills and ideas while ensuring legal compliance

External workforce management effectively enables organizations to stay agile, tap into niche expertise, and respond swiftly to evolving business needs while maintaining operational efficiency.

What is distributed workforce management?

Distributed workforce management supports employees who work outside of a centralized office, providing them with connectivity and communication, ensuring compliance with regional laws, and enabling consistent HR processes. These employees can work with fully remote, hybrid, or flexible arrangements, and possibly across time zones and locations.

Supporting remote and hybrid teams across geographies delivers multiple benefits, including:

  • Access to global talent: Tapping into a broader pool of skills and expertise, unconstrained by location
  • Increased productivity: Collaborating across time zones, enabling around-the-clock productivity and faster project turnaround
  • Cost efficiency: Reducing overhead costs related to office space, utilities, and relocation
  • Business continuity: Increasing resilience to disruptions like natural disasters or local crises
  • Employee satisfaction: Improving work-life balance, which can boost morale and retention, and reduce turnover
  • Scalability: Quickly scaling up or down based on project needs without the constraints of physical infrastructure

Similar to on-site employees, a distributed workforce needs access to corporate systems, real-time collaboration tools, and consistent employee experiences regardless of location. Supporting these needs requires technology such as:

  • Cloud-based human capital management (HCM)
  • AI-enabled tools
  • Mobile accessibility

Driven by the demand for flexibility and the evolution of digital collaboration tools, many organizations prioritize distributed workforce management for operational continuity and to remain competitive in a digitally connected world.

What is total workforce management?

Total workforce management is an integrated approach to achieving more seamless management of both permanent and contingent staff, including freelancers, contractors, and gig workers. It emphasizes the importance of HCM integration with a VMS to ensure centralized visibility.

Collaboration between HR and procurement is essential for effective management of the entire workforce to meet business needs and support a shifting future. Total workforce management helps ensure that, regardless of the type of worker or nature of their employment, your company delivers consistent experiences and is fully compliant and fair in all hiring and management.

What is mobile workforce management?

Mobile workforce management refers to an organization’s use of digital tools—including mobile technology like smartphones and tablets—and applications to manage employees who work outside of a traditional office setting. This includes field technicians, delivery teams, or remote staff.

Businesses can improve productivity, ensure compliance, and deliver better service in real time with mobile access to scheduling, time tracking, task updates, and communication.

How to choose a workforce management solution

Workforce management software can come as a standalone program or as part of a broader HR system, such as a human resource information system (HRIS) with data management capabilities. Or it can fit into a complete human resource management system (HRMS) that unifies all human resource processes and data, from core HR and payroll to talent management. The functions of workforce management solutions are further enhanced when organizations can integrate them into ERP and procurement systems.

The ideal WFM software should also:

  • Use cloud technology for enhanced accessibility and scalability
  • Include advanced analytics and AI capabilities for predictive insights and intelligent workforce planning
  • Easily integrate with a VMS for effective total talent management, ensuring seamless total workforce management

Empower your HR professionals, analysts, and business partners to answer questions quickly and accurately about your workforce.

The future of workforce management

Businesses today face changing cultures, global uncertainty, and fluctuating customer demands. Workforce expectations are evolving as employees expect flexibility, personalization, and purpose-driven environments. Work models are also more dynamic with hybrid, remote, and distributed teams requiring more agile workforce planning. To thrive in the working world of tomorrow, businesses will rely more heavily on their HR teams to find efficient and profitable solutions for modern workforce challenges.

And HR tech is certainly providing many of the answers to jumpstart their organization’s digital transformation—from automation to strategic enablement. Tasked with driving innovation and creating strategic value, today’s HR teams increasingly embed AI into core HR functions for automation, personalization, and predictive analytics.

To streamline operations, personalize employee experiences, and build dynamic, skills-based workforces, organizations should consider adopting integrated workforce management technology that delivers:

  • Better alignment of talent with business goals
  • Enhanced employee experiences and engagement
  • Improved agility and resilience in workforce operations

As the desire for remote work continues, organizations that support distributed workforces and have the right technology and HR processes in place can offset a talent crunch. However, creating a meaningful and satisfying workplace for employees who can’t work remotely is just as important.

Integrated and intelligent workforce management systems offer the flexibility and insights needed to support the future of work as it evolves—and wherever it occurs—even in times of unprecedented change.

Workforce management FAQs

  • What is remote and external workforce management?

    Remote workforce management involves overseeing and coordinating employees who work from various locations outside the traditional office. External workforce management oversees and coordinates non-employees, including freelancers, contractors, consultants, and service providers. Both of these workforce management tasks use technology to maintain communication, productivity, and engagement.

  • What is contingent workforce management?

    Contingent workforce management refers to the strategies and practices for managing non-permanent workers such as freelancers, contractors, and consultants, ensuring their effective integration and utilization. It involves coordinating procurement, onboarding, compliance, performance tracking, and payment to ensure these external contributors align with organizational goals and workforce strategies.

  • How does WFM software integrate with other business systems?

    WFM software often integrates seamlessly with other business systems like a human resource information system (HRIS), payroll, ERP, and a vendor management system (VMS), allowing for streamlined data management and enhanced operational efficiency.

  • How does WFM software support decision-making in workforce planning?

    WFM software provides data-driven insights and predictive analytics, helping managers make informed decisions about staffing, scheduling, and resource allocation, aligned with business objectives.

  • What is workforce management vs. workforce planning?

    Workforce management (WFM) focuses on the day-to-day operations of managing employees, including scheduling, time tracking, and compliance.

    Workforce planning, on the other hand, is a strategic process that helps organizations forecast future talent needs and align workforce capabilities with long-term business goals.

    In short, WFM is tactical and real-time; workforce planning is strategic and long-term. Both are essential to human capital management (HCM) solutions.

  • Is workforce management part of HR or operations?

    WFM software provides data-driven insights and predictive analytics, helping managers make informed decisions about staffing, scheduling, and resource allocation, aligned with business objectives.

  • What role does data analytics play in workforce management?

    Data analytics plays a critical role in workforce management by providing real-time insights into labor trends, productivity, and compliance. With predictive analytics, organizations can forecast staffing needs, optimize schedules, and make more informed decisions that align workforce operations with business goals. These goals include reducing costs, improving employee engagement, and boosting operational efficiency.
