resources/global-sourcing.html.description: Global sourcing is the practice of procuring goods and services from a global network of suppliers, and is a critical part of a modern procurement strategy.
resources/global-sourcing.html.body:
What Is

Global sourcing explained: How to source successfully across borders

Global sourcing is the strategic process of procuring goods or services from international suppliers.

Published on August 12, 2025

What is global sourcing?

Global sourcing, also known as international sourcing, is the practice of procuring goods, materials, or services from suppliers located across international borders. Unlike traditional sourcing models that focus on local or regional vendors, global sourcing takes a broader, more strategic view to optimize cost, quality, innovation, and supply chain resilience by tapping into a worldwide network of suppliers.

While traditional sourcing prioritizes convenience and proximity, global sourcing emphasizes value creation across multiple dimensions, often requiring greater coordination, risk management, and technological support.

Global sourcing vs. offshoring

While global sourcing and offshoring are sometimes used interchangeably, they mean significantly different things. Global sourcing is the strategic practice of using international suppliers for procurement. It focuses on where products or services are obtained.

Offshoring, on the other hand, refers to relocating a business process or operation—such as manufacturing or customer service—to another country, often to reduce labor or operational costs. In short, global sourcing is about buying globally, while offshoring is about moving operations globally.

Global sourcing vs. global procurement

Unlike offshoring, global sourcing and global procurement—also called international procurement—are closely related but still not the same. While global sourcing refers broadly to the ongoing process of identifying, selecting, evaluating, and managing a global supply base, global procurement specifically focuses on the purchasing of goods or services from international suppliers.

The role of global sourcing in modern procurement

In today’s highly interconnected and competitive marketplace, global sourcing is a foundational component of modern procurement strategy. No longer just a cost-cutting measure, international sourcing now plays a strategic role in helping organizations access innovative suppliers, specialized manufacturing capabilities, and emerging markets.

Sourcing globally enables procurement teams to broaden their supplier base, reduce dependency on single-source vendors, and build resilience in the face of regional disruptions or supply chain bottlenecks.

Beyond financial advantages, global sourcing encourages organizations to think more holistically about their supply networks—evaluating not only price, but also factors such as agility, compliance, and corporate social responsibility.

As supply chains grow more global and digital, sourcing professionals must integrate data-driven insights, robust risk management, and ethical oversight into their procurement practices. In this context, global sourcing is not simply a tactic—it’s a strategic enabler of long-term growth and operational excellence.

Why global sourcing is more complex—and critical—than ever

Global sourcing today operates in an environment marked by rapid change, heightened risk, and growing stakeholder expectations. From trade tensions and climate events to pandemics and geopolitical shifts, procurement teams are navigating an increasingly volatile landscape. At the same time, businesses face pressure to reduce costs, drive innovation, ensure ethical practices, and meet sustainability goals—all within global supply chains that span multiple continents.

This complexity makes global sourcing more challenging but also more critical to long-term success. Strategic sourcing decisions can now directly impact business continuity, brand reputation, and competitive advantage. Organizations that can successfully manage this complexity position themselves to respond faster to change and seize new opportunities in the global marketplace.

Research

What are procurement leaders focused on?

Check out this Economist Impact report to learn more about C-suite perspectives on procurement risks in 2025, including geopolitical dynamics.

Read now

Overcoming common global sourcing challenges

While global sourcing offers significant strategic benefits, it also introduces a unique set of challenges that can impact cost, quality, and continuity if not properly managed. Understanding these obstacles—and how to address them—is essential for procurement teams aiming to build strong, sustainable global supply networks.

Logistical complexity and lead times

Coordinating shipments across multiple time zones, borders, and transportation modes can lead to delays, miscommunications, and inflated costs. Long lead times make responding quickly to market changes or supply disruptions difficult.

Businesses can mitigate these difficulties by investing in advanced logistics planning tools, building in buffer inventory where necessary, and working with reliable freight partners. Close collaboration with suppliers on production and shipping schedules can also help avoid surprises.

Language, culture, and communication barriers

Misunderstandings caused by language differences, time zone gaps, or unfamiliar business customs can hinder relationship-building and delay critical decisions.

Providing cultural competency training for procurement staff and establishing multilingual communication protocols can help address potential issues. Procurement teams can also use collaboration platforms with built-in translation tools and schedule regular check-ins to maintain alignment.

Regulatory and compliance risks

Navigating trade laws, tariffs, import/export regulations, labor standards, and environmental requirements across countries can be daunting—and non-compliance can lead to penalties or reputational damage.

Companies can reduce these risks by bringing in legal and compliance experts familiar with international trade regulations. They can also use sourcing tools that flag regulatory risks and incorporate compliance criteria into supplier selection and contracts.

Quality control and consistency issues

Without direct oversight, maintaining consistent quality across international suppliers can be challenging, especially when production is outsourced to lower-cost regions.

Businesses can meet this challenge head-on by establishing rigorous supplier qualification processes, including audits, certifications, and quality checkpoints. Building continuous improvement clauses into supplier agreements and tracking performance with data-driven scorecards are other ways to avoid slippage in quality.

Currency fluctuations and cost volatility

Exchange rate shifts, inflation, tariffs, and fluctuating raw material costs can erode cost advantages and create budget uncertainty.

Creating financial hedging strategies and including price adjustment clauses in contracts can help minimize these difficulties, as well as regularly monitoring economic indicators in supplier regions and maintaining cost modeling tools that reflect total landed cost (TLC).

Overcoming these challenges requires a proactive, strategic approach to procurement. By building strong internal capabilities, leveraging digital tools, and fostering transparent supplier relationships, organizations can more easily navigate the complexities of global sourcing.

How technology enables smarter global sourcing

Technology is transforming global sourcing from a manual, reactive process into a strategic, data-driven discipline. With the help of digital tools, procurement teams can make faster, smarter decisions while improving visibility, collaboration, and risk management across global supply networks.

Advanced sourcing platforms and AI-driven analytics provide real-time insights into supplier performance, pricing trends, and market conditions. This enables more accurate demand forecasting, cost modeling, and supplier selection.

Tools like supply chain control towers and digital twins offer end-to-end visibility, allowing teams to anticipate disruptions and respond proactively. Meanwhile, smart contracts improve transparency and trust, especially in complex international transactions.

By integrating these technologies, procurement teams can streamline workflows, reduce errors, and build more resilient and agile global sourcing strategies—ultimately driving greater value across the organization.

How to build a resilient global sourcing strategy

Resilience in global sourcing means more than simply having backup suppliers. It involves proactively designing a supply network that can withstand disruptions, adapt to changing market conditions, and continue delivering value over time. A resilient global sourcing strategy is built on data, diversification, and deliberate planning. Here are some key steps procurement leaders should follow:

  1. Align sourcing strategy with business goals
    Start by clearly defining what the organization needs from global sourcing—whether it’s cost efficiency, supply continuity, innovation, or access to specific capabilities. Align sourcing priorities with broader corporate objectives, such as growth targets, Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) commitments, or geographic expansion.
  2. Conduct a comprehensive risk assessment
    Evaluate potential risks across geopolitical, economic, environmental, and operational dimensions. Identify high-risk suppliers, regions prone to disruption, and single points of failure in the supply chain. Use risk scoring and scenario planning to inform sourcing decisions.
  3. Diversify the supplier base
    Avoid dependency on a single country, region, or supplier by strategically sourcing from multiple geographies and vendors. Diversification increases flexibility and reduces exposure to localized shocks.
  4. Establish robust supplier relationships
    Build partnerships based on trust, transparency, and performance metrics. Strong relationships with suppliers encourage better communication during crises, faster recovery, and greater willingness to collaborate on problem-solving and innovation.
  5. Invest in digital visibility tools
    Leverage technology such as supply chain control towers, real-time dashboards, and supplier collaboration platforms to gain end-to-end visibility. These tools enable faster response times, improved forecasting, and early identification of potential disruptions.
  6. Continuously monitor and adapt
    Global sourcing resilience isn’t static. Monitor geopolitical developments, trade policies, and supplier performance on an ongoing basis. Use real-time data and periodic reviews to refine the sourcing strategy and stay ahead of emerging risks.

By following these steps, procurement teams can transform global sourcing from a cost-focused function into a strategic advantage—one that not only withstands disruption but also drives growth, agility, and long-term sustainability.

Global sourcing trends shaping 2025 and beyond

As procurement evolves, businesses must adapt to a dynamic environment influenced by technology, geopolitics, and sustainability goals. Here are three key trends defining the future of global sourcing:

  1. Digitally driven supply networks
    Advanced technologies like AI, machine learning, and predictive analytics are transforming how procurement teams manage global sourcing. In 2025, real-time data integration, automated supplier scoring, and digital twins are enabling faster, smarter decisions. These tools give greater visibility across global supply chains and support proactive risk mitigation, improved forecasting, and better supplier collaboration.
  2. Nearshoring and regional diversification
    The disruptions caused by geopolitical instability, shifting trade policies, and ripple effects from the pandemic that are still being felt have made overreliance on distant suppliers a liability. In response, many organizations are embracing nearshoring—sourcing closer to home—to reduce lead times, improve flexibility, and build more resilient supply chains. This trend doesn’t replace global sourcing but rather complements it with a more diversified and risk-aware approach.
  3. Sustainability and ethical sourcing
    ESG expectations are higher than ever. From investors to consumers, stakeholders demand that global sourcing strategies align with sustainability and ethical standards. In 2025, procurement teams are embedding ESG metrics into supplier evaluation, investing in low-carbon logistics, and increasing transparency into labor practices. Compliance, reputation, and competitive differentiation all hinge on responsible sourcing practices.

Essential questions to guide your global sourcing strategy

Success in global sourcing requires careful planning, risk management, and alignment with business objectives. Before initiating or expanding a global sourcing strategy, procurement teams must assess their readiness and address several key questions.

  1. What is the primary objective in pursuing global sourcing?
    Is the goal to reduce costs, diversify the supply base, access specialized capabilities, or increase supply chain resilience? Clear objectives shape supplier selection, risk mitigation, and performance metrics.
  2. Do we fully understand the total landed cost?
    Beyond unit prices, TLC includes shipping, tariffs, customs duties, taxes, handling, insurance, and potential currency fluctuations. Are we prepared to calculate and optimize for these?
  3. What risks are associated with sourcing from a specific region or supplier?
    Such risks include political instability, regulatory changes, natural disasters, intellectual property (IP) risks, and logistics disruptions. Have we assessed and quantified these risks?
  4. Do we have the internal capabilities and infrastructure to manage global suppliers?
    Do your procurement, legal, logistics, and compliance teams have the necessary expertise, tools, and bandwidth to support international sourcing?
  5. How will we ensure compliance with local and international regulations?
    Are we knowledgeable about labor laws, environmental regulations, export/import restrictions, and anti-corruption laws in target sourcing regions?
  6. Is our supply chain agile and resilient enough to absorb potential disruptions?
    What contingency plans do we have if a supplier fails to deliver or if geopolitical tensions arise?
  7. What quality assurance mechanisms are in place?
    How will we monitor, inspect, and maintain product or service quality from overseas suppliers—especially without on-site visibility?
  8. How do global suppliers align with our ESG standards?
    Are we sourcing responsibly? Do our partners follow ethical labor practices and sustainable production methods?

resources/guide-to-spend-analysis.html.body:
What Is

Spend analysis: the ultimate guide

Spend analysis is the process of reviewing procurement spend metrics and assessing performance data to reduce costs, improve strategic sourcing, and strengthen supplier relationships.

Published on July 24, 2024

In today’s world of dizzying competition and lightning-fast change, you may only have moments to seize an opportunity or spot a risk that could be a game-changer for your company. To pivot quickly and make rapid business decisions, you need confidence—you need to feel like you have reliable intel to back you up and give you a clear view of your situation. That’s where the process of spend analysis, and the spend analytics tools and methodologies that support it, comes in.

Not only does spend analysis provide key insights about your past expenditures, it also provides the basis for analytics tools to forecast spending patterns and make strategic predictions for future planning.

According to a recent report from The Economist Group, about a third of C-suite respondents cited spend analytics as a top priority for the coming year. Powerful spend analysis tools, especially those incorporating AI-driven capabilities, are crucial for navigating modern complexities and empowering you to optimize your business and procurement operations.

By systematically reviewing and analyzing disparate data sets, spend analytics solutions and practices can help you uncover inefficiencies, negotiate from a stronger position, and build better relationships with your suppliers.

What is spend analysis?

Spend analysis is the data-driven process of collecting, cleansing, classifying, and analyzing complex expenditure information. Its goal is to help you meet key objectives, such as lower procurement costs, greater efficiency, and higher compliance. At its core, it addresses some questions that help you better understand and optimize your spending:

  • What are we spending money on?
  • How much have we paid?
  • Who are we buying from?
  • Is there a better way to do this?

Historically, spend analysis was a labor-intensive and manual process. Procurement teams had to sift through disparate data sources and spreadsheets, often missing opportunities or risks. But fortunately, today’s AI-powered spend analysis tools automate these tasks and provide on-demand data insights. This streamlines the integration and standardization of data from multiple sources and makes it easier to analyze the information in real time—helping you make intelligence-based decisions that improve business results.

Spend analysis process

While the spend analysis process may vary to reflect a company’s unique needs and challenges, it’s nonetheless a structured and systematic undertaking that relies on access to continually updated reports and datasets as well as robust analytics. Here’s how a typical process works:

Capture direct, indirect, and services spend data

This includes capturing data from different systems across your business, including ERP, accounts payable (AP) systems, e-procurement platforms, expense management systems, and business units. Information for both direct spend (such as raw materials for production) and indirect spend (office supplies and utilities) must be gathered to provide a complete picture of the organization's expenditures.

Cleanse, de-dupe, and enrich data

Once data is collected, you can cleanse and standardize it to make it useful. This involves unifying formats, eliminating duplicates, and handling any blank fields. You can then enrich the information with further data points such as credit score numbers for each supplier.

Categorize all spend data

After cleansing, you must categorize your data into standard spend categories. This step involves creating a logical taxonomy that groups similar types of spend, making it easier to analyze and manage. Category management can include direct spend categories like raw materials and indirect spend categories like IT services.

Merge with external data

Integrating external data with internal spend data provides a more comprehensive analysis. Modern software solutions enhance this process by allowing for customized data mergers and reports to deliver findings that would not have been possible with manual systems from the past.

Transform raw data into actionable insights

With the application of analytics and predictive modeling, you can quickly and more accurately identify trends, forecast future spend, and uncover opportunities for cost savings.

Identify risks and opportunities for cost savings

You can then analyze your transformed data to identify potential risks, such as supplier dependencies or compliance issues. This process also reveals opportunities to cut costs by highlighting areas of inefficiency or overspending.

Use insights to empower end users

Data is knowledge, and knowledge is power. The customized information and reports available today can provide some game-changing insights. But ultimately, people must take responsibility to act on them. In this last important step, it’s essential to ensure that you are sharing (with the right teams) your findings and access to critical intelligence.

Benefits of spend analysis in procurement and across the business

Thanks to increased visibility and intelligence, spend analysis makes it easier for your procurement team to realize some of the following benefits:

  • Lower costs: Spend analysis highlights savings opportunities and potential risks, helping you negotiate better terms, consolidate purchases, and switch to more cost-effective suppliers.
  • Better risk management: Analyzing spend helps you identify overpayments or patterns that could indicate potential supply chain vulnerabilities.
  • Improved strategic sourcing: Detailed insights into spending trends let you make faster decisions, negotiate from a stronger position, and better align your strategic sourcing processes with your cross-business goals and objectives.
  • Streamlined procurement processes: Spend analysis helps you identify inefficiencies and bottlenecks. These discoveries can lead to process improvements, faster cycle times, reduced labor costs, and better procurement performance overall.
  • Enhanced supplier relationship management (SRM): You can use insights into SRM and supplier performance to develop stronger partnerships and ensure your suppliers meet the standards and expectations you set.
  • Optimized contract management: Adding analytics to the contract management process helps you see beyond the fine print to spot challenges and opportunities. These insights let you negotiate the best ongoing and renewal terms throughout the lifecycle of the contract.
  • Ability to benchmark performance: Spend analysis allows your organization to benchmark performance internally and against industry standards, identifying best practices, setting targets, and driving continuous improvement.

Spend analysis example

By integrating spend analysis solutions, the powerhouse clothing brand American Eagle Outfitters optimized its spend visibility and compliance across multiple procurement categories. This allowed for quick access to detailed spend data, which helped the company maintain a high level of compliance with its procurement policies. Notably, American Eagle Outfitters consistently achieved an 80% target for PO compliance, translating into substantial savings.

Additionally, the integration of multiple source systems facilitated real-time spend analytics, allowing American Eagle Outfitters to identify and act on cost-cutting opportunities. This strategic use of integrated spend analysis solutions strengthened American Eagle Outfitters’ vendor relationships and enhanced its overall procurement efficiency.

What is maverick spend?

Maverick spending, also known as rogue spending, happens when your employees make purchases that bypass your procurement policies. With the ease of online buying, even B2B goods and services can increasingly be acquired by anyone with an internet connection. This type of spending can lead to many problems and risks, including higher costs, lost visibility, unreliable quality, and potential compliance issues if the buyer doesn’t stick to legal or regulatory requirements. It can also damage your relationships with preferred suppliers, who may not appreciate being sidestepped.

By setting up your spend analysis solutions to spot the trends associated with maverick spend—and by educating your teams about the risks of this practice—you can help protect yourself against the problems it causes.

Spend analysis metrics and KPIs

The best spend analysis solution can help you monitor various metrics and agreed-upon key performance indicators (KPIs) through real-time dashboards and reports. Such metrics give you a window into overall spend and performance across suppliers, categories, sourcing processes, pricing, and more. Here are some common KPIs used in spend analysis:

  • Savings: This core, basic KPI measures the reduction in expenditure achieved through improved procurement strategies, better supplier negotiations, and more efficient processes. By tracking cost savings, you can quantify the financial benefits of your spend management efforts.
  • Spend under management: This KPI refers to the total spend that is actively managed by the procurement team. It helps you understand how much of your expenditure is being controlled and optimized. Higher levels of spend under management indicate better oversight and more effective procurement practices. The metric ensures that all spend is visible and accounted for, reducing the risk of maverick spending.
  • Supplier performance: You can compare metrics such as on-time delivery rates, defect rates, and compliance with contract terms to assess supplier performance. Regular monitoring sets a visible and agreed-upon bar and fosters stronger supplier relationships.
  • Operational KPIs: Operational KPIs measure the efficiency of procurement processes. These can include metrics such as cycle time for processing purchase orders, the accuracy of order fulfillment, and the efficiency of invoice processing. Improving operational KPIs leads to more streamlined procurement processes and reduced operational costs.
  • Payment terms: An often-underutilized tool, payment analysis examines the conditions under which payments are made to suppliers. This means assessing things like average payment days, early payment discounts taken, and compliance with agreed-upon payment terms.
  • Employee KPIs: Employee KPIs measure the performance and productivity of procurement staff. These can include metrics such as the number of purchase orders processed per employee, the accuracy of order placements, and the level of compliance with procurement policies. Tracking employee KPIs can help you identify training needs, improve overall team performance, and boost the efficiency and effectiveness of the procurement function .

What to look for in spend analytics software

Cloud-based, AI-powered spend analytics solutions are essential to any serious procurement and supply chain strategy. Regardless of what stage you are at in your digital transformation journey, every step you take toward improving data integration, visibility, and accuracy will pay off in both the short and long term. Look for the following as just a few of the key features you should expect in your spend analysis software:

  • Comprehensive data integration: The software should integrate with existing financial, ERP, and supply chain systems to consolidate all spend data in one place.
  • Real-time dashboards and reporting: Look for customizable, real-time dashboards that provide quick insights into key spend metrics and workflow processes.
  • Advanced analytics and AI capabilities: The software should leverage AI to transform raw data into actionable insights and predict future spending trends.
  • User-friendly interface: Ensure you are getting an intuitive, easy-to-navigate interface that requires minimal training and works on both desktop and mobile devices.
  • Scalability and flexibility: Choose software that can scale with your organization, integrate with new systems, and adapt to changing procurement needs.
  • Robust security and compliance features: The software must include strong security measures and comply with relevant regulations to protect sensitive data.
  • Customizable reporting and analytics: Select software that allows for the creation of bespoke reports and detailed data analysis tailored to specific needs.

resources/maximizing-ai-roi.html.description: Learn how to improve your ROI with AI, build a business case, and measure impact with our six-step framework for business leaders.
resources/maximizing-ai-roi.html.body:
Best Practice How-To Guide

A practical guide for maximizing AI ROI

Six steps to help ensure AI pays off for your enterprise—from business case to boardroom impact.

Published on September 10, 2025

How to measure AI ROI and prove business impact

AI is on the minds of nearly every business leader today. The promise of intelligent automation, better decision-making, and new ways of working feels immense. Despite the urgency, a common challenge remains—turning AI potential into measurable business impact.

For many executives, there’s a gap between recognizing AI’s potential and achieving measurable results. The journey requires a clear definition of AI readiness, a direct link between business priorities and targeted use cases, and a disciplined approach to measuring ROI. Without these elements, even well-intentioned initiatives risk stalling before they deliver meaningful AI business impact.

This guide explores key steps in determining ROI with AI—from assessing your readiness to sustaining value over time—with real-world examples of AI business impact from enterprise organizations.

Step 1. Align AI initiatives with business objectives

Key takeaway: Start every AI project with a clearly defined business goal to maximize impact and secure executive buy-in.

The first step toward a successful AI strategy is to evaluate your business goals. AI isn't valuable on its own. It's valuable when it moves the needle on something the business already cares about.

Before you invest, you need to know why you're investing. Are you trying to reduce costs, make faster decisions, or increase customer retention? AI solutions that start with a clear objective are more likely to succeed. They also make it easier to secure buy-in and justify the investment.

Having a single, unified interface for all of your AI capabilities can make a difference. It can proactively recommend next best actions and insights within the flow of work so employees can get more done.

Real-world example: Delta Airlines

Delta Airlines aligned its AI initiative with a core business objective—to connect employee happiness with customer experience. By using SAP SuccessFactors, they successfully filled nearly 50% of their managerial roles with customer-facing employees. The result created a virtuous cycle of positive customer and shareholder outcomes.

Step 2. Estimate ROI through use case modeling

Key takeaway: Model ROI through specific, high-value use cases and take a multi-year view to strengthen your investment case.

Before you implement any new AI technologies, you need a solid business case. For AI, that means modeling the return on investment through use cases. This is where you move beyond general ideas of efficiency and start to quantify the potential impact.

Think about the potential business AI value categories:

  • Cost optimization and efficiency gains: How many hours could you save by automating a manual process?
  • Revenue growth: Could better personalization lead to higher conversion rates?
  • Risk mitigation and compliance: Could AI help you detect fraud or automate compliance checks, reducing your exposure to risk?
  • Decision quality: What is the value of more accurate forecasting or fewer errors in your financial reporting?

One way these categories come to life is through the connection between the customer experience (CX) and your operational back end (ERP). A CX platform might have the front-end data on customer behavior and order history. But the operational data—what allows you to generate quotes, handle delivery, and provide order and invoice status—is all in the back end. The two parts must be in lockstep for a modern enterprise to deliver on what it promises.

An economic validation report by Enterprise Strategy Group shows that integrating AI into your CX and ERP systems can deliver a conservative ROI of 214% over five years—rising to 761% with maximum improvements.1 The report also highlights that this kind of integration can lead to a 10% to 30% increase in average deal sizes, directly boosting revenue.2

When you model these benefits, remember to think about recurrence. Are these one-time savings, or will they compound over time? A multi-year view of the resulting cash flow can paint a much more compelling picture than a single-year projection. This is a critical step in building a strong business case that resonates with your fellow executives and helps you measure AI performance over time.

Real-world example: Microsoft

Microsoft faced challenges with manual processes and poor forecasting in its supply chain. By targeting these pain points, it achieved a 50% reduction in manual planning processes and a 75% increase in on-time planning. These improvements directly showcase how a well-defined use case can translate into tangible ROI.

Step 3. Quantify value through baseline comparisons

Key takeaway: Establish a clear performance baseline to measure AI’s true impact and highlight the cost of inaction.

To realize meaningful AI business impact, start by defining a clear performance baseline. Document current KPIs—such as processing times, error rates, customer satisfaction scores, or revenue per transaction—and project how AI could shift these numbers. This establishes a realistic payback period and break-even point.

The true value of AI often extends beyond simple calculations like “X hours saved at Y dollars per hour.” When automation removes repetitive tasks, teams can focus on strategic initiatives, drive innovation, and contribute to higher-value outcomes. This cascading effect amplifies ROI with AI far beyond the initial efficiency gains.

Equally important is recognizing the cost of inaction. Delays in improving a critical process can mean missed revenue, diminished competitiveness, and lower customer retention. Framing AI as a strategic necessity—not a discretionary spend—strengthens your investment case.

Real-world example: Chobani

Take Chobani, for example. By using AI to streamline its financial processes, the company achieved a 75% reduction in time spent on expenses. This freed up its finance team from administrative work and allowed them to focus on more strategic initiatives like financial analysis and improving compliance.

Step 4. Track real-world metrics post-deployment

Once your AI solution is live, shift from projections to performance data using an AI measurement tool. It’s important to focus on metrics that demonstrate whether the solution is delivering as intended:

  • Measure before and after KPIs to confirm the results
  • Monitor adoption and usage rates to ensure the solution is effectively used
  • Track the downstream impacts. Did improved throughput in one department lead to a faster time to market and a revenue boost in another?

A transparent consumption model gives you complete visibility into what’s used, how often, and where it’s delivering value. These insights allow you to optimize performance, communicate results clearly, and justify ongoing or expanded investment.

AI agents can be a powerful tool for this. These agents are infused with business process expertise, giving them the ability to reason, make decisions, and adapt to dynamic conditions. They can also automate time-consuming work across business functions like supply chain, procurement, and finance.

Real-world example: Nestlé

Nestlé struggled with slow, paper-based expense processes that were prone to errors. By implementing AI-driven tools in SAP Concur, they were able to track and measure significant improvements. The company achieved a 100% elimination of manual expense management processes and saw a 3x increase in employee efficiency when creating reports.

Step 5. Include qualitative and strategic returns

Key takeaway: Factor in both measurable financial gains and strategic, long-term benefits when evaluating AI’s success.

Not every return shows up in a financial report—especially early on. It’s important to include qualitative and strategic returns when building your business case and progress reviews.

Some organizations achieved up to 300% improvement in daily productivity by automating routine processes like data entry, order processing, and customer support.3 Sales teams have also reported productivity increases of up to 90% through streamlined workflows and better access to customer data. These gains aren’t just about time saved—they free up teams to focus on higher-value work.4

Operational costs can also drop sharply. By simplifying operations and reducing the need for complex integrations, businesses can save up to 70% of the time they previously spent managing and maintaining systems.5

Some other things to consider:

  • Faster experimentation cycles: AI can accelerate innovation
  • Talent retention through innovation: People want to work for forward-thinking companies
  • Competitive differentiation: Early adoption can give you a significant market advantage
  • Future-proofing your infrastructure: Investing in AI today builds a more resilient, adaptable foundation for tomorrow

Finally, AI can significantly improve customer experience and retention. Companies have seen faster transaction completions, fewer service issues, and higher satisfaction rates—reducing churn by up to 55%6.

Real-world example: SA Power Networks

SA Power Networks faced the challenge of managing an aging infrastructure across a vast, sparsely populated area. By using an AI-powered app, they not only saved $1M in a single year—they also achieved a 99% success rate in identifying poles likely to corrode. The AI solution also gave field technicians access to 50 years of asset history with a simple natural language query to improve safety and reliability.

Step 6. Build a feedback loop for continuous justification

Key takeaway: Create a feedback loop to refine models, discover new opportunities, and sustain AI’s business value over time.

AI technologies improve as they learn from new data. The most successful organizations establish a feedback loop that tracks outcomes, refines models, and applies insights to future initiatives.

This feedback loop ensures that your AI investment continues to deliver value long after the initial deployment. It also helps you identify new use cases, optimize existing solutions, and build on your successes.

A suite of tools can help you build, extend, and orchestrate AI solutions at scale. With centralized management and governance, AI agents can be aligned to business needs and reveal new opportunities across the organization.

By continually exploring new use cases, developing custom solutions, and extending AI at your own pace, you transform AI from a single project into an ongoing engine for growth.

Starting your AI journey

Achieving a measurable ROI with AI is often more straightforward than it appears. You don’t need to have all the answers to get started. You just need the right plan, the right people, and the right support.

Whether you’re defining your first AI proof of concept or scaling AI enterprise-wide, choose technologies that are relevant, reliable, and responsible.

These systems should be protected by end-to-end security measures, including threat intelligence and vulnerability management, and governed by strong data policies to ensure responsible management, privacy, and legal compliance.

Embedded into core business processes, they deliver tangible results you can measure and build on over time.

For executives, here’s a six-point leadership checklist to help your organization maximize ROI:

  • Start every AI project with a clearly defined business goal to maximize impact and secure executive buy-in
  • Model ROI through specific, high-value use cases and take a multi-year view to strengthen your investment case
  • Establish a clear performance baseline to measure AI’s true impact and highlight the cost of inaction
  • Use post-deployment metrics and transparent tracking tools to prove value and guide future AI investments.
  • Factor in both measurable financial gains and strategic, long-term benefits when evaluating AI’s success
  • Create a feedback loop to refine models, discover new opportunities, and sustain AI’s business value over time

1.–6. "Analyzing the Economic Benefits of Using AI-Powered SAP CX Solutions Natively Connected to SAP ERP," Enterprise Strategy Group by TechTarget, August 2024.

resources/supplier-relationship-manageme.body:
What Is

What is supplier relationship management (SRM)?

Supplier relationship management (SRM) is the ongoing evaluation of vendors that supply your organization with goods, materials, and services.

Updated on January 26, 2026

Not too many years ago, your customers were happy to wait days or even weeks for products to be delivered. You knew who all your competitors were, and market trends were often gradual and steady. Today, none of that is true. Modern consumers shop in real time from a global, and typically digital, catalog. Product (and even industry) trends can take hold in weeks, if not days. Throw into the mix a confounding collection of supply chain disruptions from pandemics to politics and weather events—and that equals quite a dizzying situation. As much as your customers build your business, your suppliers are the foundation upon which it exists. Today’s best software solutions and operational innovations are helping companies develop the supplier relationship management strategies they need to not only compete but thrive in today’s complex and fast-changing world.

Supplier relationship management meaning

The practice of supplier relationship management (SRM) originated in the 1980s as a way to give companies a systematic and consistent strategy for assessing their suppliers. SRM’s roots can be traced back to the work of the renowned procurement and supply chain analyst Peter Kraljic, who introduced an innovative perspective on supplier segmentation. He developed something called the Kraljic Matrix which essentially maps suppliers against two pivotal dimensions: risk and profitability. For example, an electronics company needs both microprocessors and office supplies, but the vendor that supplies them with the former is far more essential to their success than the latter. For this reason, supplier relationship management posits that while good interactions are important with all your vendors, it’s especially crucial to cultivate robust, transparent relationships and ongoing assessment strategies with those suppliers upon whom your business is the most dependent.

Modern supplier relationship management practices and solutions leverage analytical and strategic components that can help businesses revolutionize their approach to managing vendor relationships.

SRM vs. supplier management

The terms “supplier relationship management” and “supplier management” are often used interchangeably, but they are not technically the same thing. Supplier relationship management is just what it sounds like: the practice of managing relationships with suppliers. Supplier management, however, is broader than that. It includes relationship management, but also supplier information, performance, and risk management—as well as activities like forecast collaboration.

As a term, SRM has been around a lot longer and is still used by many businesses, especially small and midsize companies that don’t need the full functionality of an end-to-end supplier management suite. Today, however, supplier management is the more modern term and is often used to describe new and advanced cloud-based tools that meet the complex needs of upper midmarket and large enterprises.

The supplier relationship management process

The SRM journey is comprised of five critical steps:

  1. Supplier segmentation: This initial phase involves categorizing the supplier base. This helps to deliver insights, highlight potential risks, uncover savings opportunities, and enhance supplier relationships. Segmentation can occur based on various criteria such as item type, quantity, risk (using the Kraljic matrix), location, price, sustainability, and more, depending on what holds the most value for the business.
  2. Supplier strategy development: Armed with the insights from segmentation, the next step is to craft a tailored strategy. This involves negotiating contracts and prices, enhancing communication processes, and attempting to diversify business across additional suppliers to minimize risk and dependency.
  3. Relationship building: This stage focuses on deepening your connection with suppliers. It transcends transactions, fostering a relationship that includes end-to-end communication which can include things like early notifications of price changes, promotions, and potential shortages. Essentially, it ensures that your suppliers know you and are attuned to your business needs.
  4. Strategy execution: Putting into action the tactics and initiatives identified during the strategy development stage to enhance performance, drive value, and achieve the set objectives with each segmented supplier group. It can encompass contract management, order fulfillment, performance management, and proactive collaboration with suppliers to ensure that the strategic goals are translated into tangible outcomes that benefit both the buying organization and its suppliers.
  5. Monitoring and continuous improvements: Continuous monitoring of supplier performance is essential to effective supplier relationship management. This can include evaluating timeliness and accuracy of deliveries, product quality, cost efficiency, lead time, and responsiveness. Performance data feeds back into the cycle, informing the next round of segmentation and strategy development, creating a loop that gets stronger and more illuminating each time it goes around.

Goals and benefits of supplier relationship management

When you improve your ability to engage with your suppliers, you boost your opportunities for success.

  • Closer relationships with suppliers: Building closer relationships with suppliers means deepening your interactions beyond the transactional level. It involves forging partnerships and building trust, mutual understanding, and shared objectives. This gives both you and your suppliers a better understanding of each other’s goals, threats, and opportunities.
  • Lower costs: By understanding suppliers' operations and cost structures, businesses can work with their vendors to identify areas for cost reduction without compromising quality. This can lead to better price negotiations, bulk purchasing advantages, and reduced total cost of ownership.
  • Reduced supplier risk: A well-implemented supplier relationship management strategy brings greater awareness and real-time visibility - which helps you identify, assess, and mitigate risks with greater speed and assertion. As the saying goes: You don’t know what you don’t know. Leveraging smart procurement solutions and SRM practices ensures that you are more prepared and confident.
  • Better supplier responsiveness: When your suppliers know you and feel invested in your success, they are more likely to go the extra mile to meet your needs, especially in urgent situations. This responsiveness can make all the difference in time-sensitive or unexpected scenarios. The tighter the relationship between buyers and sellers, the greater the responsiveness.
  • Faster supplier collaboration: By providing your suppliers with digital and real-time methods of collaboration and information sharing, you can react faster to disruption and improve business agility. Often, this is done on a multienterprise supply chain business network—a many-to-many B2B collaboration platform where buyers and sellers can connect, transact, and partner on shared processes and information.
  • Greater visibility and transparency: Good supplier relationship management is transparent. It clearly communicates performance metrics, their importance to all, and the fact that everyone is subject to scrutiny. This no-nonsense, honest approach gives a good impression and encourages suppliers to maintain high standards as part of their partnership with you, rather than simply out of fear of surveillance.
  • Optimized value chain: By aligning supplier operations with your business objectives, supplier relationship management strategies help to support an increasingly streamlined supply and value chain. This ensures that from end to end, each link in the chain is visible, functioning efficiently, and contributing to overall business success.
  • Insight into suppliers’ capabilities: With access to data and intel, you can better understand the strengths, capabilities, and potential within your suppliers’ businesses. If you’re introducing new products or business models, for example, you can assess whether your current supply base can meet those needs—or if you need to find new suppliers. By grasping the capacity and limitations within your supplier landscape, you can speculate and pivot with greater assurance and foresight.

Protecting against supply chain disruption

It took the catastrophe of COVID-19 for people to fully appreciate how dependent we all are on supply chains. Aware of how close they’d come to the brink, the best businesses began to aggressively optimize their supply chains and the systems and processes that run them. Part of this has led to the urgent adoption of better supplier relationship management practices to help navigate uncertainties with resilience and confidence. By cultivating strong supplier relationships and maintaining continuous oversight, you can anticipate disruption and respond with agility.

Challenges of supplier relationship management

Even with strong supplier relationship management processes in place, there are still risks and challenges to which you should always remain alert.

  • Lack of supplier diversity: Building great relationships with a small number of suppliers is terrific for a lot of reasons. But there is always vulnerability and risk associated with having too many eggs in one vendor’s basket.Fortunately, SRM software solutions can help to manage a lot of the time-consuming, administrative elements of relationship management, leaving you free to build new 1:1 relationships and bring on more vendors than you otherwise would have had time for.
  • Misalignment: Sometimes suppliers can become competitors. Or their agendas and business models can change to where you’re no longer aligned on terms and prices the way you once were. This can be awkward when you’ve built close and friendly relations, so it’s essential to anticipate these scenarios and build diplomatic communication and negotiation plans in case this happens.
  • Obstacles to risk and continuity: From global politics to pandemics and weather crises, we’re learning to “never say never” when it comes to the next potential supply chain event. Ensuring excellent relationships with your suppliers is an essential buffer against uncertainty—but unfortunately, it’s not a panacea. These days, it’s also crucial to double down with AI-enabled procurement solutions to help you better grapple with data, see around corners, and put contingency plans in place.
  • Visibility challenges: While supplier relationship management enhances visibility into supplier operations, it is impossible to achieve complete transparency. Balancing trust with technological aids like IoT sensors, blockchain, and GPS tracking can help in maintaining a clear line of sight without encroaching on the supplier’s autonomy.

Supplier relationship management examples

Supplier relationship management strategies and solutions are helping these important sectors manage their unique needs and issues.

  1. Healthcare: From medicine to surgical equipment, product quality is literally a matter of life and death in this sector. Supplier relationship management in healthcare often involves rigorous vetting processes for suppliers, regular quality audits, and strict compliance checks to adhere to healthcare standards and regulations. For example, a hospital could receive real-time alerts if a supplier’s product has been subject to recalls or quality issues, enabling swift action to find alternative sources and prevent potential harm.
  2. Retail: With the pace of social media, fashion trends come and go—sometimes literally overnight. Supplier relationship management in retail facilitates collaborative forecasting and planning with suppliers to ensure that the right products are available when they’re hot and not sitting around gathering dust once they’re not. For instance, a retailer of a high-priced, limited edition item can work closely with suppliers to tailor their orders by region, ensuring supply without surplus.
  3. Energy: Utility companies are often dealing with assets that are decades old and require rare and unusual parts and equipment to keep them running. Furthermore, they are facing mounting pressure to reduce emissions and develop more robust sustainability measures. The old-school parts suppliers and the modern high-tech vendors of smart power equipment have very different practices and methods. Supplier relationship management can help utility companies centralize and unify the way they manage these disparate types of suppliers—making sure they meet the crucial energy needs of customers and remain compliant with sustainability standards.
  4. Transportation: These companies depend on reliable equipment and timely delivery of supplies. Effective SRM in this sector could, for example, involve closely managing relationships with parts suppliers for vehicle maintenance, ensuring everything is available when needed without carrying excessive inventory. A logistics company might use supplier relationship management tools to evaluate the reliability of a diverse network of suppliers, giving them the confidence to expand and diversify their business.
  5. Construction: Businesses in this sector are under constant deadline pressures and must maintain relationships with a dizzying variety of material suppliers. A construction firm could use supplier relationship management software to track supplier performance across multiple projects, identifying those who consistently deliver on time and meet quality specifications. This helps them stay on track with both costs and timing.

resources/supply-chain-optimization.html.body:
What Is

What is supply chain optimization today?

Modern supply chain optimization uses data and AI to build resilient, efficient supply chains.

Updated on October 27, 20267 minutes

Modern supply chain optimization at a glance

Supply chain optimization enhances the efficiency and effectiveness of a supply chain using modern technologies and data analytics. It matters today because businesses face unprecedented disruption—from climate events to geopolitical challenges—that demands faster, more informed decisions. Technologies like AI, cloud computing, and real-time analytics have turned optimization from a static planning exercise into a continuous, dynamic practice. Modern supply chain optimization helps businesses improve performance, balance supply and demand, and respond more effectively to change.

The top supply chain optimization priorities

When it comes to supply chain optimization, the top priorities have never changed: Make sure customers are happy, increase efficiency and profitability, and balance supply and demand. Those core priorities remain at the fore. But businesses today face levels of change and uncertainty that they’ve never seen before.

Climate events, economic upheaval, and geopolitical unrest have an increasingly disruptive effect on supply chains, which have become more complex compared to the past. An event that once affected a single region or supplier can now ripple across the globe in days. The good news is that you can now use smart technologies and tools to better power increasingly sophisticated supply chain optimization strategies—turning disruption from a threat into a competitive advantage.

Key priorities for today's supply chain leaders include:

  • Meeting customer expectations for faster delivery and greater transparency.
  • Increasing operational efficiency and profitability across the supply chain.
  • Balancing supply and demand in real time, not just on seasonal cycles.
  • Adapting to sustainability requirements and evolving regulations.
  • Reducing waste and improving resource utilization.

Understanding supply chain management (SCM) provides the foundation for these optimization efforts, since it builds on the broader SCM framework. While management covers all activities that turn raw materials into finished goods, optimization focuses specifically on making those activities run as efficiently and resiliently as possible.

The evolution of supply chain optimization

With globalization and technological advancements, the scope and potential company-wide benefit of supply chain optimization have expanded significantly over the years.

  • In the past: Before there was overnight delivery and online shopping, there were fewer warehouses and, frankly, less stuff available to both B2B and B2C customers. Companies devoted much of their resources to logistics—transporting products from manufacturing sites to markets. A major focus was on reducing transportation costs.
  • Strategic integration: As businesses recognized the strategic value of supply chains, the focus shifted toward integration. This involved aligning supply chain processes with business goals and strategies. Companies began realizing the benefits of centralized coordination across their operations, improving visibility, collaboration, and planning across functions.
  • Digital transformation: The advent of technologies like material resource planning (MRP) and later, ERP systems, marked a significant milestone. These innovations gave organizations a connected, enterprise-wide view of supply chain operations, helping unify data from procurement and manufacturing to logistics, service, and fulfillment.
  • AI-enabled optimization: Today, supply chain leaders are moving beyond visibility to intelligence. By combining data, AI, machine learning, the Internet of Things (IoT), and advanced analytics, organizations can improve forecasting, automate decision-making, and evaluate potential scenarios before taking action.
  • Sustainability and resilience: Modern supply chain optimization extends beyond efficiency and cost savings. Organizations increasingly rely on AI and timely insights to strengthen resilience, improve supplier collaboration, and support sustainability goals across their supply chain. By connecting people, processes, data, and trading partners, companies can balance service levels, risk, cost, and environmental impact while building more agile and adaptive supply chains.

Use AI to detect invoice errors, accelerate supplier onboarding, and generate insights across your B2B network.

See AI capabilities

What modern supply chain optimization looks like

Today, supply chain optimization brings together planning, execution, and monitoring together on a common, cloud-based data foundation. As organizations become more interconnected, optimization increasingly relies on timely information, automation, and collaboration across suppliers, manufacturers, logistics providers, and customers.

Traditional optimization

Modern optimization

Linear, siloed processes

Connected, networked processes

Reactive problem-solving

Predictive and proactive

Cost-focused

Value and resilience-focused

Manual data sharing

Digital data exchange

Periodic planning cycles

Continuous, dynamic planning

Historical forecasting

AI-driven predictive forecasting

The stages of supply chain optimization

To achieve the most efficient and effective results, the process of supply chain optimization is typically segmented into the following phases. This approach aims to meet strategic business goals while boosting overall performance and improving customer experience.

1. Supply chain strategy

This stage sets the groundwork for all subsequent activities. It involves crafting your supply chain framework to align with the strategic objectives of your business.

  • Strategic alignment: Determine your long-term business goals and how your supply chain can support them. Decisions made here include the selection of suppliers, manufacturing locations, and logistics networks, all aimed at optimizing cost, efficiency, and responsiveness.
  • Risk assessment and planning: Prepare for potential risks down the road—both operational and external—and develop contingency plans. This involves analyzing various scenarios and their potential impact on your business, thereby ensuring preparedness for unforeseen events.
  • Sustainability considerations: Incorporate sustainability goals. This involves choosing eco-friendly materials, optimizing logistics to reduce carbon footprint, and ensuring compliance with environmental regulations.
  • Technological infrastructure: Select the technology platforms that will support supply chain operations. Today, this involves the implementation of ERP systems, a business network, and cloud-based supply chain solutions that promote visibility and collaboration.

2. Supply chain planning

Strategic planning is a critical component of supply chain optimization, focused on building your ongoing business model and establishing achievable goals and key performance indicators (KPIs).

  • Long-term vision-setting: Set KPIs and targets based on market trends, customer needs, and how your supply chain can adapt to meet evolving demands.
  • Resource allocation: Decide where to invest in terms of technology, human resources, and physical infrastructure to maximize efficiency and meet your strategic objectives.
  • Demand planning and forecasting: Use historical data and predictive analytics to anticipate future demand, allowing you to optimize inventory levels and reduce waste. During times of inflation and shifting markets, this is a highly essential activity.
  • Collaboration and communication: Work closely with suppliers, distributors, and other partners to ensure a cohesive approach to supply chain management and alignment with shared goals.

3. Supply chain execution

Execution in supply chain optimization is where strategic planning meets real-world application. It's the stage where the strategies and plans are put into action.

  • Operational efficiency: Ensure the day-to-day management of supply chain activities such as procurement, manufacturing, transportation, and distribution, all work as intended.
  • Ongoing monitoring and adjustment: Let everyone make quick adjustments as needed. With smart technology, you can track supply chain activities, allowing for immediate responses to disruptions or customer needs.
  • Collaboration and integration: Connect suppliers, manufacturers, and other stakeholders to ensure the fulfillment of all promises made further up the chain. This can include things like meeting delivery deadlines and making sure products arrive in safe, good condition.
  • Customer satisfaction: This stage is where goods are delivered on time and in good order, and where customer feedback is gathered and (ideally) actioned upon.

4. Supply chain monitoring

Supply chain monitoring brings another layer to the process, and it's increasingly important in today's fast-changing environment.

  • Continuous performance tracking: Monitor operations, identify emerging risks, and measure outcomes against business goals.
  • Analytics-driven insights: Use data and AI to detect issues early and support informed decision-making.
  • Continuous improvement: Feed operational insights back into planning activities to strengthen future performance.
  • Shared visibility: Use dashboards and alerts to provide a consistent view of supply chain performance across teams and partners.

Collaboration and B2B integration in supply chain optimization

Collaboration has become a core component of supply chain optimization because most organizations operate within complex partner ecosystems. A connected B2B network on a unified platform enables organizations to exchange information, coordinate activities, and respond more effectively to changing market conditions. Digital collaboration helps improve planning accuracy, accelerate execution, and strengthen overall network performance.

Explore the solution

Examples of supply chain process optimization

Here are some key optimization goals to help make your core supply chain functions more resilient.

  1. Warehouse optimization: Advanced AI algorithms analyze historical data to predict future stock requirements and optimize warehouse space. IoT devices track inventory, providing valuable insights into stock movement, reducing waste, and ensuring products are available when needed.
  2. Inventory optimization: Sophisticated predictive analytics tools process sales data, seasonal trends, and market fluctuations to forecast demand accurately. This prevents surplus, reduces carrying costs, and minimizes the risk of stockouts, ensuring a balanced inventory.
  3. Logistics optimization: AI allows you to integrate real-time data from various sources, helping you devise more efficient delivery routes and schedules. This reduces fuel consumption, lowers delivery times, and enhances overall transportation efficiency and sustainability
  4. Manufacturing optimization: Customer feedback combined with rapid prototyping and agile manufacturing processes means quicker adaptation to market trends and faster product development cycles, reducing time-to-market.
  5. Customer service optimization: Analysis of sales and review data provides deeper insights into customer behavior and preferences. This lets you offer tailored support and services and improve customer satisfaction and loyalty.
  6. Optimized sustainability: Analysis of resource consumption and supply chain practices helps you make informed decisions that reduce environmental impact, such as optimizing routes for lower emissions and selecting sustainable materials.
  7. Sourcing optimization: Evaluation of supplier performance, reliability, and risk factors leads to more effective sourcing strategies. This ensures efficient, cost-effective procurement while maintaining supply chain integrity and quality standards.

Using supply chain optimization software to tie it all together

Supply chains are no longer just about moving stuff from A to B. Today’s best supply chain optimization solutions enable you to take a holistic look at your business, considering your supply chain in context with all your other goals, threats, and strategic plans—meaning your supply chain teams and partners can work together to respond to anything that this fast-changing market may throw at them.

Why SAP for supply chain optimization software

Having the right technology partner for supply chain optimization matters. Even strong optimization strategies fail without the tools to execute them. SAP offers a portfolio of solutions designed to help businesses plan, execute, and monitor their supply chains with greater agility and resilience.

With SAP Business Network, you can digitally collaborate with your supply chain trading partners to help sidestep disruption before it happens, and respond with speed and agility when it does. It closes the break points between trading partners by enabling transaction exchange, information sharing, and trading partner discovery—all on a single cloud-based platform.

With SAP Integrated Business Planning for supply chain, you can create coordinated, adaptable plans for a sustainable, risk-resilient future. The planning tool brings together demand forecasting, supply planning, and response management in one place, so teams can model scenarios, test assumptions, and adjust plans as conditions change.

And with the broader portfolio of SAP Supply Chain Management, you can optimize processes across manufacturing, logistics, PLM, and more. Whether you're managing a single factory or a global network of suppliers, the portfolio supports every function.

Together, SAP Business Network, SAP Integrated Business Planning, and SAP Supply Chain Management support end-to-end optimization across planning, collaboration, manufacturing, logistics, and execution. Organizations can work from a shared foundation of data and processes while adapting to changing business needs.

FAQ

  • What is supply chain optimization?

    Supply chain optimization is the practice of improving the efficiency, effectiveness, and adaptability of a supply chain. It combines planning, execution, and monitoring activities to help organizations balance supply and demand, improve customer satisfaction, reduce costs, and support long-term business goals.

  • What are the benefits of supply chain optimization?

    The benefits of supply chain optimization include enabling organizations to improve efficiency, reduce costs, balance supply and demand, increase customer satisfaction, strengthen resilience, and improve visibility across supply chain networks.

  • What are the stages of supply chain optimization?

    The primary stages of supply chain optimization are design, planning, execution, and monitoring. Together, these stages help organizations align supply chain activities with business objectives while continuously improving performance.

  • How does AI improve supply chain optimization?

    AI helps improve forecasting, automate repetitive tasks, identify patterns in large data sets, and support faster decision-making. These capabilities can increase efficiency and help organizations respond more effectively to changing conditions.

  • What’s the difference between supply chain planning and supply chain optimization?

    Supply chain planning is the process of forecasting demand and determining how to meet it—it's about creating the plan. Supply chain optimization is broader: It encompasses planning but also includes execution and monitoring, with the goal of continuously improving the entire network.

  • How do you measure supply chain optimization success?

    Success in supply chain optimization is measured through key performance indicators such as order fulfillment rates, inventory turnover, on-time delivery, cost-to-serve, and supply chain cycle time. The most effective measurement approaches combine operational metrics with financial and customer satisfaction metrics, giving a complete picture of how well the supply chain is performing and where improvements are needed.

  • What technologies are used in supply chain optimization today?

    Today's supply chain optimization relies on cloud-based platforms, AI and machine learning, real-time data analytics, IoT sensors, and digital twin technology. Cloud platforms offer connectivity for real-time collaboration across partners. AI and machine learning allow predictive analytics and automation. IoT sensors give real-time visibility into inventory and shipments. Together, they transform supply chain optimization into a continuous, data-driven practice that adapts as conditions change.
