resources/what-is-data-strategy.html.body:
What Is

What is a data strategy?

A data strategy is a comprehensive blueprint guiding the processes, policies, and technologies for data collection, storage, management, and analysis across every area of the business.

Published on September 9, 202412 minutes

Why a data strategy matters

Motivated by recent innovation in AI and advanced analytics, companies are eager to strengthen their business intelligence. Yet, this ambition often remains unrealized in businesses without a strategic approach to data management.

Recent research in data management underscores an undeniable truth: a comprehensive data strategy is paramount for aligning data initiatives with business goals and unlocking the full potential of data assets. According to Gartner, 85% of companies that fail to manage and use their data effectively are unlikely to achieve their digital transformation aspirations. Equally alarming is the revelation that poor data quality costs businesses an average of US$15 million annually.

A data strategy is not just a nice-to-have—it’s the cornerstone of effective data that drives true business innovation and growth. Organizations will only continue to collect and analyze increasingly vast quantities of data. For that reason, a clear and actionable plan for managing, using, and protecting data is critical to a future of efficient operations, well-informed decisions, and tough-to-beat competitive advantages.

dgl

What is a Data Strategy?

Data strategy: A detailed definition

A data strategy is a well-defined plan designed to improve the effectiveness of company-wide data management. It establishes the processes, technologies, and policies needed to collect, store, manage, and analyze data in ways that support business goals. This foundational approach sets the stage for using data as both a strategic asset and a competitive edge, fueling impactful innovation and continuous business growth.

A broad range of strategic tasks, policies, procedures, and practices are covered in a data strategy, including:

  • Data creation, access, storage, and updates: Manage the data lifecycle across multiple cloud and on-premise environments.
  • High availability and disaster recovery: Help ensure data is consistently accessible and protected against cyber threats, breaches, and unauthorized access.
  • Data use: Use data more effectively among a growing variety of AI algorithms, analytics, applications, and mobile apps.
  • Data privacy and security compliance: Implement measures to protect data and comply with government and industry regulations.
  • Data archiving and deletion: Follow retention schedules and compliance standards for data management.
  • Data administration: Guide business users and administrators on the capabilities of existing data management technologies, regulatory requirements, and organizational needs for optimizing data value.

By establishing a clear data management strategy, organizations help ensure the accessibility and productive use of quality data—improving decision-making and enhancing operational efficiency.

Benefits of a data strategy

Most companies are eager to enhance their business intelligence using the latest AI and analytics tools. But to achieve this vision, they need a clear approach that makes sense for their data, aligns with their business strategy, and develops the necessary AI capabilities and data analytics solutions.

With the right data strategy, companies can set up a foundation that brings seven critical competitive advantages:

  • Informed decision-making: Access to accurate, high-quality, and timely data insights allows business leaders and employees to understand trends, forecast outcomes, and make strategic choices with confidence, ease, and speed.
  • Improved operational efficiency: Managing data effectively helps streamline processes, reduce redundancy, and enhance overall operational efficiency. This leads to cost savings and more efficient use of resources.
  • Cost reduction: Effective data management reduces data redundancy, which minimizes costs associated with data storage, retrieval, and processing. It also reduces the financial impact of data breaches and noncompliance penalties.
  • Foundation for AI success: AI relies on high-quality, well-integrated, and secure data to function effectively. Organizations produce accurate, reliable, and trustworthy outcomes when their data meets the specific needs of applications, such as generative AI, predictive forecasting, image recognition, intelligent search, and machine learning.
  • Continuous innovation: A complete data management strategy fuels innovation by providing the flexibility to explore new opportunities, develop new products, and improve existing services. Data-driven insights reveal emerging market trends and often-ignored customer needs that, when addressed, drive business growth.
  • Regulatory compliance: Following regulations is a critical aspect of a data strategy. Adhering to data privacy and security standards helps organizations avoid legal issues and penalties.
  • Enhanced data security: Data privacy and security measures strengthen the protection of sensitive information and build trust with customers and stakeholders.

Eight steps for building an effective data strategy

Fully realizing the potential of data requires more than just technical expertise. It also demands reflective assessment, creative decision-making, persuasive storytelling, and cross-functional support. A well-crafted data strategy is a sign that all these elements are done effectively.

The following eight-step data strategy framework provides a road map to a plan structure and implementation that maximizes the strengths of the organization's teams, talents, and resources.

Step 1: Assessing the current data landscape

The first step is a thorough evaluation of the organization’s existing data assets, processes, and challenges. Understanding where data is stored, how it’s currently being used, who accesses it, and where gaps or inefficiencies exist creates a clear picture of the organization’s starting point and highlights areas for improvement.

Step 2: Defining strategic goals

Establishing clear, measurable objectives helps align the data strategy with broader business objectives. This includes helping ensure a purposeful and relevant approach that advances the company’s data management maturity.

Step 3: Developing a data governance framework

Creating a comprehensive framework that includes policies, standards, and roles for managing data. Effective data governance is critical for maintaining data integrity and supporting regulatory compliance. This framework defines who is responsible for various aspects of data management, establishes guidelines for data quality, and helps ensure data is handled consistently across the business.

Step 4: Designing the data architecture

Outlining a technical structure for data storage, integration, and management is a critical step. A well-designed data architecture sets the stage for data that not only supports the organization’s analytical needs but is also accessible and scalable. This involves choosing the right data storage solutions, designing data integration processes, and setting up data flow mechanisms.

Step 5: Establishing data quality management

Adopting processes for data cleansing, validation, and monitoring helps ensure data remains accurate, consistent, and reliable with comprehensive data quality management practices. A key benefit from this task is delivering high data quality that drives informed decision-making and increases user and stakeholder confidence in the value and accuracy of the information and analytical insights.

Step 6: Deploying data analytics

Effective data analysis requires the right tools and technologies. Selecting and deploying appropriate software for data visualization, statistical analysis, and machine learning enables the extraction of valuable insights from data to drive business innovation and efficiency.

Step 7: Setting data security measures

Customer trust and compliance with data protection regulations require the implementation of comprehensive security measures. Protecting sensitive data from unauthorized access and breaches requires encryption, access controls, and regular security audits.

Step: 8: Improving the strategy continuously

A data strategy is not static—it requires continuous monitoring and improvement. Organizations should regularly review and update their data management practices to adapt to changing business needs and technological advancements. Doing so helps ensure data is managed well to realize its full potential, driving informed decision-making, operational efficiency, and competitive advantage.

What to consider when building a data strategy

Creating a comprehensive data strategy is a significant undertaking. Organizations must understand, analyze, and improve internal and external conditions and capabilities that impact business decision-making, innovation, and competitiveness.

The components

The following key components of a data strategy create a comprehensive framework that supports the effective use of data:

Data governance

Data governance sets the rules and standards for data management and encompasses policies, procedures, and responsibilities that help ensure data quality, integrity, and security. When done effectively, it increases data trust, focusing on accuracy, consistency, and reliability for actionable decision-making.

The policies, procedures, and standards that should be defined for managing data across the organization include:

  • Data quality management: Implement proven best practices to maintain data completeness, timeliness, and relevance.
  • Compliance: Adhere to regulations to help ensure data privacy and security.
  • Roles and responsibilities: Define who is responsible for various aspects of data management—from data creation to data archiving.

Data architecture

A well-structured data architecture supports scalability and flexibility, enabling organizations to adapt to evolving requirements for data storage, integration, and management. Key elements include:

  • Database selection: Choose the right databases, data warehouses, and data lakes for efficient data storage.
  • Data integration methods: Allow data to flow smoothly across various sources and be accessible to those who need it anytime and anywhere.
  • Scalability and flexibility: Design an architecture that supports growth and adapts to changing data needs.

Data quality management

High data quality is critical for making informed business decisions, as inaccurate or inconsistent data often leads to misguided strategies and lost opportunities. Implementing processes and tools that keep data accurate, consistent, and reliable demands:

  • Data cleansing: Remove inaccuracies and inconsistencies from data.
  • Data validation: Meet predefined data standards and requirements mandated by the government, industry, and business policies.
  • Regular monitoring: Check for errors continuously and correct them before they create a problem for the business.

Data integration

Data integration helps break down silos within an organization, providing a holistic view of operations and enabling better analytics. Combining data from disparate sources creates a unified view that is comprehensive and useful when the following steps are used:

  • Data consolidation: Aggregate data from different systems and sources.
  • Data extraction: Simplify and expedite the retrieval of master data from various sources.
  • Data transformation: Convert legacy data from different systems into a consistent format for analysis, automation, AI algorithms, business processes, and cross-organizational collaboration.
  • Data loading: Store integrated data in a central repository that keeps it synchronized, up to date, and accessible.

Data analytics and business intelligence

Using data analytics, organizations can make data-driven decisions that enhance business performance and drive innovation. Analyzing data and deriving meaningful insights from it calls for the following advanced tools and techniques:

  • Data visualization tools: Present data in an easily understandable format—such as charts, graphs, and dashboards—to quickly grasp concepts and trends.
  • Statistical analytics: Uncover patterns and trends quickly with statistical methods, including descriptive analytics, inferential analytics, predictive analytics, prescriptive analytics, and diagnostic analytics.
  • Machine learning models: Use algorithms to predict future trends and behaviors based on learning from historical data and automate repetitive tasks and decision-making processes.

Data security

Data security measures are established to safeguard sensitive information and ensure compliance with privacy regulations, so the business can maintain customer trust and comply with legal and regulatory standards such as General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and the California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA).

Protecting all data from unauthorized access and breaches calls for:

  • Encryption: Safeguard data during transmission and storage by converting data into a coded format that can only be accessed and deciphered with the correct decryption key from an authorized user.
  • Access controls: Restrict data access to authorized personnel, ensuring only individuals with appropriate permissions view, modify, or delete data.
  • Regular security audits: Conduct periodic checks to identify and address weaknesses within the data management system through vulnerability assessments, penetration testing, and compliance audits.

The methodology of choice

Organizations can choose from a range of methodologies to align their data strategy with specific business goals and fulfill unique requirements. Each approach has its advantages and challenges. Nevertheless, choosing the methodology that best fits an organization’s unique needs and circumstances paves the way toward an effective data strategy that supports business objectives and drives long-term success.

Here are four fundamental methodologies to consider:

1. Top-down

In the top-down methodology, senior management defines the strategic objectives and data requirements, setting the overall direction for the data strategy. This approach helps ensure the data strategy aligns with the organization's goals and priorities.

Key benefits include:

  • Strategic alignment: Link the data strategy closely to the organization's overarching goals to choose initiatives and design programs that support business objectives.
  • Clear direction: Provide clarity and focus with a unified vision to ease the organization's implementation of data policies and procedures.

However, this approach does have its drawbacks. While the data strategy is aligned with corporate goals, specific needs and challenges faced by individual departments are often overlooked, leading to gaps in the strategy.

2. Bottom-up

The bottom-up methodology gathers input from various departments to understand their specific data needs and challenges. This grassroots approach grounds the data strategy in practical realities and is more likely to be adopted business-wide.

Key benefits include:

  • Departmental insights: Capture diverse perspectives and address practical issues that may be missed by a top-down approach by incorporating feedback from different levels of the organization.
  • Higher adoption rates: Support and comply with the latest data practices by creating a strategy that reflects each department’s specific needs.

A key challenge of the bottom-up approach is consolidating diverse inputs into a single, coherent strategy. The process can be time-consuming and complex, potentially delaying implementation.

3. Hybrid

The hybrid approach combines elements of both top-down and bottom-up methodologies, seeking to balance strategic alignment with practical relevance. Senior management provides the overall direction, while individual departments contribute their insights and requirements.

Key benefits include:

  • Balanced strategy: Help ensure the data strategy is comprehensive and practical, aligning with corporate goals while addressing departmental needs.
  • Inclusive process: Involve stakeholders at all levels to foster collaboration and buy-in from all parts of the organization.

Despite the advantages, balancing input from senior management and various departments is a complex task. To deliver a unified data strategy, effective coordination and communication are needed.

4. Agile framework

The agile framework focuses on developing a flexible and iterative data strategy that allows organizations to adapt to changing business needs and technological advancements. In addition, continuous feedback and improvement are necessary to advance innovation and responsiveness.

Key benefits include:

  • Iterative development: Evolving the data strategy through continuous cycles of feedback and refinement helps ensure relevance and effectiveness in a dynamic environment.
  • Flexibility: Making the data strategy adaptive to changing conditions allows businesses to respond to new challenges and opportunities quickly.

The successful implementation of an agile framework can be significantly disruptive to organizations with a culture that does not support ongoing experimentation, learning, and collaboration.

The strategic business owner(s)

Creating a data strategy is not done by a single decision-maker in a vacuum. It’s a collaborative effort that involves various roles within the organization.

The ownership of the data strategy is a shared responsibility, with each role playing a critical part in its development and execution. Senior management typically acts as the primary owner, providing oversight and ensuring alignment with the business strategy, while the other roles contribute their specialized expertise to bring the strategy to life.

Working together, the following roles contribute their unique expertise and perspectives to help ensure comprehensiveness and alignment with organizational goals:

  • Senior management is responsible for providing strategic direction. This stakeholder sets the vision, allocates resources, and secures cross-functional support. Above all, its involvement provides the necessary buy-in from all levels of the business to coordinate financial support and motivate company-wide adoption.
  • Data architects are tasked with designing the technical infrastructure and integration processes that support the data strategy. They outline how data will be stored, accessed, and integrated across systems, helping ensure that the architecture is scalable, secure, and capable of supporting advanced analytics and AI tools.
  • Data stewards oversee the implementation of data governance policies. Their role is essential for maintaining the integrity, quality, and reliability of the organization’s data. They define and enforce data standards, manage data catalogs, and monitor compliance with regulatory requirements.
  • Business analysts identify specific data needs and use cases to drive business value. They work closely with various business units to understand their requirements and help ensure the data strategy addresses those needs. Their insights help prioritize initiatives and measure the impact of the data strategy on business outcomes.
  • IT teams handle the technical implementation of the data strategy, including data storage, integration, and security. They are responsible for deploying and managing the technology stack in ways that support data accessibility, performance, and protection. Their expertise is vital to help ensure the data strategy is technically feasible and addresses the entire IT landscape.
  • Data scientists and analysts use advanced analytics tools to derive actionable insights from the data. They develop models, perform statistical analysis, and create visualizations that help the organization make data-driven decisions. Their work translates raw data into meaningful information that drives innovation and efficiency.

Emerging data management trends to prepare for

The landscape of data management is constantly evolving, fueled by technological advancements, dynamic economic shifts, and changing business needs. Understanding the latest data management trends empowers businesses to stay ahead of the curve and make the most of their data assets.

AI integration

The integration of AI and machine learning in data strategies is becoming increasingly common. These technologies enhance data analytics capabilities, providing accurate and actionable insights and automating complex data processing tasks. In return, businesses have the tools to predict trends, identify anomalies, and optimize operations across various industries, leading to more effective decision-making and innovation.

Data privacy and security

As data breaches become more prevalent, businesses are sharpening their focus on data privacy and security within their data strategies. However, this growing emphasis is not only about building customer trust—it's also a must-have tactic to avoid legal repercussions and monetary loss associated with cybersecurity breaches. As a result, organizations are investing in advanced encryption, access controls, and compliance measures to protect sensitive information.

Real-time data processing

The advent of real-time data analytics and edge computing is revolutionizing how organizations process and use data. By analyzing data as it’s generated, businesses make quicker, more informed decisions. This capability is particularly valuable in industries such as finance, healthcare, and manufacturing, where timely insights significantly impact outcomes and efficiency.

Data democratization

Data democratization is the practice of making data accessible and usable for nontechnical users within an organization. By providing intuitive tools and training, companies empower employees at all levels to incorporate data into their decision-making processes. This trend fosters innovation while enhancing overall business agility.

Advanced data governance

Developing sophisticated data governance frameworks is essential for effectively managing data quality, integrity, and compliance. These frameworks establish clear guidelines for data management, ensuring consistency and reliability across the organization. Advanced data governance also supports regulatory compliance and helps organizations navigate the complexities of data management to set a secure foundation for business operations.

How industries transform with a data strategy

Organizations across every industry constantly search for new opportunities to unlock the full value of their data. With a data strategy, they have the guidance necessary to innovate and implement use cases that unlock operational improvement, address risks early, drive innovation, strengthen compliance, and boost revenue growth.

Below is a small glimpse into how data strategies steer industry-specific use cases:

Finance

Financial institutions implement data strategies for comprehensive fraud detection, risk management, and regulatory compliance. Take banks, for example. They have set parameters to analyze transaction data and identify unusual patterns to prevent fraud and mitigate risks. Their institutional credibility and stability are also improving, thanks to well-defined regulatory reporting capabilities and compliance processes that fully address financial mandates.

Government

Government agencies apply data strategies to enhance public services, improve resource allocation, and support data-driven policymaking. Analyzing demographic and economic data enables public sector organizations to make informed decisions that better serve the community. Moreover, by increasing operational transparency and improving service delivery, they gain constituents' trust in the management of public resources.

Healthcare

Data strategies are transforming the healthcare industry by enabling better data sharing and predictive analytics. For example, personalized treatment plans, early disease detection, and efficient allocation of patient caregivers are improving patient outcomes. In addition, hospitals and clinics are adopting comprehensive data management and analytics tools to streamline their operations to reduce costs while enhancing the quality of patient care.

Manufacturing

Data strategies are crucial for predictive maintenance, production process optimization, and supply chain management improvements in the manufacturing industry. Monitoring equipment performance and analyzing operational data empowers manufacturers to predict failures before they occur, reducing downtime and maintenance costs. Data-driven insights also help streamline production workflows and help ensure timely delivery of products.

Retail

Retailers use data strategies to create personalized marketing campaigns, optimize inventory levels, and improve customer experiences. By analyzing consumer behavior and purchasing patterns, they can tailor promotions and product offerings to meet customer needs more effectively. Furthermore, data-driven insights guide improvements in supply chain management, waste reduction, and overall profitability.

The start of a future-proof competitive edge

A data strategy is essential to manage data assets and drive operational efficiency. Yet, it also enhances decision-making, fuels innovation, and, most importantly, brings an unparalleled edge over the competition. The key is building a strategy that clearly defines processes, policies, and technologies that turn data into a valuable asset.

As organizations look to the future, emerging trends such as AI, data privacy and security, real-time data processing, data democratization, and advanced data governance will continue to shape and change the landscape of a data strategy. Staying informed about this ongoing evolution and the increasing importance of data management will remain critical in maximizing the value of data and achieving long-term business success.

resources/what-is-intelligent-automation.body:
What Is

What is intelligent automation?

Intelligent automation combines traditional process automation with AI to streamline workflows.

Published on March 17, 2025

Intelligent automation overview

Intelligent automation is the use of artificial intelligence to optimize business processes that previously could not be automated by traditional process automation alone. The combination of both intelligent and traditional technology enables enterprises to automate more complex processes. As a result, organizational efficiency can increase as AI learns from its experiences.

Optical character recognition (OCR), used to “read” paper or digital-based documents (like PDFs), is one example. Traditionally, OCR depended on pattern recognition software to identify letters and numbers. However, because fonts and especially handwriting can vary wildly, it had limits to how accurately it could do this.

The advent of machine learning in OCR negated this limitation. A machine learning neural network can “read” characters by identifying unique patterns in each one and learning new patterns to account for variation. Over time, this enables it to better consistently distinguish between Os and 0s or 5s and Ss—recognizing that a narrower circle matches the pattern of a zero more than a letter O. Some other applications of intelligent automation are:

  • Document information extraction (DOX). The evolution of OCR. DOX can extract data formatted in headers and tables in spreadsheet files (structured data) as well as scanned documents (unstructured data). This enables enterprises to process large amounts of invoices, purchase orders, receipts, forms, applications, and others quickly and ensure they match other records.
  • Smart customer interactions. Using natural language processing, intelligent process automation-powered chatbots understand and respond to customer inquiries with context-aware, tailored answers, which not only accelerates response times but also improves overall customer satisfaction while reducing the workload for support staff.
  • Predictive maintenance. By continuously analyzing historical and real-time sensor data, intelligent process automation can detect early warning signs of equipment failure, allowing maintenance teams to schedule timely interventions and adjust service intervals dynamically, which reduces downtime and repair costs.

This shows how AI can automate previously manual processes to dramatically increase accuracy and speed. In this article, we’ll also explore how it leads to better decision-making, streamlined maintenance workflows, and more operational efficiency for an enterprise and its human workforce.

Components of intelligent automation

Intelligent automation consists of three main components. Together, they provide a strategic framework for how enterprises can increase operational efficiency:

  1. Artificial intelligence (AI): Technology that enables computers to learn and solve problems like humans do. Fields of AI include machine learning, natural language processing, computer vision, and generative AI.
  1. Business process management: This component encompasses the design, operation, and optimization of digitized business processes with formal rules.
  1. Robotic process automation (RPA): Software robots that execute repetitive manual, low-level tasks like data extraction.

How does intelligent automation work?

To understand how intelligent automation works, it’s helpful to understand two more basic forms of automation first:

Traditional process automation is the use of software and technologies following programmed rules to automate repeated business processes. Integrating multiple automated processes creates an end-to-end process—this is known as workflow orchestration.

Robotic process automation is a primary component of BPA. It refers to bots programmed to emulate and copy human actions to complete repetitive tasks. By integrating them into business systems, RPA bots can automate a wide range of rule-based tasks.

Intelligent process automation is the next evolution. It integrates advanced AI techniques, including machine learning (ML) and natural language processing (NLP) capabilities, with robotic process automation to perform advanced tasks for which it isn’t necessarily preprogrammed. It can also infer the business context behind data and learn from its experiences, making it much more flexible and adaptable than older forms of automation. Examples:

  • In the lead-to-cash process (the cycle of finding leads and turning them into paying customers), sales staff can use intelligent process automation to create sales orders from either structured data (like in Microsoft Excel spreadsheets) or unstructured data (like in scanned PDFs.) They can spend the time they save on providing personalized customer service instead.
  • Within the hire-to-retire process (the cycle of finding employees and managing their journey until they exit), HR staff can use intelligent process automation to screen resumes during recruitment.

Why is intelligent automation important?

Intelligent automation is important because it merges the efficiency of automated, rule-based processes with advanced artificial intelligence capabilities that can analyze complex data and learn from experience. This enables enterprises to automate tasks that were previously beyond automation, leading to more consistency, better decision-making, and lower operational costs.

The benefits of intelligent automation

Intelligent automation enables enterprises to streamline processes and make better decisions, leading to these benefits:

  • Increased efficiency, accuracy, and consistency: AI systems can run repetitive tasks at an increased rate of automation. This improves productivity and frees human workers to focus on higher-level, strategic activities.
  • Improved ROI: With the cost reductions, time savings, and risk mitigation that comes with intelligent automation, enterprises that choose to invest in can expect significant ROI.
  • Improved customer experience: Chatbots can offer personalized customer support 24 hours a day. The faster they can resolve their issues, the less likely they’ll consider a competitor.

Challenges of intelligent automation

The benefits are clear. However, enterprises that choose to adopt intelligent process automation should prepare for the effect it may have on their human workforce.

While some employees may feel liberated from menial tasks, others may feel threatened by it. Management can alleviate this anxiety by implementing policies that encourage employees to upskill and retrain. Ideally, an enterprise can emerge with more strategic and creative thinkers focused on innovation—their decision-making reinforced with insights provided by AI.

Enterprises contemplating AI adoption should also examine issues concerning bias in AI, transparency in how it draws conclusions, and accountability. These are all topics that an organization’s AI ethics committee can help define.

Another consideration is the technical debt that arises during the migration to AI technology while also maintaining older legacy apps. Factors like poor data quality, inadequate infrastructure, and skill gaps can all hinder the effectiveness of intelligent automation in an enterprise. AI can help organizations reduce years of technical debt by automating operational tasks, such as refactoring code, that developers must often handle.

Intelligent automation technologies

Intelligent automation emerges when enterprises apply AI technologies to traditional process automation. These technologies include:

  • Artificial intelligence
    AI is the foundation of intelligent automation, enabling systems to process information, identify patterns, and make decisions without human intervention. Unlike traditional automation, which follows predefined rules and uses structured data, AI-driven systems can analyze complex data—both structured and unstructured—to extract insights and adapt to new information. This ability allows businesses to automate decision-making processes, enhance efficiency, and improve accuracy in ways that rule-based automation cannot.
  • Machine learning
    Machine learning is a branch of AI involving complex algorithms. This enables advanced pattern recognition capabilities that go beyond traditional statistical methods. With large and diverse datasets, models can deliver insights that inform decision-making in real time. In addition to continuous learning, it can also adapt over time, factoring previous actions and outcomes in its recommendations.
  • Natural language processing
    NLP is a subset of machine learning that specializes in language-based tasks and the unstructured voice and text data that come with it. NLP enables chatbots and virtual assistants to understand human commands through natural language, considering sentiment and intent to deliver tailored responses. The result is better customer service on behalf of the business. Automated document classification is another application of NLP. It enables faster routing and processing, easier compliance, and more efficient document management. Developers can also apply NLP during the coding process. It can help with everything from coding suggestions to debugging to document generation.
  • Computer vision
    Computer vision is the application of intelligent automation to visual information (like image or video data). Enterprises can use this for tasks like the monitoring and inspection of wear on the transformers, substations, and powerlines of an electrical grid.

Intelligent automation use cases

Enterprises are already putting intelligent process automation to use. Here are a few examples:

  • Finance and accounting
    The finance and accounting departments of businesses use intelligent automation to accelerate a range of workflows. With invoice processing, it can extract data from invoices and match them with purchase orders. With expense management, it can categorize employee expenses and flag anomalies for review. And with financial reporting, it can consolidate data from multiple sources, generate reports, and ensure compliance with regulations.

  • Supply chain logistics
    Intelligent automation helps supply chains stay resilient by enhancing inventory management, automating stock replenishment, and optimizing shipping routes. This results in minimized delivery times and costs, reduced shortages and overstocking, as well as increased transparency through real-time shipment tracking.

  • Customer service automation
    Enterprises are increasingly using intelligent automation to facilitate customer service. Chatbots and virtual assistants, for example, can handle customer inquiries and provide support. If an issue is too complex and they can’t, they direct it to a human agent in the appropriate department.

    AI can also analyze customer feedback and interactions to detect sentiment and improve response strategies. This is called sentiment analysis.

The future of intelligent automation

To adopt intelligent process automation is to remain competitive. Enterprises that find a strategy to orchestrate it with traditional process automation and agentic AI systems can expect to increase productivity, improve accuracy, and save on costs on their end-to-end processes.

AI agents can specialize in more complex tasks, enabling them to collaborate across different departments and organizations. Imagine one managing the inventory and delivery components of a supply chain and working with another to track the associated invoices and ledgers.

This shifts the burden of these repetitive workflows away from human teams, who are now free to focus on other, higher-level roles in R&D, corporate social responsibility, or technical support. These jobs require skills AI struggles with, like empathy, ideation, and nuance.

By investing in adopting intelligent automation and upskilling human talent, an enterprise can emerge with a workforce enhanced by AI—rather than one replaced by it. The collaboration between both can bring levels of efficiency previously thought impossible.

resources/what-is-predictive-analytics.h.title: What Is Predictive Analytics? Definition, Models, and Examples | SAP
resources/what-is-predictive-analytics.h.description: Predictive analytics is the use of data, statistical algorithms, and machine learning techniques to forecast future outcomes and trends.
resources/what-is-predictive-analytics.h.body:
What Is

What is predictive analytics?

Predictive analytics is a branch of advanced analytics that uses historical data, statistical algorithms, and machine learning to forecast future outcomes.

Updated on January 26, 2026

Predictive analytics explained

Predictive analytics is an essential component of informed decision-making in the modern world. Predictive analysis involves applying advanced techniques (such as statistical models and machine learning) to historical data to anticipate the likelihood of various future outcomes. To put it simply, predictive analytics allows organizations to go from understanding what has happened to predicting what’s likely to happen next.

Predictive analytics: definition

Predictive analytics is the use of historical data, statistical modelling, and machine learning to predict future outcomes, trends, and behaviors.

Given the numerous disruptions in recent years and the intense pressure of competition, it’s not surprising that predictive analysis has become a staple tool in organizations worldwide. As a key element in decision-making, predictive analytics is used across industries and job functions, including finance, marketing, healthcare, sales forecasting, and business strategy. So, how exactly does the predictive analytics process work?

How predictive analytics works

Predictive analytics examines past data, uncovers patterns and relationships, and uses them as insights to forecast what’s likely to happen next. The predictive analytics process typically involves the following steps:

  1. Data collection: Gather relevant historical data from various sources; for example, customer databases, patient records, sensor readings, transaction logs, or social media.
  2. Data preparation: Clean, preprocess, and standardize raw data. This usually involves removing errors and duplicates, handling missing values, and ensuring everything is in a consistent, usable format.
  3. Model selection and training: Choose predictive analytics techniques and machine learning algorithms, and apply them to the prepared data to build and train the model. During training, the model analyzes historical data related to known outcomes; then, it identifies which factors matter most and how they’ve affected these outcomes.
  4. Model validation: To test the model’s accuracy, analysts will run it on historic data it hasn’t seen, with known outcomes, and use various metrics to measure its performance. Once it’s optimal, the model is ready to deploy.
  5. Forecasting: The trained models are then applied to new data, where outcomes are unknown, to predict what they’re likely to be, based on the patterns uncovered in the historical data.

Predictive analytics process beyond deployment

Once the models are deployed and running, the work is rarely over. The models are continuously monitored and refined as new data emerges and conditions change—sometimes, they may even need to be retrained to avoid model drift. And the insights and forecasts obtained from predictive analytics need to be put to use: guiding decisions, informing strategy, optimizing operations, helping anticipate business opportunities, and flagging risks that need to be avoided or mitigated. Now that we’ve established how predictive analytics works, let’s break down a few of the most common use cases.

Types of predictive analytics models

Predictive analytics techniques encompass various approaches, including regression, classification, clustering, decision trees, neural networks, time series analysis, and anomaly detection. Many of the same techniques are used for data mining. The main difference between data mining and predictive analytics is their purpose: while data mining is typically more exploratory, predictive analytics is goal-oriented and aimed at forecasting specific outcomes.

Predictive analytics models help answer specific questions about the future; in contrast, data mining might uncover answers to questions the analyst didn’t even consider or reveal patterns that are completely unobvious.

Predictive analytics vs. prescriptive analytics

The primary difference between predictive and prescriptive analytics lies in their scope and purpose. Let’s break it down. There are four types of advanced analytics: descriptive analytics, diagnostic analytics, predictive analytics, and prescriptive analytics.

Put very simply, descriptive analytics is used to accurately assess the current state of things or understand what has happened: think monthly sales reports or customer demographics. Diagnostic analytics helps understand why it happened, which factors influenced the current status: for example, why sales dropped in a particular month. Predictive analytics uses historical data, machine learning, and AI to forecast future outcomes; an example of predictive analytics would be forecasting how a particular decision might affect sales. Prescriptive analytics takes it a step further, suggesting actions based on the prediction to achieve desired outcomes, such as recommending marketing strategies to reduce customer acquisition costs.

Think of it as questions being answered by the different types:

  • Descriptive analytics: What happened?
  • Diagnostic analytics: Why did it happen?
  • Predictive analytics: What will happen?
  • Prescriptive analytics: What should we do to make it happen?

Predictive analytics applications and real-world use cases

The use of predictive analytics in business is very extensive, with a near-endless supply of possible applications—and it’s used in more than business too. Before we break down some of the more industry-specific predictive analytics examples, let’s first look at the most common use cases that are found across industries.

Some of the most common predictive analytics applications include:

Sales

Predictive analytics models are widely used in sales forecasting and to anticipate customer behavior or demand shifts. Businesses use predictive analytics to identify high-value prospects, guide budget planning, and optimize sales strategies by modeling the impact of potential strategic changes before implementing them.

Marketing

Certain predictive modeling techniques can be invaluable for marketers trying to deepen their understanding of customer preferences and personalize customer communication. Predictive analytics helps improve ad targeting, segment customers, and tailor offers based on the stage of the customer journey and other factors.

HR

Predictive analytics is an excellent tool for optimizing staffing levels, especially for roles where rapid scaling may be required during particular seasons or due to other circumstances. For example, in the hospitality sector, analyzing staffing and business data from past years can help HR managers plan the workforce accordingly, preparing contingent staff for peak seasons or busy hours.

Supply chain management

Predictive analytics applications in supply chain management are varied and depend on the specific industry. But, in just about every sector, it’s essential to be able to anticipate supply chain disruptions and prepare for shortages, bottlenecks, and price surges. For example, manufacturers can analyze historical demand patterns, supply time leads, and transportation data to forecast material needs and adjust procurement schedules proactively.

Business development and strategy

Having more accurate forecasts of the future, backed by data, helps business leaders make informed decisions and guide their companies in the right direction. Whether performing market analysis before expanding into a new sector or assessing regional regulations and competitive landscape before entering a new market, decision-makers rely on predictive analytics in business strategy.

Operations

Whatever the industry, having a better idea of the issues that are likely to occur makes it easier to optimize how the business operates. From predicting equipment failures to optimizing resource allocation and anticipating delivery delays, predictive analytics help operations run smoothly and without interruptions.

Customer support

Predictive analytics models can help organizations forecast customer needs and remedy potential issues before they start affecting customer satisfaction. Transitioning from reactive problem-solving to proactive support would not only enhance the customer experience but also conserve support resources in the long run.

Real-world predictive analytics examples

Now that you have a general idea about the use of predictive analytics in business, let’s look at some real-world examples from various industries.

Finance & banking

Predictive analytics applications in the finance sector are varied. For one, predictive analytics models are widely used in stock market forecasting, credit scoring, and risk assessment. For example, calculating the likelihood of a stock rising before investing. But they’re also a key component in detecting and preventing fraud, supporting cybersecurity, and identifying vulnerabilities.

Healthcare

Predictive modeling techniques can help healthcare organizations anticipate disease outbreaks and spread. Healthcare providers use them to identify patients at risk for certain conditions and suggest preventative measures or timely screenings. For example, by analyzing which lifestyle factors have correlated with the diagnosis of a particular health issue in specific patient populations, healthcare providers can figure out which other patients should be screened for it or offered lifestyle interventions.

Manufacturing

Manufacturers use predictive analytics to help prevent equipment failure and optimize maintenance, protect supply chains from disruptions, and anticipate pricing changes on raw resources and energy. For example, by analyzing historical maintenance data, they might find that equipment had broken down more often with manual inspections too far apart; at the same time, the increase in equipment lifespan diminishes beyond doubling the number of checks. Compared to trial and error, predictive modeling techniques are a more efficient way to find the sweet spot to reduce equipment failure without expending maintenance resources unnecessarily.

Retail and e-commerce

Retail companies rely heavily on predictive analytics for demand forecasting, inventory management, dynamic pricing, personalized marketing, and other purposes. For example, they can segment customers based on spending patterns and purchase history. Then, they’ll see which customers haven’t yet ordered products bought by other customers in that segment with similar purchasing patterns and target them with personalized offers. For example, if most customers who regularly buy dog toys also typically stock up on dog treats from that retailer, those who bought one but not the other are more likely to use a personalized discount code or seize a limited-time offer. On a personal level, it keeps recommendations more relevant, improving customer experience, and at scale, it adds up to better sales numbers.

Telecommunications

Telecom providers use predictive analytics models to reduce customer churn and increase customer retention and service renewal (among other things). Predictive analytics techniques help identify customers that are likely to cancel their service or unlikely to renew, so the company can personalize marketing offers or, in some cases, customer education efforts to encourage them to stay. This is especially important if customer acquisition costs are high: intervening proactively before existing customers switch providers is critical for profitability.

This list of predictive analytics examples is by no means exhaustive—in today’s economy, there are uses for it in just about every industry. But the key takeaway is that the use of predictive analytics in business is practically essential to staying competitive.

Key benefits of predictive analytics

The wide range of applications we’ve discussed shows the importance of predictive analytics. Across industries and use cases, the common thread is that it gives companies a tremendous advantage. Key benefits of predictive analytics include:

Risk reduction: From combating fraud or avoiding investments with poor prospects to reducing the chance of supply chain disruptions—predictive analytics help companies mitigate risks.

Efficiency: Predictive analytics help companies maximize performance with minimal changes. Additionally, modeling possible outcomes before making any change is a good way to avoid disruption and resource waste.

Better decision-making: One of the main predictive analytics’ advantages is that it gives specific, data-derived input to guide decisions. Even the top experts in their field can make better decisions if their experience and professional intuition are supported by hard data. Besides, informing strategic decision-making by data makes it easier to secure internal buy-in.

Improved customer experience: Many of the applications of predictive analytics we’ve discussed benefit not only the company but the customers, too. Custom recommendations and offers, proactive support, personalized communication—all these benefits of predictive analytics make the customers’ experience better. And customer experience often affects customer retention, trust, spending patterns, customer lifetime value, and sometimes even the cost of customer acquisition.

Competitive advantage: Predictive analytics provides organizations with the foresight they need to avoid costly mistakes, reduce disruptions, anticipate market trends, seize business opportunities, and respond to changes faster. In other words, it helps them stay ahead of the competition.

Given the benefits of predictive analytics, one might wonder why it’s not used by every single company in the world. In fact, although more and more companies are recognizing the importance of predictive analytics, there are a few challenges and limitations that may be holding some organizations back.

Turn data into smart decisions

Find out how intelligent applications can transform real-time insights into timely action across your business.

Explore the deep dive

Challenges of predictive analytics and best practices for overcoming them

Challenges of predictive analytics can be loosely grouped into three categories based on the key components of the predictive analytics process: data, people, and model. Data-related limitations of predictive analytics have to do with data quality, governance, and availability. “People challenges” typically involve human error and bias introduced at various stages of the predictive analytics process, as well as resistance to technology adoption. And finally, predictive analytics models can pose certain challenges as well, such as model drift. Let’s break down some of the most common challenges of predictive analytics—and the solutions to overcome them.

Limited data availability

Challenge: Predictive analytics relies on data. If too few data sources are available, it’s challenging to ensure that predictive analytics provides accurate output. In fact, even training predictive analytics models would be difficult without a vast and varied supply of data.

Best-practice approach: Strive to use IoT hardware and software that generate high-quality data in usable formats. Depending on the industry and line of business, this might involve investing in a reliable CDP, installing equipment monitors and trackers, or modifying specific company procedures. Sometimes, thinking outside the box could help too: there are external data sources that might be relevant—as long as they’re publicly accessible and the applicable regulations allow their use for commercial purposes.

Poor data quality

Challenge: Predictive analytics needs clean, complete, and relevant data to provide accurate output. Missing, inconsistent, or outdated data can lead to inaccurate predictions.

Best-practice approach: Ensure robust data governance and cleaning processes. One way to do it is to use software ecosystems that work well together and standardize data by default. The alternative is to invest more time or allocate additional analyst resources to data cleaning and preprocessing. This step is a part of the predictive analytics process anyway, but a good, unified IT landscape can make it easier and faster.

Bias

Challenge: Data-derived and AI-generated insights are especially valued as objective, unbiased input; the thinking goes that, since they’re generated by models rather than humans, there’s no reason for there to be any bias. In reality, models and AI can actually be biased. With models, it’s the selection and preparation of training data that can introduce bias.

Best-practice approach: An effective intervention to avoid model bias can occur at two stages of the predictive analytics process. During data preparation and selection, ensure your datasets are diverse and don’t reflect historical inequalities. And once the models are trained, validate them regularly to monitor for bias, underfitting, and overfitting.

Model drift

Challenge: Real-world conditions evolve, sometimes very rapidly. A model trained on outdated data, even if it was accurate originally, may become less effective over time. Fraud detection is a good example because fraud methods change very dynamically, so a model trained on last year’s data may miss new fraud patterns emerging this year.

Best-practice approach: This is where upkeep becomes very important. Here, too, regular validation and continuous monitoring of model performance are crucial. Sometimes, models even need to be retrained with updated data.

Difficulties with employee adoption

Challenge: It’s discouraging to see great predictive analytics tools that you’ve invested effort and resources in remain underutilized. And while change is rarely easy, such sophisticated tech can be particularly difficult to adopt.

Best-practice approach: Try to understand why your people are resisting adoption. Is it a lack of expertise that makes predictive analytics tools seem too difficult to use? Is there an underlying distrust of automation in general? Once the core issues are clear, focus on addressing them: demonstrate value, provide training, or hire specialized talent to help bridge the gap between technology and key non-technical stakeholders.

Best practices: Predictive analytics checklist

  • Prioritize the use of clean, relevant, high-quality data in compliance with all applicable regulations (such as GDPR), privacy laws, and data security standards.
  • Ensure that your datasets are diverse and do not reflect personal biases, historical inequalities, or outdated notions.
  • Monitor predictive analytics model performance continuously, validate accuracy regularly, and retrain on new data as needed to avoid model drift.
  • Support employee adoption by demonstrating value, providing training, and integrating predictive analytics in business workflows.
  • Opt for user-friendly analytics software that supports predictive analytics, ideally with robust data governance built in, and uses relevant innovations, such as generative AI, to facilitate adoption and use.

Modern predictive analytics: AI, machine learning, and automation

A number of modern technologies have significantly advanced predictive analytics: machine learning, advances in AI, cloud computing, and automation, to name a few. Thanks to these technologies, organizations can analyze huge volumes of data in real time, reveal underlying patterns, and make accurate predictions about future outcomes. They make it much easier to accurately anticipate shifts in customer behavior, spot emerging market trends, and understand operational needs. Predictive analytics AI tools empower business decision-makers to transition from a reactive approach, focused on catching up with opportunities and mitigating challenges, to proactive strategies informed by data.

One of the biggest drivers of this transformation is the rise of AI-enhanced cloud platforms. These platforms enable companies of all sizes to use their data to access advanced predictive analytics, machine learning capabilities, and sophisticated enterprise planning. AI supports real-time analytics powered by a business data cloud and makes it easier and more intuitive for users. And automating repetitive tasks, such as reporting, allows teams to focus on responding to changes in forecasts, anticipated disruptions, and new opportunities.

Predictive analytics in business is a vital part of the broader data science ecosystem, connecting business data, statistical modeling, and AI to provide actionable intelligence. As the use of predictive analytics becomes more widespread, it enables more organizations to stay agile and competitive.

Through predictive analytics, data science helps businesses turn insights into foresight—an ability that’s rapidly becoming a prerequisite for success.

FAQs

  • What is predictive analytics used for?

    Predictive analytics is used to forecast future outcomes by analyzing historical data. These forecasts are then used for guiding decisions, informing strategy, optimizing operations, helping anticipate business opportunities, and flagging risks that need to be avoided or mitigated.

  • How does predictive analytics work in simple terms?

    In simple terms, the predictive analytics process involves analyzing what has happened in the past (historical data) to predict what will likely happen in the future. To do it, predictive analytics models are trained on information from the past, where we have data on both the factors and the outcomes; after “seeing” which factors have contributed to particular outcomes in the past cases, the model can then predict likely outcomes when it analyzes new data, which describes the factors but not the outcomes.

  • What are the benefits of predictive analytics?

    The key benefits of predictive analytics include risk reduction, increased operational efficiency, improved decision-making, enhanced customer experience, a competitive advantage, and more precise and accurate forecasting.

  • What are examples of predictive analytics in real life?

    Examples of predictive analytics use are found across industries and business functions, including sales, marketing, supply chain and logistics, human capital management, customer support, and operations. For example, marketers use predictive analytics to forecast customer behavior, healthcare providers use it to identify patients at risk for certain conditions, finance leaders use it to inform investment decisions, and manufacturers use it to anticipate equipment failure.

  • What are the challenges of predictive analytics?

    The main challenges of predictive analytics include limited data availability, poor data quality, bias, underfitting, overfitting, model drift, and difficulties with employee adoption.

  • Predictive vs. prescriptive analytics: What’s the difference?

    The difference between predictive and prescriptive analytics is that, while predictive analytics uses historical data, machine learning, and AI to forecast future outcomes, prescriptive analytics builds on these predictions and actually suggests actions that should help achieve desired outcomes, such as recommending sales strategies to increase lead conversion.

resources/what-is-sourcing.html.body:
What Is

What is sourcing?

Sourcing is the process of identifying, assessing, and engaging suppliers to procure goods and services for a business.

Published on July 24, 2024

The core aims of sourcing have never really changed: Find reliable suppliers who can deliver fast at a good price. But today’s world is growing more complex by the minute. Modern digital solutions allow for unprecedented speed, intel, and visibility. This helps you manage your business better, but it also means that competition is fiercer than ever and that your customers have more choices than at any time in history.

Your company must also navigate an increasingly rocky landscape when it comes to sustainability, ethical sourcing, and unpredictable global and environmental events. As one of the earliest links in your global supply chain, sourcing can set a great example of how consistent practices and integrated digital solutions can help you cut costs, speed up cycles, and boost your performance.

Sourcing definition and meaning

Sourcing is all about finding, evaluating, and onboarding suppliers that can provide the best goods and services—with the best terms—for your business. It impacts cost, quality, and the availability of products or services. By securing reliable and cost-effective suppliers, you can ensure a steady flow of materials to not only keep your operations running smoothly, but also to meet your customers’ fast-paced demands.

As a preliminary step in supply chain management, sourcing involves evaluating supplier capabilities, negotiating terms and prices, and managing relationships to ensure a continuous supply of quality goods and services. This directly impacts production costs and product affordability—and if done right, leads to savings, improved quality, and better supply chain resilience and agility. Additionally, sourcing decisions are crucial for meeting sustainable and ethical practices—which also helps you build and maintain a positive brand image.

Sourcing vs. procurement: What’s the difference?

Sourcing and procurement are often used interchangeably, but they actually refer to distinct parts of the supply chain management process. In reality, sourcing is an early-stage component of the procurement process. The due diligence and rigor associated with the sourcing role adds enormous value to procurement, offering an additional layer of confidence and strategy to support their later acquisition activities. Here’s how sourcing and procurement fit together:

  • Sourcing focuses on identifying, evaluating, and engaging suppliers to provide goods and services. It involves market research, running sourcing events, and negotiating favorable contract terms—helping you to build a resilient supply chain and ensure great relationships with your suppliers.
  • Procurement encompasses the entire process of acquiring goods and services, from early needs recognition to supplier payments. It includes steps such as recognizing needs, requesting goods and services, reviewing and approving requests, creating purchase orders, receiving goods, and processing payments.

Different types of sourcing in supply chain management

In reality, most of today’s businesses use a combination of different sourcing models to meet increasingly complex opportunities and challenges. Here are some of the most common ones:

Outsourcing

Contracts third-party suppliers (rather than in-house teams) to carry out specific tasks. This model can reduce costs, access specialized skills, and increases flexibility.

Insourcing

Uses internal resources to perform tasks instead of contracting them out, providing greater control over processes and quality.

Near-sourcing

Relocates sourcing activities closer to the market where products are sold, reducing transportation costs, improving communication, and shortening delivery times.

Global sourcing

Procures goods and services from different countries, often using electronic data interchange (EDI), allowing businesses to benefit from lower production costs and access to new markets.

Single sourcing

Selects one supplier for all required materials, goods, or services, strengthening supplier relationships and bargaining power.

Captive service operations

Establishes wholly-owned subsidiaries or facilities in other countries to handle business functions.

Joint ventures

Involves partnering with another organization to share resources, expertise, and risks in sourcing activities.

What is strategic sourcing?

Strategic sourcing is a methodical, data-driven approach that evaluates and continuously re-evaluates your activities to align with your long-term goals. Unlike traditional sourcing, which often focuses primarily on cost and speed, strategic sourcing considers a broader range of factors, including supplier quality, reliability, sustainability, and long-term partnerships. This approach helps you secure the best prices, build strong supplier relationships, and enhance supply chain efficiency.

Key components of strategic sourcing include the following:

  • Spend analysis: Evaluating and analyzing an organization's expenditure to identify cost-saving opportunities and areas for improvement.
  • Supplier evaluation: Assessing potential suppliers based on their capabilities, reliability, and alignment with the organization's values and objectives.
  • Supplier relationship management (SRM): Building and maintaining strong relationships with suppliers to ensure long-term collaboration and mutual benefits.
  • Market research: Conducting thorough research to understand market trends, supplier landscapes, and competitive dynamics.
  • Risk management: Identifying and mitigating supply chain disruptions such as geopolitical instability, supplier insolvency, natural disasters, and risks associated with inventory control.
  • Integrating across the supply chain: Integrating cross-business solutions to ensure that related operational areas are co-informed. For example, integrating with material requirements planning (MRP) systems to correlate supplier activity with inventory levels and scheduling.

Responsible sourcing

Responsible sourcing involves incorporating ethical, social, and environmental considerations into procurement decisions. This means selecting suppliers that adhere to fair labor practices, environmental sustainability, and ethical business conduct. The goal is to ensure that sourcing activities contribute positively to the world around us, and also align with your broader corporate social responsibility (CSR) objectives. And as today’s customers and investors expect greater transparency and more responsible business practices, the companies that prioritize sustainable sourcing and ethics can boost your brand image, build customer loyalty, and mitigate risks.

Impact sourcing

Impact sourcing is a socially responsible sourcing strategy focused on providing employment opportunities to people from disadvantaged communities or backgrounds. It aims to create positive social and economic impacts by offering sustainable work to people who may not have had access to traditional employment channels. This typically involves making existing and new jobs more accessible to marginalized or differently-abled candidates and offering training programs to build long-term skills and opportunities. When done with strategy and care, it can help to build a more cohesive and loyal workforce—boosting retention, value, and lasting community impact.

Three main sourcing models

A sourcing model defines the level of involvement, control, and risk in the sourcing process. Depending upon the nature of your business and product range, one (or all) of these models may work for you.

Direct sourcing

Involves procuring goods and services directly from manufacturers without intermediaries. This model provides greater control over the quality and cost of products and often leads to stronger supplier relationships.

Indirect sourcing

Means purchasing goods and services through intermediaries such as distributors, wholesalers, or agents. This model can provide access to a broader range of products and services, but it may come with higher costs due to intermediary markups.

Hybrid sourcing

Combines elements of both direct and indirect sourcing. This model is often used for critical or high-volume items to control costs and quality, while employing indirect sourcing for less critical or lower-volume items to benefit from intermediaries' expertise and broader product ranges.

Key steps in the sourcing process

Every company is unique, so there is no “cookie cutter” sourcing process. However, best practices tend to include most of the steps below:

  • Assess sourcing needs: Use experience and data-driven intel to help determine your company’s specific needs and demands, including required products or services, quantity, and delivery timeline. This step defines the scope and objectives of your sourcing activities.
  • Identify potential suppliers: Conduct market research to find suppliers who meet your requirements. Consider factors such as supplier reputation, financial stability, and delivery capacity. Quantifying your selection criteria can help streamline the process.
  • Issue requests for proposals (RFPs): Issue standardized RFPs to potential suppliers, detailing requirements, timelines, and evaluation criteria. This allows suppliers to submit the most relevant proposals as to how exactly they can meet your needs.
  • Evaluate RFPs: Evaluate and shortlist received proposals against your criteria. Using e-procurement platforms can streamline this process by supporting digital submissions and analyses—for faster communication and more efficient decision-making.
  • Negotiate contracts: Enter detailed (and meticulously documented) negotiations with shortlisted suppliers to finalize terms and conditions. This process will focus on the big factors such as pricing, delivery schedules, and payment terms. But it should also consider written commitments to transparency and accountability.
  • Execute contracts: Formalize the agreement with the chosen supplier through a legally binding contractual document. This officially kicks off the supplier relationship—and it goes without saying that you should secure the appropriate legal counsel for this step.
  • Monitor performance: Continuously monitor the supplier’s performance through regular audits, reviews, and feedback sessions to ensure they meet agreed standards. For best results, address issues promptly and maintain a strong, consistent—but respectful—stance.

Benefits of effective sourcing

With competition and customer choice being what it is these days, it’s essential to leverage every opportunity to create savings, efficiency, and greater visibility and integration.

  • Cost savings: Companies that adhere to strategic sourcing strategies have been shown to save over 8% on their annual sourcing costs—by leveraging data-driven solutions and committing to holistic analysis of their sourcing operations.
  • Product quality: Never in history have customers had more sellers to choose from. Competition is fierce and good sourcing can help you lock in quality goods and services from your suppliers. Quality feedback from customers can also support better category management, focusing on supplier performance around very specific categories of goods.
  • Supply chain predictability and resilience: If the pandemic taught us anything, it’s the vulnerability of supply chains. When the supplier links in your supply chain are strong and reliable, your business is more robust.
  • Reduced risks: Everything from natural disasters to politics can have an impact on supply and demand. Good sourcing helps you anticipate and respond quickly to a wide variety of risks. Furthermore, recent stats show that companies that use contract- and catalog-based invoices have a 60% higher rate of managing supplier compliance.
  • Brand image and loyalty: In today’s business world, success can be won or lost on the strength of your reputation and image. Transparent supplier relationships and unwavering sourcing standards can help to both protect and promote your brand.

Sourcing challenges

Like it or not, your business is enormously dependent upon reliable suppliers. And with that dependency come some challenges and hurdles:

  • Long sourcing/supplier onboarding processes: Traditionally, background research, evaluations, and approvals have delayed procurement. Streamlining onboarding with standardized procedures and modern cloud technology can help reduce these slowdowns.
  • Reduction in quality of goods: Particularly with global suppliers, even reliable partners can suddenly be bought out or restructured before you know it. Cloud-based solutions that offer real-time supplier visibility can help reduce surprises.
  • Contractual risks: To minimize risks that come from neglecting due diligence, today’s sourcing teams look for customizable templates, automated workflows, detailed audit trails, and the ability to easily collaborate with internal contract management stakeholders.
  • Supplier over-dependence: It’s golden when you have a supplier that you can trust and depend upon. But unexpected disruptions happen. So, yes, be loyal to your proven partners, but always have a few vetted alternates waiting in the wings.
  • Weak supplier relationships: As in all human relationships, complacency is a bad thing. Consistent communication and streamlined supplier relationship strategies and solutions are essential to managing expectations and strengthening partnerships—rewarding good performance, and spotting and addressing potential problems before they happen.

How to set a successful sourcing strategy

Setting a successful sourcing strategy is crucial for optimizing the procurement process and achieving long-term business goals. Here are the key steps involved in developing an effective sourcing strategy:

  • Establish goals: Define specific goals and key performance indicators (KPIs) for your sourcing strategy. Include the obvious ones like cost reduction and supplier performance. But be sure to also encourage and reward targets like team leadership and innovation.
  • Analyze current and past sourcing activities: Today’s AI-powered analytics and data management tools let you amalgamate both real-time and historical data sets into customized reports. And don’t forget to ask your teams on the ground. Your best insights may come from the shop floor rather than the top floor.
  • Bring in market research and competitor data: Information is power. Make “research” a core focus. Explore your competitors’ websites and media. Listen to your customers. And follow the news in your sector and in the world. You can even use the same AI-powered analytics tools that you use on your own data to provide insights into your external market research findings.
  • Conduct regular audits and performance monitoring: If you haven’t been rigorous about expecting your longstanding suppliers to undergo ongoing performance monitoring and regular audits, it can feel awkward to do so all of a sudden. But it’s an essential step in the process. Here’s where implementing a consistent SRM strategy from the start can help you in the long run.

What to look for in sourcing software

When selecting sourcing software, ensure that it aligns with your organization’s needs and can effectively support the sourcing process. Here are a few key features and capabilities to look for:

  • Cloud deployment: Opt for a cloud-based solution that offers scalability, flexibility, and remote access.
  • Process management workflows: Ensure the software provides robust workflows to automate and streamline various sourcing activities, including supplier onboarding and qualification.
  • Comprehensive supply chain insights: The software should offer a 360-degree view of supply chain activities, powering better decision-making and risk management, and integrating smoothly with existing ERP and business management systems.
  • Cost management tools: Look for features that support detailed cost breakdown analysis and total landed cost calculations for global sourcing, including logistics, import duties, and taxes.
  • Collaboration and communication tools: Sourcing solutions should provide tools that support your collaboration with suppliers on all documentation, reporting, compliance, and more.
  • Advanced analytics and reporting: It’s essential that you can track performance in real time, identify trends, and manage sustainability and efficiency from a single platform.

The key capabilities of SAP Business Data Cloud include a business data fabric that unifies SAP and third-party data with enterprise-wide governance and provides flexibility for AI workloads with intelligent compute. These capabilities help organisations automate processes and power AI agents and applications that can reason and act across the business.

 

SAP Business Data Cloud capabilities are offered through a variety of SAP products and services, including SAP Datasphere, SAP Analytics Cloud, SAP Business Warehouse, SAP Databricks, SAP HANA Cloud, SAP Master Data Governance and SAP Reltio.

Existing SAP Datasphere and SAP Analytics Cloud customers can continue their services without interruption but they have the option to transition their current solutions to a fully managed solution with SAP Business Data Cloud.
